The Religious Tract Society printed this penny tract on dangers on the ice off Labrador. Moravian missionaries on that coast suffered climate severity and native hostility for many years. In 1782, brethren Liebisch and Turner faced a remarkable preservation of life on the ice. Further particulars show their labours bore fruit.

Liebisch, pained in the throat, could not bear close air and sat at an entrance covered with skins. A woman, a child, and two missionaries share the peril. The tract teaches providence through a true adventure. Its plain style suited Sunday readers. The story remains a vivid missionary narrative.
14023-life-of-daniel-boone-the-great-wes:
Cecil B. Hartley's life of Daniel Boone follows the hunter from early days to his fame as Kentucky's first settler. Border fighting, Indian captivity, and long hunts fill the narrative, with Boone's coolness under danger as its steady theme. A full autobiography, dictated by Boone himself, closes the book and states his belief that he was ordained to settle the wilderness.

Frontier custom gets equal space. Chapters describe house-raisings, where neighbors gathered to set a young couple up on a parent's land, and Sabbath rests, when hunters stayed home for luck or piety. Clark's Illinois campaign and Detroit's threats frame the wider war for the West. Hartley writes in the heroic mode of his age, yet the book keeps value as a popular record of how Americans in the nineteenth century remembered their pathfinders.
14110-kernel-cob-and-little-miss-sweetcl:
George Mitchel wrote this 1918 children's fantasy for Ursula, Dordie, Hutch, Bob, and children the world over, with pictures by Tony Sarg. Jackie and his little sister Peggs live with an aunt of thirty-two, so long past childhood that she forgot children need toys. Left to make-believe, the pair meet Kernel Cob, a brave toy soldier, and Little Miss Sweetclover, and set out on a quest.

Adventure piles upon adventure. Kernel Cob creeps alone into a toy shop, salutes a row of tin soldiers, and asks help to find the South Pole, where Jackie and Peggs's mother and father may wait. The soldiers stay silent, being deaf or merely tin, until another voice answers. Nights on the road, haystack beds, moonlit longings, and a villain's trail keep the pace brisk. Toy soldiers, dolls, and children share one world here, and courage matters more than size.
14128-toni-the-little-woodcarver:
Johanna Spyri, author of Heidi, wrote this Alpine tale of Toni, a boy who carves from childhood and longs to earn his bread by the craft. Helen B. Dole translated it in 1920. Toni's mother shows a pastor two little carved goats, but no path to training or sales appears. Small animals and boxes alone, the pastor warns, will waste his time and earn nothing.

A master in Frutigen offers hope. Skillful and well known, he makes large works that travel far, even to America, and could teach Toni properly. Trouble strikes when Toni falls silent and strange, far from his mother, with no relatives near. A herdsman's boy carries him to the pastor, who tries every means to make him speak and asks if he longs for his mother. Kindness, craft, and Alpine faith carry a gentle story of a boy's gift finding its way.
14211-wanted-a-match-maker:
Paul Leicester Ford's Wanted: A Match-Maker follows Constance Durant, a young woman whose mother wishes her married, in love, but with a nudge toward suitable matches. Mrs. Durant hesitates, petulant and fond, over words she almost speaks. Illustrations catch Constance comforting a hospital boy called Swot, lifting a patient's head, and sitting at a bedside through worry and talk.

Hospital scenes test Constance's heart. A doctor, hurrying to operate, asks her to calm a poor patient who dreads the knife, though she must miss dinner in satin and lace. She follows orderlies past steady eyes and amused accents, then reassures a boy who fears his money was taken for keeps, offering her own purse as pledge. Romance grows from kindness shown under pressure, and Ford writes society comedy with warmth. A match, the novel suggests, forms where character shows, not where mothers plot.
14278-the-radio-boys-on-the-mexican-bord:
Gerald Breckenridge's 1922 boys' book sends the Radio Boys to the Mexican border, with directions for installing an amateur radio receiving telephone. Jack, Tom, Frank, and Stone track treachery by airwaves, while a cry in the air, an enemy near, a daring leap, and shots at night raise the stakes. Remedios plays a part in the day's adventures, and a Mexican chauffeur recognized beside Mr. Rollins deepens suspicion.

Listening becomes detective work. Jack takes Tom into confidence behind a closed door, fearing he knows not whom to trust after what he has seen. Stone crawls to a rock fissure where radio wires descend into a cave, kneels in darkness, and hears Spanish murmurs rising through the hole. Frank, with limited Spanish, catches the language if not the words. Radio, border intrigue, and boy loyalty combine in a brisk adventure for young wireless fans.
14361-carmen-s-messenger:
Harold Bindloss wrote this 1917 adventure novel of the Border hills and the Canadian wheat lands. Foster, the hero, crosses rough moorland with Pete, a dour Scot whose face is lined and whose stride stays young. The tale follows messages, mines, and a chase across farms and rail lines. Featherstone changes his plans, and Foster makes a promise that binds him. Bindloss writes of men, ground, and loyalties that do not bend.

Pete crossed quaking moss with Foster and climbed to a tableland torn into peat rifts. The men who wrung a living from these barren hills, Foster thinks, thrived when they reached Canada's soil. Later a snow slide blocks the rail line, and Foster walks past stalled cars toward a gang at work round the bend. The novel pairs Border grit with Canadian scale. Its charm lies in country, friends, and a puzzle worked out step by step.
14377-the-queen-like-closet-or-rich-cabi:
Hannah Wolley's 1672 cookbook and household guide, in its second edition, gathers receipts for preserving, candying, and cookery, addressed to women running a house. Wolley was among the first English women to publish such a book under her own name.

Recipes cover cakes, syrups, pickles, meats, and sweets, with quantities in quarts, pounds, and spoonfuls, plus cordials and remedies for common ills. A second part adds further receipts and household advice. Later editions expanded the book for new readers across England. The volume shows Restoration kitchens at work, and it marks a milestone in women's printed cookery.
14409-esther:
Published anonymously in 1884, this New York novel opens in the new church of St. John's on Fifth Avenue, where Esther, a young woman of artistic taste, meets the clergyman George Hazard. Their friendship grows amid sermons, pictures, and talk of faith.

Esther weighs Hazard's devout world against her own freer circle, while her cousin Catherine falls under his influence. The novel probes religion, art, and a woman's independence in Gilded Age Manhattan, with sharp dialogue and careful social observation. Its authorship was long a secret, and its quiet irony still rewards patient readers.
14428-the-life-and-correspondence-of-sir:
Ferdinand Brock Tupper edited this 1845 biography of his uncle, Major-General Sir Isaac Brock, from family papers opened after decades in storage. Brock commanded British forces in Upper Canada during the War of 1812 and died at Queenston Heights.

Letters, orders, and memoir passages trace Brock from Guernsey to Canada, with long notices of the Shawnee leader Tecumseh, his ally. The volume also sketches Brock relatives and fellow officers. It remains a key early source on the Canadian war, written by family hands and full of firsthand detail on frontier command. Later historians still mine its letters for the war's northern campaigns.
14441-wagner:
John F. Runciman's short 1913 life of Richard Wagner, in Bell's Miniature Series of Musicians, traces the composer from his Leipzig youth through Magdeburg, Riga, Paris, Dresden, Zurich, Munich, and Bayreuth. A second edition, it pairs a life with a survey of works.

Runciman sets Wagner against Bach, Mozart, Haydn, and Beethoven, then discusses Lohengrin, Tannhäuser, and the Ring, with attention to leitmotifs such as the Montsalvat theme. The book is enthusiastic and partisan, written for general readers rather than scholars. It offers a compact Edwardian introduction to a towering and quarrelsome genius.
14508-the-christmas-dinner:
Shepherd Knapp wrote this children's play, published in Philadelphia in 1921, for boys and girls to act, with Mother Goose as narrator. The play was dedicated to its first performers and their trainers.

The first scene opens in a farmhouse kitchen, with a fireplace, a mantel lamp, a wood box, and a broom, as the family saves its appetite for Christmas dinner. Mother Goose steps before the curtain between scenes to tell what happened while it was closed. The play is homely and direct, made for school stages and family audiences at Christmas.
14579-simon-called-peter:
Robert Keable's 1921 novel follows Peter, a chaplain in the Great War, through France and its temptations. He dedicates the book to Julie, who never lived yet never dies. Keable had written The Drift of Pinions.

Peter reads letters on a terrace by the sea and talks with Arnold and Donovan. He faces the glamour of war that Keable warns has filled the world's cup of sorrow again and again. A woman kisses him twice and leaps away with the words be good, and if you can't, be careful. The novel is a frank, controversial war romance of faith and desire.
14656-the-sword-maker:
Robert Barr's The Sword Maker, published by Frederick A. Stokes in New York in June 1910, is a romance of the medieval Rhine by the author of Tekla and In the Midst of Alarms. Its table of contents promises guilds, counts, and freebooters.

The plot opens with an offer to open the river, a bargain struck, and dissension in the ironworkers' guild over shared money. A disturbing journey by Father Ambrose, the Countess von Sayn, the Archbishop of Cologne, a mutiny, missing gold, and the laughing Red Margrave of Furstenberg follow. The prisoner of Ehrenfels and a lovers' meeting close a lively historical adventure.
14668-mcguffey-s-second-eclectic-reader:
McGuffey's Second Eclectic Reader, in its revised edition, taught American schoolchildren to read in the schoolroom of 1900. William Holmes McGuffey's name, though not listed in the text, stands behind the series.

Lessons cover articulation, punctuation, and selections in prose and poetry, with Roman numerals numbering the exercises. A tiger lesson describes the giant cat's stripes, bounds, and whiskers, teaching both reading and natural fact. The reader's moral tone is plain and direct, and its exercises still suit a teacher working with beginners. McGuffey readers shaped American schoolrooms for generations. Teachers prized their plain moral lessons and steady drills.
14680-the-continental-monthly-vol-1-no-5:
The Continental Monthly for May 1862, devoted to literature and national policy, asks what the Union should do with slavery and secession as the Civil War deepened. Its opening essay traces the road from Boston in 1770 to Lexington.

Other pieces weigh slave population growth, a philosophic bankrupt, and the Molly O'Molly papers. A constitutional essay argues that Congress, acting for the United States as a unit, annuls separate state integrity. The magazine's Union voice is firm and legalistic. The issue is a strong source on Northern war aims in the spring of 1862.
14766-mcguffey-s-third-eclectic-reader:
William Holmes McGuffey's Third Eclectic Reader, revised edition dated 1879, taught American schoolchildren to read in the schoolroom of 1900. Its moral tone is plain, as in the lesson that she is kind to the old blind man, and much is left to the teacher.

Lessons build reading and writing step by step, with explanations enough to start a child, and Roman numerals as lesson numbers as a bonus. Some material survives only as images, since specialised characters have no plain text form, and old contractions appear with a space. The reader remains a landmark of American schooling: simple stories, clear morals and steady practice.
14868-the-tailor-of-gloucester:
Beatrix Potter's 1903 tale was told to her friend Freda, who had been ill and loved fairy tales. It claims to be true, at least about the tailor, the waistcoat and the cry of no more twist. Potter says she heard it in Gloucestershire at Christmas 1901, and made a new story nobody had read before.

In the time of the tale, a tailor in Gloucester works on a waistcoat for the mayor's wedding, helped by small, shrill voices from behind a wall. The book, with a motto from Richard the Third about entertaining tailors, blends workshop realism with fairy help. Potter's pictures give the tailor's shop, the mice and the finished waistcoat a warmth that has kept the story loved.
14880-mcguffey-s-fourth-eclectic-reader:
William Holmes McGuffey's Fourth Eclectic Reader carries American schoolchildren a stage beyond the third reader, in the schoolroom of 1900. Its moral tone stays plain, its exercises stay suitable, and much is left to the teacher, as the transcriber's note explains.

Explanations in the text are enough to start a child reading and writing, Roman numerals appear as lesson numbers, and old contractions are spaced as in the original. Passages with special characters are rendered approximately in text, with original images in other formats. Section numbers are decimal in contents and Roman in the body. The reader remains a classic of American primary schooling.
1489-the-new-mcguffey-first-reader:
The New McGuffey First Reader opens the famous series for the youngest pupils, with short words, simple sentences, and pictures in the original books. Lessons teach letters, sounds, and good conduct together. The First Reader, with its short lessons, taught millions of American children to read.

Children learn to read through stories of home, farm, and school, each ending with a moral. The First Reader shaped American childhood for generations, and it remains a classic of early reading instruction. Its moral tales, of honesty and kindness, matched the school values of its age.
14896-the-diamond-master:
Jacques Futrelle's 1909 mystery begins with a plain yellow package, about the size of a cigarette box, tied in thin scarlet twine and addressed to the head of a great business house. Inside lies the first diamond, and more follow in a supply that seems unlimited.

Tweedledum and Tweedledee, Thursday at three, the astute Mr. Birnes, a mysterious woman and a winged messenger deepen the puzzle. Some conjectures, and more diamonds, lead to a big game, a silent bell, the third degree and Mr. Czenki, who appears, is caught in the net and at last explains in part. The great cube closes a tale of gems, greed and clever detection.
1490-the-new-mcguffey-fourth-reader:
William H. McGuffey's Fourth Reader, in its new edition, gathers prose and verse for schoolchildren at the fourth level of reading. Lessons mix stories, poems, speeches, and moral tales, each chosen to teach reading and character. McGuffey's Readers, first issued in the 1830s, sold over a hundred million copies.

The Fourth Reader is harder than the First, with longer pieces and richer language, and it trained generations of American pupils. The book remains a window on nineteenth-century schooling and its values. The Fourth Reader's longer lessons prepared pupils for speeches, essays, and serious reading.
14943-an-american-idyll-the-life-of-carl:
Cornelia Stratton Parker writes the life of her husband, Carleton H. Parker, as an American idyll, published by the Atlantic Monthly Press in 1919. A poem by Robert Louis Stevenson, reprinted by permission of Scribner, frames the memoir: a being who lived the better part of human days in April, never knowing December's chill.

Parker came, stayed and went, nor ever ceased to smile, taking his fill of music, joy of thought and seeing, while his wife alone crossed the melancholy stream after him. The book is a widow's tribute and a portrait of a short, bright life in California labour and university circles, told with grief held in check by admiration.
14979-cape-cod-and-all-the-pilgrim-land-:
Cape Cod and All the Pilgrim Land for June 1922, volume six number four, is a monthly magazine devoted to southeastern Massachusetts, published at Hyannis and edited by Lemuel C. Hall. A frontispiece of dancing on the sands sets a summer tone.

From the publisher's desk and the portal of the Cape come first. Where shall I spend my vacation, Wellfleet, a squeak for a life and Cape trout streams follow. Ocean travels, editorials, Falmouth inner harbour, Bass River and Cape Cod notes come next. A delayed letter and a million quarts of strawberries close the local news. The issue is a bright regional magazine of place and season.
15040-mcguffey-s-fifth-eclectic-reader:
McGuffey's Fifth Eclectic Reader, revised edition copyrighted in 1879, carries older schoolchildren further in reading, elocution and literature. Preliminary remarks, articulation, inflections, accent, emphasis, modulation and poetic pauses open the volume, teaching how to read aloud well.

Particular attention is invited to notices of authors, and selections grow longer and harder than in earlier readers. The plan of revision matches other books in the series, considerably enlarged from earlier forms. McGuffey's readers shaped American schooling for generations, and the fifth reader shows the top of that ladder: clear speech, good prose and moral tales for young citizens.
15077-the-tale-of-mr-jeremy-fisher:
Beatrix Potter's 1906 tale follows Mr. Jeremy Fisher, a frog who lives in a damp little house among buttercups at a pond's edge. On a rainy day he sets out to catch minnows for dinner, dressed in a macintosh and goloshes, with rod, basket, and a round green boat like a lily leaf. His plans run to five fish and guests.

Fishing brings mishaps: a stickleback, a hungry trout, and a wet landing teach Jeremy that pond life bites back. Potter's prose is neat and funny, and her pictures, absent from this plain text, are part of the tale's fame. Small children will enjoy Jeremy's pluck and his very damp day.
15089-the-deserter:
Richard Harding Davis sets this short war story among American correspondents waiting at Salonika during the First World War. The group includes a veteran reporter, a brash young newcomer, and a kindly cartoonist known for giving his money away. Their talk about news, duty, and home sets the scene for what follows.

At the heart of the tale stands a soldier who has left his post, and the moral puzzle his case poses for men who write about war from the sidelines. Davis keeps the focus on character and choice rather than battle scenes. The result is a compact, humane look at courage, loyalty, and the gap between reporting a war and fighting one.
151-the-rime-of-the-ancient-mariner:
An old sailor stops a wedding guest and holds him with a glittering eye. Samuel Taylor Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner, in seven parts, tells how the mariner shot an albatross and doomed his ship. Thirst, Life-in-Death, and ghostly crew follow on a windless sea.

The mariner's blessing of water snakes breaks the curse, and penance sends him wandering to tell his tale. Coleridge's ballad mixes sea lore, guilt, and grace in haunting verse. The poem's images entered the language: albatross, water everywhere, and a sadder, wiser man. It anchors English Romantic poetry.
15167-london-river:
H. M. Tomlinson's 1921 book on London River begins at Poverty Corner, on the north side of the City, where a seamen's foreshore hides in plain sight along Fenchurch Street. Chapters follow a midnight voyage, a shipping parish, ship-runners, a coffee shop, and an old Lloyd's Register. The river's shadows shape every page.

Tomlinson writes as a lover of ships and watermen, with lyrical prose on tides, docks, and the men who work them. His London is built of old shadows, as he puts it, and the river keeps its secrets. Readers who love river books will find this one atmospheric, wise, and beautifully observed.
15170-the-child-s-world-third-reader:
Hetty Browne, Sarah Withers, and W. K. Tate prepared this third reader for rural schools, issued by Johnson Publishing in Richmond. Aimed at young pupils, it offers graded reading lessons with charts, a manual, and cards sold as teachers' aids. The aids promise to save time for trained and untrained teachers alike.

Lessons mix stories, poems, and schoolroom pieces suited to third-grade readers, with an eye to country classrooms. The book shows how reading was taught in early twentieth-century America: by steps, with helps at hand. Historians of schooling will find it a plain, useful sample of its kind.
15315-gladys-the-reaper:
Anne Beale's 1881 novel Gladys, the Reaper opens on a June evening after rain, as farmers tap barometers and plan to mow hay in coming sunshine. Gladys stands, in the book's motto, like Ruth amid alien corn. The farmer's wife chapter sets a rural, harvest-time scene.

Gladys, a country girl of spirit, faces love, work, and family trials through harvests and seasons, in Beale's warm, moral style. The novel blends farm detail with romance and faith. Fans of Victorian rural fiction will find it gentle, wholesome, and rich in harvest color.
15327-a-library-primer:
John Cotton Dana's Library Primer, in a third edition of 1903, teaches how to organize and manage a public library. A preface traces the primer to articles in Public Libraries in 1896, drawing on Poole on library organization, Fletcher on American libraries, and Plummer's hints for small libraries. Dana dedicates it to Green, Fletcher, and Cutter.

Chapters cover founding, housing, buying, cataloguing, and serving readers, with practical advice for small towns. The primer helped build America's public libraries. Librarians and local historians will find it a clear, useful classic of library practice.
15342-notes-of-a-twenty-five-years-servi:
John McLean's Notes of a Twenty-Five Years' Service in the Hudson's Bay Territory, volume one, printed in London in 1849, records a fur trader's long northern life. He began writing to pass lonely hours, and friends urged him to publish. The territory, he notes, still lacked a full account despite earlier books.

McLean describes posts, journeys, Native peoples, and trade, with a trader's eye for hardship and routine. His notes run plain and firsthand, without literary polish. Historians of Canada's fur trade will find the volume a valuable, ground-level record of a vast, hard country.
15353-a-first-spanish-reader:
Erwin W. Roessler and Alfred Remy, teachers at New York's High School of Commerce, wrote this Spanish reader for pupils near the start of their course. The first twenty-three pieces use only the present tense, and hard sentence forms are kept out on purpose. Each piece ends with questions to help a pupil prepare the lesson, and a vocabulary backs the whole book.

Early readings cover school, family, the house, coins, months, seasons, and the human body, in short and simple Spanish. Later pieces move on to Mexico, Brazil, the theatre, and short tales adapted from Spanish writers and other sources. The aim is steady practice, not grammar drills: a beginner reads real Spanish from the first lesson and builds up word by word.
15385-a-cathedral-singer:
James Lane Allen published this novel in 1916, with a frontispiece by Sigismond de Ivanowski. It opens on Morningside Heights in New York, where the Cathedral of St. John the Divine rises slowly above the city. Across the street stands St. Luke's Hospital, and nearby sit the studios of the National Academy of Design, where young artists labor under a low skylight.

The story centers on a singer drawn to the cathedral's music and faith, set against that grand building and its neighbors. Allen contrasts the hospital of human suffering, the studios of visible beauty, and the cathedral of unseen hope. A later passage recalls a Southern boy born on an old battlefield, linking the singer's past to the wider American story. The novel is quiet and reflective, more portrait than plot.
15402-what-answer:
Anna Dickinson's 1868 novel What Answer opens on a crowded Fifth Avenue at afternoon height, with a gallant throng in purple, fine linen, and sweeping robes. Faces proud and self-satisfied gaze from windows and streets, as if dress, dining, and mirth were all of existence. A Dryden motto on youth and beauty's pride fronts the book.

Dickinson, a famous lecturer, turns from that glitter to ask what answer wealth and fashion give to deeper claims of love, duty, and faith. The novel blends social satire with moral earnestness. Readers of Reconstruction-era fiction will find it sharp, stylish, and searching.
15503-the-underworld-the-story-of-robert:
James C. Welsh published this mining novel in New York in 1920, with Frederick A. Stokes. Its hero is Robert Sinclair, miner. Its twenty-five chapters run from the thong of poverty through a young rebel. Black Jock's threat, the coming of a prophet, and heroes of the underworld follow. A strike, rivals, and a red hose race follow.

The opening finds a woman finishing a sock by lamplight while her husband, Geordie, lies restless with a sore back, tired of lying always in one position. That domestic scene sets the book's method: pit life told through families, not statistics. Later chapters bring Mysie running away, a conference, a meeting with Mysie, and a fight with death. Welsh writes a Scottish mining novel of labor, love, and danger underground.
15523-getting-together:
Ian Hay, author of The First Hundred Thousand, published this wartime book in 1917, with Doubleday in Garden City and Houghton Mifflin in Boston. For months, Hay says, it had been his pleasant duty to travel around the United States, lecturing on war topics to indulgent American audiences. The book grows out of that tour.

Hay admires the average American's instinct for public affairs, and the quickness with which he seizes a live topic. The opening question, by day from a newspaper man and by night by telephone, is always the same: when is the war going to end? No one asks how it will end, Hay notes, as if that were settled. The book argues for Anglo-American getting together, in a friendly, anecdotal style meant to draw two peoples closer in war.
15617-cyclopedia-of-telephony-and-telegr:
This first volume of a four-volume Cyclopedia of Telephony and Telegraphy appeared in Chicago in 1919. The American School of Correspondence published it as a general reference work by telephone and telegraph experts and electrical engineers of high standing. A frontispiece shows Alexander Graham Bell, inventor of the telephone, and over two thousand engravings illustrate the set.

The subtitle lists the field in full. It covers phones, shared lines, boards worked by hand, boards worked by machine, power plants, and special services. It covers building, running, and repair work. Wire messages, and wireless wire and voice work, complete the range. Collaborators include Kempster B. Miller, George W. Patterson of Michigan, Charles Thom of Western Union, and Robert Andrews Millikan. The volume serves as a technical manual for a new network age.
15620-recreations-in-astronomy-with-dire:
Henry White Warren, author of Sights and Insights, published this popular astronomy in 1879, with eighty-three illustrations and maps of stars. A front picture shows Orion and Taurus, with notes on red stars, double stars, and the Crab Nebula. Warren's preface declares astronomy moving at the double-quick: since Copernicus settled its principles four hundred years ago, it has never had to beat a retreat.

Chapters cover creative processes and progress, the constitution of light, and the chemistry of suns revealed by light. Instruments follow: the telescope, the reflecting telescope, and the spectroscope, with celestial measurements. The sun, the planets as seen from space, shooting stars, meteors, and comets, and the planets as individuals close the set. Warren writes for amateurs with telescopes: how to look, what to measure, and what the new science of starlight means.
1563-the-crystal-stopper:
Maurice LeBlanc's Crystal Stopper follows Arsene Lupin, gentleman thief, through arrests, a home life of Alexis Daubrecq, and a chief of enemies who holds a list of twenty-seven names. A crystal stopper, hiding a secret paper, becomes the key to blackmail, murder, and a death sentence that Lupin must overturn.

Through Paris houses and country chateaux, Lupin matches wits with police and villains, rescuing friends and outwitting a master blackmailer. The plot is intricate and the pace is swift. It is a classic Lupin adventure, full of disguise, daring, and the thief's gallant code.
15659-the-beacon-second-reader:
James H. Fassett wrote this Beacon Second Reader, published by Ginn and Company in Boston, New York, Chicago, and London in 1914, with Atlanta, Dallas, Columbus, and San Francisco on the title page. The Athenæum Press printed it. The contents mix fairy tales, poems, and folk tales for young readers learning to read with pleasure.

Early pieces include the ship, an old English rhyme, the wolf and the seven young kids by the Grimms, and Phoebe Cary's they didn't think. Tom Thumb, Cinderella, and raindrops follow, with the four friends and little birdie by Tennyson. Mother Frost, why the bear's tail is short, and Rumpelstiltskin lead to bed in summer and a good play by Robert Louis Stevenson. The golden touch, over in the meadow, the bell of Atri, and Dick Whittington close a classic early reader, built on stories children already love.
15705-the-silly-syclopedia-a-terrible-th:
Noah Lott, an ex-relative of Noah Webster, offered this silly syclopedia in New York in July 1905, from G. W. Dillingham Company, embellished with numerous and distracting cuts and diagrams by Louis F. Grant. The subtitle calls it a terrible thing in the form of a literary torpedo, launched for hilarious purposes only, inaccurate in every particular, with copious etymological derivations and other useless things.

An epigraph adapts Longfellow on leaving excuses for a smile behind us. The book is dedicated to the author's automobile, which jumped a fence, climbed a telegraph pole, burst its cylinder head, exploded its tires, and barked at him. Abbreviations decode slang: at the bat, butt in, catch on, easy street, and pass the butter. Entries mock cookery, hamburgers, and the Milk Trust. The book is pure Edwardian nonsense, a joke dictionary for readers who like their learning laughed at.
15706-winchester:
A short illustrated guide to Winchester, described by Sidney Heath and pictured by E. W. Haslehust. Blackie and Son issued it in London, Glasgow, and Bombay in 1911, as part of the Beautiful England series. Sister volumes cover Oxford, Canterbury, Windsor, York, and the English Lakes. The format pairs brief, loving prose with colour pictures.

Heath walks the reader through the cathedral city: its close, gate, streets, and old stones. Haslehust's pictures give the close and the town in soft colour. History and present-day charm share the pages in equal part. The guide still charms as a snapshot of Edwardian travel writing, when a small book and a train ticket were enough for a day's delight.
15728-the-indiscreet-letter:
A short comic novel by Eleanor Hallowell Abbott, author of Molly Make Believe, issued by the Century Company in New York in 1915. Abbott builds her tale on a train journey, a letter, and the trouble it causes. A travelling salesman, short, quick, and dressy in a new buff suit, shares a car with a young electrician. Talk, flirtation, and a misdirected letter set the plot spinning.

The letter, written without care, falls into wrong hands and stirs love, jealousy, and laughter. Abbott writes with light wit and a keen eye for manners on the move. Her characters talk fast and feel faster. The book delights as a small comedy of modern life: one careless page, and a whole journey changes course.
15746-the-flamingo-feather:
An adventure novel for young readers by Kirk Munroe, set in Florida during the French settlement of the 1560s. The hero, Rene de Veaux, is caught between French colonists at Fort Caroline and the native peoples around them. Munroe, a popular boys' writer, mixes history with escapes, traps, and battles. Harper and Brothers issued the tale in 1887, with pictures to match.

Rene befriends Has-se, a young native, and the two face capture, revenge, and a mutiny at the fort. A flamingo feather serves as a token of trust between them. Later chapters bring Jean Ribault's fleet, a night of terror, and Rene's return. The book keeps its pace brisk and its morals plain: loyalty and courage matter more than rank or birth.
15747-reading-made-easy-for-foreigners-t:
A reader for immigrants learning English, by John L. Hulshof, teacher of modern languages in New York City public schools. Hinds, Noble and Eldredge issued the third reader in 1909. Short lessons build vocabulary through American life, with remarks to the teacher at the front. The book aims at newcomers who can read a little and want more.

Lessons treat Flag Day, the national flag, and the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor. Independence, George Washington, the first steamboat, and the American Indian follow, beside pieces on coffee, pure air, and good behaviour. Rosa Bonheur and Alexander and the robber add story colour. The reader shows how schools in 1909 taught English and citizenship together.
15751-a-selection-of-books-published-by-:
A publisher's catalogue from Methuen and Company of Essex Street, London, listing books then in print. Catalogues of this kind served booksellers and readers as a guide to a firm's whole list. Entries are grouped by series, with short notes on each title's scope. The range runs from school texts to art, history, and devotion.

Series named here include Ancient Cities, Arden Shakespeare, Classics of Art, and the Little Guides and Little Library sets. Leaders of Religion, Library of Devotion, and Handbooks of English Church History show the firm's weight in church books. New Library of Medicine and New Library of Music mark its push into fresh fields. As a record, the list maps what a leading London house sold and prized in its day.
15790-esther:
A school edition of Racine's tragedy Esther, in three acts, edited by I. H. B. Spiers of William Penn Charter School. D. C. Heath and Company issued it in Boston, New York, and Chicago in 1891, as part of Heath's Modern Language Series. Spiers calls Esther the easiest and shortest masterpiece of French tragic literature. His text updates spelling and grammar for students of his day.

Esther, a Jewish queen in Persia, risks her life to save her people from a court plot. Racine, writing for girls at Saint-Cyr, keeps the verse pure and the action spare. Spiers adds an introduction, notes, and appendices to guide young readers through the French. The edition still serves as a gentle first step into classical French drama.
15797-the-seeker:
A 1904 novel by Harry Leon Wilson, author of The Spenders, with pictures by Rose Cecil O'Neill. Doubleday, Page and Company issued the book in New York. Bernal Linford, grandson of an old clergyman, grows up in the village of Edom and seeks a faith he can hold. Wilson follows him from childhood fable to adult doubt and duty.

Bernal tests the Christmas saint as a boy, then meets preachers, a village atheist, a worldly aunt, and Nancy Crealock, a wondering child turned woman. His brother Allan takes the pulpit while Bernal searches wider. Truth, Wilson argues, must survive friction like a diamond. The novel stands as a humane study of belief in an age when old certainties were breaking.
15798-clover:
A girls' novel by Susan Coolidge, author of What Katy Did, issued by Little, Brown and Company in Boston in 1907. Jessie McDermot supplied the pictures. Clover, Katy's younger sister, grows up in the later Katy books, and this volume follows her own path. Coolidge writes with warmth for girls leaving childhood behind.

Chapters open with a talk on the doorsteps and a day of happy letters. The first wedding in the family and two long years follow, as Clover learns love, work, and loss. Home, sisters, and friends anchor every change. The book charms as a gentle sequel: a girl becoming a woman, in a house full of love.
15825-new-national-fourth-reader:
A school reader by Charles J. Barnes and J. Marshall Hawkes, issued in 1884 as part of Barnes' New National Readers. Fourth readers served pupils moving from simple tales to longer prose and verse. Lessons mix stories, poems, history, and nature, each with notes on hard words. An illustration of Pompeii's destruction fronts the book.

Lessons open with Charlotte Daly's I'm Going To, then move to Mayne Reid's adventure with dusky wolves. The bean and the stone, and other fables, teach morals in short form. Pronunciation marks guide young readers, with notes at each lesson's end. The reader still shows how American schools in the 1880s taught reading: varied, moral, and steadily harder.
15902-poker:
A short play by Zora Neale Hurston, copyrighted in 1931, transcribed from an original manuscript by the Library of Congress American Memory Project. Pencilled notations, possibly Hurston's own, appear as handwritten notes in the text. The play is set in the present, in New York, in a shabby front room of a shotgun house. Its cast lists seven players and one onlooker.

Nunkie, Too-Sweet, Peckerwood, Black Baby, Sack Daddy, and Tush Hawg gather round a plain centre table, with Aunt Dilsey nearby. Gaudy calendars, a battered piano, and kerosene lamps dress the room. Talk, bluff, and pride drive the game. The play gives a vivid slice of Black folk life: humour, speech, and stakes, in one taut room.
15930-a-dutch-boy-fifty-years-after:
A memoir for young readers by Edward Bok, adapted from his Americanization of Edward Bok and edited by John Louis Haney of Central High School, Philadelphia. Charles Scribner's Sons issued it in 1921, with a photograph of Bok as frontispiece. Bok dedicates the story to the schoolboys and schoolgirls of America. His lesson is that an obstacle is not a wall.

Bok, a Dutch immigrant boy, lands in America poor and works his way up by thrift, study, and sheer will. Newspapers, books, and a famous magazine editorship lie ahead. Haney's edition trims the tale for school use. The memoir still inspires: a boy from abroad, becoming American by work and by hope.
15934-his-excellency-the-minister:
A French political novel by Jules Claretie of the Academie Francaise, completely translated by Henri Roberts. George Barrie and Sons printed it in Philadelphia in 1900 for subscribers only, in a limited edition of one thousand numbered sets, this copy number three hundred and fifty-eight. Eugene Wallet made the etchings, Adrien Marie the drawings. Claretie dedicates the book to Alphonse Daudet.

His Excellency the Minister follows a minister's rise, intrigues, and fall in the Third Republic. Salons, newspapers, and chambers frame a tale of ambition and love. Claretie writes with a journalist's eye and a novelist's warmth. The handsome edition suits collectors: a political romance, finely printed and finely pictured.
15991-japhet-in-search-of-a-father:
Captain Frederick Marryat's novel follows a young man named Japhet who sets out to find the father he has never known. The 1896 Dent and Little, Brown edition runs to seventy-nine chapters, and a prefatory note recalls its first run in the Metropolitan Magazine. Marryat, a former naval officer, wrote sea tales and adventure stories that were widely read in his day.

Japhet's search carries him through many turns of fortune, new friends, false leads, and hard lessons about rank and family. The book moves at a brisk, old-style pace, with dialogue and incident doing most of the work. It will appeal to readers who enjoy classic adventure, mistaken identity, and a hero piecing together his own past.
1603-the-blue-flower:
Henry Van Dyke's The Blue Flower gathers short stories of longing for something afar, from the sphere of sorrow, as the Shelley epigraph puts it. Dedicated to the memory of Bernard Van Dyke, the tales move between real places and dreamlike quests, with characters seeking a flower, a star, or a lost love.

Van Dyke's prose is gentle and idealistic, and his stories end more often in hope than in triumph. The preface warns that such tales are parcels in a basket, varied by design. The book is a quiet, old-fashioned collection for readers who like their fiction tender and thoughtful.
16070-the-empire-of-austria-its-rise-and:
A history of Austria by John S. C. Abbott, in his Monarchies of Continental Europe series. Mason Brothers issued it in New York, with Rickey, Mallory and Company in Cincinnati. Abbott, a popular historian, traces the empire from its rise to its present power. His narrative favours kings, battles, and vivid scenes over dry annals.

Habsburg marriages, wars, and reforms carry the story through centuries of European strife. Vienna, its court, and its armies stand at the centre. Abbott writes for general readers who liked history as story. The book still serves as a nineteenth-century view of Austria: an old empire, told with admiration for its endurance.
16079-some-old-time-beauties-after-portr:
Boston publisher Joseph Knight Company issued Thomson Willing's volume in 1895, pairing famous English portraits with short life sketches. Each chapter takes one celebrated woman of an earlier age and the painter who caught her likeness, from Gainsborough and Reynolds to Romney and Lawrence. Ten women appear, among them Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire, Emma, Lady Hamilton, and Marguerite, Countess Blessington.

The sketches mix looks, manners, politics, and gossip, so each woman comes alive as a person of her own time rather than a face on a wall. Georgiana's charm, her Whig circle at Devonshire House, and her canvassing for Charles James Fox get full treatment. Readers who like art, high society, and eighteenth-century England will find a light, anecdote-filled way into that world.
16373-mrs-red-pepper:
Grace S. Richmond's Mrs. Red Pepper, published in 1913, continues the story of Red Pepper Burns, physician and surgeon, and his wife. Chapter one, wholly given over to sentiment, opens with the Green Imp. The long, low, powerful car is loaded with passengers, a motor trunk, bulky parcels, and mud. It pulls aside in the fifth April shower of the afternoon. Burns descends from the car, ready for whatever the country practice brings.

Later chapters cover Burns doing his duty, a red head, broken steel wires, points of view, an apple tree, a practical artist, a runaway road, and the country surgeon at work. Richmond writes warm, popular domestic fiction with humor and heart. Readers of the Red Pepper books will find a comfortable, engaging sequel.
16530-the-ridin-kid-from-powder-river:
Henry Herbert Knibbs follows young Pete, the Ridin' Kid from Powder River, through a long western tale in this 1919 novel. Chapters run from firearms and new fortunes through warnings, justice, and a change of base to Pop Annersley's boy, the pit, the black sombrero, the spider, and a gamble. Fugitive, El Paso, and Doris mark the later course.

Knibbs writes with a Westerner's ear for speech, horses, and showdowns. The plot mixes ranch life with outlaw trouble and a love thread. Readers of classic westerns will find a full, colorful yarn, brisk in pace and rich in frontier detail.
16552-the-next-of-kin-those-who-wait-and:
Nellie L. McClung writes of those who wait and wonder at home while war takes their kin, in this 1917 Canadian book. A poem on hope opens the volume, answering ages of weeping women with a new note. Hope has dawned in lonely hearts, and a message is being sent over the waste of grief. The prose that follows gives voice to mothers, wives, and sisters.

McClung, known for Sowing Seeds in Denny, writes as a reformer and storyteller, plain and heartfelt. The book speaks to wartime Canada, where waiting was itself a kind of service. Readers of women's war writing will find it moving and of its moment.
16557-the-deserter:
Captain Charles King's 1887 novel opens far up in the Northwest, along the Elk River, where a train of white-topped army wagons crawls eastward in October sun. Dust powders every face in the guarding battalion, and four companies of infantry stride along, rifles slung, covering the exposed southern flank. The prelude sets a frontier march in full.

King, himself an army captain, writes with inside knowledge of troops, dust, and danger. The Deserter pairs with From the Ranks in one Lippincott volume. Readers of military fiction will find a vivid, authentic tale of the old army on the plains.
16589-the-killer:
Stewart Edward White tells western tales in this 1920 volume, opening with the title story, written twenty years after the events at his wife's and Buck Johnson's urging. The narrator warns that his yarn has no love story and no plot: things just happened, one after another. The Road Agent, The Tide, Climbing for Goats, and The Ranch follow.

White writes from ranch life he knew well, with dry humor and a keen eye for men, horses, and hard country. The stories are plain and unsentimental. Readers of western fiction will find a classic voice here, honest about the West as it was lived.
166-summer:
Charity Royall, a ward of lawyer Royall in the hill village of North Dormer, longs for a wider life. Edith Wharton's Summer, published in 1917, follows Charity through a June of work, reading, and first love. A young architect visiting the village opens her world.

Charity's guardian watches her with mixed care and desire, while the mountain folk she came from beckon her back. Wharton sets passion against duty in spare, sunlit prose. The novel's frank treatment of a young woman's longing shocked its first readers. It now ranks among Wharton's finest short novels.
16600-cecil-rhodes-man-and-empire-maker:
Princess Catherine Radziwill portrays Cecil Rhodes, man and empire-maker, in this 1918 biography with eight photogravure plates. Chapters run from Rhodes and Milner through the foundations of fortune, a complex personality, the Raid and its aftermath, the Afrikander Bond, concentration camps, martial law, and flight from the Rand. An estimate of Milner closes the main text.

Radziwill writes as a society insider with strong views, mixing personal sketch with imperial politics. The book gives Rhodes as his age saw him: builder, schemer, and dreamer of empire. Readers of South African history will find it vivid, partisan, and full of period color.
16623-letters-of-a-woman-homesteader:
Elinore Pruitt Stewart writes genuine letters from Wyoming homestead life in this 1914 book, printed as written save for omissions and changed names. A young widow who lost her husband in a railroad accident, she worked in Denver, then kept house for a Scotch cattleman, Mr. Stewart, on his quarter-section. Letters to a former Denver employer tell the rest.

Chapters run from arrival at Burnt Fork and filing a claim through a busy summer, a Thanksgiving wedding, proving up, horse-thieves, and the joys of homesteading. Stewart writes with humor, grit, and warmth. The book remains a classic of women's frontier writing, plain and unforgettable.
16706-a-sixth-century-fragment-of-the-le:
E. A. Lowe and E. K. Rand wrote this 1922 study of six leaves of a sixth-century uncial copy of Pliny the Younger's letters, kept in the Pierpont Morgan Library in New York. Lowe taught palaeography at Oxford and Cambridge, Rand taught Latin at Harvard, and the Carnegie Institution issued the work as publication number 304.

The study reads the old leaves letter by letter, hand by hand, to date and place the copy and to judge its text. It shows how scholars use script, ink, and page to recover a lost book's past. Readers keen on old books will find a model of close manuscript work, short, exact, and full of plates and notes.
16720-marzio-s-crucifix-and-zoroaster:
F. Marion Crawford bound two novels in this authorized edition, Marzio's Crucifix and Zoroaster, issued by P. F. Collier in New York. Marzio's tale opens with the sculptor Marzio Pandolfi striking his hammer on a table. He cries that modern life is a living lie, while his handsome apprentice Gianbattista looks up from his work. Zoroaster's frontispiece shows a man who moved not through long hours of day.

Crawford pairs a Roman artist's tale of pride, art, and faith with an eastern tale of a prophet's long vigil. Both novels turn on strong wills and hard choices. Readers who like rich, old-style historical romance will find two full tales in one volume, each with its own world and its own moral fire.
16751-mcguffey-s-sixth-eclectic-reader:
William Holmes McGuffey's Sixth Eclectic Reader, in the schoolroom form of about 1900, gathers graded reading pieces with short lives of their authors. Each piece is followed by notes enough for a teacher to start a child on reading and writing. Roman numerals mark the lessons, and the moral tone is plain throughout.

The reader mixes verse, prose, and short moral tales, with care for clear speech and good conduct. A child learns to read aloud, spell, and weigh right action in the same lesson. The book now serves as a window on old American schooling, and as a still-usable set of short, plain pieces for young readers.
16771-jacqueline-of-golden-river:
H. M. Egbert wrote this 1920 tale of love, gold, and peril in a French Canadian river land, issued by Doubleday, Page in Garden City. Chapters move from a dog and a damsel in Madison Square, through a priest, a captain, a cliff, a chateau, snow blindness, a roulette wheel, a hidden chamber, and swords at last. A frontispiece by Ralph Pallen Coleman opens the book.

Egbert mixes romance with adventure: a hero who parts without a backward glance, a villain named Leroux, and a gold river that lures men on. The tale runs fast, with chases, confessions, and a chateau's fall. Readers who like old north-country romances will find plenty of dash, danger, and a love that holds through the worst.
1679-hiram-the-young-farmer:
Burbank L. Todd follows Hiram, a country boy who leaves a dreary job in town when spring calls him back to the fields. There he must learn farming by doing it: bargaining for land, handling horses, and earning the trust of neighbors. A runaway horse and a girl riding into the story mark the turns of his first season.

The novel is a straightforward tale of a young man finding work he can stand behind, told with affection for farm routines and small-town talk. Readers who enjoy stories of apprenticeship — mistakes made, lessons kept, and a slow rise toward independence — will find Hiram an easy companion, earnest without ever turning solemn.
16845-arthur-a-short-sketch-of-his-life-:
Frederick J. Furnivall copied and edited this short sketch of Arthur's life and history. It is in English verse of the first half of the 1400s, from the Marquis of Bath's manuscript. The Early English Text Society issued it through Trubner in London in 1864. Latin side notes in italics and stops in parentheses follow the manuscript. The verse opens with a call to hear of King Arthur and his labor, and how he was first begotten.

Furnivall gives scholars a plain, faithful text of a rare Arthur poem, with notes to help reading. The verse is short, old, and full of early English forms. Readers of Arthurian legend and medieval verse will find a valuable primary text, best read with a glossary, for its glimpse of Arthur as the 1400s knew him.
16864-notes-of-a-twenty-five-years-servi:
John McLean wrote these notes on twenty-five years of service in Hudson's Bay territory, volume two issued by Richard Bentley in London in 1849. Chapters take up a trip to Norway House, York Factory, a voyage to Ungava, an exploring trek through Labrador's interior, deer hunts, short rations, influenza, and a distressing bereavement. The first volume covers earlier years.

McLean writes as a fur trade officer who lived the north, not as a distant traveler. He notes posts, natives, reindeer, weather, and the hard facts of supply and loss. The book gives a plain, first-hand view of the fur trade's far edge, valued for its detail and its sober tone about a hard life.
16868-adventures-of-a-despatch-rider:
Captain W. H. L. Watson wrote this 1915 book of a despatch rider's war, issued by Blackwood in Edinburgh and London with maps. It opens with a letter to Second Lieutenant R. B. Whyte, recalling old Oxford days, Balliol, and a first book that was to be a clever Oxford novel full of character sketches. War changed that plan into a rider's tale.

Watson tells of carrying orders by motorbike and horse through the Fifth Division's lines, with maps to track each ride. The tone mixes schoolboy humor with the grim facts of the front. The book gives a vivid, first-hand view of Great War staff work from the saddle, prized for its wit and its plain sense of danger.
16871-skyrider:
B. M. Bower wrote this 1919 western tale of Johnny and the sky, issued by Little, Brown in Boston. A frontispiece by Anton Otto Fischer shows Johnny daring a steep dive at a herd. Chapters move from a poet without honor and one fight, two quarrels, and a riddle into Johnny's gay trip to Sinkhole. Desert glimpses, salvage, and finder keeper follow. A midnight ride, thieves riding boldly, and Mary V facing Johnny appear. A rider of the sky closes the set.

Bower mixes ranch life with early flying, as Johnny trades horses for wings and luck holds its pace. The tale is brisk, funny, and full of desert air. Readers who like westerns with a new twist will enjoy a hero who rides both horse and plane, and a story that moves from range to sky without losing its humor.
16872-percy-bysshe-shelley-as-a-philosop:
Charles Sotheran wrote this 1876 New York study of Percy Bysshe Shelley as thinker and reformer, with a sonnet by Charles W. Frederickson, a portrait, and a view of Shelley's tomb. Sotheran dedicates it to Frederickson, praising him as one of the few who grasp Shelley's hidden essence. Shelley's own motto, let us see the truth whatever it may be, heads the book.

Sotheran reads Shelley not just as a poet of clouds and winds, but as a moral thinker who sought truth and reform. He links verse to Shelley's views on faith, power, and human freedom. The book suits readers who want Shelley the thinker, in an early, earnest study that still shows why his ideas stirred his age.
16904-hello-soldier:
Edward Dyson wrote this book of khaki verse called Hello, Soldier. Much of it first printed in the Bulletin, Punch, the Leader, and the Melbourne Herald. A few pieces are new in print. Dyson notes a paper famine left him no choice but to print on peculiar paper or delay the book. He pleads unusual times for its bizarre craft look. The opening poem calls Australia his native land and says its rating now is A1.

Dyson writes of Australian soldiers with humor, pride, and plain speech, in verse meant to be read aloud. His soldiers joke, march, and face war with a larrikin grin. Readers who like war verse will find a lively, Australian collection, full of slang, mateship, and the pride of a young nation at war.
16914-the-life-of-nelson-volume-1-the-em:
Captain A. T. Mahan of the United States Navy wrote this first volume of his life of Nelson, issued by Sampson Low in London in 1897. His preface owns that Nelson's life has been written so often that a new attempt needs an excuse. Mahan's excuse is completeness: his great study of sea power needs its own portrait of the one man who summed up and embodied all that sea power could mean.

Mahan tracks Nelson from youth to command, weighing genius and opportunity together as the forces that made him the personification of Britain's navy. The volume is a masterwork of naval history, dense with orders, moves, and judgment. Readers of sea war will find a deep, authoritative life, best read before its second volume.
16915-the-life-of-nelson-volume-2-the-em:
Captain A. T. Mahan of the United States Navy wrote this second volume of his life of Nelson, issued by Sampson Low in London in 1897. Chapter fourteen opens in August 1799, with Nelson in temporary command in the Mediterranean, relieved by Lord Keith, seeking return to England for ill health. Rome, Naples, Minorca, Malta, and Lisbon all press on his command.

Mahan reads Nelson as the embodiment of British sea power, weighing his tactics, his temper, and his dealings with allies. The volume is a masterwork of naval history, dense with orders, moves, and judgment. Readers of sea war will find a deep, authoritative life, best read beside Mahan's own books on sea power.
16929-treat-em-rough-letters-from-jack-t:
Ring W. Lardner wrote this book of letters from Jack the Kaiser Killer, issued by Bobbs-Merrill in Indianapolis in 1913 with pictures by Frank Crerie. It opens at Camp Grant on September 23. Jack writes to his friend Al from the recreation room. Twenty other boys write letters around him, half of whom can barely talk English, let alone write it. Jack has felt sick since Wednesday night. He jokes he will be murdered in his bunk before he ever reaches the trenches.

Lardner writes in Jack's comic, misspelled voice, full of army slang, bunk jokes, and home news. The letters mix camp life with wartime brag and bluster. Readers who like Lardner's humor will find a funny, period book of soldier letters, best read for its voice and its view of training camp life.
1699-the-vanished-messenger:
At a quarter to nine on an April evening, a traveller carrying secret papers disappears from Liverpool Street station. A young woman finds herself caught between rival agents. London drawing rooms, country houses, and quiet railway platforms become places where a word dropped at dinner can matter as much as a gun.

The plot turns on who holds a missing message and what it would reveal about naval plans and foreign spies. Oppenheim keeps the pace brisk and the cast polished. The novel is a good sample of the Edwardian spy story: patriotic and romantic, built on the fear that enemies were already moving unnoticed through England.
1701-the-story-of-waitstill-baxter:
Kate Douglas Wiggin sets this Maine novel around Waitstill Baxter and her sister Patrice, two young women keeping house under the rule of their stern stepfather, Deacon Baxter, near the Saco River. Waitstill's patience and Patrice's spirit carry them through seasons of farm work, church, and small-town talk.

A romance with the joiner Ivory, and the sisters' slow push toward lives of their own, give the story its shape. Wiggin writes with warmth about New England village life — its chores, its kindnesses, and its narrow judgments. And the book's charm lies in two sisters who hold together while the world around them expects them to simply obey.
17032-the-lieutenant-and-commander:
Captain Basil Hall's 1862 sketches, drawn from his Fragments of Voyages and Travels, show life as a naval lieutenant and commander. Chapters cover taking a line in the service, shore leave in Ireland, the Admiralty list, promotion hopes, and the tropics at sea. The editor praises the book for young men bound for any walk of life, and most of all for young officers.

Hall mixes personal yarns with firm lessons on duty, tempered by care and humanity in command. The tone is lively and plain, with humor in the shore tales and grit in the sea scenes. Readers keen on the old navy will find a vivid, instructive memoir of rank, work, and command at sea.
17053-kate-bonnet-the-romance-of-a-pirat:
Frank R. Stockton's 1901 romance follows Kate Bonnet, daughter of the pirate Bonnet, through ships, ports, and perils of the pirate age. Early chapters pair two young people, a ship, and a fish, then move to quarter-decks, a fruit basket friend, and a governor of Jamaica. Dickory, Ben Greenway, and Captain Vince all shape Kate's path as she plans, laughs, and faces blade and law.

Stockton mixes humor with adventure, and Kate herself, brave and quick, steals each scene. The tale asks what a daughter owes a pirate father, and how she can find an honest life of her own. Readers who like pirate yarns with wit and a strong heroine will enjoy this long, colorful romance.
17063-a-lost-leader:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's 1907 novel follows Mannering, a rising statesman who falters, and Borrowdean, a rival who drives bargains and debts of honor. Book One sets up a woman with an alias, a duchess at home, and the Mannering mystery. Later books add love against politics, a journalist's meddling, treachery by telegram, and Mannering at last as M. P.

Oppenheim mixes political intrigue with romance, in the smooth, popular style that made his name. Duchesses, debts, and double lives fill four books of plot twists. Readers who like Edwardian tales of power, love, and conscience will find a fast, absorbing novel with a hero who must earn back his lost lead.
17158-armageddon-and-after:
W. L. Courtney's 1914 book, dedicated to young idealists of all lands, reads the Great War through the lens of Revelation. Its first chapter sets out problems of the future, with Kipling's poems and John's vision of kings gathered at Armageddon side by side. Later chapters draw lessons of the past and suggest reforms for the days after the fighting.

Courtney writes as a moralist, not a strategist, urging youth not to let war tarnish their dreams. His prose is earnest and high-minded, typical of early war writing before the full cost was known. Readers of wartime thought will find a short, sincere plea for a better peace after Armageddon.
17255-the-wings-of-icarus-being-the-life:
Laurence Alma Tadema's 1894 novel tells Emilia Fletcher's life in her own words: thirty-five letters to Constance Norris from July to the next March, a fragmentary journal, and a postscript. The first letter, written near midnight at Fletcher's Hall, finds Emilia in a strange room in a strange land, with visions of Constance, mists in a valley, and moths round her candle.

Emilia's tale is one of love, art, and a fall like Icarus, told in intimate, emotional prose. The letter form keeps the story close and confessional. Readers who like Victorian epistolary novels will find a moving, if melancholy, portrait of a woman who flew high and paid the price.
1728-the-odyssey-of-homer:
Held by Calypso, wrecked by storms, and guided at last by Athena, Odysseus makes his long road home from Troy in this prose version by Butcher and Lang. Guided at last by Athena after Calypso's hold and wrecking storms, he faces the Cyclops, Circe, the Sirens, and the suitors who feast in his hall at Ithaca.

Butcher and Lang's version, with its prefaces and introduction, was made for readers who wanted the epic in clear prose rather than verse. It keeps the poem's order across all twenty-four books. Its plain style lets the story's cunning hero, its loyal wife Penelope, and its patient son Telemachus stand out without ornament.
17294-essays-in-liberalism-being-the-lec:
Lectures and papers given at the Liberal Summer School at Oxford in 1922 make up this collection, printed in London the same year. Each piece comes from a different speaker, so the book reads as a shared platform rather than one author's argument. Lord Robert Cecil opens on the League of Nations and the repair of Europe, and John Maynard Keynes takes up reparations and debts between allies.

Other essays cover the balance of power, disarmament, national finance, free trade, India, Egypt, the machinery of government, industry, wages, unemployment, mines, land, and farming. Taken together, they show how British liberals in the early 1920s framed peace, empire, and the daily economy. The volume remains a clear window onto that party's hopes just after the war.
17355-the-runaway-skyscraper:
Murray Leinster's Runaway Skyscraper starts when the Metropolitan Tower clock begins to run backward. A crash, a shiver, and groaning give way to calm: elevators run, lights burn, and clerks return to ledgers. Arthur Chamberlain, dictating to his stenographer Estelle Woodward, pauses, listens, and resumes, even as his letter to creditors Gary and Milton waits.

Soon the whole tower proves loose in time and space, and its people must face a wild, funny predicament. Leinster writes in brisk pulp style, with office humor and science wonder in turn. Science fiction fans will enjoy an early, inventive tale of a building on the run, and the folks trapped inside it.
17398-the-cabman-s-story-the-mysteries-o:
The Cabman's Story, subtitled The Mysteries of a London Growler, opens on a family holiday from Hammersmith to Alexandra Palace in a four-wheeler. With wife, sister, Tommy, Fanny, and Jack inside, the narrator climbs beside the driver, a weather-beaten veteran with white side whiskers. A glass of gin at the Green Anchor loosens the old cabman's tongue.

His talk covers hansoms versus four-wheelers, respectability, fares, and London streets, in shrewd, chatty prose. The tale suits readers who love Victorian London from the box seat. Short and vivid, it gives a cabman's-eye view of a city on the move, with humor and horse sense to spare.
17495-the-stolen-singer:
Martha Bellinger wrote this novel, published in Indianapolis in 1911 by the Bobbs-Merrill Company, with pictures by Arthur William Brown. A frontispiece catches Miss Redmond detecting a passage of glances between two others. Chapters open with twilight in the park, Hambleton of Lynn, and midsummer madness. Mr. Van Camp makes a call, Melanie dreams, and the party boards the Jeanne d'Arc.

A rope ladder, the breast of the sea, and a camp on the beach carry the adventure on. Readers get a popular romance of music, society, and seaside daring, in Bellinger's light style. The book suits readers of Edwardian popular fiction.
17584-letters-from-mesopotamia-in-1915-a:
Robert Palmer's letters from Mesopotamia in 1915 and January 1916 were printed for private circulation only. Palmer was killed in the battle of Um El Hannah on June 21, 1916, aged twenty-seven. He had gone with a draft from the 6th Hants to reinforce the 4th Hants, after the 6th had served in India since November 1914. That service frame opens the volume.

Readers get a young officer's letters home from the Mesopotamian campaign, personal, observant, and unpolished by later editing. The book suits readers of Great War letters and of the campaign in Iraq. Its private origin gives it an intimate, memorial character.
1763-the-nature-faker:
Richard Herrick is a rich young man with a gentle temper and no sense of humor, whose one aim in life is to marry Miss Catherweight. For three years she has told him it cannot be. At last she sets him a test: prove he understands nature — the animals he claims to love — before she will hear him again.

Herrick's efforts with bears raised on milk from a bottle make the comedy. Keepers warn him that the beasts have forgotten what a pine forest smells like. Davis uses the tale to poke at sentimental nature writing, and at a suitor whose earnestness outruns his knowledge of the wild.
17636-the-mystery-at-putnam-hall-the-sch:
Arthur M. Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer, wrote this Putnam Hall school story, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. It belongs to a cadet series that also includes The Cadets of Putnam Hall, The Rivals of Putnam Hall, and The Champions of Putnam Hall. Chapters open with an encounter on the road, the cadets of Putnam Hall, and something about a runaway.

A fruitless search, a fight in the gymnasium, and Captain Putnam's investigation follow, with Pepper's discovery and a football eleven and game ahead. Readers get a brisk boys' school tale of friendship, sport, and mystery, in Stratemeyer's reliable style. The book suits young readers who enjoy school stories.
17658-the-harbor-master:
Theodore Goodridge Roberts, author of Rayton and Captain Love, wrote this novel of the coast, published in Chicago and New York by M. A. Donohue and Company, copyright 1911 and 1913, first impression January 1913. The English edition bore the title The Toll of the Sea, as the title page notes. The story opens at Chance Along, a hamlet hidden at the back of a deep cleft in formidable cliffs.

Chance Along lies somewhere between Cape Race and St. John's, with great boulders almost closing the mouth of its cove. Black Dennis Nolan gives the first chapter its name. Readers get a Newfoundland coast tale of wreckers, fishermen, and hard lives, in Roberts's vigorous style. The book suits readers of sea fiction.
17737-the-schemes-of-the-kaiser:
Juliette Adam, a French writer who fought German power in print for forty-five years, wrote this book of war-time essays, turned into English by J. O. P. Bland and printed in New York in 1918. Adam had dueled in words with Bismarck and then with Kaiser Wilhelm II, and she saw both as foes of France.

Dated notes from 1890 onward track Wilhelm's pose as a peace-loving social monarch, his trips to Russia, and Germany's steady build-up of its army while its press preached calm. Adam's voice is sharp, angry, and personal, full of scorn for what she calls the Kaiser's tricks. The book gives a fierce French view of the road to the Great War.
17764-king-winter:
King Winter is a short picture book verse tale from Hamburg, printed by Gustav W. Seitz and entered at Stationers' Hall. It is made for small children, with rhymes to be read aloud and pictures to pore over on a cold night.

A mother by the fire tells Jenny and Johnny of King Winter, who dwells in the far north in a palace of snow and sits on an icy throne. His queen stuffs his cushions with soft snowflakes, and Jack Frost serves as his man. The verse is simple, cozy, and sweet, a small winter treat for the youngest readers.
17789-molly-mcdonald-a-tale-of-the-old-f:
Randall Parrish wrote Molly McDonald in 1912, a tale of the old frontier with color pictures by Ernest Blumenschein. The book, printed by A. L. Burt in New York, follows a young woman caught in the hard, swift life of forts, stages, and border towns.

Chapters run from an unpleasant fix to Brick Hamlin, an attack, the defence of a stage, a flight across a river, and arrest at Fort Dodge. Molly holds her own among soldiers, scouts, and rogues, with pluck and a quick tongue. Parrish writes brisk frontier romance, and this is a lively sample, full of dust, danger, and young love.
17882-consolations-in-travel-or-the-last:
Sir Humphry Davy wrote Consolations in Travel in his last days, printed by Cassell in 1889 from the great chemist's dying work. Davy, born at Penzance in 1778 and dead at Geneva in 1829, was president of the Royal Society and one of England's foremost men of science.

The book makes reason the companion of faith, as Davy looks back on a life of inquiry, from a boyhood garret lab to fame. He writes of nature, spirit, and the light beyond earth, with calm and hope. It is a gentle, grave farewell by a scientist-philosopher, and a window on how a great mind faced death.
18000-phineas-finn-the-irish-member:
Anthony Trollope wrote Phineas Finn, the Irish Member, first run in St. Paul's Magazine from 1867 and printed in book form in 1869. The novel follows a young Irishman who seeks a seat in Parliament and finds that politics tests his honor, his purse, and his heart.

Phineas stands for Loughshane, takes his seat, and moves among Lady Laura Standish, Violet Effingham, and Lord Chiltern, with debates, dinners, and duels of wit. Trollope writes with his usual calm mastery of manners and motive. It is a great Victorian political novel, still the best door into how Westminster once worked.
18025-the-story-of-isaac-brock-hero-defe:
Walter R. Nursey wrote The Story of Isaac Brock in Toronto in 1908, printed by William Briggs, with a portrait of Major-General Sir Isaac Brock. Nursey calls Brock the foremost defender of the flag Western Canada has ever seen, a claim few Canadians would dispute.

Chapters run from Brock's home in Guernsey and his school days to ensign, colonel, Egmont-op-Zee, Copenhagen, and Canada. Mutiny, fur traders, and the war of 1812 fill the later pages. Nursey writes with warm, patriotic pride. It is a stirring life of a hero of 1812, best for readers who love Canadian history and bold soldiers.
1805-the-gentle-grafter:
Jeff Peters and Andy Tucker are con men who prefer a soft touch to a hard crime, selling patent cures and running small swindles with a certain courtesy. They sell patent cures, run small swindles, and once try to win office by honest means, only to give the plan up on a hotel clerk's advice.

The humor lies in the pair's code: they cheat, but they cheat with a certain courtesy, and their victims are often greedier than they are. O. Henry keeps the tales short and the endings turned. The book is a good sample of his comic manner, where the grafter is less a villain than a mirror held up to respectable ambition.
18056-the-tin-soldier:
Temple Bailey wrote The Tin Soldier, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, first printed in November 1916 and reprinted through 1919. Bailey, author of Glory of Youth and Contrary Mary, here gives a war-time romance with a toy-shop frame.

Book one, On the Shelf, opens in a toy shop, with Cinderella, Drusilla, a question, a slacker, a promise, and Hilda. A tin soldier watches human love and duty from his shelf, and the tale moves from toys to soldiers. Bailey writes with warmth and patriotic feeling. It is a sweet, war-time love story, best for readers who like romance with a touch of fancy.
18076-the-boy-trapper:
Harry Castlemon wrote The Boy Trapper, printed in Philadelphia by Henry T. Coates, as the first of the Boy Trapper series. Castlemon, famed for his Frank and Gunboat books, here gives boys a hero who lives by trap, gun, and woodcraft.

David, a poor lad, takes visitors, an offer of partnership, and bad news in stride, then hunts bear, traps quail, and chases a ten-dollar reward. A barrel of eighty thousand dollars and a talk with General Gordon haunt his past. The tale is brisk, clean boys' fiction, full of dogs, bears, and pluck, in the hearty style of the day.
1809-bucky-o-connor-a-tale-of-the-unfenc:
Along the unfenced line between the United States and Mexico rides Bucky O'Connor, a Texas ranger of the old school, quick, decent, and hard to fool. Bucky meets showmen and gunmen. He also meets Frank Anderson, who explains, in a low, sweet voice, that his show would not draw without him, since he does legerdemain.

Raine dedicates the book to his brother Edgar, the wanderer who answered the call of the frozen North, and the dedication sets the tone: loyalty to restless men. The novel moves through chases, disguises, and standoffs, and its hero is the ranger as Raine liked him best — quick, decent, and hard to fool.
18233-animal-ghosts-or-animal-hauntings-:
Elliott O'Donnell, author of Werwolves and Haunted Houses of London, published this book of animal ghosts in London in 1913. O'Donnell asks whether animals haunt, and whether they share in a hereafter, and he answers with case after case collected from correspondents and old tales. The book is arranged by creature, so readers can follow one kind of ghost at a time.

Cats open the set, with the black cat of the old manor house at Oxenby and the headless cat of Seedley, Manchester. Dogs follow, with the grey dog of Birmingham, a dog that saved a life, and spectral hounds such as the Mauthe Doog. Horses close the main part, with phantom cavalcades and heralds of death. Readers get ghost lore with fur, feather, and hoof, told as evidence rather than as mere fright.
18234-a-girl-s-student-days-and-after:
Jeannette Marks wrote A Girl's Student Days and After, printed in 1911 by Fleming H. Revell, with an introduction by Mary Emma Woolley, president of Mount Holyoke College. Marks, a Wellesley graduate, writes for school and college girls at a time when their education drew new thought.

Woolley notes that buildings, courses, and teachers achieve little without the girl's own cooperation, and Marks shows how the new girl must bear her share. The book treats study, friendship, and life after school with earnest, practical wisdom. It is a warm, period guide for young women, and a window on women's education in 1911.
18266-death-and-after:
Annie Besant wrote this short Theosophical manual, number three in the series, published in London and Benares in 1906 at one shilling. Besant says the manuals meet a public demand for a simple exposition of Theosophical teachings, since the larger literature seemed too abstruse, too technical, and too expensive for ordinary readers. Theosophy, she insists, is not only for the learned; it is for all.

The book opens with a Saxon king's hall, where a missionary preaches of life, death, and immortality while a bird flies through the lighted room. Besant then sets out what Theosophy teaches about death and what follows it, in plain terms meant to make life easier to bear and death easier to face. Readers get a short, earnest guide to a spiritual view of mortality.
18277-the-training-of-a-public-speaker:
Grenville Kleiser wrote this 1920 manual for people who must speak in public. Kleiser had taught public speaking at Yale Divinity School, and he builds the book step by step. Early chapters take up rhetoric and eloquence, the exordium or introduction, narration, division and argument, and the peroration or close.

Later chapters turn to passion and persuasion, the study of words, elegance and grace, composition and style, copiousness of words, and knowledge and self-confidence. Kleiser draws on old writers such as Isocrates, Plato, and Cicero. A reader gets a practical course: how to open, how to order a case, and how to end with force.
18283-life-of-father-hecker:
Rev. Walter Elliott wrote this 1891 life of Father Isaac Hecker, founder of the Paulist Fathers, published in New York by the Columbus Press. Elliott calls himself Hecker's first biographer and says he felt the joy of a son in telling his achievements and virtues. He loved Hecker, he writes, with a sacred fire of holy kinship, and the book holds together what he calls the heaven-made wisdom of a great teacher.

Chapters trace childhood and youth, the turning point, Brook Farm, Fruitlands, self-questionings, and a search among the sects. Hecker moves through Concord, stands at the door of the church, and crosses its threshold. Readers get a spiritual biography: an American seeker who tried reform communities and philosophies before finding his life's work in the Catholic priesthood.
18297-the-story-of-a-summer:
Cecilia Cleveland wrote this 1874 journal of a summer spent at Chappaqua, New York. Cleveland says the little volume is no work of fancy, but a simple record of a pleasant summer stay. It gathers facts and incidents not before published about a man who once held a large place in the public mind, seen here in his home circle rather than in public life.

Chapters follow the return to Chappaqua, walks over the grounds, the side-hill house, drives to Mount Kisco, and evenings of music and mail. Cousins Ida and Gabrielle share the house, and visitors, suitors, and a musical squirrel pass through its days. Readers get a quiet domestic portrait, told day by day, of a famous household at rest.
1833-the-case-of-the-registered-letter:
