Friends crowd to see him off, yet at the sailing he feels oddly alone. No part of the parting ceremony, he thinks, belongs to him personally, and the lively scene only sharpens his loneliness.

Aboard ship he meets the little grouch of the title, a spoiled girl with a tongue. Adams, a veteran magazine writer, turns the voyage into light comedy with a romantic wake. The ship's log device gives the tale a diary's freshness. It is Edwardian ocean travel in story form: decks, dinners, and flirtation.
22227-the-4-d-doodler:
The 4-D Doodler ran in Comet magazine in July 1941, a pulp tale of the fourth dimension. Its professor explains the problem with a shadow. A shadow has length and breadth but no thickness; to enter our world it would have to bulge into a dimension it cannot reach. By the same logic, we cannot simply step into the fourth dimension — until the doodler finds a way.

The cover scene shows the professor's head suspended above his body, glaring about while the mouth moves rapidly. Wonder and horror mix in the pulp proportion. Such stories taught readers to play with geometry as magic. This one is a brisk survivor of Comet's five-issue run.
22302-the-western-united-states-a-geogra:
School readers once taught geography through story-like lessons, and The Western United States follows that pattern. Its full title calls it a geographical reader for the West. No author or date appears in the catalog record.

The prose follows water through the land in close detail. Storms send streams dashing down mountain slopes to the plains below. On the western slope, small streams join into one great river. That river winds across the plateau, seeking the easiest route to the Gulf of California. Young readers learned the shape of the western land by following its rivers from source to sea.
22332-brain-twister:
Brain Twister is a science fiction novel preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its back matter jokes about its own authors in an odd way. Their personal lives, readers are told, differ widely.

One author's hobbies include close-order drill and river pollution. The other prefers quiet games such as humming or blinking. That deadpan humor hints at the book's playful tone. A title like Brain Twister promises mental tricks and strange ideas. The story belongs to the era of pulp science fiction paperbacks. Readers get a period romp built on a twisted premise, told by writers happy to tease themselves in print.
22350-the-red-blooded-heroes-of-the-fron:
The Red-Blooded Heroes of the Frontier recalls the hard push across unknown country. Early markets drew men toward northern New Mexico and Colorado. The Mormon settlements of Utah also attracted attention and trade.

Reaching those markets seemed almost hopeless at first. The country north of them was trackless and practically unknown. All anyone knew was that it swarmed with hostile Native nations. Nobody knew the conditions for water and grass. Both were prime needs for moving herds across the land. Against those odds, the book tells its frontier stories. Readers meet traders and herders whose courage was tested by distance itself.
22369-notes-and-queries-number-182-april:
Notes and Queries number 182 appeared on April 23, 1853. Like every issue, it traded in readers' questions and findings. One correspondent had been researching British poets on a small, charming point.

He studied the character of the nightingale's song in verse. The quantity of epithets applied to the bird struck him greatly. Their diversity struck him just as much. Such a query shows the journal's range and spirit. No fact about books or nature was too small to chase. Readers today get Victorian literary curiosity at its most dogged, preserved in a single weekly number.
22512-the-stutterer:
The Stutterer is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its passenger feels a ship's drive through his own body and feet. Vibration runs through his feet to the floor beneath him.

He sits tense and immobile for what seems a long time. Abruptly the strain is relieved, and sound returns around him. He hears the rising and falling whine of rockets then. They tell him the ship is in pulse drive now. It flickers back and forth across the speed of light. A stuttering drive, by the title, gives the tale its name. Readers get space travel felt in the bones. Small sensations carry the wonder here.
22564-great-artists-vol-1-raphael-rubens:
Great Artists, volume one, studies Raphael, Rubens, Murillo, and Durer for general readers. It opens with Raphael, called the most praised of all painters. He is also the most beautiful and most loved, it claims.

When such delightful things can truthfully be said of one man, pleasure follows. Readers may look forward to a detailed study of his life. His works receive the same close, admiring attention in turn. Rubens brings Flemish energy, Murillo Spanish devotion, Durer German precision. Together the four span the glory of European painting between them. The volume served art study in homes and schools. It offers biography and appreciation in clear, enthusiastic prose.
22583-the-highgrader:
The Highgrader is a novel published in 1915, set in the American West of mining country. The catalog record here names no author. The title word points to a mining crime: stealing rich ore from the mine where one works. That world of camps, claims, and quick fortunes forms the story's backdrop.

The sample opens far from the mines, with a small child selling paper stars she cut herself to put in the sky. Such tender scenes sit inside a tale of ambition and rough frontier justice. Western readers of the era favored clear heroes, moral tests, and a strong sense of place. The Highgrader offers that period flavor, along with a look at how mining shaped western towns.
22596-measure-for-a-loner:
Measure for a Loner is a science fiction story about the fame that gathers around a lone space pioneer. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its narrator notes how many people thought the coming flight important, from comic-strip readers to newspaper editors hungry for a hero.

The press builds the pilot up as a Lindbergh of Space, while comics hero Wild Bill Star blasts through his own decades of invented adventures. That contrast between real risk and packaged glory sits at the story's heart. It is a wry period piece about celebrity, media, and the first star flight. Readers of classic magazine science fiction will find the satire still sharp.
22629-the-vortex-blaster:
E. E. Smith wrote The Vortex Blaster, a science fiction story presented here complete in one issue, as its original magazine billing boasted. The catalog record gives no year. Smith, a founder of space opera, here turns to atomic disaster work: his hero Neal Cloud is an atomic physicist who defuses runaway vortexes of atomic fire.

The sample finds Cloud crushed by grief, sitting in dull apathy, his lifeless eyes staring past a small portrait of everything that once gave his life meaning. Loss, not adventure, loads the story's spring. Smith mixes hard talk of physics with raw feeling in his pulp manner. Fans of early space opera get a compact, complete-in-one-issue tale from one of its inventors.
22770-the-continental-monthly-vol-5-no-5:
The Continental Monthly offers its issue of May 1864, volume 5, number 5. The magazine, devoted to literature and national policy, was published in New York. It appeared in the middle of the Civil War. The catalog record names no editor. Northern monthlies of the war years mixed poems and tales with hard arguments about the Union's future.

The sample argues economics with census figures. In 1790 and 1800 Kentucky stood far in advance of Ohio. By 1860 Ohio's product was nearly triple Kentucky's. Per head, the gap was wider still. Free labor against slave labor is the unstated engine of the comparison. Essays of this sort were war work by other means. The issue preserves the Union's case as its intellectuals made it, month by month.
22781-32-caliber:
Donald McGibeny wrote 32 Caliber, a novel whose title names a small pistol and whose sample opens, surprisingly, on a golf course. The catalog record gives no year. The mix is the book's signature: country-club ease on the surface, a killing underneath, and a narrator who reads a green as calmly as a clue.

There's a small clay bank abutting the green, the narrator explains, and you can play around it or over it to the hole directly behind. Real golfers play over the bank, landing a good mashie shot dead on the green. Dubs like Paisley play around it, taking two easy mid-iron shots. Such exact, unhurried talk, in a murder story, builds the chill. McGibeny's tale is period crime fiction with a sporting accent.
22795-the-ontario-high-school-reader:
The Ontario High School Reader is a schoolbook of reading lessons for Canadian high school pupils. The catalog record names no editor and gives no year. Readers of this kind, set by provincial authority, put the same poems, speeches, and essays into the hands of a whole generation of students.

The book opens by teaching its own art: there are several reasons for every boy or girl to strive at good reading. Good oral reading, the introduction argues, is an accomplishment in itself. It pleases others greatly, and ourselves as well. Lessons in elocution stand before the selections themselves. Historians of education can read in such volumes exactly what a province wished its young people to admire.
22841-mr-joseph-hanson-the-haberdasher:
Shop signs tell the story in Mr. Joseph Hanson, the Haberdasher, by Mary Russell Mitford. After Waterloo, she notes, every market town and village boasted a Wellington house or a Waterloo house, each hoping to catch a ray from the great name's glory. Belford Regis's drapers and haberdashers were not about to be left behind.

Hanson's shop becomes a lens on trade, patriotism, and small-town ambition. Mitford delights in the puffing of wares and the pride of a respectable tradesman. The humor stays gentle, and the detail stays exact, from window displays to local rivalry. Her Belford Regis sketches endure because people like Hanson fill them. This is a shopkeeper's portrait, drawn by a customer who missed nothing.
22884-the-dragon-painter:
Mary McNeil Fenollosa sets The Dragon Painter, her 1905 novel, in old Japan. Snow falls on temple roofs in her opening weather, swinging in wet masses from bamboo plumes and balancing along green-black pine branches. Summer then bakes the capital, and its rains fall in broad, shining sheets.

Against those seasons stands a painter obsessed with dragons. Fenollosa, who lived in Japan and wrote on its art, builds the tale around creation, love, and madness in an artist's household. The dragon he chases is both subject and symbol. American readers of 1905 met Japan largely through books like this one. Its mix of romance and art lore still gives it charm, period framing and all.
23008-the-sheriff-and-his-partner:
Frank Harris rides west in The Sheriff and His Partner, one of his frontier tales. He recalls a figure of grim resolve shot through with humor. His one regret is arriving too late to watch the man work. Office days dragged for the newcomer. Stephen's Commentaries grew as monotonous as the bare uncarpeted floor.

Law books make poor company where sheriffs settle things in person. Harris builds the tale on that gap between statute and six-gun practice. His West is talkative, violent, and observed by an English-born writer with a reporter's appetite. The sheriff and his partner stand for an order older than courts. Readers get a compact Western with a literary polish not always found in the genre's early years.
23026-the-phantom-of-the-river:
Daniel Boone moves through Kentucky shadow in The Phantom of the River. Boone hugs the Ohio shore as he slips eastward. Kenton, meanwhile, works deeper into the shadowed forest, hunting for signs of danger. Disturbed by evidence of danger, Kenton trended left and met Boone near the river.

Edward S. Ellis built this frontier novel on the two most famous scouts of the Ohio valley. Shawnee danger, river crossings, and a phantom that haunts the banks drive the action in the classic dime-novel manner. Ellis wrote history as well as fiction, and his facts about Boone's world are sound. The romance laid over them gallops. Boys of the 1880s devoured such books, and their pace has not slackened.
23034-captain-canot-or-twenty-years-of-a:
A wanderer's tale becomes a book in Captain Canot, or Twenty Years of an African Slaver. As acquaintance ripened, the editor writes, his friend gradually drew from the captain the story of his adventurous life. The incidents impressed the editor as remarkable, and the African portraits as faithful. He urged the captain to set everything down fully for publication.

Theodore Canot spent two decades in the slave trade on the West African coast, and his memoir describes barracoons, voyages, and markets in plain detail. Published in 1854, it was used by abolitionists as evidence from inside the trade itself. The voice stays disturbingly matter-of-fact. That flatness is the book's power. It records a crime as routine business, and convicts itself.
23050-peter-biddulph-the-story-of-an-aus:
A barge baby opens Peter Biddulph, the story of an Australian settler. The narrator can recollect nothing clearly before the barge stuck off the mud onto dry ground. He was born on board a river barge, he says, and never left it, winter nor summer, until he was fully six years old.

From that floating childhood the tale moves toward emigration and the making of a settler in Australia. River life, poverty, and departure fill the early chapters in the manner of the popular settler novel. The new country waits as both promise and test. Such books recruited as much as they entertained, picturing colonial life for readers in crowded Britain. Peter's barge is a fine start, a home that moves and a boy who must learn to stay.
23059-my-friend-the-murderer:
A. Conan Doyle introduces a numbered prisoner in My Friend the Murderer. You'd like it, doctor, says Warder McPherson, insinuating one shoulder into the room. The warder rates the prisoner's untold story highly. Getting him to tell it is the hard part, since the man speaks freely to nobody. Maybe you don't know who 82 is?

Number 82 turns out to carry one of the strangest true-crime tales Doyle ever framed, a mass murderer turned informer, living under guard in an Australian prison. The doctor narrator draws the story out visit by visit. Doyle wrote it before Sherlock Holmes made him famous, and the seeds show, a cool observer, a monstrous case, a tale within the tale. It remains a gripping early work.
2307-the-depot-master:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Depot Master runs the railroad station of a Cape Cod town, and through his eyes we see the whole community pass by. The novel follows the depot master as he sorts mail, gossip, romance, and trouble for his neighbors, with Lincoln's trademark dialect humor softening every conflict. Cape Cod's shore and speech give the book its flavor.

The story is episodic and warm, built from small crises rather than one grand plot. Readers who like gentle regional fiction will enjoy its humor and its affection for small-town life. It is a pleasant example of Lincoln's popular Cape Cod tales.
23104-the-blue-tower:
Evelyn E. Smith questions the servants in The Blue Tower. Surely the Belphins exist to serve mankind, one thinker reasons. Gloating over servants would be ungrateful. Besides, they probably enjoy the labor, he decides, and stops a passing Belphin to confirm the comforting thought.

That smug little argument sits at the story's heart. A served humanity, a tower, and a race bred or built to serve make a fable about masters who call obedience happiness. Smith wrote witty, pointed science fiction, often about power wearing a smile. The Blue Tower shows her method, a pleasant surface, a hook underneath. Readers should watch whose comfort the tower actually serves.
23132-marcia-schuyler:
Grace Livingston Hill paints a morning in Marcia Schuyler, published in 1908 under her married name, Lutz. Marcia wears her hair in smooth brown braids, her round cheeks flushed, perhaps from the rosy eastern light. Her face looks as untroubled as the summer morning itself. Her eyes dream like the soft clouds along the horizon.

Marcia steps into her older sister's place, and nearly into her sister's wedding, in Hill's best-loved early novel. Set in old New York in 1830, the tale tests a young girl asked to grow up in a single day. Hill became America's queen of clean romance, and this book shows the making of the crown, faith, freshness, and a heroine equal to her emergency.
23149-in-the-control-tower:
Will Mohler rides a ruined landscape in In the Control Tower. The gloom counts as mercy, given what industry has done to the sky. His train creeps past slag hills and the rusting carrion of machines, then bolts between endless advertising walls and through concrete troughs of grimy light.

That approach by rail sets the story's world, industry and advertising grown over the sky itself. A control tower waits at the journey's end, and with it whatever governs this damaged future. Mohler's descriptive power is the main event, sentence after sentence of beautiful disgust. Readers get atmosphere thick enough to breathe, which is precisely the problem his characters face.
23170-a-brace-of-boys-1867-from-little-b:
Fitz Hugh Ludlow praises uncles in A Brace of Boys, dated 1867, from Little Brother. Unclehood, Ludlow writes, is its own category. No responsibility shakes an uncle's judgment the way it shakes a father's. Bachelor uncles, he claims, judge children, and parents too, far more coolly for exactly that reason.

Two boys, a brace, give Ludlow his pair of subjects, watched by the bachelor uncle whose judgment the passage advertises. Ludlow, better known for his book on hashish, writes family life here with a humorist's detachment and a brother's knowledge. Elsewhere he warns of the worst family skeleton, the kind that claws free through our own flesh and blood. The story keeps that shadow under its comedy, and is better for it.
23182-the-brigade-commander:
J. W. De Forest wrote The Brigade Commander, a work of war fiction told close to the ground of a battlefield. Men rest where they can, some dropping into calm sleep. Yet at an order they can leap up and answer with the red flash and harsh roar of battle.

The scene sets out two lines of battle, each made of three infantry regiments. The first line stands well ahead of the second. De Forest writes as a close observer of soldiers, showing both their ease in waiting and their speed when the call to fight comes.
23184-monte-cristo-s-daughter:
Monte Cristo's Daughter is an anonymous sequel to the famous Count of Monte Cristo story. It opens far from France, in Rome. The Count has rented the Palazzo Costi, one of the city's many private palaces, on a broad street near the bridge of Sant'Angelo.

From there the setting looks across the river toward the Leonine City, also called Trastevere. Placing the Count in a Roman palace keeps the grand scale of the first tale: wealth, fine rooms, and a hero who moves through Europe's great cities. Readers get a fresh stage for the Count's family story.
23190-mary-liddiard-or-the-missionary-s-: Mary Liddiard, or the Missionary's Daughter is a tale named for a missionary's child. The sample shows her world through its buildings. One floor is a raised platform of coral stone, some two feet high. A wide roof reaches well past the walls. Stout bread-fruit posts hold it up, lashed tight to the rafters with ropes of sinnet.
23212-notes-and-queries-number-72-march-:
Number 72 of Notes and Queries, dated March 15, 1851, carries the journal's usual mix of literary notes. One writer is glad to see correspondents turning to Chaucer. The text of that father-poet, he says, has lain fallow since the days of the editor Tyrwhitt, and now offers a rich field for work.

He hopes the journal will give free entry to all comments and hints on the poems. Sifted and stored in its pages, they could form a store from which later scholars might draw ample material. Readers see Victorian scholars building knowledge together, one small note at a time.
23214-fostina-woodman-the-wonderful-adve: A. A. Burnham's Fostina Woodman, the Wonderful Adventurer names its heroine in its title as a woman of adventures, and promises a life out of the ordinary. Its scene is set in northern Massachusetts, near the Connecticut River. The river winds through hills and valleys before dropping into a deep basin. That meeting of settled farmland and wild, falling water frames the country Fostina moves through.
23215-old-ebenezer:
Opie Read's Old Ebenezer is a novel of a sleepy town and the man who settles into its pace. Sam Lyman came out of the keen air of Vermont. In the drowsy neighbourhoods around the town of Old Ebenezer, he loafed and dreamed, at first looked on as a marvel of energy.

The soft air of a south-western state soon eased the Yankee worry out of his stride. He grew content to sit in the shade and wait for the other man to come to him. Read builds his tale on that change, in a town where the other man is in no hurry either.
23225-notes-and-queries-number-73-march-:
Number 73 of Notes and Queries, dated March 22, 1851, opens with church and family history. The editors recall calling attention to the Monumentarium of Exeter Cathedral in an early number of the volume. They had hoped Mr. Hewett's work there would serve genealogical, antiquarian, and historical inquirers well.

That hope, they report, bids fair to be fully met. More workers are entering the same useful field of recording monuments and inscriptions. The issue shows the journal's core business: saving local records, praising careful compilers, and pointing readers to sources before stones and memories fade.
23235-notes-and-queries-number-197-augus:
Number 197 of Notes and Queries, dated August 6, 1853, takes up the history of party names. One writer suggests that a full history of party, tracing where party names began, would be a welcome addition to literary history. The journal, he notes, has already printed studies of names like Whig and Tory.

Terms such as Puritan, Malignant, and Evangelical can be traced to their first use, he argues. Other names still hide the date of their coining, and those are the ones he sets out to examine. Readers see the journal's method at work: small word histories used to unlock big political ones.
23244-the-dude-wrangler:
Caroline Lockhart's The Dude Wrangler, from 1921, is a comic western novel. Its opening listens before it looks. For a full minute, a man hears nothing out of the way. Surf beats on the sea wall below the Colonial's lawn. The courthouse clock strikes the hour.

Then come ripping, tearing, slashing noises, like a sash-and-blind factory at work. Lockhart reveals their source with a straight face: they pour through the long, thin nose of an old gentleman nearby. The joke sets the tone. Readers get a dude-ranch story told with dry western humour and a sharp ear for absurd detail.
23274-lost-in-the-forest-wandering-will-:
Lost in the Forest continues Wandering Will's adventures, this time in South America. Trouble is already brewing aboard ship. In a low voice, the captain confides his fear to the doctor: this may be the last voyage either of them makes, at sea or anywhere else.

Their skipper, the captain says, does not look after his men. He calls the crew as rascally a bunch as he ever set eyes on. From words dropped here and there, he is sure mischief is in the wind. Readers get a sea adventure that opens under threat of mutiny, before the forest is even reached.
23282-notes-and-queries-number-74-march-:
Number 74 of Notes and Queries, dated March 29, 1851, takes up the short life of portraits. One writer argues that portraits of men must fade and yield the scene to those who follow, almost as fast as the human race itself gives place to rising generations.

Costly portraits, bought for twenty, thirty, or sixty guineas, take proud possession of a drawing room. In the next generation they descend to the parlour, slightly mentioned as a father's and mother's pictures. Readers get a sharp Victorian note on fame, family, and how quickly even expensive remembrance fades.
23315-young-soldier:
This Turner and Fisher infantile toy book pictures a young soldier for the very young. An ensign looks fine with banner and sword, and the verses ask whether the child would like to be a soldier and fight for country.

Later pictures show the soldier on leave, hunting with horn, whip, cap, and dog. Small, bright, and patriotic, the book is a Victorian toy book of soldier play, made to stir pride and imagination. Bright pictures suit the very young, with soldier play and hunting scenes. One plate shows the soldier on leave with hunters, horn, whip, cap, and dog in tow.
23318-the-nine-lives-of-a-cat-a-tale-of-:
Charles Bennett wrote this tale of wonder about a cat's nine lives, published in London in the mid eighteen hundreds with pictures on every page. Kitty is hung while still young, but pulls a knife and escapes, beginning a string of narrow escapes.

Each life brings a new peril and a new trick, told in verse and picture for children. Bennett's book is a classic of Victorian animal fantasy, funny, grim, and full of feline pluck. Each escape brings a new peril and a new trick for quick young readers. After the hanging comes a drowning attempt by a boy, the second of Kitty's narrow escapes.
23326-me-re-giraud-s-little-daughter:
Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote this French village tale, published in the late eighteen seventies. Neighbors gossip about Madame Giraud, once plain Mere Giraud, now proud since fortune gave her a pretty daughter who won a rich husband.

Annot, her sabots clattering on brick floors, leads the talk, while others echo her spite. Burnett's short story turns on envy, luck, and the price of a daughter's beauty in a small community. Gossip and envy drive the short tale, with sabots and brick floors for color. Mère Giraud herself slips off to Paris to visit Madame Legrand, shutting up her small trim cottage.
23351-the-yacht-club-or-the-young-boat-b:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William T. Adams, wrote this eighteen seventy three boys' book as part of his Yacht Club series, with thirteen pictures. It follows a young boat builder who learns his craft, joins a club of keen young sailors, and takes to the water in boats of his own making.

Races, cruises, and club rivalries fill the pages, with lessons in seamanship, fair play, and hard work tucked into the fun. Miss Nellie Patterdale and Don John appear in the frontispiece, hinting at the friendships and scrapes ahead. Boys who love boats will find clear talk of sails, hulls, and handling, plus a hero who earns his place by skill rather than by swagger.
23369-mrs-dud-s-sister:
Josephine Daskam set this tale on a terrace at tea, where Varian wishes his friend Hunter, long absent from America, could see Mrs. Dud and her pretty maids. Hunter, away for thirty years, still thinks in terms of help and caps, and laughs at how much Binghamville has changed.

Mrs. Dud herself anchors the talk: once a girl who carried her father's dinner to the store on Saturdays, now a wonder of the town, with a household run in fine style. The tale turns on the sister of the title and on the gap between old memories and new manners. Daskam writes it with light satire, poking fun at snobbery while liking her people, and at how towns remake themselves while old friends look on.
23384-gascoyne-the-sandal-wood-trader:
R. M. Ballantyne set this Pacific tale on a low, black hulled schooner with trim sails and bright brass, a craft that might be a yacht or a pirate ship. Its master, Gascoyne, trades sandalwood among the islands, and the question that drives the tale is plain: is he a trader, or is he a pirate?

Island scenes, shipboard life, and clashes with rival crews fill the pages, as Gascoyne's past and his crew's loyalties come slowly to light. Ballantyne writes the sea with zest, from calm mornings on a slumbering ocean to sharp action when sails appear on the horizon. Young readers will enjoy the riddle at its heart and the warm, adventurous spirit of Pacific trade in the age of sail.
23440-edward-barry-south-sea-pearler:
Louis Becke wrote this nineteen fourteen South Seas tale of Edward Barry, a pearler who opens the book dead broke. From the Maynards and the brig Mahina to Ponape, Arrecifos Lagoon, and a Samoan prophet named Velo, Barry chases fortune among islands, traders, and captains.

Alice Tracey and her mother's strange story cross his path, with a little celebration proposed by Captain Rawlings, talk of marriage, and a flag hoisted for England. Becke, who knew the Pacific trade, fills the tale with lagoon colour, ship talk, and island manners. Readers who love sea adventure will enjoy Barry's rise, falls, and second chances, told with the ease of a man who had lived among the scenes he paints.
23441-lady-betty-across-the-water:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson edited this nineteen hundred six novel of Lady Betty, a young Englishwoman who crosses the water for a visit to America. America is the great, delightful, and hospitable land that gives her the time of her life. Pictures by Orson Lowell add to the charm.

Betty chats with cadets as if she had grown up with them, tours, calls, and falls into American social life with wide eyed delight. The Williamsons write her letters and scenes with light, fond humour, contrasting English manners with American ease. Readers who like travel romance will enjoy Betty's voyage of discovery, as a titled visitor learns that a new country can feel, at once, strange and like home.
23483-dame-wonder-s-picture-alphabet-amu:
McLoughlin Brothers printed this Dame Wonder picture alphabet for small children, with a picture and a rhyme for each letter. A stands for an archer, B for his bow, C for the crow he shot at, and D for his dog, setting the pattern for the book.

An ensign, flag, and fort, a goat, a horse, an Italian, a jug, and Jane follow, with kite, lobster, Mary, numbers, owl, and parrot after them. Queen, rose, sword of state, throne, table, uncle, violin, windmill, ten, yacht, and zebra close the round. The rhymes stay short and bright, made for pointing and naming. Tiny readers will love learning letters through pictures that tell small stories of their own.
23568-the-mississippi-saucer:
Frank Belknap Long wrote this weird tale, first printed in Weird Tales in March nineteen fifty one, of Jimmy, a shantyboat boy on the Mississippi. He watches the Natchez Belle draw near, toes poking from his socks, heart knocking, as the packet purples the water with shadow and belches soot.

Jimmy has a wild talent for collecting things and for vexing captains without risking his neck. Other shantyboat boys from Louisiana bayous to the Great Sandy envy him. The saucer of the title, a wonder from the sky sought by men of old for magic, enters his river world with eerie force. Long writes the river with love and the wonder with dread, making a short, strange tale of a boy, a boat, and a sky that answers back.
23571-general-max-shorter:
Kris Neville wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Galaxy in December nineteen sixty two, on the high cost of spreading mankind to the stars, in lives both human and not. The first landing on Miracastle, the first two stage planet men tried to colonise, sets the scene: a flat plateau among steep, foreboding mountains that float through briefly cleared air.

An iron grey castle of rock, carved by alien winds and acid tears from acid clouds, stands in the distance. It stands under a halo where an orange sun, barely larger than Sol, splinters rays through fog and gloom. Neville writes the alien world with vivid, eerie force, as General Max Shorter faces a colony's price. Readers who like planet tales with a moral edge will enjoy Miracastle's gloom and the general who must pay for it.
23575-adventures-in-africa-by-an-african:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote this short African adventure of a hero fresh from school in England, who joins his uncle, a trader with the peoples of central Africa. Attacked soon after setting out by natives led by Boers, the party turns back with few beasts left, horses and an ox, across the Kalahari Desert.

A night camp in tsetse fly country kills the horses, while thirst, elephants, a hippopotamus, and other wild beasts test the travellers, and one of their number dies. Kingston tells the journey briskly, in the Victorian manner, with much hunting that modern readers will view with distaste. Still, the tale gives a vivid, if period bound, picture of trade, desert, and danger in nineteenth century Africa.
23612-the-leader:
Murray Leinster wrote this science fiction tale of the Leader, whose career remains a mystery of history. Illegitimate and uneducated, hysterical and superstitious, the man gathers discontented followers and turns them into fanatics, seizing by sheer force of personality, without resistance, the government of a great nation.

As ruler, he imposes the absolute despotism of a primitive sultanate, honeycombs society with spies, and imprisons, tortures, and executes without trial. His subjects give him impassioned loyalty and abandon morality at his command. Leinster's warning lies in the tale's central riddle: a superman who overlooks the chance of a super superman. Readers who like political science fiction will find a chilling, prescient fable of charisma, fear, and power.
23638-reminiscences-of-a-south-african-p:
William Charles Scully published these memories in 1913, looking back on a youth spent first in Ireland and then in South Africa. The early chapters recall his family, school days, and the sea voyage that carried him to Cape Town. Once ashore, he tries sheep farming, meets Xhosa leaders such as Chief Sandile, and drifts toward the diamond diggings.

The heart of the book is camp life at the diamond fields: scarce water, claim disputes, and diamond theft. The rush to Colesberg Kopje follows, where Scully nearly finds the Kimberley mine and loses his first diamond. Told in a plain, anecdotal voice, it gives a first-hand view of frontier South Africa before the mines grew into big business.
2365-the-princess-de-montpensier:
Madame de Lafayette's Princess de Montpensier is a short, perfect novella of love and honor in the French Wars of Religion. The princess, married to a prince she does not love, is courted by the Duke of Guise, her first love, and by the Count of Chabannes, who loves her nobly and hopelessly. Lafayette's cool, precise prose turns passion into tragedy.

The story's famous discretion, its refusal to explain too much, gives it a modern feel. Its portrait of a woman trapped by marriage and war still moves readers. Lovers of French classical fiction will find a small masterpiece.
23735-the-story-teller:
Maud Lindsay published The Story-Teller in Boston in 1915, with pictures by Florence Liley Young. She dedicates it to her cousin Judith Winston Sherrod, in whose joyous company she journeyed through the wonderland of youth. The book is a storyteller's own set of tales, meant to be read aloud.

Twelve stories fill its pages, from The Two Brothers and The Jar of Rosemary to The Plate of Pancakes and Little Maid Hildegarde. Later tales bring the Great White Bear, the Song That Traveled, and the Quest for the Nightingale. Lindsay writes in a warm, old-fashioned manner, and each tale ends with its small moral plainly in view.
23811-the-good-ship-rover:
The Good Ship Rover, published by T. Nelson and Sons in 1888, tells of a gallant model ship three feet long, with white sails, sturdy masts, rigging, pennon, and figurehead. It had never seen the sea. For nearly a year it had cast anchor in the Leslies' nursery, a pleasant, airy room full of toys, and nothing like the sea at all.

Harry Leslie, about eight years old, has never seen the sea either, though he has read much about sailor life. His dearest friend is Walter Hammond, the doctor's eldest boy next door, and the two intend to go to sea together when old enough. Mrs. Leslie fears damp feet and colds, but the boys' dreams sail on, with the little Rover as their first vessel.
23821-yorke-the-adventurer:
Louis Becke published Yorke the Adventurer in 1901, a South Seas tale narrated by a man who first met Yorke early in the 1870s. The narrator recalls Captain Joshua Slocum's trick for night attacks in Tierra del Fuego. Sprinkle the cutter's deck with sharp tacks, then sleep soundly, for even horny Fuegian feet fear the business end of a tack.

Reading Slocum, the narrator smiled and thought of dear old Yorke and the Francesco. His own vessel had run under the lee of New Britain's South Cape to wood, water, and repair. It had lost a foretopmast in heavy weather among the Solomons. There, on a coast with no white men for three hundred miles, Yorke's story begins.
23870-the-teesdale-angler:
R. Lakeland published The Teesdale Angler at Barnard Castle in 1858, a guide to trout fishing drawn from upwards of thirty-five years of practical angling. Though its title is local, Lakeland intends it for trout fishers generally, especially in Yorkshire, Durham, Westmoreland, and Cumberland.

Contents cover river fish, advice to beginners, and useful hints, with chapters on fly fishing and the angling months. Natural flies get their due: the stone fly, the flesh fly, and the cow dung fly, with lists of palmer flies, hackle flies, and select killing flies. Lakeland's hope is modest: that his hints may aid the diversion of all who wish to be proficient in a pleasing recreation.
24003-confessions-of-a-book-lover:
Maurice Francis Egan published Confessions of a Book-Lover in Garden City in 1922, dedicating it in memory of Theodore Roosevelt, a man of action in love with books. Egan's chapters run from boyhood reading through poets and poetry to certain novelists, letters, biographies, memoirs, and books at random.

To get the best out of books, Egan insists, you must learn to love these lasting friends while still young. Late, serious reading makes technique and grammar seem too important, and the glamour is lost. Through Fenimore Cooper's verbiage you must still feel the real lakes and woods, and beneath Sir Walter's mat of words the wild fervour of romance. A great author, unlike a lost friend, can never be irretrievably lost.
24071-special-messenger:
Robert W. Chambers wrote this novel of the American Civil War era, opening with a Union cavalry column riding into the town of Sandy River. The troopers wear forage caps and fur-trimmed hussar tunics, and a mounted band rides ahead under a young bandmaster. The townsfolk, who have scowled at Yankee cavalry before, watch in silence, loyal only in spots.

The story follows a special messenger moving through divided country, where a careless word or a wrong road can be fatal. Chambers fills the march with local color: dusty streets, watching faces, and soldiers trying to read a town that will not cheer them. Readers get a brisk war adventure about duty, daring, and the risks of carrying orders behind enemy lines.
24097-the-story-of-red-feather-a-tale-of:
Edward S. Ellis wrote this frontier tale for young readers, published by McLoughlin Brothers. It follows a brother and sister on the American frontier, where a visit to relatives, a homesick girl, and a ride home along a familiar trail set the story moving. The chapters carry titles such as Caught Fast, A Friend in Need, and Surrounded by Peril.

Danger gathers as the Muddy Creek band and the warrior Tall Bear threaten the settlement, and a child, as one chapter title promises, shall lead them through it. Ellis mixes escapes, councils, and narrow rescues with a plain moral about courage and family loyalty. Young readers get a fast-moving adventure from the days of cabins, trails, and frontier forts.
24161-all-day-september:
Roger Kuykendall wrote this science fiction tale for Astounding Science Fiction in June 1959, with pictures by van Dongen. A meteor no larger than a match head, born when a star died long before lungfish left the sea, falls on the Moon and drills through the casing of Evans' tractor turbine. At eight thousand revolutions a minute, the shaft knots, blades fly through the casing, and the turbine stops for good.

Evans is a prospector on the Moon, two days from sunrise, his tractor worth two hundred and fifty thousand dollars, only fifty thousand paid, the rest in notes and grubstake shares. When broke, he hauls uranium ore and metallic sodium from Potter's dike to Williamson Town. Readers get a hard-luck survival tale, told against the cold lunar day.
24179-conversion-of-a-high-priest-into-a:
The Reverend Meletios Golden tells his own conversion story in this book, edited and presented in a second edition published in New York in 1912. It is dedicated to his father, who called the eight-year-old boy to his deathbed and told him God would be his father, Jesus his savior, and work for righteousness his path. Golden directs all his efforts in life toward that destination.

Chapters follow a farewell, an arrival, a first day in New York, and life as a high priest before his change of faith. A farmhouse where Golden wrote his conversion and a Greek-American Christian association appear among the pictures. Readers get a first-person account of faith remade, from priesthood to Christian work.
2422-introduction-to-the-compleat-angler:
Andrew Lang introduces Izaak Walton's Compleat Angler with an essay on Walton's life, his fishing, and his gentle philosophy. The introduction sketches the seventeenth century angler-author, his friendships, and the book's long popularity, arguing that Walton teaches patience and contentment as much as fishing. Lang's own charm matches his subject.

The piece serves as a gateway to Walton's classic, explaining why a book about fish has endured for centuries. Readers approaching the Angler will find Lang a delightful guide. Anglers and literary historians alike will enjoy it. Lang was a prolific scholar who also wrote fairy books and histories.
24301-the-camp-in-the-snow-or-besieged-b:
William Murray Graydon wrote this boys' winter adventure, copyrighted by Street and Smith in 1902. Its chapters run from A Merciless Enemy and Into the Wilderness through A Double Peril, The First Deer, The Face in the Trees, Besieged by Wolves, Through the Ice, Mr. Raikes of Portland, The Great Storm, and A Great Disaster to Under the Snowdrift and Decoyed to Danger.

Later chapters bring the last of the catamount, a herd of deer, and a successful battle. On the trail, found and lost, Hamp's peril, and Bogle showing his hand follow. Brick's defence, plunged underground, an unexpected ally, and back to freedom come next. A struggle for life, a vial of chloroform, and a perilous ride close the book. It opens on a Boston express on a December night in Maine. Readers get a breathless snowbound adventure.
24380-shock-absorber:
E. G. von Wald wrote this science fiction story, with pictures by van Dongen, for Astounding Science Fiction in June 1955. Its epigraph warns that a man acts on what he believes the facts are, not on the facts, and lives or dies by what the facts are. Sometimes there is no time to correct a man's beliefs, yet he must act correctly.

An aging little psychologist, a full captain, scowls at a junior commander on Mars who argues with him. Out with the fleet, discipline is now virtually nonexistent, though a discipline of a sort, strict and effective, has replaced the academy kind. Despair is the lowest common denominator among combat patrols, bringing mutinies, disobedience, and defections. After the aliens are kicked out of the solar system, old ideas may return. Readers get war, belief, and command.
24389-blue-bird-weather:
Robert W. Chambers wrote this novel, published by D. Appleton and Company in New York and London in October 1912, copyrighted in 1912, with pictures by Charles Dana Gibson. It is dedicated to Joseph Lee of Needwood Forest. Its frontispiece shows a woman trotting away to Marche's door and tapping softly, and an early picture carries the line, spoken gravely, that she is afraid it will be blue-bird weather.

The book stands among Chambers's many works, from The Streets of Ascalon, Japonette, and The Adventures of a Modest Man. The Danger Mark, Special Messenger, and The Firing Line lead to The Younger Set, The Fighting Chance, and Some Ladies in Haste. The Tree of Heaven, The Tracer of Lost Persons, and A Young Man in a Hurry follow, with Lorraine, Maids of Paradise, and Ashes of Empire. Readers get a Chambers novel, bright with Gibson pictures.
24394-gossamer:
G. A. Birmingham wrote this novel, published by George H. Doran Company in 1915. Its first chapter finds the narrator and Gorman going over the case of poor Ascher yet again, perhaps for the twentieth time. Gorman reminds the narrator that he cannot understand Ascher, being a man of no country who knows nothing of patriotism. The narrator, whose leg was mangled in battle, agrees in part: he went to fight only because he could not avoid going.

He denies fighting for his country, yet claims to understand Ascher as well as Gorman does. Ascher suffered severely when loyalty to his native land gripped him at a critical moment. The narrator's rending of body matches Ascher's rending of soul, without the consolation of feeling a hero. Gorman, Irish by birth, sympathy, and conviction, is a member of Parliament pledged to Ireland. Readers get patriotism, Ireland, and a man without a country.
24470-japhet-in-search-of-a-father:
Captain Frederick Marryat published this novel in 1836, the seventh book from his pen. It was the first of his books without a nautical setting. Japhet, a young man who does not know his father, sets out to find him. His search carries him through many corners of nineteenth-century English life.

Marryat had retired from the Royal Navy in 1828 to write. He was famous for inventing episodes as he went, and the novel is full of lively scenes, odd characters, and sudden turns. Readers get both an entertaining quest story and a vivid picture of the world Marryat knew, told by a popular novelist of his day.
24471-tobacco-its-history-varieties-cult:
E. R. Billings published this large illustrated book at Hartford, Connecticut, in 1875. It treats tobacco from its first discovery to his own day, covering its history, varieties, culture, manufacture, and commerce, with an account of its many modes of use.

Billings notes that over three hundred books had already been written on tobacco, yet most covered only its trade or its medicine. His own book gives a fuller account of growing the plant, in America and in nearly every great tobacco country of the world. Its Virginia chapters draw on unpublished sources. The book remains a rich record of a crop that shaped empires.
24482-zip-the-adventures-of-a-frisky-fox:
Frances Trego Montgomery wrote this children's book, published in 1917 with pictures by Violet Moore Higgins. It had first appeared serially in the Detroit News Tribune. Its hero is Zip, a frisky fox terrier whose curiosity keeps landing him in trouble.

Chapters follow Zip as he digs up stolen silver, takes a disastrous jump, gets stuck in a stovepipe, and meets Peter-Kins and a turkey gobbler. A candy pull and a fight follow before curiosity undoes him once more. Young readers get a lively, funny animal story, told in short chapters that suit reading aloud or alone.
24582-field-and-forest-or-the-fortunes-o:
Oliver Optic wrote this boys' story, published at Boston in 1870 with fourteen illustrations, as part of his Upward and Onward series. Its hero is a farmer, and its opening picture shows Old Matt and the horse-thieves. The tale follows a young man's fortunes in field and forest, where farming, hunting, and hard work meet.

Optic's story rewards industry, honesty, and courage, as his hero faces thieves, bad seasons, and the daily labour of the land. The book belongs to a series that taught boys to rise by steady effort. Young readers get a warm, old-fashioned tale of country life and a farmer's luck.
24589-the-tale-of-benny-badger:
Bailey's Sleepy-Time Tales continue in this story of Benny Badger, one of a long shelf of animal books for small children. A picture shows Benny disliking Mr. Coyote's singing, a joke that sets the tone: Benny is a sturdy, opinionated badger, and the farmyard folk around him are full of music, mischief, and advice.

Arthur Scott Bailey tells Benny's adventures in short chapters, with pictures by Harry L. Smith, in the simple style of his Cuffy Bear and Ferdinand Frog books. Small children get a bedtime tale of a badger learning to rub along with neighbours, funny, gentle, and easy to follow.
24599-a-young-mutineer:
Mrs. L. T. Meade, author of A Girl in Ten Thousand and Girls New and Old, wrote this girls' story of a young mutineer. Its frontispiece asks whether the person was fickle, and did he break his promise, a question at the heart of the tale. Meade's heroine faces a trial of loyalty, temper, and truth.

The story follows schoolgirl friendship, family trouble, and a mutiny of spirit, as its heroine learns to hold her course. Meade wrote dozens of girls' books, and her tales mix adventure with moral courage. Young readers get a spirited, old-fashioned story of a girl who dares to stand alone.
24635-exeter:
Sidney Heath described Exeter in this volume of the Beautiful England series, pictured by E. W. Haslehurst and published by Blackie and Son at London, Glasgow, and Bombay in 1912. Its frontispiece shows Exeter from the canal, and later plates show the quay and the city's streets and churches.

Heath's text guides readers through the cathedral city of Devon, its Roman walls, medieval lanes, and river scenes. The book belongs to a series that also covered Oxford, Canterbury, Winchester, York, and the English Lakes. It gives a charming, well-illustrated portrait of Exeter before the First World War.
24674-expositions-of-holy-scripture-ephe:
Alexander Maclaren, the Baptist preacher, wrote these expositions of Holy Scripture, published at New York by George H. Doran. The volume covers Ephesians and the Epistles of St. Peter and St. John. Its Ephesians sermons open with saints and faithful, and the truth that a Christian is a saint because he believes.

Maclaren's expositions move verse by verse, with clear divisions and practical application, in the style that made him famous in Victorian pulpits. His readings of Peter and John treat faith, love, and holy living. Readers of devotional literature will find here a classic of evangelical preaching, warm and scholarly.
24791-the-marooner:
Charles A. Stearns wrote this science fiction tale of a two-man spaceship crew on a strange world. Mr. Wordsley, a slight, ingenious engineer, watches the stars through photon collectors of his own making. Captain DeCastros, a huge and moody clown of a man, holds command and keeps reminding Wordsley of it.

The two crossed half the universe for a breath of rare perfume, and their landing on the dry world Avis Solis brings hardship, odd creatures, and broken gear. Stearns mixes humor with wonder, letting the odd couple's friction carry the plot. Fans of pulp-era space tales will enjoy its strange suns, dry winds, and quest for a scent worth a voyage.
24797-a-history-of-sea-power:
William Oliver Stevens and Allan Westcott, professors at the United States Naval Academy, published this history in 1920. It traces sea power from the first navies through Athens and Rome. Chapters on Venice and the Turks follow, then the ocean routes opened by Portugal and Spain, down to the rise of English sea power and Nelson's wars.

Chapters pair battles with strategy: the Armada, wars with the Dutch and French, and the fights of the First of June and Camperdown. Maps and diagrams back the text. The book gives a clear, naval-eye view of how command of the sea shaped empires, and it long served as a standard text for midshipmen.
24825-the-ghost-of-chatham-a-vision-dedi:
The Ghost of Chatham, printed in London in 1821 by William Hone for sixpence, is a verse vision on the trial of Queen Caroline. The ghost of Chatham, the elder Pitt, rises to speak against the Bill of Pains and Penalties, the cruel and unconstitutional attack on the Queen that had roused the whole nation.

The preface rejoices that the Queen was delivered and the constitution saved from a tremendous explosion. Hone's pamphlet mixes satire, loyalty, and high feeling for the House of Peers. It gives a vivid taste of radical print culture in the year of Caroline's trial, when pamphlets fought politics in verse.
2483-janice-day-the-young-homemaker:
Helen Beecher Long's Janice Day: The Young Homemaker follows a girl who takes charge of a household and learns the arts of cooking, sewing, and managing a home. The story mixes practical lessons with friendship and mild romance, aimed at young readers learning domestic skills. Janice's cheerfulness carries the book.

The novel belongs to a popular series for girls, earnest and instructional in its way. Modern readers will note its period ideals of homemaking. It charms as a piece of girls' fiction history. Long wrote a whole series following Janice through school and married life.
24911-young-glory-and-the-spanish-cruise:
Young Glory and the Spanish Cruiser, number three of the Young Glory dime novels, appeared in New York on April 22, 1898, priced at five cents. The story follows Young Glory, a brave American lad, through the Spanish-American War: a prisoner shot, a comrade rescued, and a bold flight for life.

Chapters carry him to the camp of the patriots with Captain Ruiz Calderon, to San Juan de Porto Rico, and aboard the Brooklyn and Nashville. Dan Daly rows down creeks, brings in forty rifles and cutlasses, and helps board the cruiser in a last stand. The tale gives young readers a breathless, patriotic adventure from the year of the Maine.
24920-the-book-of-all-power:
Edgar Wallace wrote The Book of All-Power, a thriller of magic, murder, and old Russia. At its center stands a book said to hold the black magic of Kensky, by which its owner can torment enemies and bring sorrow on Christians who oppose him. Sophia Kensky, baptised in the Christian faith, has told the Archbishop of the book.

Malcolm, the hero, hears why men would kill for it: Ivan Nickolovitch threw a stone at its keeper, and a thousand reasons are given for murder. Wallace spins the tale with his usual pace, mixing faith, fear, and conspiracy. Readers who like his thrillers will find a dark, strange story of a book too dangerous to own.
2493-the-adventures-of-paddy-the-beaver:
Thornton W. Burgess's Adventures of Paddy the Beaver follows the busy beaver as he builds his dam, outwits trappers, and teaches the meadow folk about work and patience. The story mixes animal adventure with natural history, as Paddy's engineering shapes the pond for everyone. Burgess's woodland characters return in force.

Young readers learn how beavers live while enjoying a gentle plot. The book belongs to Burgess's beloved animal series. Nature-loving children will find a warm classic. Burgess based his meadow tales on walks near his Massachusetts home. The book teaches how a beaver dam changes a whole pond.
24975-the-gift-bearer:
Charles L. Fontenay's story, first printed in Amazing Science Fiction Stories in September 1958, follows Richard J. Montcalm, a solid family man who chairs Traskmore's censorship board. The morning after a stormy meeting, his forces, including ministers and heads of women's clubs, face Patrick Levitt's liberals over a nude statue called Dawn in the park. Montcalm rules the statue must be removed from public view, despite Levitt's sarcastic offer to dress it in underwear.

Then a flying saucer whizzes over Traskmore and vanishes into the sky, opening a stranger question: what priceless gifts might visitors from other worlds bring, and would Montcalm accept them? He debates the matter long and decides as before, with the children in mind. The story is a neat satire of small-town moral policing.
25061-the-penal-cluster:
Ivar Jorgensen's Penal Cluster is a science-fiction novella about a future society that punishes its worst mental criminals in a novel way. Agent David Houston, working undercover in a London bank, tracks suspects whom ordinary prisons cannot hold, since their crimes are committed by thought alone.

The solution is a drug-induced coma in bodies exiled to a cluster of tiny dark asteroids trailing Earth in its orbit. Jorgensen uses the strange prison to ask how far a society may go in pursuit of vengeance. He asks whether a punishment no one can see is justice or cruelty dressed up as progress.
25127-the-tiger-hunter:
Captain Mayne Reid's Tiger Hunter is his free English version of Gabriel Ferry's 1851 French novel Costal l'Indien, first published under Reid's name in 1861 as A Hero in Spite of Himself. The Routledge edition used here, from 1890, gives the book the title by which its hero, the jaguar hunter Costal, is known.

Set during Mexico's war of independence from Spain in 1811 and 1812, the story follows dragoon officers, insurgent bands, and deserted villages in Oaxaca. Costal, brave and feared, moves between the camps, and the novel mixes adventure with a picture of a country in revolt. The tigers of the title are jaguars of the Mexican wilds.
25150-the-young-bank-messenger:
Horatio Alger Jr.'s Young Bank Messenger, copyrighted in 1898, is a rags-to-respectability adventure in the author's familiar formula. Ernest, left alone in the world after a deathbed revelation and a robbery, takes work as a bank messenger. He falls into the orbit of outlaws, a Quaker detective, and a robber's cave.

Chapters follow Ernest through an armed escort, an outlaw's escape, a strange meeting, and a startling disclosure about Stephen Ray and his son. Alger rewards honesty, pluck, and hard work, and punishes greed, and the novel remains a clear example of the boys' success stories that made his name.
25151-slow-and-sure-the-story-of-paul-ho:
Horatio Alger Jr.'s Slow and Sure tells the story of Paul Hoffman, a young New York street merchant rising from the sidewalk to the shop. It belongs to Alger's series of New York street-life tales begun with Ragged Dick.

Much of the book follows a street waif raised by burglars, torn between gratitude to his guardians and duty to honest life. Scenes include Barnum's Museum, a tenement fire, and Paul's hope of a house on Madison Avenue. Alger's moral is plain: steady work and honesty beat quick gains.
2527-the-sorrows-of-young-werther:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe wrote this short novel in letters, here translated by R. D. Boylan, and it made its young hero famous across Europe. Werther, a sensitive artist, pours out his heart to a friend about nature, books, and his growing love for Charlotte, a kind young woman already promised to another man.

As his hope fades, Werther's letters turn from joy to despair, and his feeling for Charlotte grows into an obsession he cannot escape. Goethe writes with great tenderness about first love, loneliness, and the pain of a mind at war with itself. The book remains a landmark of feeling, and a warning about love that refuses all limits.
2541-character:
Samuel Smiles wrote this study of character as the force that shapes both private lives and whole nations. He opens with poets and thinkers who call character moral order seen in a single nature, and argues that a country's wealth lies less in revenues or forts than in cultivated citizens.

Smiles draws on lives of workers, soldiers, and reformers to show honesty, patience, and duty in action. The chapters preach thrift, courage, and self reliance without sneering at failure. Victorian readers took it as a guide to conduct, and it still reads as a plain, earnest case for living by steady principle.
25464-the-king-of-root-valley-and-his-cu:
R. Reinick's 1856 fairy tale opens in Root Valley, where a curious princess rules her father's fancy. Story-telling guests, an aerial chariot, and town festivities fill the first chapter. A spring festival brings migrating birds, a nut-field, and strange visitors: Nutcracker and Harlequin, who come to life from a box of Nuremberg toys.

Three wishes, a wonderful brook, and wandering rats lead to battle, homage, and a procession to Root Valley. Nutcracker is betrothed to the princess and takes the Nutfield as her dowry, though pride soon troubles the puppet kingdom. Chapman and Hall published the tale in London, with eight illustrations by T. Von Oer and Reinick.
25472-blackbeard-buccaneer:
Ralph D. Paine writes a pirate adventure around Blackbeard, the buccaneer captain Teach. The contents open with the courteous pirate Captain Bonnet and the merchant trader Plymouth Adventure, then move to hostages held to Blackbeard and captive seamen in the forecastle. A voyage by little raft, the mist of the Cherokee swamp, and the winding creek carry Jack Cockrell through swamp and ambush.

Jack hides his canoe in a stagnant cove, climbs an oak, and watches open water for Bonnet's men. Later chapters bring the great fight of Captain Teach, Blackbeard loyal to the last, and a quest for pirates' gold. Ned Rackham's plans go amiss, and Mr. Peter Forbes mourns his nephew. The Penn Publishing Company issued the book at Philadelphia in 1922, illustrated by Frank E. Schoonover.
25473-frontier-boys-on-the-coast-or-in-t:
Capt. Wyn Roosevelt follows Jim, Joe, and Tom Darlington to the California coast in this sixth Frontier Boys book. Captain Bill Broom and his pirate gang seize the boys' valuables and hand them a cruel defeat. Chapters lead through a cove and cave, barbed wire, and Pete's yarn, toward a chase to rescue Tom and Juarez from pirate power.

Jim gallops ahead with a Spaniard at his side, exulting in a victory over the Black before onlookers who hoped to see him beaten. Fresh sea air brings hope that the boys will overtake the pirates and free their comrades. Hurst and Company published the book in New York, with copyright held by Platt and Peck in 1909.
25481-little-grandfather:
Sophie May writes the fifth volume of Little Prudy's Flyaway Series, set among the Parlin family. Willy Parlin looks funny in his first pocket-clothes, his tight green breeches like pods of marrow-fat peas. Chapters follow the trundle-bed, the ox-money, the boy who wore home the medal, and the boy who meant to mind his mother. The boy who cheated, the Never-Give-Ups, and the muster follow, with going to sea and a trip to the forks.

Willy whistles faintly as he lays sticks on the fire, hoping his mother will not find him out, and she sings the Gaffer Gray ballad when he comes in cold. The book closes with a chapter titled I Ha'e Naebody Now and a conclusion. Lee and Shepard published it at Boston in 1874, from a copyright of 1873.
25507-little-grandmother:
Sophie May, author of the Little Prudy and Dotty Dimple stories, writes this tale for young readers in her Little Prudy's Flyaway Series. Published in Boston in 1873, with a front picture of Little Grandmother herself, it belongs to a planned set of six volumes about Prudy and her circle.

May dedicates the book to a young Cuban friend, Maria Arozarena, and keeps the story simple, domestic, and affectionate. A grandmother figure stands at the centre, giving child readers a warm elder to love while small home adventures unfold around her.
25585-shakespeare-ben-jonson-beaumont-an:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge supplies notes and lectures on Shakespeare, Ben Jonson, Beaumont, and Fletcher in this new edition, published in Liverpool by Edward Howell in 1874. Contents move from a definition of poetry and Greek drama to the progress of drama and public taste.

Coleridge judges Shakespeare a poet generally, praising judgment equal to genius. He then works through plays in order. Notes on the Tempest, Love's Labour's Lost, and Midsummer Night's Dream come first. Comedy of Errors, As You Like It, and Twelfth Night follow. Histories such as King John, Richard II, and Henry IV appear beside Coriolanus, Julius Caesar, and Romeo and Juliet.
2561-robert-falconer:
George MacDonald tells the story of Robert Falconer, a Scottish boy growing up among broad Scots speech, strict faith, and hard work. A glossary at the end of this text helps modern readers with the Scots words woven through the talk.

Robert loses his father to a wandering life, clings to his grandmother's stern love, and fights his way toward learning and a trade. MacDonald writes with warmth about conscience, forgiveness, and the pull of home. The novel endures as a Scottish coming of age tale, rough in dialect but tender at heart.
2563-memoirs-of-the-comtesse-du-barry-wi:
Baron Etienne Leon Lamothe-Langon wrote these memoirs in the voice of the Comtesse du Barry, the last favorite of Louis XV, though the book is a pseudonymous work, not her own writing. A note in this text warns readers that the narrator tells truth only as she sees it, which is seldom quite the fact.

The comtesse recalls her rise from low birth to Versailles, her rivals, her lovers, and the court's glitter and spite. The pages mix gossip, scandal, and sharp portraits of a monarchy near its fall. Readers get a vivid, unreliable tour of old France, best enjoyed as brilliant storytelling rather than strict history.
25646-child-s-health-primer-for-primary-:
This child's health primer, first in the Pathfinder Physiology series, teaches primary pupils about the body, with special reference to alcoholic drinks, stimulants, and narcotics. Barnes and Company published it in New York and Chicago in 1885. The scientific department of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union endorsed it.

A picture of wasting money fronts the lessons, linking drink with loss. Suited to pupils at third reader grade, the primer introduces anatomy, physiology, and hygiene in short, plain lessons. Health, temperance, and careful habits form its core message for young schoolchildren. The series covers anatomy, physiology, and hygiene for school use.
25672-in-the-boyhood-of-lincoln-a-tale-o:
Hezekiah Butterworth writes this tale of Lincoln's boyhood, centred on the Tunker schoolmaster and the times of Black Hawk, in a ninth edition from Appleton in 1898 with a 1892 copyright. A rescue fronts the book, and Lincoln's own words give the epigraph: faith that right makes might.

Butterworth calls the book a true picture in a framework of fiction, showing how Lincoln's character, which commanded hearts and confidence, was formed. The preface argues Lincoln became the typical character of American institutions, and youth spent unselfishly shaped the man who later led a nation.
25677-the-history-of-minnesota-and-tales:
Judge Charles E. Flandrau writes this history of Minnesota with tales of the frontier, published in St. Paul by E. W. Porter in 1900. The state seal of Minnesota and a portrait of Flandrau front the book, with the motto A ma puissance.

Flandrau dedicates the history to old settlers who laid the state's foundation on freedom and toleration and defended it gallantly. His introduction explains the work first formed part of an encyclopedia of Minnesota biography. Frontier tales then carry readers from early settlement to statehood in a judge's clear, firsthand style.
25733-tam-o-shanter:
Robert Burns writes Tam o' Shanter, a tale in Scots verse, in this Saalfield edition with decorations by Harry L. Miller, copyrighted in 1908. A front picture shows a wife telling Tam he was a scoundrel, setting the comic domestic frame.

When chapmen leave the street and drouthy neighbours meet as market days wear late, folk take the gate while Tam sits bousing at the nappy, getting fou and unco happy. He thinks not of the long Scots miles home, and Miller's decorations follow Tam on his grey mare Meg, the landlady growing gracious, and dancers flying quick and quicker.
2574-on-the-frontier:
Bret Harte gathers frontier stories in this volume, opening at the Mission of San Carmel on August 10, 1838, along the hard coast line between Monterey and San Diego. Dome shaped hills, rare traders, and the glitter of the Pacific set a stark stage for the tales.

A Blue Grass Penelope waits, a man is left out on Lone Star Mountain, and mission life meets American restlessness. Harte writes of Spanish California fading before the new order, with sympathy for both. The stories blend romance and irony, and they capture a borderland moment just before it vanished.
25772-little-lost-sister:
Virginia Brooks, author of My Battles with Vice, writes Little Lost Sister, published in New York by the Macaulay Company in 1914. Brooks argues it is not always fashion, costume, or blazing show windows that tempt little lost sisters.

More often, she says, human need for love and shelter tempts them, with lack of a friendly handclasp to lighten tomorrow's labour, and sympathy breeding hope. Chapters open at the button mill, where Elsie Welcome works, then seeing Millville from the button factory. Brooks writes a social novel of working girls, danger, and rescue.
25795-lord-kitchener:
G. K. Chesterton writes this 1917 life of Lord Kitchener, published in London with a portrait photograph by Elliott and Fry. Horatio Herbert Kitchener, born in County Kerry to an English colonel, was Irish-born yet English in descent.

Chesterton sees in that first fact a simple, practical man amid mystical western problems distant from his mind, an element clinging to his career with unconscious poetry. Chesterton credits him with an epic hero's qualities, while noting he was the unlikeliest man to write epic poetry. The short life sketches soldier, empire, and war.
25823-the-story-of-leather:
Sara Ware Bassett writes The Story of Leather, published by Penn in Philadelphia in 1927 with a 1915 copyright and pictures by C. P. Gray. Bassett, author of stories of lumber, wool, glass, sugar, silk, and porcelain, dedicates the book to Mr. A. C. Lawrence, whose friendship and aid made it possible.

Revolving drums front the book, and chapters open with Peter Coddington sitting in afternoon sunshine, then Peter winning another name. Bassett traces leather from hides and tanning to finished goods, in a story-of-industry book that teaches children how everyday materials reach their hands.
25826-the-gospel-of-the-hereafter:
J. Paterson-Smyth, rector of St. George's, Montreal, sets out what the Bible says about life just after death. Part one treats the near hereafter: the self that lives on, the crisis of death, meeting loved ones again, the communion of saints, and growth and cleansing in the unseen life. He argues that the dead watch, recall, and care for the great events of faith, not least the work of Christ.

Part two turns to the far hereafter and the end of all things. The book leans on Scripture throughout, with long looks at the Transfiguration and the letter to the Hebrews. Printed in 1910, it aims at plain readers who grieve or wonder, offering comfort that death is a passage and a ministry, not a sleep without thought or love.
25829-the-dark-tower:
Phyllis Bottome writes The Dark Tower, published by the Century Company in September 1916 with pictures by J. H. Gardner Soper. A Browning epigraph opens the book, with Child Roland coming to the dark tower, and a Maccabees verse on dying manfully for brethren without staining honour.

Winn Staines, a man loyal to God, crown, and regiment, opens the tale, arriving at the Fanshawes at eleven o'clock and wanting, if possible, a home without rows. Winn tells Miss Rivers gently he shall never be dangerous for her, in a front picture, as Bottome builds a wartime novel of honour, love, and duty.
25858-the-radio-boys-trailing-a-voice-or:
Allen Chapman sends the Radio Boys after a voice that will not be caught. Bob and his friends pick up strange messages in the stuttering voice of Dan Cassey, and an older hand, Mr. Brandon, tells them he too has caught them. Brandon thinks the notes form a criminal code, clever and near impossible to read without a key, and the boys set out to trace the sender.

Printed by Grosset and Dunlap with a foreword by Jack Binns, the book is the fifth Radio Boys tale, after first wireless, Ocean Point, the sending station, and Mountain Pass. Scenes move from home sets to the open air, with a man plainly taking a message in the frontispiece. The boys use skill, patience, and teamwork to turn stray signals into a solved case.
25875-the-woman-from-outside-on-swan-riv:
Hulbert Footner sets a Northland tale on Swan River, printed in 1921. It opens on a January afternoon at Fort Enterprise, where the company store gang round the stove debates the one question that never stales: when will the mail come. Into this closed world comes Clare, the woman from outside, and her arrival stirs talk, pursuit, and a hearing that tests every claim.

Chapters follow the white medicine man, Hooliam, the Kakisas, a log shack, a foot trail, a rescue, and a last stage down the river. Etzooah's tale of signs and half known words, of a red coat and a white girl gone down river unseen, deepens the mystery around a man named Eembrie. Footner writes of fur country, law, and loyalty, with the river itself as the road home.
25886-the-young-lieutenant-or-the-advent:
Oliver Optic, pen name of William T. Adams, tells the Civil War tale of Lieutenant Thomas Somers of Massachusetts. The book opens in a railroad car, where an officer with two bars greets Somers as a regimental brother and hails him as a first rate soldier. Somers soon faces the senator's daughter, friends at court, and the hard school of camp and field.

The climax finds the line giving way before a fierce charge, with the safety of the army and the fate of the country hanging on one man's stand. Somers cries rally round me, fires his revolver, and holds his ground for the flag. Optic writes for boys who love brave deeds, and his young lieutenant earns his rank by pluck, duty, and steady nerve.
2589-the-experiences-of-a-bandmaster:
John Philip Sousa, the march king, wrote this memoir of eighteen years making music for the masses, twelve with the United States Marine Band and six with his own band. At the White House he played state functions and watched presidents and their guests at close range.

Sousa recalls tours, mishaps, rival bands, and the curious incidents that crowd a conductor's life. His tone is genial and anecdotal, full of backstage detail. The book gives a lively view of American musical life at its most public, from the Executive Mansion to the concert hall.
25899-the-prodigal-father:
J. Storer Clouston tells a comic Edinburgh tale of respectability turned upside down, printed in 1909. It opens in a cable tram car, where two citizens speak in hushed tones of the most extraordinary thing ever heard: Mr. Walkingshaw, of Walkingshaw and Gilliflower, has done something no one can credit. The firm name itself, one says, seems a surer pledge of worth than the senior partner's honored name.

The prodigal father of the title upends his family's staid life, and the novel follows the shock waves through kin, trade, and town talk. A later scene finds a man studying a picture splashed with red ocher, which he takes for the grandstand at a football ground, and musing on art, widows, and modern daubs. Clouston, known for The Lunatic at Large, writes with dry wit and a keen eye for Scots pride.
25926-the-1926-tatler:
The 1926 Tatler is a school yearbook full of senior portraits, class notes, and student writing. Evelyn McCue Baker, president of the senior class, leads the roll, praised as good as she is fair. Mary Barber Eaton of the League, editor Margaret Louise Newhall, and a dozen more seniors follow in turn. Each girl gets a motto, a childhood portrait, and a senior portrait.

Student pieces fill the later pages, such as Shirley Woodward's essay on gardens read about in books. She visits an Italian garden through print alone, entering by a vine covered Tuscan arch to a terrace, cool ferns at her feet, and a terracotta pool below. The Tatler thus keeps a year of school life, its officers, its wit, and its daydreams, bound in one keepsake volume.
25960-the-desert-fiddler:
William H. Hamby tells a desert tale of fiddles, ranches, and water rights in The Desert Fiddler, printed by Grosset and Dunlap. The book grew from a photoplay titled Percy, a Thomas H. Ince production released by Pathé, with Charles Ray as Bob Rogeen and Barbara Bedford as Imogene Chandler. Pictures from the film mark scenes of fiddling, wiles, and ranch war.

Bob sleeps in the east wing of a squat adobe house when a midnight shake at the screen door brings news from Red Butte Ranch. Reedy Jenkins schemes against Imogene's crop, warning that shutting off water will wither all the valley's cotton in a day. Holy Joe shanghaies ranchmen and finds Percy a willing ally. Hamby's tale mixes music, humor, and desert justice.
25968-newspaper-reporting-and-correspond:
Grant Milnor Hyde, instructor in journalism at the University of Wisconsin, writes a manual for reporters, correspondents, and students of newspaper writing, printed by Appleton in 1912. Chapters move from gathering the news and news values to the news story form, fire stories plain and feature, faults in news stories, follow ups and rewrites, speeches, interviews, and court reporting.

Later chapters cover social news, obituaries, sport, human interest, dramatic reporting, and a style book, with study hints and stories to correct. Hyde notes a key difference in sourcing. A man on a platform speaks to be quoted. A man speaking privately dreads full quotation and hopes the reporter will forget half his words. The manual is a clear, workmanlike guide to the reporter's craft.
25982-thrilling-narratives-of-mutiny-mur:
Printed by Hurst and Company, this collection of thrilling narratives tells of mutiny, murder, piracy, shipwreck, and disaster from the early part of the century to the present time. The preface ranks shipwreck among the greatest evils man can face, never void of danger, often fatal, and always productive of regret. Patience, fortitude, and ingenuity, it says, can at best prolong a struggle with destiny.

Tales include Captain Woodward and five seamen in Celebes and an occurrence at sea, with accounts of providential escapes and heart rending fatalities. One wreck scene shows a French sailor, Pierre Henin, praised by London's Humane Society, vowing to reach a grounded ship alone at low water and warn her crew to flee. The book is a grim, stirring shelf of sea disasters.
26011-the-prairie-mother:
Arthur Stringer tells a prairie wife's story in diary form in The Prairie Mother, printed by Bobbs Merrill in 1920 with pictures by Arthur E. Becher. The book opens on a Sunday, the fifteenth, with the narrator waking to a pea green world. A doctor's far away voice says give her another whiff or two, as if through the Simplon Tunnel. The prairie mother writes of birth, home, and marriage with humor and grit.

Later entries spar with her husband over his Edmonton trip without a goodbye kiss. It felt like glory ending, as when a circus manager mounts a tub to hawk an after concert for a dime. She counters his jibe that marriage grows tougher like Hogan's Alley. Stringer, author of The Prairie Wife, writes of western women with warmth, wit, and a keen ear for talk.
26056-a-booke-called-the-foundacion-of-r:
