Printed in 1563, A Booke Called the Foundacion of Rhetorike survives in only five known copies, this text transcribed from microfiche of the Bodleian Library original. The transcribers kept the book's old spelling, capitalization, punctuation, and its use of u for v and i for j, with long s regularized and paragraph marks rendered plain. A dedication in modern italics fronts a text otherwise in blackletter.

The rhetoric lesson draws on ancient history, as when Assyrians under Darius rebel, seize mighty Babylon, and stir the king to wrath over his Persian realm. Zopyrus, one of seven noble peers, sees the danger to country and prince. The book gives modern readers a rare, raw taste of Tudor prose and the art of persuasion as taught four centuries ago.
26156-hopes-and-fears-or-scenes-from-the:
Charlotte M. Yonge's 1899 novel follows Honora Charlecote, an unmarried woman torn between two homes. One is a City house in Woolstone-lane, near the Thames, inherited from City kin and older than the Great Fire. The other is Hiltonbury Holt, the old family seat, where her father, a London rector, sought rest from his work.

Honora recalls St. Wulstan's church as her youthful boast, large and light and Grecian beside damp old Hiltonbury. Later scenes bring Lucilla and Horatia, home cures, and family strains that test Honora's duty and patience. The book treats a spinster's life with respect, showing how faith, kin, and daily care shaped a woman's choices in Victorian England.
26177-the-book-of-stories-for-the-story-:
Fanny E. Coe's 1914 volume, issued in London by George G. Harrap, gathers tales for parents and teachers who tell stories to children. Its preface argues that story-telling has won a place as a real art in home and school. It also notes a plain problem: parents run short of fresh material, while teachers know good tales but lack time to hunt them down.

The collection draws from many nations and many kinds of source. Folk tales, modern fairy tales, and myths stand beside a newer field, real life, with tales of child heroes, adult heroes, and animals. The book aims to give tellers a full store to draw on, so story time stays fresh week after week.
26234-far-past-the-frontier:
James A. Braden's 1902 adventure tale opens with the flight of Big Pete Ellis, a red-bearded giant who snatches a wagon and lashes its horses into a wild dash. Two boys watch him vanish toward the setting sun, and a bound boy's story soon sets a perilous journey in motion. Chapters promise a man under a bed, a shot in the dark, and lonely mountain roads.

The party pushes into a wild country rich in deer, bears, wolves, and panthers, with Indians all about. They build a cabin, face the hatred of Big Buffalo, and camp for maple sugar in the wilderness. Return Kingdom and John press on, seeking the right place to settle. The book offers frontier danger and pluck for young readers.
26241-antony-gray-gardener:
Leslie Moore's 1917 novel, issued by G. P. Putnam's Sons, follows Antony Gray, a gardener, through letters, memories, and an English country life. Its prologue opens in March storm, with wind tearing at bare elms around a big grey house. Chapters list a letter, a lady of the blue book, a friendship, a stay at Teneriffe, and amazing conditions that force a decision.

Later titles promise an English cottage, doubts, a discovery, a meeting, and a manor house. Trix arrives on the scene, moonlight brings theories, and an old man in a library tells his story. A boyhood memory of a masked coach holdup, played in the manner of Claude Duval, adds comedy. The book blends garden work, mystery, and romance at a gentle pace.
26334-the-map-of-life-conduct-and-charac:
William Edward Hartpole Lecky's Map of Life, first printed in September 1899 and reissued in 1904 by Longmans, maps conduct and character. Its opening asks how far talk and reasoning can promote happiness at all, since circumstances and temper fix most of our lot. Chapters weigh determinism against free will, and happiness as a state of mind often confused with its means.

Lecky contrasts nations that seek happiness by shaping disposition, through religion, Stoicism, and eastern thought, with nations that seek it in better circumstances, through industry and progress. English character, the body's action on mood, and the fear of death all get chapters. A closing chapter treats death as terrible chiefly through its trappings, with pagan and Christian views compared.
26391-the-unknown-wrestler:
H. A. Cody's 1918 novel opens on a city street, where a blind old man plays a wheezy violin while his weary daughter holds out his hat for coins. Passersby mock the broken music, but the old man keeps his post, driven by a purpose he will not drop. The scene sets the book's concern with pride, hardship, and quiet endurance.

The action moves to a village where a domineering figure, Simon Stubbles, gives John Handyman written notice to quit for showing spirit. Chapters titled Conscience Money, Secret Plans, Perversion of Justice, and The Challenge trace quarrels, a will, and a public test of nerve. The title's wrestling proves as much moral as physical, as characters are forced to stand or yield.
2640-st-martin-s-summer:
Rafael Sabatini published this historical romance in 1921, and its chapters follow the Seneschal of Dauphiny, Monsieur de Garnache, and a dowager whose compliance opens doors at the Chateau de Condillac. Garnache loses his temper, keeps it, and walks into traps that open and close around him.

Sabatini writes with his usual swordplay, intrigue, and gallant dialogue, setting French nobles and rogues against each other in a summer of plots. The novel charms as a brisk adventure of honor and deception. Readers who love his sea tales will find the same dash on land.
26433-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for November 1847 opens with an essay on the navigation of the Antipodes, praising English discovery as a work of benevolence begun by Cook. The writer holds that voyages to new regions aimed to benefit their peoples, and that James Bruce, lawyer turned traveller, set his gaze on Africa as a land of marvels. Geographical knowledge, the essay argues, stands among the age's most intellectual advances.

Other pieces treat American copyright, evenings at sea, and the question whether Rubens was a colourist, weighing his lucid harmony against Rembrandt's ideal colour. Research and adventure in Australia, Highland destitution, and valedictory visits to Roman villas complete a number that mixes travel, art, and current affairs in Blackwood's Tory manner.
2644-isaac-bickerstaff-physician-and-ast:
Richard Steele created Isaac Bickerstaff for his Tatler papers, and this volume gathers the Bickerstaff writings with an introduction by Henry Morley. Morley sets out the relations between Steele and Addison, and how the Tatler grew into the Spectator.

Bickerstaff, physician and astrologer, predicted deaths, mocked quacks, and commented on London life with urbane wit. The papers show Augustan journalism at its birth, shaping public taste through a fictional voice. The book delights as a window on coffeehouse London, and on the friendship that made the periodical essay famous. Steele's London feels close at hand, from coffeehouse talk to printed squibs.
2646-john-leech-s-pictures-of-life-and-c:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote this appreciation of John Leech, reprinted from the Quarterly Review of December 1854. Thackeray recalls childhood amusements, from Boydell's Shakespeare gallery with its murky Opies and glum Northcotes to the pictures children were allowed to look at.

Leech's drawings of English life, with their humor and social bite, earn Thackeray's warm praise. The essay blends memoir with criticism, and it shows a novelist judging a fellow artist. Readers get a double portrait: Leech the draughtsman, and Thackeray the fond, sharp eyed observer. Thackeray's own boyhood memories give the praise a personal warmth.
26482-madeline-payne-the-detective-s-dau:
Lawrence L. Lynch, himself of the Secret Service, published this detective novel in 1883, reissued at Chicago in 1888. Its heroine, Madeline Payne, takes up her detective father's work and pursues justice against wretches with a strong cause in her hands. A friend, hearing her story, wishes for a fairy godmother to turn her into a six-foot brother to share the burden.

Chapters move through an old tree's revelations, the story of a crime, a shrewd scheme, and wheels within wheels. Claire, Cora, a French maid, a message from the dead, and a silken belt tangle the clues, while snares are set and a veritable ghost appears. Lynch, author of Shadowed by Three, keeps the mystery turning through thirty-nine chapters.
26498-peter-cooper:
Rossiter W. Raymond's 1901 biography, number four in the Riverside Biographical Series, traces Peter Cooper from ancestry to public fame. Obadiah Cooper came from England to New York about 1662 and settled at Fishkill on the Hudson, and his descendant John Cooper, born in 1755, fathered Peter as his fifth child. Boyhood, business ventures, and inventions follow, including the Tom Thumb locomotive.

Municipal affairs and national politics widen the story, but the Cooper Union for the Advancement of Science and Art stands as Cooper's monument. Raymond pauses on American giving, noting that private benefactions and endowments far surpass government support for such institutions elsewhere, while businessmen give time to boards and committees without pay. Cooper embodies that public spirit.
26548-the-tale-of-a-trooper:
Clutha N. Mackenzie, a trooper in the Wellington Mounted Rifles of the New Zealand Expeditionary Force, published this memoir with John Lane in 1921. It opens on a New Zealand station in a winter storm, where Mac and Charley check stock in the hills and yarn with old George the rouseabout. Enlistment soon turns the station hand into a soldier bound overseas.

Troopship life, desert days, Cairo tours, and a lunch with the Sultan fill the middle chapters before Mac reaches Gallipoli at last. Anzac, Table Top, Suvla Bay, and the night battle on Chanak Bair follow, until Mac is wounded and his campaigning days end. Homeward closes a cheerful, plain-spoken account of a colonial trooper's war.
2660-early-australian-voyages-pelsart-ta:
John Pinkerton gathered these early Australian voyages in an 1886 Cassell volume, with an introduction on how imagination reached new worlds before mariners did. Plato fabled Atlantis, Bacon dreamed of new lands, and then real ships followed.

Pelsart's wreck, Tasman's sailing, and Dampier's roving each get a full narrative, drawn from the voyagers' own accounts. The book traces how Europe slowly learned the shape of Australia. It serves as a compact, vivid history of discovery, told by the men who risked the southern seas. Pinkerton's notes link the three voyages into one story of slow discovery.
26615-black-beaver-the-trapper:
J. C. Lewis published this frontier memoir in 1911, calling it the only book by a trapper and covering twenty-two years with Black Beaver. Lewis opens by confessing he can neither read nor write. He dictated instead to his old backwoods chum, the Kidd. His brother rewrote the tale under orders to fix it up but not change it. The result is plain, boastful, tall-tale speech from a man of six-shooter literacy.

Black Beaver's travels run from the Amazon to the Mackenzie rivers, with four dog-team crossings of Alaska from Dawson to Point Barrow. Five hundred skins cached at Iditarod were to stock an Arctic Alaskan Educational Exhibition. Grizzly kinds, from silver tip to Kodiak, and hunts told in rough detail fill a book best read as a trapper's own legend of himself.
26622-how-to-read-the-crystal-or-crystal:
Sepharial, author of The Book of Cards and The Little Book of Magic, published this guide with Foulsham at London in 1922. It teaches crystal seering, the practice of seeing visions in a crystal, ovoid, or mirror, and it opens by admitting that no full scientific account of the phenomenon exists. Sepharial leans on atomic vibration and Swedenborg's doctrine of correspondences, by which every spiritual force has a matching material form.

Chapters set out the seer's qualifications, preliminaries, the vision itself, its difficulties, and its symbols, with some experiences from practice. Directions for using ovoids and spheres for crystal or mirror vision follow, and a concise dictionary of astrological terms closes the book. It is a period manual for readers curious about occult practice, not a work of modern science.
26662-the-first-distiller:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this comedy in six acts in 1886, in Louise and Aylmer Maude's translation. It opens with a peasant ploughing at noon, hungry for the chunk of bread his wife cut for him, while an imp hides behind a bush and steals it. The imp expects curses, but the peasant only says, let the thief eat it, and much good may it do him, leaving the devil at his wits' end.

In Hell, the Chief of the Devils complains that few peasants arrive, while tradesmen and gentlefolk flock in daily. A devil disguised as a labourer then works beside the peasant, horns and hoofs hidden, teaching him craft after craft toward a reckoning in the third year. Tolstoy's joke turns serious: the path to ruin runs through drink, and the first distiller is its inventor.
26695-make-or-break-or-the-rich-man-s-da:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William T. Adams, published this boys' story with Lee and Shepard at Boston, entered in 1868 and copyrighted in 1896. It is the fifth Starry Flag story, first serialized in Our Boys and Girls, and its preface promises excitement that warms hearts and stirs blood without corrupting young minds. Patient, striving, toiling Leo Maggimore and gentle, self-sacrificing Maggie are its models.

Chapters run from Mr. Wittleworth Gets Shaved and Boy Wanted through Mr. Checkynshaw's violence, Leo's workshop, Mon Pere, the mouse business, and Leo's wonderful performers to Wittleworth versus Checkynshaw. A banker, satisfied that Marguerite Poulebah is his lost daughter, traces her from a hospital through the Sisters of Charity to Strasburg. It is a moral adventure of work, family, and found identity.
26753-notes-and-queries-number-183-april:
This number of Notes and Queries, number 183, dated Saturday, April 30, 1853, priced at fourpence, calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, is When found, make a note of. Notes, queries, replies, and miscellaneous matter fill pages 421 to 442.

Notes include Joseph Burtt's proclamation of Henry VIII against possessing religious books, Latin and Latiner, inedited poems, round towers of the Cyclades, and Shakespeare correspondence. Queries ask about Jacob Bobart and his dragon, Bishop Berkeley's portrait, selling a wife, Inigo Jones, and whence the word Cossack. Replies cover the legend of Lamech, Lord Coke's charge, white roses, Psalmanazar, and photographic correspondence on glass baths and calotype negatives.
26828-a-red-wallflower:
Susan Warner, author of The Wide, Wide World and Queechy, published this novel with James Nisbet and Company at London, in a 1913 edition of the 1884 book. Warner's note insists the story's whole chain of skeleton facts is true. The denominational feeling in both families, and the forms it took, are part of that truth and no invention of hers.

An English family, headed by retired army officer Colonel Gainsborough, tall, thin, grey, and grave, settles in a small Connecticut shore village with no business and a life of placid domestic pleasure. Nobody can solve why he came, though whispers blame a disagreement with his relations. His wife, one little girl, and two old retainers, Christopher Bounder and Mrs. Barker, complete the household. Chapters run from dandelions and learning through college, dissent, strawberries, hay and oats, London, the Tower, and a settlement.
26896-notes-and-queries-number-76-april-:
A week before number 77, Notes and Queries issued number 76 on Saturday, April 12, 1851, at threepence, or fourpence stamped. Notes ask whether Shakespeare could have called Cleopatra yond ribald-rid nag of Egypt, citing the folio text where Enobarbus and Scarus watch the Antoniad and her sixty ships fly and turn rudder. C. Forbes writes on Browne's Britannia's Pastorals, and minor notes cover the sweat of thy brow, honeymoon, and fees at Westminster Abbey.

Queries seek the authors of the Rolliad and Pursuits of Literature, and an account of a large ancient wood-engraving. Minor queries cover Barlaam and Josaphat, the Knights of Malta, and general pardons. Replies treat Thomas May, the Duchess of Buckingham, the San Grail, the frozen horn, and Cromwell's dealings with the devil. Minor replies range from Gig Hill and God's Acre to a whale caught at Greenwich before Cromwell's death.
26897-notes-and-queries-number-77-april-:
Saturday, April 19, 1851, brought number 77 of Notes and Queries, priced threepence, or fourpence stamped, as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, borrowed from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of. Notes inside cover a Latin drinking song by Richard Braithwait, strange appearances in the sky by the Reverend A. Gatty, Douglas Jerrold on after me the deluge, and Bishop Thornborough's monument.

Queries ask for portraits of Spenser, for the vendace, and for the family of Queen Katherine Parr. Minor queries cover the word news, Quakers' attempt to convert the Pope, and religious teaching in German universities. Replies treat Sir Balthazar Gerbier, the travels of Baron Munchausen, Pope Joan, tobacco in the East, and swearing by swans. Notes on books, sales, catalogues, and notices to correspondents close the number.
26898-notes-and-queries-number-78-april-:
The last April number of Notes and Queries came on Saturday, April 26, 1851, at sixpence, or sevenpence stamped, opening with the proposed record of existing monuments. Notes give illustrations of Chaucer, number four, the academies of Sir Francis Kynaston and Sir Balthazar Gerbier, Shakespeare and Fletcher, and illustrations of Tennyson. Folk lore covers sacramental wine and the cure of disease by means of sheep, and Sydney Smirke writes on the Republic of San Marino.

Minor notes explain a surname's origin. A deserted infant found in a church porch was given the surname Denial, as one whom all deny, and christened Daniel from the same letters. Queries ask for the bellman and his history, the country of the Angles, and Dutch books published outside the Netherlands. Replies treat haybands in seals, the north side of churchyards, the Rolliad writers, Quakers' attempt to convert the Pope, and snail-eating.
26935-conservation-reader:
Harold W. Fairbanks wrote this school reader for the Conservation Series, published by World Book Company, Yonkers, in 1920, with photographs and color paintings. Its frontispiece shows the passenger pigeon, an extinct species. Its preface quotes Henry Fairfield Osborn: the momentum of conservation cannot yet halt and reverse destruction's tide. Only enlightened public sentiment, built by the schools, can save natural resources.

Thirty-one chapters move from how our first ancestors lived and how our needs differ. They treat the soil as the most important gift of nature, the use and care of water, and the enemies of the trees. They cover forest fires, government help for forests, and forest playgrounds. Later chapters ask what to do when coal, oil, and gas are gone. They mourn the tragedies of milady's hat and cape, and show how to bring wild creatures back again.
26956-alien-offer:
Al Sevcik's science-fiction short story opens with General James Rothwell facing an offer he cannot easily trust. Commander Aku, a golden-furred alien, tells him that Earth's children must board alien ships within a week, while a vengeful fleet waits in space.

Rothwell must weigh the aliens' promise of rescue against the chance of a trap, as parents watch their children loaded aboard and soldiers move against the ships. The story turns on one question: when strangers offer salvation on a deadline, how does a commander tell rescue from capture?
26957-star-mother:
Robert F. Young's short story Star Mother opens with Martha standing in her garden, watching her son rise as the first star of the evening. Terry, a young astronaut aboard Explorer XII, circles the earth in an airtight capsule, a boy grown up too soon on a celestial carousel.

Martha keeps her Tuesday egg route and answers her customers' questions while she waits for word that they can bring Terry down. The story's ache lies in a mother's pride and fear, and in her silent wish that the stars be left to God.
2696-elsie-venner:
Oliver Wendell Holmes first published this romance in the Atlantic Monthly as The Professor's Story, beginning in December 1859. Elsie Venner, a strange, beautiful girl, seems touched by something wild and serpentine, and a young doctor and a professor puzzle over her nature.

Holmes calls the book a romance, and he uses it to argue about heredity, will, and moral responsibility. The tale mixes New England village life with medical mystery, in Holmes's learned, witty prose. It remains a curious landmark, where a novelist doctor tests how far nature shapes a soul.
27101-life-of-rear-admiral-john-randolph:
Captain James Henry Rochelle's 1903 life of Rear Admiral John Randolph Tucker follows a naval officer who served three flags. Tucker commanded in the navy of the United States, then as captain and flag-officer in the navy of the Confederate States, and finally as rear admiral in the navy of Peru.

The book adds his presidency of the Peruvian hydrographical commission of the Amazon, with an appendix on navigating the upper Amazon and its tributaries. Battle scenes include the Galena and Monitor engaging batteries before Richmond, grounding a life of war, science, and far-flung service.
27115-the-cattle-baron-s-daughter:
Harold Bindloss's 1906 novel The Cattle-Baron's Daughter follows Hetty among the cattle-barons of the range country. Early chapters bring a portent, Hetty taking heed, and Muller standing fast, before Hetty comes home to face an incendiary, a sheriff, and a prisoner.

Larry proves intractable, stands trial, and wins acquittal, while Torrance warns and Hetty offers a bounty. Bindloss writes of range war, loyalty, and hard choices, with a fierce white frothing about a rider on the frontispiece, in the vigorous western style of his Alton of Somasco. The edition was published in September 1906 by Frederick A. Stokes Company. Larry's peril and a futile pursuit follow before the close.
27188-the-wonder:
J. D. Beresford's The Wonder, published by Doran in 1917 and dedicated to Hugh Walpole, unfolds in two parts: the narrator's early associations with Ginger Stott, and the childhood of the Wonder. Notes for a biography and the disillusionment of Stott open the book.

Stott enters his house with dread, not fear of his wife, but terror sleeping there, and rubs his armchair vigorously, as if a child of evil had polluted it. Later chapters trace the incipience, progress, and relaxation of the narrator's subjection to the Wonder, closing with release and the uses of mystery.
27198-the-explorer:
W. Somerset Maugham's The Explorer, published by Doran in 1907, opens on a desolate beach where a woman stands alone, her torment unassuaged by sea, sky, and silence. Nature, Maugham reflects, smiles with indifference on the light at heart and brings deeper sorrow to the heavy.

The novel follows an explorer whose golden city of dreams proves no more than a poverty-stricken village, a symbol of all earthly endeavours. Through Alec's studies and journeys, Maugham weighs ambition, love, and the price of a life spent chasing horizons. The book is dedicated to Mrs. G. W. Steevens. Maugham's copyright dates run 1907 with Heinemann and 1909 with Baker and Taylor.
27245-food-for-the-traveler:
Dora C. C. L. Roper's Food for the Traveler, published at Oakland in 1916 for twenty-five cents, promises what to eat and why, with over one hundred menus for three meals a day. Roper, a doctor of osteopathy, opens with a maxim: a person is made of what he takes in, from spiritual, mental, and physical food.

Long do-not-mix lists warn against fat pork and cucumbers, milk and meat, cooked vegetables and nuts, and potatoes with tomatoes or acid fruits. Menus run from clam broth and cream soup to rice with milk and fig butter, in a practical handbook for travelers who eat on the road.
27344-the-faithful-promiser:
The author of The Words of Jesus and The Morning and Night Watches wrote this devotional book, published by Stanford and Delisser in New York in 1858, from notes dated December 1849. Its plan is simple: take one Bible promise night by night, and plead it in prayer. It follows the example of the Psalmist who pointed to a particular word and said, remember thy word unto thy servant.

Each entry gives a text, such as Isaiah's promise that sins scarlet shall be as white as snow, under a heading like Pardoning Grace, followed by a short meditation. The pieces are gleanings from the promise treasury, meant for closet meditation or seasons of sorrow. Readers seeking a slow, daily devotional will find its method plain and steady.
27476-the-sign-of-the-spider:
Bertram Mitford, author of A Veldt Official and 'Twixt Snow and Fire, published this adventure novel with Dodd, Mead in 1897, from an 1896 copyright. Its chapters move from Sweet Home and Adam's first wife through warnings against unholy spells, a land of promise, King Scrip, and Pirate Hazon, toward a sign, a shadow, and a horror.

The hero passes dark days, a guardian angel, preparation, and the twelfth hour. He meets dissensions and two perils, and reaches Lindela, a place of horror, a deep solitary grave, and a farewell to his ideal. Mitford writes adventure with mystery and dread in the mix. Readers of late Victorian romance will find a fast, strange tale.
27534-cobwebs-from-a-library-corner:
John Kendrick Bangs published this book of verses with Harper and Brothers in New York and London in 1899, dedicated to Sister Anne. The verses had appeared from time to time in Harper periodicals and elsewhere, and Bangs gathers them here.

Contents run from Bookish and A Pessimistic View through Bookworm Ballads, Ideas for Sale, and The Author's Boomerang, to No Copyright Needed and Ingredients of Greatness. Later pieces include The Bibliophile's Threat, My Treasures, A Poet's Fad, and Satisfaction on Reading Walt Whitman. Bangs writes bookish humor with a light, teasing touch.
27550-the-mother:
Norman Duncan published this book of stories with Fleming H. Revell in New York, Chicago, and Toronto in 1905. H. E. Fritz designed the decorations, and Duncan dedicates the book to E. H. D.

Contents include By Proxy, The River, A Garden of Lies, The Celebrity in Love, At Midnight, and A Meeting by Chance. Later stories are called Renunciation, The Chorister, Alienation, A Child's Prayer, and His Mother, closing with Nearing the Sea and The Last Appeal. By Proxy opens at the distinguished funeral of old Senator Boligand, ordered by his young widow with exquisite taste. A child, a blonde lady, and a veiled man sit unnoticed in the shadows.
27594-an-eagle-flight-a-filipino-novel-a:
An Eagle Flight is a Filipino novel adapted from Noli Me Tangere by Dr. José Rizal, published by McClure, Phillips in New York in 1901, with a 1900 copyright. Its epigraph, from Timon of Athens, promises a bold eagle flight that leaves no track behind.

Chapters open with the house on the Pasig, Crisóstomo Ibarra, the dinner, and heretic and filibuster, then a star in the dark night and Captain Tiago and Maria. Later come Sisa and Basilio, the story of a schoolmaster, the story of a mother, and the meeting at the town hall. The eve of the fête, the sermon, the crane, and the procession follow. Rizal's novel of the Philippines under Spanish rule reaches English readers here.
27605-notes-and-queries-number-227-march:
Notes and Queries, a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, published this number, 227, on Saturday, 4 March 1854, at fourpence. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, runs: when found, make a note of.

Notes here treat Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy, the derivation of a Greek word for age, and William Lyons, Bishop of Cork, Cloyne, and Ross. A curious marriage agreement and ancient American languages appear too, with Conduitt and Newton. Minor notes cover music in Middleton's Witch and the phrase paid down upon the nail. Queries range from the Hunter of Polmood to fading ink and Sir Ralph Killigrew.
27611-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 361, dated November 1845, was published by William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London, and printed by Ballantyne and Hughes. Its contents mix fiction, history, poetry, and travel, as the magazine always did.

The number opens with The Student of Salamanca, part one, set on a September evening in 1833, as two young men step out. Humboldt, Hakem the Slave, and the Lay of Starkather follow, with Mozart and an account of a visit to the volcano of Kirauea. The Days of the Fronde, sketches of Italy, and pieces on railways complete a varied number.
27702-mr-stubbs-s-brother-a-sequel-to-to:
James Otis wrote this 1882 sequel to Toby Tyler, following Toby and his friends as they try to start a circus of their own. The boys have enthusiasm and Toby's circus knowledge, but no tent, wagons, or trained animals.

Chapters follow the scheme, a blind horse, a pony, a lost monkey, and a dinner party, building to a show that breaks up and the death of Abner. Illustrated and briskly told, the book mixes boyish adventure with the practical troubles of putting on a performance. The contents run from the scheme and a blind horse to stealing ducks, a lost monkey, and Abner's death.
27752-aphrodisiacs-and-anti-aphrodisiacs:
John Davenport privately printed these three essays in London in 1869 on the powers of reproduction, under the title Aphrodisiacs and Anti-Aphrodisiacs. The volume also gives an account of the judicial congress as practiced in France during the seventeenth century.

Davenport opens with ancient worship of the reproductive powers and then surveys substances and practices said to excite or restrain desire. Frank for its time and dense with historical and medical lore, the book is now read mainly as a document of Victorian attitudes toward sex, medicine, and the law.
27789-a-royal-prisoner:
Pierre Souvestre and Marcel Allain wrote this 1918 Fantômas detective novel, published in New York by Brentano's. It follows reporter Jérôme Fandor and Inspector Juve through a tangle of disguise, theft, and murder linked to the master criminal Fantômas.

Chapters run from a New Year's Eve celebration and a tragedy in the Rue de Monceau to a mysterious prison, a stolen diamond, and the arrest of Fantômas. Fast, lurid, and full of twists, the book shows why the Fantômas series thrilled readers across Europe and America. Later chapters include a kingdom called Hesse-Weimar, a queen named Hedwige, and an explosion on the Nord-Sud line.
27862-the-cauliflower:
A. A. Crozier wrote The Cauliflower, published in New York by the Rural Publishing Company in 1891, with testimonials from growers in Pennsylvania, Texas, and Wisconsin. One grower claims more money has been made per acre from cauliflower than from any other vegetable yet discovered.

Chapters cover origin and history, management of the crop, cauliflower regions of the United States, insect and fungus enemies, seed selection, varieties, broccoli, and cooking. Practical and thorough, the book shows American market gardening turning to a specialty crop near large cities. The book closes with cooking receipts, a glossary, and references, after a descriptive catalogue of varieties.
27983-the-orphans-of-glen-elder:
Margaret Murray Robertson wrote The Orphans of Glen Elder, opening with Aunt Janet's visit to a smoky town, after walking seven-and-twenty miles from the heather hills near Kirklands. Weary and anxious for her only brother's orphan children, she climbs a dark, narrow staircase to a fifth landing.

In a room she finds a boy of ten on a low bed, his face recalling her beloved brother, and familiar objects such as her father's desk and her mother's carved chair. Robertson's Scottish domestic tale follows orphans, kinship, and care, with the warmth and moral feeling of her popular fiction.
2810-plunkitt-of-tammany-hall-a-series-o:
George Washington Plunkitt, a Tammany Hall politician, explains his craft in these plain talks recorded by William Riordon from Plunkitt's rostrum at a New York courthouse bootblack stand. Plunkitt defends what he calls honest graft, meaning profit taken openly through knowledge of city business, and separates it from outright theft. Chapters cover becoming a statesman, holding a district, and the curse of civil service reform.

The talks give a firsthand view of machine politics, ward loyalty, and the exchange of favors that kept Tammany running. Plunkitt's voice is blunt, funny, and unashamed, and his advice on studying human nature still gets quoted. The book endures as the classic insider account of how urban politics actually worked.
28107-the-complete-golfer:
Harry Vardon, Open Champion in 1896, 1898, 1899, and 1903, wrote The Complete Golfer after his first American title in 1900. The book, first published in June 1905 with sixty-six pictures, mixes memoir with plain teaching. Vardon recalls his boyhood in Jersey, his start as a caddie, and his slow rise to the top of the game.

Later chapters work through grip, stance, swing, and play from tee to green, with notes on famous matches and rivals. Vardon's advice stresses steady practice and calm nerves over tricks. Golfers still read it as both a manual and a window on the game before the First World War.
28123-the-scarlet-feather:
Houghton Townley's The Scarlet Feather, published in New York in June 1909, is a novel of debts, love, and a family secret. Dora Dundas, tied to a household of sorrow and a tiresome patient, must choose between duty and a man she fears and tries to hate. Will Grefe drew the pictures, and the sheriff's writ that opens the book sets the trouble in motion.

Chapters follow dinners, confessions, a will, and a public confession, as Mrs. Swinton, Colonel Dundas, and Dick Herresford each press Dora toward a choice. A scarlet feather, at last, marks the truth. Townley keeps the plot brisk and the feelings plain, in the style of Edwardian romance.
28152-sword-and-pen-ventures-and-adventu:
John Algernon Owens wrote Sword and Pen: Ventures and Adventures of Willard Glazier, a life of the soldier-author Captain Willard Glazier. Glazier fought in the Civil War, was captured, escaped from prison, and later wrote popular books on battles, cities, and the great river. Owens gathers his campaigns, writings, and public career in one volume.

The book also lists Glazier's works, from Soldiers of the Saddle to Down the Great River, and adds publisher's notes on his claim about the Mississippi's source. Modern notes in the text correct that claim in favour of Lake Itasca. It serves as a record of a once-popular author-soldier.
28161-the-master-mummer:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's The Master Mummer, copyright 1904, is a novel of writers and artists chasing fame. Arnold, a young author with sheets of blank paper and much smoked tobacco, cannot choose among his brimming ideas. His friend Mabane, a tall Scotch painter in a smock, urges him to write something, even if he must tear it up.

The book follows their search for a subject worth immortality, through studios, talk, and false starts. Oppenheim, already known for Anna, the Adventuress and A Prince of Sinners, writes with wit about the artist's life. The novel amuses readers who know the itch to make something lasting.
28194-notes-and-queries-number-231-april:
Notes and Queries, number 231, for Saturday, April 1, 1854, is a weekly medium for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, priced at fourpence. Its notes treat Kennington Common, life and death, Trafalgar and Nelson's death, and a heraldic anomaly, with folk lore on three maids and Shrove Tuesday custom. Minor notes cover Jacobite clubs and an epigram falsely given to George Herbert.

Queries ask about quotations, Sir Edmund Plowden, an ancient clock, and a marvellous combat of birds, with replies on many points. The number shows Victorian scholars trading facts in print. It offers a snapshot of antiquarian talk in the spring of 1854.
28294-pilgrimage-from-the-alps-to-the-ti:
Rev. J. A. Wylie wrote Pilgrimage from the Alps to the Tiber in 1855 on the influence of Romanism on trade, justice, and knowledge. Wylie, author of The Papacy, travels from the Alps through Piedmont, Milan, Venice, Ferrara, Bologna, and Florence to Rome, noting Vaudois valleys, reformers, and the present as image of the past. Shepherd and Elliot published the book in Edinburgh.

Chapters treat constitutionalism in Piedmont, the Duomo of Milan, Venice as death of nations, and modern and ancient Rome. Wylie's tone is Protestant and earnest, praising reform and lamenting Rome's power. The book offers a Victorian pilgrim's view of Italy.
28309-christopher-hibbault-roadmaker:
Marguerite Bryant wrote Christopher Hibbault, Roadmaker in 1908, published in January 1909, as a novel of a workhouse boy and the road to London. On a hot July day, a small boy in workhouse garb loiters by a milestone sixty-three miles from London, parcelling the distance into days' journeys against the few pennies in his pocket. Grosset and Dunlap published the book.

Christopher's bitter memories of hungry days and fortune's shifts drive him to seek a better life. Bryant's dedication verse calls love the divine roadmaker, smoothing paths for those who follow. The novel offers a tender, earnest tale of a boy making his own road.
28342-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
November 1844 brought the 349th number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, a monthly miscellany published in Edinburgh and London. It mixed essays, fiction, verse, and comment for educated readers. Its lead piece argues that the House of Lords wrongly reversed the Irish State trials.

Daniel O'Connell and his fellow defendants had been found guilty by a jury. The Lords freed them on a technical point, and the magazine protests the decision. Other contents include a memoir of college friends, a poem signed Delta, French socialists, a serial instalment of Marston, poems by Elizabeth Barrett, and steamboat memories. Together they show British opinion in the mid-1840s.
28418-the-black-buccaneer:
Stephen W. Meader's The Black Buccaneer, copyrighted in 1920, opens on July 15, 1718, on the Penobscot Bay shore of Maine. A clumsy boat loaded with sheep makes its way against the tide, steered by Amos Swan, with his fourteen-year-old son Jeremy soothing the flock.

Jeremy, raised on the wild frontier, has already faced Indian raids and fought at a blockhouse loophole at twelve. His father leaves him alone on an island with the sheep, and the boy is soon drawn into the company of Stede Bonnet's rovers. Meader, who illustrated the book himself, writes a brisk pirate adventure for young readers.
28450-stopover:
William Gerken's short story Stopover is set in America after an atomic war that separated more than ten million families and destroyed their old way of life. The narrator and his wife Marty take in a tired young traveller who knocks at their door asking for food.

The boy, who calls Oregon home, is a Lifter: an axe hangs in mid-air in the shed where he works, held by no visible hand. Like other wanderers, he searches town records and signs the stopover book, hoping a relative passed the same way. Gerken's story links a strange new talent with the plain human need to find family after disaster.
28476-notes-and-queries-number-194-july-:
Two weeks later, the July 16, 1853, number of Notes and Queries carried the same weekly exchange for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. This number opens with notes on the derivation of the word island, weather rules, the modern practice of assuming arms, and Shakespeare correspondence.

Minor notes touch the Order of the Garter, an old ship, and the letter h in humble, while queries range from Bishop Gardiner to Lord Byron and Cromwell's portrait. Replies cover place names, cleaning old oak, and burial in an erect posture, with photographic correspondence on a new process. The issue shows Victorian readers pooling small facts into shared knowledge.
28477-notes-and-queries-number-195-july-:
The July 23, 1853, number of Notes and Queries, number 195, continues the weekly exchange at fourpence for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Notes here treat William Blake, a poem by Shelley not in his works, the impossibilities of history, and the Dance of Death.

Queries ask about fragments of manuscripts and the electric telegraph, while minor queries range from Sir Walter Raleigh to the Southwark pudding wonder. Replies cover authors' remuneration, hour-glasses in pulpits, and ladies' arms borne in a lozenge, with photographic correspondence on multiplying photographs. The issue again turns readers' small questions into shared knowledge.
28478-notes-and-queries-number-196-july-:
By July 30, 1853, Notes and Queries had reached number 196, still priced at fourpence for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its notes include books chained to desks in churches, real signatures versus false names, popular stories of the English peasantry, and Shakespeare correspondence.

Queries ask about Lord William Russell, ancient furniture, and a prie-dieu, while replies treat the Rosicrucians, inscriptions on bells, and whether Cook discovered the Sandwich Islands. Photographic correspondence covers stereoscopic angles and yellow bottles for chemicals. Like its sister numbers, the issue turns small questions into a shared conversation among readers.
28480-the-frontier:
Maurice Leblanc's The Frontier, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and copyrighted in 1912, is a novel of tension on the Franco-German border. Leblanc was already famous for Arsene Lupin, but here he writes a serious drama of nations and families rather than a detective tale.

The story opens at the Butte-aux-Loups, where old Morestal shows his wife through a telescope that the German frontier post has been felled with an axe, the third such incident that year. His son Philippe, his wife, and two women are drawn into lies, enquiries, and an armed vigil. The novel builds toward a thunderclap in which private choices carry the weight of war.
28483-legends-of-vancouver:
E. Pauline Johnson, writing as Tekahionwake, published Legends of Vancouver in 1911, with an eighth edition in 1913. Johnson credits the late Chief Joe Capilano of Vancouver as their teller, and the legends first ran in the Vancouver Daily Province.

Their first meeting came in London in 1906, during Capilano's visit to England, when Edward VII and Queen Alexandra received him at Buckingham Palace, where Johnson greeted him in Chinook. He shared them only when the mood took him, telling Johnson things no other English speaker had heard. The book preserves Coast Salish stories in Johnson's vivid prose.
28522-laura-middleton-her-brother-and-he:
Laura Middleton; Her Brother and Her Lover is an anonymous Victorian erotic novel, printed in 1890 under the St. Kitt's imprint. The narrator, visiting distant relations of his mother, renews an old friendship with Laura Middleton, a handsome girl two years older than himself.

Laura, her brother Frank, and the narrator form the triangle of the title, as the visitor uses what he has learned about Laura's private life to press his own advances. The novel belongs to the underground erotica of its period, and it is included here as a historical text of Victorian sexual writing, not as a mainstream romance.
28590-the-dust-flower:
Basil King's The Dust Flower, published by Harper & Brothers in 1922 with illustrations by Hibbard V. B. Kline, opens in a lovers' quarrel. Rashleigh Allerton tears his hair as his fiancée Barbara demands he choose between her and a set of club friends she calls profligates. She twists her engagement solitaire while he pleads that a cocktail or a glass of sherry undoes him.

From that strained engagement the novel follows Letty and the people around her through pride, tenderness, and second chances. The frontispiece shows Letty sinking to her knees, bowing her head on hands that draw her closer. Readers get a society romance about reputation, feeling, and the hard work of forgiveness.
28663-the-ranger-or-the-fugitives-of-the:
Edward S. Ellis's The Ranger, or The Fugitives of the Border, published by Hurst and Company of New York in 1911, opens on the Ohio. Sir William Leland, emigrated from Europe, built a large and imposing dwelling in the western wilderness. He and his wife died within a year of each other, leaving George, twenty, and Rosalind, seventeen, with a faithful servant.

Sir William had bought every foot of his land from its claimants, following Penn's example, and friendship held for three quiet years. Then terror breaks the peace, and Kent the ranger enters the tale. Chapters follow captives, a raft, a meeting on the river, Zeb's revenge, escape, and rescue. Readers get a border adventure of flight and pursuit.
2905-the-burning-spear-being-the-experie:
John Galsworthy wrote The Burning Spear as the wartime experiences of John Lavender, a dreamer who wanders England with a burning spear and a horse of air. Galsworthy later admitted authorship, calling the book revenge of the nerves against the dreads, strains, and griefs of war. The epigraph from Tom O'Bedlam sets the tone, with ghosts, shadows, and a tourney ten leagues beyond the world's end.

Lavender questions farmers about German prisoners, shouting at a stolid Englishman in a bowler hat and Bedford cords who gazes over his land. The comedy comes from a Quixote loose in wartime England, asking patriotic questions nobody wants. The book stands as Galsworthy's strangest war work, satire shaped by nerves rather than strategy.
29104-the-web-of-the-golden-spider:
Frederick Orin Bartlett published this adventure novel in 1909. Its chapters open with a closed door, a stranger's arrival, and a golden god that speaks, then move to gold and jewels long hidden, a stern chase, and strange fishing. Love and queens, powder and bullets, and the shadow of the Andes follow.

Bartlett mixes treasure-hunt excitement with romance, as his hero chases a hidden fortune through South American settings. Illustrations by Harrison Fisher and Charles Relyea add to the period flavor. Readers get a turn-of-the-century adventure yarn, brisk and colorful, about a web of gold that draws everyone it touches.
29110-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 360, for October 1845, volume fifty-eight, was published by William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London. Its contents include an essay on Montesquieu, a reminiscence of boyhood by Delta, De Burtin on pictures, and manner and matter. Marston, or the Memoirs of a Statesman, concludes, beside a famous piece on how the writers got up the Glenmutchkin railway.

The Montesquieu essay calls him the founder of the philosophy of history, beyond doubt. He first sought lasting causes behind the fate of nations and general laws for the rise and decline of peoples. Other pieces cover the science of languages, scrambles in Monmouthshire, and Neapolitan sketches. Readers get a single number of a great Victorian monthly, rich in history, humor, and criticism.
29170-the-hoofer:
Walter M. Miller Jr. wrote this science fantasy story about a space rover's return home. A spacer has no business with a family, the tale begins, but what can a young man do when his heart longs for a home? The rover, known by the pale goggle marks on his sunburned face, is tolerated and helped by strangers on his way.

The story follows his stumbling pursuit of a harassed housewife on a bus, his fall in the aisle, and his decision to sleep where he fell. Miller, praised as a brilliant newcomer, tells a wayfarer's return without pulling punches. Readers get a warm, sad story about homecoming after long absence, where time itself has changed the family left behind.
29196-mutineer:
Robert J. Shea wrote this science fiction story about Trooper Lane, a New York trooper hovering three thousand feet above Tammany Square. A cool cybrain, surgically implanted in him, works on his problem, but Lane has no patience left. Denied time off after fighting in Chicago, he bowled city police over at the armory and now plans to take his case over everyone's head to the mayor himself.

Lane flies on humming paragrav-paks, glaring down at the three towers bordering the square. Shea's tale turns on its title: a mutineer against his own force, with the deadliest weapon being man himself. Readers get a tense future-city story about a trooper pushed past his limit, told from inside his angry, hovering flight.
29203-ruth-fielding-at-briarwood-hall-or:
Alice B. Emerson published this girls' school story in 1913, the second Ruth Fielding book after Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill. Ruth arrives at Briarwood Hall, a beautiful old boarding school, where rival societies, the Upedes and the Fussy Curls, compete for new girls. A marble harp, a ghostly tribunal, and a campus mystery give the term its plot.

Emerson writes the familiar school-story pleasures: friendships, rivalries, pranks, and a heroine who solves what baffles others. The book was part of a long series for girls, with later volumes at Snow Lodge, Lighthouse Point, and Silver Ranch. Readers get a cheerful period school tale, and a good entry point to a popular series.
29296-the-ministry-of-intercession-a-ple:
Andrew Murray of Wellington, South Africa, wrote this plea for more prayer, published in London in 1898 in a third edition. Murray, author of Abide in Christ and Waiting on God, takes his text from Isaiah: watchmen on Jerusalem's walls who never hold their peace day or night. Intercession, he argues, is a ministry in its own right, not an afterthought.

Murray inscribes the volume to fellow ministers and gospel laborers he met at conventions across South Africa, from Langlaagte and Johannesburg to Durban, Pietermaritzburg, and Stellenbosch. Readers get a devotional classic of the prayer movement, earnest and practical, urging Christians to pray persistently for the church and the world.
29364-elements-of-foreign-exchange-a-for:
Franklin Escher, who lectured on foreign exchange at New York University, wrote this primer to teach bankers and merchants how money moves between countries. The fifth edition, printed in 1915 by the Bankers Publishing Company, builds from first principles: what bills of exchange are, who wants them, and why their rates rise and fall.

Chapters work through demand bills, cables, drafts, and the five main forces that shift exchange rates, with plain cases to show each step. The prose stays close to practice, not theory for its own sake. Students of old banking, trade, and the gold-era money system will find a clear, usable guide to a world before instant wire transfers.
29366-the-prisoner:
Alice Brown's 1916 novel, printed by Macmillan, centers on a woman whose life is bound by duty, care, and the quiet claims of kin. A younger sister, slender and sweet, guards the home with a mother's fostering care, while the heroine weighs love against the bonds that hold her fast. Brown, known for My Love and I and Rose MacLeod, writes in the restrained, domestic key of her best work.

The plot moves through home scenes, plain talk, and moral choice rather than grand events. What imprisons the heroine is not a cell but custom, conscience, and love itself. Readers who like early twentieth-century tales of women's inner lives will find a thoughtful, well-wrought novel about freedom sought inside a life of care.
29387-marcy-the-blockade-runner:
Harry Castlemon published this Civil War boys' novel in Philadelphia in 1891, in his War Series, with illustrations by George White. Marcy, the blockade-runner of the title, first appears with a visitor, then hides flags, while Beardsley betrays himself. Two narrow escapes follow, and a cat without claws crosses the plot.

Later chapters run the blockade itself, lose a prize from the Sumter, and ask the question at the book's heart: Union or Confederate, which? Julius falls into trouble, an enchanted looking-glass appears, and Marcy heads off for the fleet. Readers get a brisk Civil War adventure for young readers, full of escapes, secrets, and divided loyalties.
29416-the-mind-master:
Arthur J. Burks published this two-part novel in Astounding Stories in January and February 1932, combined here with the second part's recap removed. The novel is a sequel to Manape the Mighty, and its first chapter is titled The Tuft of Hair. Burks's archaic and variable spelling is preserved in this text.

The story opens with Ellen Estabrook whispering to Lee Bentley as their liner creeps up through the Narrows toward the Statue of Liberty. Ellen hopes a horrible nightmare is over. Burks then turns from a homecoming to the mind powers of the title. Readers get a pulp novel of mental mastery and menace, in two installments, from the early years of the science fiction magazines.
29423-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
William Blackwood and Sons published this number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 350, in December 1844, volume 56. The Edinburgh monthly, printed by Ballantyne and Hughes, mixed politics, fiction, and criticism for a conservative readership. Its contents show that range in a single month.

Contents include The Scottish Banking System, The Milkman of Walworth, Injured Ireland, and Singular Passages in the Life of a Russian Officer. Traditions and Tales of Upper Lusatia continue with The Moor Maiden, beside pieces on Edmund Burke, John Brown, Nelson's despatches, and Guizot. Readers get a month of a leading Victorian magazine, serious and varied, from the year before the Irish famine deepened.
2943-the-great-hunger:
Johan Bojer wrote The Great Hunger as a Norwegian novel of a man torn between art, love, and survival, translated by W. J. Alexander Worster and C. Archer. The book opens with a northwester gale roaring through a fjord in the long winter evenings, flinging boats up to fisher huts and lifting barn gangways like unwieldy birds. Maids fight their way on hands and knees to the cowshed at milking time.

The hero leaves Norway poor and unknown, watches his last home island sink below the sea rim, and returns to ask what life awaits him. A return at two in the morning finds his ship boring through thick woolly fog. The novel follows hunger in both senses, for food and for a life large enough to live.
29439-dr-sevier:
George W. Cable, author of Old Creole Days and The Grandissimes, set Dr. Sevier in New Orleans, in the world of Creole life he knew best. Charles Scribner's Sons printed the novel in a uniform edition with his other Louisiana books. Chapters follow the doctor himself, a young stranger, and a cast of Creole folk. Their scenes run through dinners out, the trough of the sea, and a heroine brought to bay, asking where her love has gone.

Cable writes with local color and moral care, tracing how pride, custom, and charity shape lives in the old city. The doctor stands at the center as healer, judge, and friend. Readers of American regional fiction will find a rich, humane novel of Louisiana, written by one of its finest chroniclers.
29472-select-conversations-with-an-uncle:
H. G. Wells published this 1895 book, third in the Mayfair Set, as a set of talks with an uncle now extinct, plus two other pieces of memory. The uncle, made affluent by chance in South Africa, holds forth on fashion, ideals, photography, music, marriage, and the perpetual discomfort of humanity. Wells frames each talk as a witty, half-serious sketch of late Victorian social life.

Readers meet the young Wells as a humorist: sharp, playful, and already keen on how people live and pose. The pieces are short, talky, and full of quotable turns on manners and modern life. Those who know Wells only as a prophet of science tales will enjoy this lighter, earlier voice, talking over tea about the world he saw.
29487-forever:
Ned Lang's short science tale follows Charles Dennison, a rich, careless inventor who works in his own small laboratory in Riverdale after Harvard, a hitch in the Navy, and study at M.I.T. Dennison's new find is plainly valuable and patentable, yet he guards it so poorly that a bullet from a silenced weapon chips a granite wall inches from his head. Only then does he grasp how many grasping hands feast on the work of the innocent.

Lang turns the tale on a wry, frustrating point: a discovery that will not stay discovered. Dennison's hunt for a way to keep his find safe drives the plot to its sharp close. Readers get a compact, clever story about invention, greed, and the hard cost of carelessness.
29533-the-red-hand-of-ulster:
G. A. Birmingham, author of Spanish Gold and Priscilla's Spies, wrote The Red Hand of Ulster in 1912, printed by Hodder and Stoughton in London and George H. Doran Company in New York. Birmingham tells much of the book in the impersonal manner of ordinary history, with himself as unseen spectator, while the rest rests on lived knowledge of Ulster life. The red hand of the title stands for the province and its fierce loyalties.

The novel treats Ulster politics, faith, and identity on the eve of Home Rule crisis, with humor and partisan warmth. Its narrator watches, judges, and takes sides with a light hand. Readers of Irish fiction and of the Ulster question will find a lively, partisan novel that captures a province at a moment of high tension.
29618-the-aggravation-of-elmer:
Robert Arthur's short tale opens in the darnedest traffic jam the narrator ever saw in White Plains, with Main Street gutter to gutter in stalled cars, trucks, and buses for two blocks. Nobody leans on a horn, and a quarter of the drivers peer under their hoods. The narrator hurries back to his shop, Biltom Electronics, Bill-Tom, get it, when Marge threads to the curb leading a small blonde girl of eight.

Arthur's tag line jokes that crowds would flock to Elmer, yet Elmer must lug his own door wherever he goes. The aggravation of Elmer drives a comic mystery of stalled traffic. Fans of Arthur will enjoy a witty, small-town tale with a science-fiction twist.
29642-hidden-water:
Dane Coolidge's 1910 western, printed by A. L. Burt Company of New York with color pictures by Maynard Dixon, opens after long, brooding days of sunshine in a land of clean-cut peaks. A tall cowman fresh down from the peaks orders a round, and his good humor is so broad that he invites everyone present to drink, sheepman included. A frontispiece warns that no sheepman was ever seen to fight, but this one must be watched.

Coolidge writes of hidden water, range war, and the clash of cattlemen and sheepmen in the dry country. The mouse of chapter one gives way to guns, threats, and a woman named Kitty. Readers of classic westerns will find a sturdy, sunlit tale of water, pride, and the range.
29650-the-greater-power:
Harold Bindloss, author of The Cattle Baron's Daughter and Lorimer of the Northwest, set The Greater Power in the Canadian West, printed in 1909 by Frederick A. Stokes Company of New York. Its chapters open overburdened, follow the trail to Waynefleet's ranch, and grant Laura Waynefleet's wish. Then come the flood, the breaking of the dam, and Laura making a dress. A frontispiece cries, I am afraid I am going to lose him, after all.

Bindloss writes of ranch life, water, and will, where nature's greater power tests human plans. The novel mixes romance with the hard labor of the frontier. Readers of western and Canadian fiction will find a sturdy, heartfelt tale of love and landscape.
29702-the-space-rover:
Edwin K. Sloat's tale, printed in Astounding Stories in February 1932, follows young Winford fleeing Mercury's prison mines. Evan Winford leans wearily against the controls of a little space sphere, staring at Mercury a million miles sunward. Mine guards search nearby mountains, and warnings broadcast to all planets to watch the little prison tender ship.

Six pairs of eyes look up at Winford, and Agar, forgetting he is a dog, stares with the rest at their ragged, unshaven company in dirty white canvas uniforms. Winford leaps out into space along a cable in a bid for freedom. Fans of early space pulp will enjoy a breathless escape tale of mines, guards, and the void.
29714-the-negro-farmer:
Carl Kelsey submitted The Negro Farmer to the University of Pennsylvania in partial fulfillment of the Ph.D., printed in Chicago in 1903 by Jennings and Pye at fifty cents. Its chapters run from introduction and geographic location through economic heritage and present situation, to social environment, outlook, and agricultural training. Virginia, the sea coast, the central district, and the alluvial region each get their pages.

Kelsey argues that religious sentiment against bondage did more than economics alone to shape the farmer's fate, and he maps Black farming across the South with care. The thesis remains a source on Black rural life after slavery. Students of agricultural and African American history will find a detailed, early sociological study.
29739-little-masterpieces-of-science-the:
George Iles edited this 1902 volume of Little Masterpieces of Science for Doubleday, Page, on the naturalist as interpreter and seer. Its authors are Charles Darwin, Alfred R. Wallace, Thomas H. Huxley, Leland O. Howard, and Iles himself. Darwin's summary of the Origin of Species opens the set, with fossil armadillos like living species seen on the Beagle voyage and Galapagos forms diverging island by island.

Each piece shows a naturalist reading nature as a text: observation turned to interpretation. The volume serves general readers who want science in the scientists' own words. Students of natural history will find a compact, classic anthology of Darwin and his heirs.
29776-pretty-madcap-dorothy-or-how-she-w:
Laura Jean Libbey wrote this romance of a New York working girl, with a copyright date of 1891. Dorothy is called the jolliest girl in the book-bindery, and the subtitle promises a magnificent love story of a beautiful, willful girl at work. The tale opens with her fellow binder Nadine Holt, who says working girls can hardly ever meet a lover at all.

They rise at daylight, swallow breakfast, and hurry to work, and it is dark before they reach the street again. A girl who must earn her living early, Nadine says, might as well give up hopes of marrying. Thirty-nine chapters follow Dorothy as she proves her friend wrong. Libbey keeps the tone gay, bold, and full of shop-floor talk.
29792-buffalo-bill-s-spy-trailer:
Colonel Prentiss Ingraham published this Buffalo Bill tale in 1908, subtitled The Stranger in Camp. It opens with a note on William F. Cody himself. Cody was born in Iowa in 1846 and rode pony express as a boy. Then he served as a scout and guide in the Civil War. His camp talk with Ned Buntline gave rise to the Buffalo Bill stories.

The tale itself moves from a hermit of the Grand Canyon and a miner's secret to masked foes, a strange burial, a dumb messenger, and a ransom. Buffalo Bill tracks outlaws, frees captives, and foils a spy's work in camp. Ingraham keeps the chapters short and the action steady, in the dime novel style that made Cody a folk hero.
29818-the-plunderer:
Roy Norton published this mining country novel in 1912, with a frontispiece in color by Douglas Duer. It opens at a rambling log road house, the stopping place for a mountain stage, with a watering trough, iron pails, and a rusted pump out front. Mountains stand hard and stern on every side. Into this place comes Bully Presby, whose name heads the first chapter.

The Croix d'Or, an ugly watchman, the black death, an aged engineer, and a dynamiter follow in the chapter list. A lady of the horse and a woman unafraid give the tale its heart, and a girl's advice turns more than one plot. Norton, who trailed and mined for years, writes the range with first-hand ease. The book is a brisk tale of claims, bullies, and love in high country.
29908-the-adventurer:
C. M. Kornbluth wrote The Adventurer, with pictures by Freas. Its epigraph says that for every evil under the sun there is an answer, simple and direct, or slow and seemingly unrelated, but an answer of a kind. President Folsom XXIV complains petulantly to his Secretary of the Treasury, Bannister, that he cannot understand why he cannot buy the Nicolaides Collection. It is such a bargain, he mourns, with an archaic Henry Moore figure and fifteen early Morrisons.

Bannister, with apprehension and a thread-like feeling across his throat, boils it down to no money. The Secretary of Public Opinion shakes his head at seizing the collection for the public good: the art lovers would howl in protest. Sales of the new Series W bond issue have fallen behind, Bannister starts to explain, before the president stops him. Kornbluth keeps the satire of power, money, and art brisk and dry.
29948-two-timer:
Fredric Brown offers a brace of vignettes here, short and sharp like a hypodermic, as the headnote puts it. Stone drew the pictures. The first vignette, Experiment, opens with Professor Johnson proudly showing his two colleagues a first time machine. It is a small-scale model, like a postage scale with two dials, and it works only on objects under three pounds, five ounces, for twelve minutes or less.

Johnson's test object is a brass cube of one pound, two point three ounces. He sends it five minutes into the future, and it reappears to the second. Then he tries five minutes into the past, and the paradox bites: the cube should vanish from his hand before he places it. Brown keeps the logic tight and the joke cold. The pair of vignettes shows the old vignette master at his best.
29954-there-is-a-reaper:
Charles V. De Vet wrote There Is a Reaper. Its headnote sets its bargain. Doctors gave a man just one month to live, leaving him that span to ponder what comes after death, and one way to learn is to ask a dead man. The narrator watches with a smile as his victim drinks amber brown liquor hiding poison.

The victim's contented look freezes to startled stillness, his body arches, and his voice chokes off deep in his throat. After a minute of rigid torment, the starch leaves his body and he slides down his chair, head limp against the seat. Then the narrator asks, Where are you? The moment has cost him sixty thousand dollars. The narrator himself had received a month to live from the state's best doctors three weeks earlier.
30003-law-and-laughter:
George A. Morton and D. Macleod Malloch wrote Law and Laughter, printed in London and Edinburgh in 1913 by T. N. Foulis, published in October 1913. Portraits of eminent members of bench and bar illustrate it. A Pasquin epigraph fronts it: as crafty lawyers try various arts to get a double cause and win applause, so does an author, rummaging his brain, try various methods to entertain.

Seven sections order the laughter: the judges of England, the barristers of England, the judges of Ireland, and the barristers of Ireland. The judges of Scotland, the advocates of Scotland, and the American bench and bar complete the survey. Portraits run from Lord Thurlow, the frontispiece from a painting by Thomas Phillips, through the Earl of Rosslyn and the Earl of Mansfield. The Earl of Eldon, Lord Kenyon, Lord Erskine, Lord Westbury, and Lord Brougham follow.
30114-the-journal-of-submarine-commander:
The Journal of Submarine Commander von Forstner was translated by Mrs. Russell Codman, with an introduction by John Hays Hammond Junior, and printed in Boston and New York in 1917 by Houghton Mifflin Company, published in November 1917. A frontispiece from Underwood and Underwood shows passengers and crew leaving a sinking liner torpedoed by a German submarine in the Mediterranean. The transcriber kept inconsistent hyphenation and corrected obvious typographical errors.

Eight chapters order the journal: ordered to command a submarine, breathing and living conditions under water, and submersion and torpedo fire. Mobilization and the beginning of the commercial war follow, with the journal's own part in the commercial war and the capture of two prize steamers. Off the coast of England and the method of sinking and raising ships complete the record. The journal gives a German submarine commander's own account of undersea war, from first command through commerce raiding.
30136-a-short-history-of-the-book-of-com:
William Reed Huntington, rector of Grace Church, New York, traces the Book of Common Prayer from its origins through its trials to the American revision of his own day. His short history covers the first English forms and the changes forced by politics and faith. It gives the 1892 outcome, with a tabular view of additions made at each revision from 1552 to 1892. Papers read before a liturgical class sit beside essays printed during the revision movement.

Thomas Whittaker published the volume in 1893, with papers on the Book Annexed, its critics, and its prospects, plus a sermon from before revision in 1878. Huntington writes as a churchman who took part in the work. The book blends history with a first-hand account of what was attempted, what was won, and what was left undone.
30187-death-points-a-finger:
Will Levinrew, also William Levine, opens a mystery novel in a daily newspaper at deadline, published by the Mystery League in New York and London in 1933. The tempo rises to its highest pitch as the paper goes to bed. Twenty typewriters hammer final paragraphs, new leads go on old stories, and news machines, telegraph machines, and two tickers add to the din. Copy boys shout, men at the horseshoe desk echo them, and sheets are snatched from machines before the type bars stop.

Discarded copy paper, newspapers, cigarette stubs, and burnt matches strew the floors, while coats and hats litter desks and battered chairs. Levinrew, author of Poison Plague in 1929 and three murder novels by 1932, knows the newsroom as a living organism in wild disorder. The novel promises a mystery told from inside that pressured, noisy world.
30210-comic-bible-sketches-reprinted-fro:
G. W. Foote offers comic Bible sketches reprinted from The Freethinker, in a first part published in London in 1885. His introduction notes that English letters already had comic histories, grammars, geographies, and law books, and Carlyle had foretold a comic Bible with horror. A French Bible Amusante had sold widely, and its irreverence, Foote says, crossed to England despite pious shock.

Progressive Publishing issued the short volume, and Foote recalls that the Freethinker itself had faced two prosecutions for blasphemy, a fact his foes loved to cite. The sketches treat sacred stories with deliberate laughter, in the manner of the French originals copied with more or less fidelity. As a period piece, the book shows Victorian freethought using humor as a weapon against guarded belief.
30214-the-red-hell-of-jupiter:
Paul Ernst sends Captain Brand Bowen to Jupiter in a complete novelette from Astounding Stories, October 1931. Commander Stone, grizzled chief of the Planetary Exploration Forces, recalls Bowen from leave and orders a low flight over the southern hemisphere's red area. A ship sent to explore the red spot a year before never came back, and Stone wants a report on what is wrong with that infernal death spot.

Bowen, the youngest officer in his division to wear the triple-V for distinguished service, takes the mission. Two fighting Earthmen fall to the Pipe-men, as their vanished comrades did, and learn the spot's secret. Chapter 1, The Red Spot, sets the mystery in plain pulp terms: a vast stain on a giant world, lost ships, and strange captors waiting below.
30218-joseph-the-dreamer:
Amy Steedman retells the story of Joseph for young readers, in a Nelson volume with pictures throughout. Joseph is still a little lad when his mother dies, and his father Jacob, who loved her above all, turns his love to Joseph and baby Benjamin. Elder brothers, grown men able to care for themselves, watch as Jacob makes Joseph his special favourite, dressing him in a beautiful coat of many colours.

Envy grows as the boy grows older, and his brothers ask why one child should be marked out for favour above the rest. A front picture shows Joseph later as ruler of Egypt, speaking to his brothers, so the retelling spans the whole arc from favoured son to power. Steedman writes in simple, warm prose, making an old Bible story clear and exciting for children.
30234-dead-ringer:
Lester Del Rey tells of Dane Phillips, a researcher desperate for one true success, in a short tale illustrated by Dick Francis. Phillips slouches in a window seat, watching morning crowds head to work, while editor Jordan skims his notes with an old, unreadable face. Tall and bony, Phillips has learned to look loose-jointed and relaxed whatever he feels, yet his oversized hands clench in his pockets until nails cut his palms.

Each tick of an old-fashioned clock throbs through his brain, each rustle of pages feels like a shot of adrenalin, and his mind pleads that this time it has to be right. Jordan finishes, shoves the folder back, reaches for his pipe, sighs, and nods slowly: a nice job of researching, fit for a Sunday feature. Relief floods Phillips so fast he nearly falls, braced against the seat, in unbelieving hope.
30235-six-centuries-of-english-poetry-te:
James Baldwin gathers typical selections from the great English poets, working backward from Tennyson to Chaucer across six centuries. Silver, Burdett published the volume in 1892, as the first book in a Select English Classics series arranged and annotated for school classes. Later volumes in the series, the publishers note, would add prose, drama of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and choice extracts from great essayists.

Baldwin, author of The Book Lover, selects poems that show each poet at his most typical, in an order that lets a class move from familiar Victorian verse back to medieval roots. The book suits teachers and general readers who want one compact shelf of English poetry, with notes to help, rather than a shelf of separate complete works.
30240-the-big-trip-up-yonder:
Gramps Ford, chin on hands on his cane, scowls at a five-foot television screen in a crowded future family tale by Kurt Vonnegut Jr., set in 2185, where privacy itself has grown rare. Gramps Ford scowls at a five-foot television screen and shouts at each news item that his generation did it a hundred years before. Emerald and Lou, seeking privacy on the balcony, must sit in the back row behind a long train of kin: parents, siblings, children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren.

All but Gramps seem in their late twenties or early thirties by older standards, since anti-gerasone halted aging. Gramps, already seventy when the drug appeared, has not aged in the hundred and two years since, and stays withered and bent. Kossin drew the pictures, and the story's joke is plain: a family that never thins out must still find room for one more generation.
30271-the-grecian-daughter:
Arthur Murphy's tragedy in five acts, The Grecian Daughter, comes as performed at the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, printed from the prompt book under the managers' authority. Longman, Hurst, Rees, and Orme published the London text, with remarks by Mrs. Inchbald, and a plate shows Euphrasia crying behold all Sicily, as the point glows with the tyrant's blood. The play had won rapturous applause on stage, Inchbald notes, while critics in the closet judged it severely.

Her remarks take the good-natured side first, praising splendour of decoration, glow of martial action, events of deep interest, and a moral of excellent tendency at the close. On its first appearance, she says, the tragedy met brilliant success and still held a place among dramas performed every season. Readers of Georgian theater will find a stirring, moral tragedy in its acting text.
30273-tom-and-maggie-tulliver:
Tom and Maggie Tulliver retells George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss for young readers, in a Nelson volume from London, Edinburgh, and New York in 1909. Mr. Tulliver of Dorlcote Mill wants Tom to have a good education, not merely two years at the academy fit for a miller and farmer. He plans to take Tom from the academy at Lady Day and place him at a downright good school at Midsummer, so the boy may become a bit of a scholar.

Chapters follow Tom to school, his choice of school, his homecoming, a jam puff, a family party, magic music, and Maggie's naughtiness. Maggie runs to the gipsies, the gipsy queen abdicates, and Philip enters beside a new schoolfellow and the Duke of Wellington. A frontispiece shows Tom running to stop Maggie snatching her line away, in a gentle abridgement of a great novel.
30286-the-phantom-lover:
Ruby M. Ayres tells The Phantom Lover, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1921, under a copyright by W. J. Watt and Company. Ayres, author of A Bachelor Husband and The Scar, dedicates the book to her friend Janet Moore, the real June Mason in the story. Somewhere out in the night a woman cries, a monotonous sound breaking the silence of the street and floating through the window of Micky Mellowes's room.

Micky, in a bad temper, wonders how he shall get through the evening before him. He woke with a headache and learned half an hour before that his dinner party is off, owing to the death of a relative. New Year's Eve makes matters worse, and he wonders whether Marie Deland feels as sick about it as he does. His flirtation with Marie bids fair to develop into something deeper, with engineering on his part.
30287-modern-americans-a-biographical-sc:
Chester M. Sanford and Grace A. Owen, both of Illinois State Normal University, gather twenty-seven short lives for upper-grade school readers, published by Laurel Book Company in 1918 and 1921. Calvin Coolidge opens, as the narrator sits in an old-fashioned hotel in a small Vermont village, having come from the broad prairies of Illinois to catch a little of Coolidge's spirit. Thomas A. Edison, Alexander Graham Bell, and Theodore Roosevelt follow.

Later lives treat John Pershing, William Howard Taft, Luther Burbank, Clara Barton, George W. Goethals, and James Whitcomb Riley, with Helen Keller, the Wright brothers, and Robert E. Peary among them. William Jennings Bryan, Henry Ford, Jane Addams, Andrew Carnegie, Woodrow Wilson, Mark Twain, and Warren G. Harding close the set. The reader suits classes that want modern heroes in plain, brief stories.
30348-the-last-supper:
T. D. Hamm tells a short, chilling tale of pursuit on a frozen Earth, introduced as a jolt and a chill. Guldran chases a woman hampered by a child in her arms, running less fleetly now, while exultation drowns his uneasy guilt at disobeying orders. Those orders were mandatory and concise: no capture alone, any human life reported to the ship at once, and all small craft back an hour before take-off.
