Barrie's chapters mix humor with tenderness: night watchers, a military cloak, a mud house tragedy, and a dance to a woman's piping. The minister must face his own pride and his flock's gossip. The novel endures as a warm, comic portrait of a small town and a man caught between duty and heart.
33952-what-you-can-do-with-your-will-pow:
Russell H. Conwell wrote this book on will power, copyrighted in 1917 by Harper and Brothers as volume one of a National Extension University set. Conwell, a lecturer and preacher for more than fifty years, tells young men and women that success holds no hidden secret. Will, he says, is the voice crying in the marketplace and the wilderness.

The future, Conwell argues, stands like a block of unwrought marble, to be shaped by firm, driving determination, health, and intelligence. Neither birth nor surroundings need bar the way. The book offers a classic American gospel of effort and resolve.
33967-descriptions-of-new-hylid-frogs-fr:
William E. Duellman published this 1968 study of new tree frogs in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series. No fewer than nineteen new species of hylid frogs had been found and named in Mexico and Central America in the past decade. Most lowland kinds were long known, so most novelties came from the less easy highlands.

Duellman studied hylid frogs across the region in the spring and summer of 1966, with close work on Hyla and related genera. The paper describes the new kinds with plates and measures. It serves frog students who need exact, first-hand accounts of these small-range species.
33985-manslaughter:
Alice Duer Miller wrote this novel of New York society, published in 1921 with pictures from the Paramount photoplay. Its heroine, Lydia, faces temptation, a theft, and an investigation by O'Bannon, while a bracelet she has seen and shrunk from haunts the plot. Scenes of sobbing, dread, and a firm hand on a shoulder mark the tale.

Miller, author of Come Out of the Kitchen, writes of wealth, law, and a woman's name at stake. The novel asks how far a rich young woman can go before the law catches her. It remains a brisk, dramatic tale of the Jazz Age's bright surface and hard edge.
34023-the-bread-line-a-story-of-a-paper:
Albert Bigelow Paine wrote this story of a newspaper, published in New York in 1900 by the Century Company, with copyrights in 1899 and 1900. Paine dedicates the book to those who have started papers, thought of starting papers, or are thinking of starting papers. Chapters open with a first dinner and Frisby's scheme.

Letters between Truman Livingstone of New York and Dorothy Castle of Cleveland carry much of the tale. Premiums, cash for names, the sanctum, and the gentle art of advertising fill the way. An hour of dark foreboding, final straws, and the end of the rainbow close the arc. The book offers a lively tale of paper-making.
3403-the-register:
William Dean Howells sets this short farce in an upper room of a Boston boarding house in Melanchthon Place. A plain young lady, newly arrived, puts small touches of decoration around her room while she talks with a friend in the next room. The friend, Ethel Reed, teases her about a young man and about country places with fanciful names.

The comedy turns on gossip, vanity, and the small wars of boarding house life. Howells builds the scene from voices heard through a doorway, so much of the fun lies in what is overheard and half understood. Like his other farces, the piece is short, dialogue driven, and best read as a play for the ear.
34069-a-kut-prisoner:
H. C. W. Bishop wrote this account of a Kut prisoner, published in London and New York in 1920 by John Lane, the Bodley Head, in the On Active Service series. Bishop dedicates the book to the memory of all British and Indian officers and men of the Kut garrison who suffered and died in captivity. Pictures show Kastamuni and its castle rock.

Chapters run from Ctesiphon and Kut through the march to Kastamuni, life there, escape, the first night, hills, slow progress, bluffing peasants, and reaching the coast. Recapture, rescue, hiding with Turks, delays, three days on the Black Sea, and the Crimea and home close the tale. The book offers a vivid prisoner-of-war story.
3410-the-american-spirit-in-literature-a:
Bliss Perry traces American writing from its first settlements to the early twentieth century in this volume of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1918. Chapters move through the pioneers, first colonial literature, later colonial generations, the Revolution, and the Knickerbocker group of New York writers.

Perry asks what holds American literature together across such change. He follows the shift from sermons and colonial pamphlets to a national voice shaped by war, growth, and new wealth. The book works as a short history for general readers, giving names, periods, and themes without demanding prior study of each author.
34100-lefty-locke-pitcher-manager:
Burt L. Standish's 1916 baseball novel follows Lefty Locke, a pitcher who is offered a manager's post. The offer comes with tangled deals, a shadowy backer named Weegman, and a mystery player whose true aims stay hidden for much of the book.

Thirty-seven chapters carry Lefty from the mound to the manager's bench, through tests of nerve, temptation, and games where one bad call can undo a season. Young readers get both a sports tale and a puzzle, as Lefty must judge men as sharply as he judges pitches. Standish had already told Lefty's tale in earlier books of the bush and the big league.
3412-the-golden-chersonese-and-the-way-t:
Isabella Bird records a trip across the Malay Peninsula in this travel book, whose old name for the region gives the title. The Golden Chersonese was the ancient Greek name for the peninsula, and Bird describes the route to reach it as well as the place itself. She travels by river and road through settlements, forests, and towns that few British readers then knew at first hand.

Bird writes as a keen observer of people, houses, markets, and local rule. She notes Malay customs, Chinese and Indian settlers, and the work of tin mines and plantations. The book remains valuable as a first hand account of Southeast Asia in the late nineteenth century, written by one of the great women travelers of her age.
3422-the-life-of-the-fly-with-which-are-:
Jean Henri Fabre studies flies and their kin in this volume of natural history essays, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. The chapters move from the harmas, Fabre's stony field laboratory in Provence, to the anthrax fly, the greenbottles, the gray flesh flies, and the bluebottle in its egg and grub stages. Two chapters pause for the author's memories of school and of mathematics.

Fabre watches living insects with patience, noting how parasites lay eggs in maggots and how larvae change form. He explains his terms in plain language and adds notes where a name might puzzle a reader. The book suits anyone curious about insects, field observation, and a scientist who wrote with the eye of a storyteller.
3478-legends-of-vancouver:
Pauline Johnson, whose Mohawk name was Tekahionwake, retells Coast Salish legends of the Vancouver region in this book. Johnson was the daughter of George Johnson, head chief of the Six Nations, and his English born wife Emily. A friend's preface notes that a poet has arisen to cast her art over the grey mountains, trails, and shores of British Columbia.

The legends explain peaks, inlets, and landmarks through stories of chiefs, spirits, and transformations. Johnson heard many of them from local storytellers and shaped them in graceful English prose. The book remains a treasured bridge between Indigenous oral tradition and Canadian literature, and it suits readers who love place based tales.
349-the-harvester:
David Langston, a harvester of the woods, lives by Thoreau's ideals in a modern age. Gene Stratton-Porter's Harvester follows David from Belshazzar's decision through forest harvests to a quest for a dream girl. Ruth Jameson, a city girl, and Granny Moreland join his story.

Chapters cover demonstrated courtship, snow wings, and love invading science. David's cleanliness, poetic temper, and mental force mirror Thoreau, as the book's dedication claims. Stratton-Porter's nature lore fills every chapter. The novel closes her Limberlost-era romances. Stratton-Porter's harvester closes her series of nature romances.
354-the-story-of-a-pioneer:
Anna Howard Shaw tells her own life in this memoir, written with Elizabeth Jordan. Shaw recalls first memories, a hard youth in the Michigan woods, and school and college days that led her to preach and to practice medicine. The book then follows her into the long fight for votes for women.

Chapters name the work plainly: the wolf at the door, a divided flock, Cape Cod summers, and years with Susan B. Anthony, called Aunt Susan here. Shaw later led the national suffrage group and built homes of her own. The memoir reads as a pioneer's plain record, proud yet free of boasting.
3624-chaucer:
Adolphus William Ward writes a short critical life of Geoffrey Chaucer in this volume of the English Men of Letters series. Ward builds the life partly from public records, such as the Royal Wardrobe Book, the Exchequer Issue Rolls, and the Customs Rolls, and partly from the poems themselves. He also leans on the work of the Chaucer Society, above all its director Frederick Furnivall.

The book traces Chaucer from court and customs work to the Canterbury Tales, explaining his language, his sources, and his humor for general readers. Ward differs at times from other scholars, including Fleay, and he notes those doubts with care. The volume suits readers who want a compact, scholarly introduction to England's first great poet.
3633-jezebel-s-daughter:
Wilkie Collins writes a sensation novel that he presents as a standalone work, not a sequel to his previous novel The Fallen Leaves. In his preface he explains that The Fallen Leaves had reached only a limited class of readers in England. That was due to the forms of publication used so far, and a cheap reprint would come later. This new novel therefore stands on its own, with its own heroine and mystery.

The story follows a young woman caught between a powerful mother figure and a secret from the past, in Collins's familiar mix of romance, villainy, and legal intrigue. Readers who enjoy his sensation fiction will find a brisk plot and a heroine who must fight for her name. The book suits those who like Collins without needing his earlier novel first.
3634-the-guilty-river:
Wilkie Collins writes a short mystery novel set beside a river, where a moth collector's quiet hobby turns strange. The narrator, snaring moths in the woods, reaches for a large specimen and meets an apparition that changes his summer. Later chapters introduce a deaf lodger, a portfolio that returns, a game played by Mrs Roylake, repeated warnings, and a claret jug that holds a clue.

The river itself becomes a character, carrying secrets and bodies of evidence. Collins builds suspense from small details and half understood meetings. The book suits readers who enjoy his shorter sensation tales, with a compact plot, a vivid riverside setting, and a mystery that unfolds by hints.
3669-a-woman-hater:
Charles Reade writes a novel that opens at the Golden Star hotel in Homburg, a modest house used by travelers rather than gay gamblers. At two o'clock on a fine June day, two strangers sit at small tables far apart in the dining room, absorbed in their own thoughts. One is a sharp faced, middle aged man of business, Joseph Ashmead, an operatic and theatrical agent who scribbles hasty letters.

The story follows a man who calls himself a woman hater and the women who prove him wrong, through theater, business, and romance. Reade writes with energy and strong feeling, as in his other sensation novels. The book suits readers who enjoy Victorian melodrama with a hero whose prejudice must yield to love.
3782-huntingtower:
John Buchan sends Dickson McCunn, a retired Glasgow grocer, on a walking holiday that turns into a rescue tale. McCunn, a decent and bookish man, wanders into a Galloway village where a captive princess and foreign plotters hide behind quiet walls. A bachelor's den, with red paper, a fire, and a whisky decanter, becomes one unlikely council chamber as local allies gather.

Buchan writes with a light hand for a thriller, letting an ordinary hero grow brave by steps rather than by bluster. The Scottish countryside, its speech, and its stubborn folk carry much of the charm. Readers who like adventure with humor will find Huntingtower a fine entry to Buchan, with suspense that never quite loses its smile.
3828-simon-the-jester:
William Locke opens this comic novel at a London club, where the knowing Renniker answers every question, from trimming a puppy's tail to the mind of any European potentate. Asked for the most God forsaken spot in England, Renniker names Murglebed-on-Sea, a south coast watering place in the fine flower of November desolation. The narrator sends his man Rogers to inspect it, and Rogers returns like a servant who expected a pantry and found a desert.

Later scenes bring Colonel Bunnion, a genial red faced man with a moustache too big for his body. A small figure in a devil of a top hat butts him in the stomach and bounds off like a football. Locke writes with light irony throughout. Readers who like Edwardian comedy will find a tale of odd places and odder people, told with a smile.
3831-the-secret-power:
Marie Corelli sets this mystical romance in the hills of Southern California, above the Sierra Madre. A bearded man lives in a roughly built hut with papers and books neatly piled, reading through the heat while a great cloud sails overhead like foam on a sea wave. He claims a discovery given by a Supreme Intelligence, a power meant to rid the earth of mischief, disease, and sorrow.

His friend Gwent questions him, asking why man should not leave such work to the Supreme Intelligence itself. The hermit answers that man exists to help the scheme of the universe, not hinder it, and must destroy hindrance wherever it stands. Corelli writes with earnest grandeur throughout. Readers who like spiritual romance will find a tale of faith, science, and high purpose.
396-the-lady-or-the-tiger:
Frank Stockton poses a famed riddle in this short tale of a semi-barbaric king and his arena of poetic justice. Accused men must pick one of two doors: behind one waits a fair lady, behind the other a hungry tiger. When the king's daughter loves a young courtier, her lover faces the same cruel choice.

Stockton ends without telling which door the youth picks, leaving readers to weigh love, jealousy, and pride. The tale's fame rests on that open end, which has sparked debate for generations. Brief and polished, it shows how a simple puzzle can outlive whole novels.
4053-nuttie-s-father:
Charlotte M. Yonge's novel follows Nuttie, a girl in a fresh Holland Sunday dress worked with wild strawberries by her mother's hands. In a small drawing room, nearly pushed in by Mr. Dutton, she meets a lady on the sofa through a daze of tears.

A chapter heading from King Lear frames the scene: a father wonders if the lady before him is truly his child. Yonge builds the story from family duty, faith, and the slow repair of broken ties. Readers who like Victorian domestic novels will find a gentle tale of a daughter, a father, and a home learning to hold together.
4070-the-master-builder:
Henrik Ibsen's play follows Halvard Solness, a master builder who fears the young, above all Ragnar, and schemes to keep a talented young woman in his office. If he could get her into the office, he thinks, then Ragnar too would stay where he is.

Solness tells Dr. Herdal how he stood, looked, and wished intently, speaking to her in a friendly way about one thing and another before she went away. Ibsen turns that wish into a study of ambition, guilt, and the price of building high. Readers who like serious modern drama will find a tense, symbolic play about power and fall.
4082-the-barrier:
A northern adventure novel opens with a song in dialect, as Poleon Doret sings of two brown eyes that changed everything for him. Clouds lift from the sky, winter feels like spring, and his pack grows light on the trail.

He sings of walking forty miles in a night to hear one song, and of making a fortune to marry the girl he loves. The Barrier, by Rex Beach, sets love and gold-seeking against the hard country of the far North. Readers who enjoy frontier romance will find a brisk tale of trails, traders, and stubborn hope.
414-the-pageant-of-summer:
Richard Jefferies celebrates one English summer in this short prose poem of fields and lanes. Green rushes, hawthorn, angelica, and wild parsnip fill the opening pages, each plant noted for scent, sap, and shape. Birds, pollen, and ditch water join the slow march of heat and growth.

Jefferies writes with a naturalist's eye and a poet's ear, letting small sights carry large feeling. No plot disturbs the pageant; the season itself is the hero. The book endures as a classic of nature prose, best read slowly, like a walk through high summer grass.
4284-the-window-gazer:
Isabel Ecclestone Mackay wrote this novel around Professor Spence, who begins the story perched on an upturned keg in a foggy coast city. No one warned him about the fog, and its swift arrival leaves him shivering and out of sorts. He is a reasonable man, but the day has turned strange in fifteen minutes.

The title points to the book's theme: people who watch life from outside, like gazers at a window, rather than buying what pleases them within. Mackay follows Spence and his circle through letters and encounters, mixing humor with a study of loneliness, learning, and the wish to belong.
4303-denzil-quarrier:
George Gissing opened this novel in a silent room at dusk, where Lilian sits with a large open volume she is not truly reading. The cat sleeps on the hearthrug, the fire has sunk to a red glow, and the cold autumn light thickens outside. Lilian's pose, an old childhood habit, invites reverie as a way of passing long, solitary hours.

From that quiet opening the story follows Denzil Quarrier and the woman at its center through love, doubt, and social pressure. Gissing's interest lies in inward life: what people think while they seem idle, and how silence shapes a marriage. The novel is slower than his London panoramas, and more intimate.
4308-the-town-traveller:
George Gissing wrote this comic novel around Mr. Gammon, who breakfasts in bed and sets out on a London quest. The contents promise a missing uncle, a china shop, Polly and Mr. Parish, a head waiter at Chaffey's, and a lord's will. Gammon's craft, Polly's wrath and defiance, and a pursuit of a brougham keep the plot busy.

Unlike Gissing's grimmer London novels, this one leans toward farce. Wills, names, and mistaken identities drive the action toward a double event and New Year's Eve. Readers who know Gissing only as a novelist of poverty will enjoy his lighter touch here, with London streets and shops as the stage.
431-the-fortune-hunter:
David Graham Phillips follows a handsome, penniless German actor named Feuerstein through New York society in this novel. Feuerstein, down to a ten-cent piece, lives by looks, nerve, and unpaid tailors. He hunts a rich wife with bold charm, and each conquest brings fresh risk.

Phillips tracks his hero through salons, quarrels, and a bold dash that ends in disaster. Love, pride, and hunger for rank tangle at every turn. The novel reads as a sharp study of a man who sells himself for fortune, and of a city eager to buy the act.
4316-the-romance-of-the-colorado-river:
Frederick S. Dellenbaugh, a member of the United States Colorado River Expedition of 1871 and 1872, wrote this history of the river's discovery and exploration. He begins with Ulloa in 1539 and Alarcon's ascent, then follows Onate, the trappers, Fremont, and Lieutenant Ives toward the great canyons.

The heart of the book is John Wesley Powell, the one-armed knight who attacked the canyons by boat, faced cataracts and short rations, and returned for a second voyage. Dellenbaugh tells the story with maps, pictures, and a member's knowledge. It remains a readable history of how the Colorado and the Grand Canyon became known.
4493-the-case-of-general-ople-and-lady-c:
George Meredith wrote this comedy around General Ople, a retired officer who hires a pony-carriage for an excursion beyond London's suburbs. He crosses a famous common, falls in love with it at once, then exchanges his heart for a lofty highway along a park's borders. Gradually he comes within a stone's throw of the riverside.

There he determines to bestow himself near Lady Camper, and the case of the general and the lady unfolds as a comedy of courtship, neighborhood, and military manners. Meredith treats an old soldier's second campaign, for a home and a wife, with gentle irony. The tale is short, witty, and characteristic of his lighter manner.
4622-trials-and-confessions-of-a-houseke:
T. S. Arthur published Trials and Confessions of a Housekeeper at Philadelphia in 1859. Part of the matter had already appeared as Confessions of a Housekeeper, but the book is now considerably increased. Its range covers the grave and instructive as well as the agreeable and amusing. Arthur is sure no lady reader familiar with housekeeping trials will fail to recognise her own experiences, since nearly every picture is drawn from life.

Chapters include a speculation in china ware, something about cooks, light on the subject, and cheap furniture. They go on to ask whether it is economy, to living at a convenient distance, a picked-up dinner, and who is Kriss Kringle. Later chapters cover shirt buttons, pavement washing in winter, regard for the poor, house cleaning, and broiling a lobster. Readers get a lively, practical Victorian housekeeping book, full of humour and hard-won sense.
4670-lightfoot-the-deer:
Thornton W. Burgess tells Lightfoot the Deer for children, opening with Peter Rabbit meeting Lightfoot. Later chapters follow Lightfoot's new antlers, and Lightfoot telling how his antlers grew, with the spirit of fear, Sammy Jay bringing word, and a game of hide and seek. The merry little breezes help Lightfoot, wit meets wit, and Lightfoot grows uncertain before a clever trick turns the tables.

The hunted watches the hunter, Lightfoot visits Paddy the Beaver, and the two become partners, with Paddy warning Lightfoot of danger. Three watchers, visitors to Paddy's pond, a hunter losing his temper, a dreadful sound, hounds got rid of, and a long swim follow. The hunting season ends, a mystery is solved, and a surprising discovery closes the tale. Readers get a gentle woodland adventure about fear, wit, and friendship.
4674-tennessee-s-partner:
Bret Harte's Tennessee's Partner appears here as Western Classic number three, with an introduction by William Dallam Armes. Its epigraph calls both men fearless types of a civilisation that in the seventeenth century would have been called heroic, but in the nineteenth was simply called reckless. Armes sets the tale in California after Marshall's discovery brought thousands of adventurers from almost every class and country.

Government in California then stood at its worst, Armes says, with an unpopular Mexican system and law practically unknown, until Congress made other provision. Free and slave states stood equal in number, California would turn the scale, and the congresses of 1848 and 1849 left the battle unsettled. Yet the worst elements did not win, and a de facto government was accepted. Readers get a classic Harte tale of gold-rush friendship, loyalty, and rough justice.
4677-our-world-or-the-slaveholder-s-daug:
Our World, or The Slaveholder's Daughter, published at New York and Auburn in 1855, presents itself as an honest tale plainly told. Its preface expects charges of misrepresenting Southern society and misconstruing facts, and it urges champions of things as they are to read and digest what follows. The authors believe readers will find truth stranger than fiction, and they aim to give a true picture of Southern society in its various aspects.

Slavery, they argue, is directly chargeable with the moral, social, and political evils detailed in the book. They offer the work as an incentive to those, North or South, who would rid the country of its darkest, foulest blot. Contents open on Marston's plantation, a night spent there, and things not so bright as they seem. Readers get a strong anti-slavery novel of its day, plain in style and urgent in purpose.
4699-we-of-the-never-never:
Jeanie Gunn, Mrs. Aeneas Gunn, wrote We of the Never-Never, dedicated to the bush folk of the Never-Never. Its prelude introduces the people of an Australian cattle station. They include the Maluka, the Little Missus, the Sanguine Scot, the Head Stockman, the Dandy, the Quiet Stockman, the Fizzer, Mine Host, and the Wag. Guests, a few Black boys and lubras, dogs, Tam-o'-Shanter, Happy Dick, Sam Lee, and Cheon follow.

Cheon, crudely recorded on station books as cook and gardener, is ever mirthful, ever helpful, and irrepressible. Behind the main figures moves a medley of Whites, Blacks, and Chinese, travellers, overlanders, and billabongers passing through. Gunn writes the Northern Territory with warmth, humour, and close observation. Readers get a classic Australian station memoir, full of bush life, hardship, and affection for a remote world.
4759-the-romance-of-rubber:
The Romance of Rubber, edited by John Martin, editor of John Martin's Book, The Child's Magazine, was published by the United States Rubber Company as a booklet for young readers. Its contents cover The Discovery, Charles Goodyear, The Hevea Tree, and Wickham's Idea, then Plantation Development, Plantation Life, and Harvesting the Rubber, closing with A Last Word. An introductory note explains why the company printed it.

The company, as the largest rubber manufacturer in the world, wanted coming generations to understand rubber's importance in everyday life. It hoped to interest and inform young readers, believing the rubber industry would be better off if future citizens knew more about it. Chapter one asks what Columbus discovered in 1492, then turns to what he found on his second voyage, a discovery less easy to name. Readers get a clear, company-published primer on how rubber is grown, gathered, and made useful.
4784-brother-and-sister:
Josephine Lawrence, author of Brother and Sister's Schooldays and Holidays, opens Brother and Sister with the Morrisons. The series runs from Brother and Sister, through Schooldays, to Holidays. This first volume introduces a brother and sister whose daily life fills its chapters. Contents include Grandma Hastings, Sister in Mischief, and party preparations, with Dick's buttons, Ralph's present, and more presents.

A party, time out in the barn, a haunted house, and Jimmie's surprise follow, with a little shopping and a big disappointment. Two in trouble, trouble again, and Miss Putnam complaining lead to making up with Jimmie and Mickey Gaffney. A very sick doll, plans for Mickey, a call paid by brother and sister, and Mickey owning up close the book. Chapter one has Mother Morrison urging Brother to drink his milk before leaving the table. Readers get a gentle children's story of siblings, neighbours, and small adventures.
4948-love-the-fiddler:
Frank, a young man deeply in love with Florence Fenacre, finds his neighbors already treating the match as settled, in this romance of courtship. Every old lady within three miles regards the wedding as good as arranged, and Frank looks forward to it as the dearest thing fate could give him.

Florence, however, has never said no and has not yet been prevailed upon to say yes, preferring to leave matters as they are and forestalling any set proposal. The catalog record gives no author name. Readers get a light comedy of wooing, where the comedy lies in a suitor's certainty meeting a heroine's determination to decide in her own time.
495-amy-foster:
Joseph Conrad tells of a shipwrecked stranger in an English seaside village in this short story, narrated by a country doctor named Kennedy. A man cast ashore near Colebrook, speaking no English, finds shelter and work, then marries Amy Foster, a plain servant girl. Her pity turns to love, then to fear as his strangeness grows.

Conrad writes in slow, grave prose, tracking exile, speech, and the gap between kindness and understanding. The tale ends in lonely grief. It stands as a compact study of the outsider, and of how a village can take a man in yet never truly take him home.
4959-the-life-and-adventures-of-maj-roge:
Major Roger Sherman Potter, a Cape Cod man, narrates his own life and adventures in this comic history, opening with a defense of his bleak native home. Cape Cod, he insists, is the birthplace of the most celebrated critics, though critics acknowledge her only with reluctance, and her poets and novelists set their romances elsewhere.

One solitary poet was even punished for singing to her sands, Potter complains, setting the satirical tone. The major's adventures follow in the same boastful, digressive voice. No byline appears in the catalog record. Readers get a tall-tale autobiography that pokes fun at literary fame, regional pride, and the hero himself.
4990-the-adventures-of-a-boy-reporter:
Harry Steele Morrison's Adventures of a Boy Reporter follows Archie from country life and school, where the Hut Club forms, to a longing for change that carries him to New York. A trip to the city with his uncle settles it: Archie will leave home at night, work on a farm for money, endure cruel treatment, and sleep among ruins and tramps' campfires.

Stealing a ride, kicked out by a brakeman, a night in a lodging house, dishwashing in a Bowery restaurant, and a police station all precede his kindly reception at a newspaper office. There Archie becomes the boy reporter of the title. Readers get a rags-to-newsroom tale about a boy earning his place in the city.
4993-a-texas-ranger:
William MacLeod Raine's Texas Ranger opens with a girl crouched in bear-grass, listening to wheels crunch over broken granite as a trap dips into a draw. Desperation spurs her courage. A pair of bays hitched to an open rig rounds the bend. A young man drives them, draws up, and looks down into a valley glowing golden.

The ranger's arrival sets a western tale of pursuit, danger, and rescue in motion. Raine writes the desert country with a rider's knowledge of draws, granite, and distance. Readers get a brisk Texas western, where a chance meeting on a winding road becomes a fight for a life.
5006-harriet-and-the-piper:
Richard Carter called his estate Crownlands, not to please himself or his wife, but for his mother's newly born family pride. The place had belonged to a Carter. Tradition held it a grant of the first George to the first of the name in America. Madame Carter adopted the unknown owner into vague cousinship. She told old friends Crownlands had always been in the family.

Harriet, the heroine, and the piper of the title move through this world of invented ancestry and real feeling. An author name is absent from the record. Readers get a domestic novel about family pride, property, and love, where a house's name matters almost as much as the people inside it.
5071-the-philanderer:
George Bernard Shaw's Philanderer opens in a room furnished for argument. The room is not quite square. One back corner is cut diagonally by a doorway. The opposite corner is rounded by a turret window filled with flowers around a statue of Shakespeare. A fireplace and armchair stand on the right. A small round table holds a yellow-backed French novel, open. A grand piano stands open on the left.

The play's philanderer moves through this world of actresses, critics, and new ideas, with Bernhardt, Jones, Pinero, and Grundy invoked as the theatrical background. Shaw's comedy of love and modern womanhood unfolds in drawing-room debate. Readers get an early Shaw play, witty about courtship and the new woman alike.
5093-the-little-minister:
J. M. Barrie's Little Minister opens long ago in Thrums, when caged blackbirds whistled impudently at a king's soldier to come over the water to Charlie. A minister of Thrums was to be married. Then something happened, and he remained a bachelor. In old age he passed the lady who was to have been his wife. Her hair was white, but she, too, was still unmarried.

Only a weaver witnessed the meeting. He said solemnly afterward that they did not speak, but gave one another a look, and he saw the love-light in their eyes. No more is remembered of the two. Readers get Barrie's Scottish romance of love deferred, tender, whimsical, and quietly heartbreaking.
5113-the-confessions-of-a-beachcomber:
Edmund James Banfield spent years living on a small island off the tropical coast of Queensland. These linked sketches record what he saw there day by day. Birds, fish, turtles, coral gardens, and the changing moods of sea and weather fill the pages, alongside notes on the island's early history and its neighbours.

Banfield writes as a close watcher rather than a distant naturalist, naming the creatures he meets and describing their habits in plain detail. Readers get a slow, vivid portrait of island life at the turn of the century. A beach walk could turn up a shark, a rare bird, or a story from the people who lived nearby.
5166-the-poetaster:
Ben Jonson's comedy The Poetaster, or His Arraignment, is set in ancient Rome and stages a literary war. Ovid, Tibullus, and Gallus mix with the poetasters Crispinus and Demetrius. Jonson uses the Roman scene to answer his own rivals, putting bad poets on trial before Augustus in a final arraignment.

The play is Jonson's sharpest satire on the theatre world of his day, full of classical allusion and personal score-settling. Readers interested in Shakespeare's contemporaries will find a lively, combative comedy. It opens a window into how Jacobean playwrights fought their battles in verse on the public stage.
5174-allan-and-the-holy-flower:
H. Rider Haggard's Allan Quatermain novel, first published in 1915, sends the famous hunter after a rare orchid rather than gold. Brother John, an auction room, and a slave road lead Quatermain and his companions into the African interior, where a king, a magic mirror. A people called the Motombo guard the home of the holy flower.

Haggard mixes adventure with African legend and lost-world wonder, as Quatermain faces a sentence of death and a battle for the flower itself. Readers of his earlier African romances will find the same blend of danger, mystery, and vivid landscape, told in Quatermain's dry, first-person voice.
527-the-end-of-the-tether:
Joseph Conrad follows Captain Whalley, an old master going blind, in this sea novella. Whalley commands the steamer Sofala on a Malay coast run, hiding his failing sight from owners, crew, and himself. A Malay serang, a low swamp coast, and a river estuary mark his last voyages.

Conrad writes with grave, slow power, tracking pride, duty, and the end of a working life. Whalley must choose between honor and ruin as the tether runs out. The tale stands as a somber study of age at sea, where a captain's nerve outlasts his eyes.
5302-the-land-of-the-blue-flower:
Frances Hodgson Burnett's Land of the Blue Flower is a fairy tale of a kingdom once called King Mordreth's Land, after a fierce and cruel king. The tall, strong, beautiful King Amor descends from his mountain castle. He begins to reign. The land takes its new name, and the story follows his rule.

Burnett, author of The Secret Garden, writes a parable of kingship, kindness, and the power of love to change a country. The book offers young readers a gentle allegory, illustrated in the original, in which a good king remakes a gloomy land into a place of blue flowers.
5401-old-rose-and-silver:
Myrtle Reed wrote Old Rose and Silver as a romance of music, memory, and second chances. The novel opens with an author's note about its songs, including an unpublished piano arrangement of Wilson G. Smith's Entreaty, and then follows its characters through chapters titled A Falling Star, The Voice of the Violin, and The Crosby Twins. Music threads through the household scenes.

As the story moves from welcome-home gatherings to an enchanted hour and a thirtieth of June, old affections resurface and new ones form. Reed writes in a gentle, old-fashioned style, letting violins, letters, and summer afternoons carry the feeling. Readers get a warm, sentimental romance from the early twentieth century.
5422-the-masquerader:
Katherine Cecil Thurston sets this novel in London on a foggy January night, when two events collide: a border rising against the Persian government and a strange case of mistaken identity. A man who looks exactly like a rising politician becomes entangled in the politician's life, and the resemblance soon shapes both men's fates. Parliament gossip and street fog set the opening mood.

The plot turns on doubling, disguise, and political intrigue, as the substitute is drawn deeper into public life and private danger. Thurston keeps the tension between the two look-alikes at the center, asking what happens when appearance replaces identity. Readers get an Edwardian thriller with romance, politics, and a steady sense of menace.
5611-the-satyricon-of-petronius-arbiter:
Petronius Arbiter wrote the Satyricon, a Roman satire surviving in fragments, here translated by William Burnaby with an introduction by C. K. Scott Moncrieff. The introduction opens as an open letter to a young gentleman, beginning on high ground above St. Andrews, looking seaward for the Inchcape Rock, where at first nothing shows and then a speck of whiteness lasts no longer than a wave.

The novel itself follows Encolpius, Giton, and Ascyltos through feasts, quarrels, and escapades in Nero's Rome, with the famous dinner of Trimalchio at its center. Readers get ancient satire at its most vivid: comic, frank, and full of Roman daily life.
5638-an-adventure-with-a-genius-recollec:
Alleyne Ireland wrote An Adventure with a Genius as recollections of Joseph Pulitzer, dedicated by permission to Mrs. Joseph Pulitzer. Ireland says his wanderings through life's labyrinth brought a new adventure around every corner, rich in experience for a mature and reflective mind even when lacking vivid action. His Pulitzer adventure proves the point.

Chapters run from In a Casting Net and Meeting Joseph Pulitzer through life at Cap Martin. Yachting in the Mediterranean, getting to know Pulitzer, Wiesbaden and an Atlantic voyage follow, ending at Bar Harbor and the last cruise. Readers get an intimate portrait of the press lord in private life.
5696-a-yankee-girl-at-fort-sumter:
This children's story opens with two schoolgirls, Sylvia Fulton and Grace Waite, walking to school and talking about a song that holds Sylvia's name. Grace, nearly eleven and a year older than Sylvia, explains with proper pride that the song praises Sylvia's spelling, and Sylvia, delighted, plans to tell her mother. The scene sets a warm, everyday tone before the story's larger setting, Fort Sumter and the coming Civil War, enters the girls' lives.

We follow a young Yankee girl as ordinary friendship, school, and family life meet a national crisis. The book is written for young readers, with clear scenes and gentle humor, and it uses a child's view to make a distant war feel near. It suits families reading about American history together, and children who enjoy stories where a young heroine watches her world change.
572-the-great-big-treasury-of-beatrix-po:
Beatrix Potter's best-loved tales gather in one large treasury, from Peter Rabbit and Benjamin Bunny to Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle, Jemima Puddle-Duck, and Mr. Tod. The book opens with four little rabbits in a sand bank under a fir tree. Potter wrote and drew the tales between 1902 and 1913, starting with Peter Rabbit.

Potter's stories pair small animals with precise country detail, and her pictures, in the original books, made the tales famous. This treasury lets young readers meet the whole company in one volume, story after story. Her precise natural detail, learned from years of sketching, gives the animals their truth.
579-the-poems-of-sidney-lanier:
Sidney Lanier, the Georgia poet and musician, writes verse that tries to make English poetry sing like music. His poems draw on the South, on nature, and on the sound of words themselves. Lanier died in 1881, at thirty-nine, after years of illness and hard work.

Lanier, who played the flute in an orchestra and wrote on the science of verse, believed rhythm carried meaning. The collection gathers his best-known lyrics, and it remains the standard way to meet a poet who heard poetry as song. His Marshes of Glynn, among his finest poems, shows his musical theory in full flower.
5847-the-heart-of-rome-a-tale-of-the-los:
The Heart of Rome, subtitled A Tale of the Lost Water, opens with the Baroness Volterra driving to the Palazzo Conti in the heart of Rome at nine in the morning. She hopes to find Donna Clementina at home, having tried twice to telephone the previous afternoon, only to hear that communication was interrupted. Her anxiety to see Clementina at once sets a Roman mystery in motion.

Readers follow aristocratic Rome through palaces, telephones, and old water rights, as a lost water supply becomes a matter of love, money, and honor. The novel favors atmosphere and intrigue over action, with Rome itself as a character. It suits readers of Italian historical romance, and fans of novels where a city secret drives a family's fate.
5957-the-art-of-the-story-teller:
Marie L. Shedlock sets out to defend storytelling as an art rather than a set of rules. Her preface contrasts a coming science of education with the living work of teachers who keep a direct sense of childhood. She argues that wise teachers still need artists who can read a tale with feeling and restraint.

The praise quoted in the preface points to her range across Daudet, Grimm, and deeper world philosophy. Shedlock is shown at home in wit, folk wisdom, and grave thought alike, always within the limits of the craft. The volume offers her papers on how stories should be chosen, shaped, and told aloud.
5977-bound-to-rise-or-up-the-ladder:
Horatio Alger Jr. writes for boys about rising by honest effort, and the sketch that opens this volume recalls his life among New York street boys. He mingled with them, gained their trust, showed concern for their affairs, and urged them toward honest and useful living. Over seventy stories followed his first.

The novel itself follows a boy climbing, step by step, from small beginnings toward a better place. Alger's formula pairs hard work with a fair chance and a helping hand. Readers meet a hero whose pluck matters more than his purse, in a tale built to encourage young strivers.
5990-rosamond-or-the-youthful-error-a-ta:
Mary J. Holmes opens her Riverside tale on a rainy September day, with a young man gazing at a glowing grate while rain beats the windows. His thoughts lie elsewhere than wind or weather, and the story that follows traces Rosamond Leyton, her education, and a brother and sister bound by old ties.

Chapters on Ben's visit, Marie Porter, making love, a guest at Riverside, and the end frame the main tale. Shorter pieces follow, among them Diamonds, Bad Spelling, Maggie Lee, and The Answered Prayer. Holmes writes domestic romance with a steady, sentimental hand, centered on home and heart.
5991-the-solitary-summer:
Elizabeth von Arnim writes in diary form, opening on 2 May with a wish to be alone for a whole summer and get to the very dregs of life. She plans to be idle so her soul may grow, to invite nobody, and to spend months in garden, plain, and forest, watching where she has made mistakes.

On wet days she will seek the driest pine woods, and in sun she will lie on the heath watching broom flare against the clouds. The Man of Wrath answers only, mind she does not get her feet damp. The book finds peace in silence, and humor in a solitude that others keep interrupting.
6165-cowboy-dave-or-the-round-up-at-roll:
Frank V. Webster sends Cowboy Dave to the round-up at Rolling River, opening with stray cattle, a taunt, a confession, and a small stampede. Treachery, a cry for help, a rescue, Mr. Bellmore, and Dave meeting Len follow, with Dave wondering, hazardous work, and a fight.

Webster, author of farm boys, telephone boys, newsboy partners, and boy pilots, writes brisk western adventure for boys. Dave's round-up tests riding, nerve, and loyalty among cattle, rivals, and rough country. The chapters promise news, danger, and a round-up brought home through pluck and teamwork.
6173-the-note-books-of-samuel-butler:
Samuel Butler began early to carry a notebook, writing down anything he wanted to remember, whether heard from others or said by himself. His reason, in one note, was that thoughts fly so fast one must shoot them, since trying to put salt on their tails is no use.

He bagged as many as he could hit and preserved them, rewritten on loose sheets, as a museum of wise, beautiful, and strange creatures winging across his vision's field. Henry Festing Jones arranged and edited these selections, with a photogravure portrait from an 1898 photograph. The notebooks show Butler thinking aloud.
6300-the-project-gutenberg-complete-work:
A single vast file gathers Parker's novels, tales, and poems, from The Judgment House and Pierre and His People through Romany of the Snows, Northern Lights, and Mrs. Falchion, to Valmond, The Trail of the Sword, and the Canadian and Egyptian books. The Trespasser, Seats of the Mighty, Battle of the Strong, Lane That Had No Turning, Right of Way, and Weavers all stand inside, with Embers and A Lover's Diary for verse.

The file opens, fittingly, in an opera house, where a singer named Al'mah makes Manassa the musical feast of the year at Covent Garden, while three watchers resist her spell. That scene comes from The Judgment House, first in the contents. As an omnibus it is a library in one place, for a reader who wants Parker's whole range, from prairie towns to Paris courts, without hunting volume by volume.
6307-the-story-of-a-bold-tin-soldier:
Attention is the word of command heard in a toy department at night, after customers and clerks have gone home. A Calico Clown peers round building blocks, a Candy Rabbit asks if the Sawdust Doll has returned, and a Monkey on a Stick reports no old friends in sight. Then the Bold Tin Soldier calls his men again, and the toys of Laura Lee Hope's make believe world stir into life.

Ten chapters follow the soldier through a make believe fight, saving the clown, a boy's purchase, a bean battle, a captain and a lamb, and a sad accident. A bunch of sweetness, a return to the store, and a rabbit close the tale. Hope writes for young children, with toys that talk, march, and care for one another when the shop lights go out.
6428-the-surgeon-s-daughter:
Walter Scott's Surgeon's Daughter, from the second series of Chronicles of the Canongate in 1827, was separated from the Highland Widow tales and deferred to this collection's close, for printers' reasons. An 1831 introduction explains the move, which hardly interests general readers. Johnson's verse on Levett, the village doctor whose useful care never mocked a summons with cold delay, opens the tale's praise of rural medicine.

Gideon Gray, Scott's surgeon, stands for village doctors from whom Scotland reaps more benefit than gratitude, schoolmasters excepted. Such a man serves a pretty borough or village as his practice's centre, day and night at the service of cases the village affords and beyond. Scott writes a tale of a surgeon's daughter caught between duty, love, and a father's calling, in a Scotland where medicine is also ministry.
647-the-dynamiter:
Robert Louis Stevenson and Fanny Van de Grift Stevenson write a tale of anarchists and bombs in this 1885 volume, subtitled More New Arabian Nights. The Cigar Divan in Soho frames the stories. Prince Florizel, dethroned and now a tobacconist, hears tales of the Squire of Dames, the Superfluous Mansion, the Brown Box, and Zero's explosive bomb.

The Stevensons write with wit and adventure, mixing crime, comedy, and political horror. A dedication to police officers Cole and Cox sets the tone: crime is ugly even under sounding names. The book endures as a lively sequel, where London plots and Paris bombs meet in a cigar shop.
6521-the-king-of-the-dark-chamber:
Tagore opens his play on a street where strangers ask a guard the way to a great feast, and learn that any road will lead them there. The talk is light at first, yet it points to the play's core riddle: a king who rules unseen, and a people who must trust a voice they cannot see. From that street scene, the drama moves inward, toward faith and doubt.

The king stays hidden in a dark chamber while queens, guards, and common folk weigh rumor, hope, and fear. Tagore, who made his own English version, lets the verse-like speech carry both story and symbol. The King of the Dark Chamber is a short, strange play about seeking a ruler who will not show his face.
6563-the-blunderer:
Molière's early comedy, first played at Lyons in 1653 and in Paris five years later, turns on a servant whose eager help wrecks every plan. Mascarille, drawn from an Italian play by Nicolo Barbieri, means well but bungles each step, and his master's love plot keeps falling apart at his hands. The note that opens the text traces these debts with care.

A boasting soldier, sharp talk, and a string of counterplots keep the five acts in brisk motion. Molière changes the Italian ending to one he judged better, and adds scenes from other old comedies as he goes. The Blunderer is a lively early work, full of the mischief that would mark his later stage.
6584-princess-polly-s-gay-winter:
Amy Brooks brings Princess Polly back for a gay winter at Avondale, where little Rose Atherton deems no spot lovelier in all the world. A summer at the shore gives way to school days, a sea nymph play, a new friend named Gwen, and a call that brings joy. Uncle John, Aunt Judith, and Aunt Rose all have parts in the fun.

Parties, a holiday frolic, and Gyp's small ambition fill the chapters with warm, home-like cheer. Brooks writes in a gentle voice for young girls, with manners, kindness, and play as the chief lessons. Princess Polly's Gay Winter is a cozy seasonal tale, bright with friendship and family love.
6590-quotations-from-the-pg-collected-wo:
David Widger gathers striking lines from the collected novels of Gilbert Parker, for readers who want to find a favorite passage fast. His editor's note invites new tips from readers, and notes that web publication lets him fix and add lines with ease. Each quote can be traced back to its novel by a search for a short phrase.

The set spans Parker's tales of Canada and the wider world, in his own words, without added comment. It works best as a companion to the novels, not as a stand-alone book. Widger's Quotations gives Parker fans a quick path to lines they loved, and a prompt to read the full tales again.
6600-the-moccasin-maker:
Pauline Johnson's prose, gathered soon after her death in 1913, speaks from two worlds at once. The daughter of a Mohawk chief and a white mother, she lived for years on the Iroquois Reserve, and her tales carry that life in their bones. An introduction by Gilbert Parker and praise from Charles Mair frame the set.

Stories of her mother, of a red girl's reasoning, of a pagan in St. Paul's, and of Lillooet Falls move between reserve, town, and church. Johnson writes with pride, wit, and a clear eye for both peoples she belonged to. The Moccasin Maker is a warm, important record of a Native writer finding her voice in print.
6667-poems-of-power:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox explains her title in a note: the final word means the divine power in every human being, whose recognition is the secret of all success and joy. Many verses in the book try to show that idea at work. The Queen's Last Ride, The Meeting of the Centuries, Grief, Illusion, Assertion, and I Am lead the contents.

First issued in 1903 and reprinted again and again, the volume won Wilcox a wide, loyal audience. Her verse is plain, bold, and meant to stir the will. Poems of Power is a stirring set for readers who like poetry that urges them to stand tall and trust their own inner force.
671-phil-the-fiddler:
Horatio Alger, Jr. writes of Italian street musicians in New York in this boys' tale. Phil, a twelve-year-old violin boy with a battered fiddle, sings Viva Garibaldi in uptown streets while a padrone profits from his play. A preface tells how Alger learned the trade's hard facts from Italian gentlemen and the Eco d'Italia, whose editor called such boys the White Slaves of New York.

Alger writes with plain, earnest prose, following Phil through ferries, barrooms, sieges, and escapes. The tale mixes adventure with a plea for the children. It endures as a vivid Alger story, where a fiddler's courage wins friends and freedom.
6718-cap-n-dan-s-daughter:
Joseph Lincoln sets Cap'n Dan's Daughter in Trumet Centre, where the Metropolitan Dry Goods and Variety Store opens for business in August. Sam Bartlett takes down shutters, sweeps, and dusts, then goes home for breakfast, having waited on no customers at all, for there were none. The store is ready, but trade is not.

August should bring city visitors, white duck hats, and oilskin coats for sailing, yet the town waits. Into that quiet shop world comes Cap'n Dan's daughter, with love and town talk in her wake. Lincoln writes with Cape Cod humor and warmth. Cap'n Dan's Daughter is a cozy, comic tale of a small town and its people.
6720-the-wentworth-letter:
Joseph Smith writes, at the request of John Wentworth, editor of the Chicago Democrat, a sketch of the rise, progress, persecution, and faith of the Latter-day Saints. Wentworth wanted the account for a friend writing a history of New Hampshire, and Smith asks only that it be printed entire, ungarnished, and without misrepresentation. The letter first ran in Times and Seasons in March 1842.

Smith tells of his birth in Sharon, Vermont, in December 1805, and of his family's move when he was ten. The sketch that follows is the founding statement of his faith. The Wentworth Letter is a short, historic document, central to Mormon history and to American religious life.
6754-the-tale-of-brownie-beaver:
Arthur Scott Bailey tells of Brownie Beaver in Pleasant Valley, near a village Farmer Green seldom visits, beyond Blue Mountain. Brownie must find a queer place to live, learn to fell a tree, and build with sticks and mud. A freshet, a dam in danger, and a happy thought test his skill and pluck.

Mr. Crow, Mr. Frog, Jasper Jay, and Grandaddy Beaver all have parts in the woodland fun. Bailey writes in simple, gentle prose for the youngest readers, with a new lesson in each chapter. The Tale of Brownie Beaver is a sweet, old-style animal book for small children.
6799-philosophical-letters-of-friedrich-:
Schiller's Philosophical Letters open with prefatory remarks on how reason, like the heart, passes through epochs and transitions, yet its growth is seldom portrayed. Writers show passions in extremes, aberration, and results, Schiller notes, without asking how closely they bind to a person's intellectual frame. Moral decay, he argues, roots in a one-sided, wavering philosophy that blinds the mind with a show of truth.

An enlightened understanding, by contrast, ennobles and steadies the soul. Letters on the theosophy of Julius and on the animal and spiritual natures in man follow. Philosophical Letters is a short, searching work of a poet thinking as a philosopher.
6800-the-works-of-frederick-schiller:
The Works of Frederick Schiller gathers his histories, plays, poems, philosophy, and a novel in one collected edition, translated from German and illustrated. History holds the Thirty Years' War in five books and the Revolt of the Netherlands in four. Plays run from The Robbers and Fiesco to Wallenstein and Wilhelm Tell. Don Carlos, Demetrius, and Mary Stuart also appear. Poems in three periods, aesthetical essays, philosophical letters, and The Ghost Seer complete the set.

A preface to the sixth edition calls this the best collected Schiller in English, with many corrections. For readers who want Schiller whole, this volume is the gateway. The Works of Frederick Schiller is a vast, essential shelf for any lover of German letters.
6809-the-doctor-s-daughter:
Vera, author of Honor Edgeworth, opens The Doctor's Daughter with a preface on prefaces themselves. Dickens, she notes, said prefaces, though seldom read, are continually written, and she likens them to soft explanations whispered when one person is introduced to another. Such a note, she suggests, can reconcile fastidious friends to a quaint, old-fashioned little body.

The tale that follows centers on a doctor's daughter, her home, her loves, and her trials, in the gentle style of Victorian domestic fiction. Vera writes with warmth and a touch of humor. The Doctor's Daughter is a pleasant, old-fashioned novel of family life and feeling.
683-the-compleat-angler:
Izaak Walton wrote this 1653 classic as a talk between friends on the art of fishing. Piscator, the angler, teaches Venator, the hunter, how to catch trout, pike, and other river fish, with lore on bait, tackle, seasons, and the habits of each kind. Songs, poems, and old sayings break up the lessons.

Walton praises angling as a calm, honest pastime, close to nature and far from the noise of town and court. The book is not just a manual: it is a plea for a quiet life, patience, and good company by the water. It has stayed in print for centuries as both a guide for anglers and a gentle piece of English prose.
6845-the-whistling-mother:
Grace Richmond's Whistling Mother opens with a son's praise: he has the greatest mother on earth, five feet six, weighing just what she ought, and never still long enough to grow stout. She is game for any outing, awfully good company, and more like a vigorous girl than a mother in the usual sense. A picture caption adds that a boy with work to do is immortal till his work is done.

The tales that follow show that mother in home, town, and trouble, whistling her way through life. Richmond writes with warmth and humor. The Whistling Mother is a cheerful, loving portrait of a mother who stays young in spirit.
6881-note-book-of-an-english-opium-eater:
Thomas De Quincey gathers short essays in this notebook, opening with a sequel to his famous piece on murder as a fine art. Three memorable murders leads a set that ranges widely, from the Bible and mere human science to the literary history of the eighteenth century and the Antigone of Sophocles. Later pieces weigh Wellesley, Milton against Southey and Landor, and the falsifying of English history.

Other essays touch suicide, shallow learning, English dictionaries, and Dryden and Pope at their sharpest. De Quincey writes with a playful edge even on gloomy themes, and he warns that readers who cannot meet gaiety halfway will miss his drift. The book reads as a cabinet of curiosities from a most restless mind.
6893-in-the-quarter:
Robert Chambers opens this novel in Paris in May 1888, in the crowded Cafe des Ecoles of the Latin Quarter. Art students argue over Salon news, sing half mocking songs about masters and mistresses, and trade chalk and spoons across marble tables wet with beer. Elliott, Rhodes, Clifford, and Thaxton talk of who is in and who is out, while Rhodes nurses a drink and a grudge.

The Quarter itself is the true subject, a place where young painters live cheap, love lightly, and weigh art against money and family duty. Chambers follows their evenings, studios, and quarrels through sixteen chapters, catching the noise, humor, and restless hope of Americans and others learning to paint in Paris.
6903-miss-ludington-s-sister:
Edward Bellamy opens with a reflection on how happiness falls unevenly across lives, coming all at once to some and spread thin for others. For men, he says, the bright years often arrive in manhood or later, with a hard and successful career. For women, and most of all for women who do not marry, the bright years most often come in girlhood and young womanhood, before life grows lonelier.

Miss Ida Ludington, at twenty five, feels that truth take hold, as her interests narrow and her days grow quiet. The novel that follows traces what such a life can still hold, and what a sister's bond can mean when the spring of youth has passed. Bellamy writes with quiet care about time, loss, and the search for joy.
6915-in-camp-on-the-big-sunflower:
Lawrence Leslie sends a band of boys to camp on the Big Sunflower, opening with an alarm when Toby looks as if he has seen a ghost. Steve and Bandy-legs hold the camp while Max and his cousin Owen walk the river bank looking for fresh water clams. The contents promise treasure hunting, unknown shell gatherers, a puzzler for Max, and a great find from the river.

A new cook springs a surprise, danger waits on the trail, and Max plays the good Samaritan before the man trap is set again. At dead of night the mystery deepens, and the closing chapter solves it at last. Leslie writes a lively camp tale of boys, river craft, and a puzzle worked out in the open air.
6923-the-miser:
Moliere's Miser, first acted on September 9, 1668, appears here in Charles Heron Wall's English prose translation, with a short introduction and notes. Wall notes that Moliere borrowed from Plautus and imitated others, yet far surpasses them in handling his theme. Harpagon, the miser, loves money above all natural feeling, shuns family life, and treats his own children as natural enemies.

The cast sets Harpagon against his son Cleante and daughter Elise, both in love, with Valere, Marianne, and Anselme tangled in the plot. Master Jacques, cook and coachman both, and the valet La Fleche add comic edge. Moliere himself played Harpagon, and the play remains a sharp, moral comedy on greed.
6927-the-white-feather:
Wodehouse sets The White Feather a year and a term after The Gold Bat, at the school of Wrykyn. His note jokes that the short stories bridging the two books kept away from his publishers, a painful show of the white feather itself. Sheen, the hero, faces home troubles, visitors with advice, and the charge of cowardice that gives the book its title.

Chapters follow Sheen's slow education, his progress under Mister Joe Bevan, a naval battle and its fallout, and a skirmish that ends in the rout at Ripton. Drummond retires, Seymour finds one success, and Bevan's counsel shapes the close. Wodehouse turns a schoolboy's fear into a light tale of pluck learned the hard way.
6937-a-biography-of-edmund-spenser:
John Hales writes the life of Edmund Spenser, revised in 1896 from the Macmillan Globe edition of Spenser's works. He opens with Latin verses on a life laid open like a votive tablet, then admits how little is known. Spenser's life, like Chaucer's, hides in obscurity, and like Shakespeare's it rests on meagre entries in official papers rather than on full records.

Hales therefore builds from documents, dates, and the poems themselves, tracing a poet whose great work outshines his paper trail. Footnotes mark each chapter's sources, and old spelling marks are explained for the reader. The biography serves as a compact, scholarly guide to the author of The Faerie Queene.
701-the-king-of-the-golden-river:
John Ruskin wrote this fairy tale about three brothers who live by a river in a rich valley, where gold seems to flow from the hills. Two brothers are greedy and cruel, and their selfish acts turn the valley barren. The youngest, kind and just, meets the King of the Golden River and faces a test of his heart.

Ruskin draws a clear moral: wealth kept by greed dries up, while wealth shared with care brings life back to the land. Mountain scenes, storms, and a touch of wonder carry the lesson without preaching it flat. The tale is unlike Ruskin's art writing, yet it shares its core belief that nature rewards right use and punishes abuse.
705-the-roadmender:
Michael Fairless wrote these short papers about a man who leaves town life to mend roads by hand in the English countryside. He sits by a white gate, breaks stone, and watches the seasons change. The papers first ran in The Pilot and were gathered in 1911, with three parts: the roadmender's own tale, a passage out of shadow, and a scene at the white gate.

The narrator finds peace in plain work, prayer, and the sights of hedge, field, and sky. His musings turn on faith, death, and the worth of a simple life. The book is quiet and devout, prized for its gentle prose and its belief that humble labour, done with love, can be a form of worship.
7211-the-american-union-speaker:
Philbrick's American Union Speaker, entered in 1865, serves two ends at once. It meets the demand for new selections suited to the spirit of the hour, and it gathers standard pieces for elocutionary exercise on which time has set its seal. About one hundred extracts from recent work, by more than fifty authors, appear here for the first time in a speaker.

Old and new pieces stand side by side, chosen and prepared with care for reading aloud in school, hall, or home. The book belongs to a wartime moment when public speech carried unusual weight, and its selections mix fresh feeling with lasting eloquence. Readers get a portable stage for voice, memory, and civic pride.
7224-within-you-is-the-power:
Henry Thomas Hamblin argues that a power lies hidden in every person, by whose use one may rise to higher and better things. His chapters move through infinite life and power, the overcoming of life's difficulties, and fate or free will. Cause and effect, success, health, and the secret of abundant supply follow, then turn to the subconscious and superconscious mind.

Character building, habit, happiness, and the right use and misuse of mental and spiritual powers follow, closing with the overcoming of limits and the awakening of inward powers. Hamblin writes in a calm, encouraging voice for readers seeking practical hope rather than abstract theory. The book offers plain counsel for a steadier, fuller life.
7229-rujub-the-juggler:
G. A. Henty's Rujub, the Juggler is a historical tale for young and old set in the Sepoy Mutiny in India from 1857 to 1859, while Lord Canning held the reins of British rule. The publisher's introduction recalls chupatties passed from village to village and placards against British rule at Delhi. It also recalls the greased cartridges of the new Enfield rifle, rumoured to be smeared with forbidden pig's fat.

Fanatical feeling, the introduction says, soon brought the mutiny to a head, and Henty builds his story on that storm. A juggler's craft and a boy's courage thread through camps and sieges, giving young readers adventure with a history lesson inside it. Henty keeps the pace brisk and the loyalties plain.
7252-the-women-who-came-in-the-mayflower:
Annie Russell Marble wrote this little book as a memorial to the women who came in the Mayflower. Their comrades followed in the Ann and the Fortune and kept high standards of home life in early Plymouth Colony. She makes no attempt at a genealogy of any family, and she admits frankly how much proof is lacking where accounts conflict.

Her aim is glimpses of communal life in 1621 to 1623, with silhouettes of single matrons and maidens whose influence reached into domestic life and schooling. Marble honours endurance, thrift, and care as public virtues, not merely private ones. The book keeps its scale small and its respect large.
727-the-star-spangled-banner:
John A. Carpenter traced the history of the song that became the American national anthem. He starts in August 1814, when Admiral Cockburn threatened Washington in revenge for American raids in Canada, and follows the war that led Francis Scott Key to write his verses at Baltimore. The song's words, music, and early fame are set out in turn.

Carpenter adds the story of the flag, the fort, and the men who sang the song into public life. His account is short and factual, drawn from letters and records of the day. The book serves readers who want to know how a wartime poem grew into a national symbol, and what its first singers meant by it.
7309-business-correspondence-vol-1-how-t:
Business Correspondence, Volume One, teaches how to write the business letter in twenty-four chapters on preparing to write, finding the proper viewpoint, opening, presenting a proposition convincingly, and making an effective close. Forceful style, originality, selling appeal fitted to different prospects, and getting orders by letter follow, with proved principles illustrated by extracts from two hundred and seventeen actual letters.

The book opens with what a postage stamp can do and the advantages of doing business by letter, treating the letter as a sales tool, not a formality. Its lessons stay practical throughout, showing real letters rather than preaching rules in the abstract. Clerks, salesmen, and managers get a working manual for the post.
7326-the-yeoman-adventurer:
George Gough's Yeoman Adventurer follows a hero through chapters on the great Jack, a sergeant of dragoons, Mistress Margaret Waynflete, a journey's start, an ancient high house, and his lord Brocton. Losing his Virgil, a conjurer's cap, a career as a highwayman, Sultan, a slip, and the guest-room of the Rising Sun carry him onward. Pharaoh's kine, war's risks, moorlands, and Bonnie Prince Charlie lie ahead.

Gough dedicates the book to A. D. Steel-Maitland in gratitude and admiration, and his tale mixes Jacobite adventure with rogue's comedy. A new hat, a double six, foppery, a council at Derby, and a brother who knows at last promise twists to the end. The novel reads as a brisk historical romp.
7334-with-buller-in-natal-or-a-born-lead:
G. A. Henty's With Buller in Natal, or A Born Leader, opens with a frank preface on the late war. A full, impartial history will take a long time, since even witnesses in different parts of the field differ widely. Until fuller details supplement the meagre military despatches, Henty writes, anything like an accurate history would be impossible. So he has reconciled the various narratives of fighting in Natal as best he can.

His hero, Chris, springs at the enemy in the book's illustration, and the tale follows Buller's campaign through Natal's battles with a boy's eye for action. Henty balances war story with an attempt at fair narrative, admitting gaps where sources clash. The novel gives young readers a campaign in vivid, careful form.
7359-indian-summer:
William D. Howells's Indian Summer opens midway on Florence's Ponte Vecchio, where Colville lounges against a jeweller's booth and stares at the Arno. It is a January afternoon that began bright and warm, then changed mood as clouds flew and rain threatened. A yellow torrent seethed below, fed by rain already fallen in the mountains.

From that bridge the novel follows middle-aged Americans in Italy, love renewed late, and the comedy of manners abroad. Howells writes with his usual gentle irony, letting talk and small choices carry feeling. The Florentine opening sets a mood of late light and second chances that the whole book keeps.
7395-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
Grandmother's Story of Bunker-Hill Battle gives this volume its center. Holmes retells the Revolution as a grandmother told it to a child, with a grandson promising to come right back and staying away the live-long day. Around that fireside tale sit poems from 1874 to 1877. They include a memorial to Samuel Gridley Howe, a hymn for Governor Andrew's statue, and a welcome to the nations at Philadelphia on July 4, 1876.

The centennial year runs through the book, as Holmes, now an elder statesman of letters, looks back at the Revolution his grandparents' generation fought. Old Cambridge, family records, and the ship of state fill out the volume. It is Holmes in his late, public role: the survivor who speaks for the past to a nation celebrating a hundred years.
7410-the-minister-s-charge-or-the-appren:
William Dean Howells, author of The Rise of Silas Lapham, builds this novel around a minister's conscience. On the way home from boarding in the country, the Reverend Sewell is reproached by his wife: he had no right to give a poor boy false hopes about his poetry. To discourage the boy would have been kinder, she argues, if the verses were bad. Yet Sewell has taken the boy's case on himself.

The boy is Lemuel Barker, and the novel follows his apprenticeship to life under the minister's charge. Howells uses the small story to ask large questions: what do we owe the hopeful, and when does kindness become cruelty? Told with Howells's quiet realism, the book is a study of conscience, poetry, and the education of a young man.
743-thoughts-on-man-his-nature-productio:
William Godwin gathered thirty-four years of reflection in this 1831 volume on man, his nature, his works, and his finds. The book grew from thoughts first aired in his earlier Enquirer, now given a fixed and lasting form. Godwin writes on mind, habit, genius, and the forces that shape human life.

Essays move from the growth of character to the value of books, the arts, and science, with personal notes on the author woven in. His tone is calm and inquiring, not fiery, though the views are bold. The volume gives readers Godwin the thinker at leisure, weighing what people are and what they may become.
7434-the-adventures-of-joel-pepper:
Margaret Sidney's Pepper books were beloved by generations of children, and this volume follows Joel Pepper, the family's irrepressible boy, through his own adventures. The contents promise mischief from the start: Joel and the snake, Deacon Brown's nail pile, the muffin man and the tramp, and a scramble on Bandy Leg Mountain. A birthday party, a fishing trip, and a bag of rye flour all turn into trouble.

Later chapters take Joel to Grandma Bascom's, onto the Boxford stage, and into a fight at Strawberry Hill, with Polly and Dave close at hand. Sidney writes with the warmth of the Pepper household itself, where scrapes are forgiven and courage counts. The book stands alone, but readers of the Five Little Peppers will greet old friends here.
7548-quotes-and-images-from-the-confessi:
Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer is a rollicking Irish military novel. First published at Dublin in 1839, it is gathered here in quotations and images. The title page bore no author's name, though the work is generally attributed to Lever. Harry is a young officer in a British regiment stationed in Ireland in the early 1800s, and his confessions are misadventures in love and soldiering.

The edition's story is part of its charm. The first edition's pages were too stained and friable to scan, so a colleague typed the book out in the old-fashioned way for this eBook. The quotations catch Lever's high spirits. There is a set of raps, and curses at being in such quarters. Comrades smoke, sigh, and snore, and men who never prayed before pray for the route to Cork or Galway.
7553-quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of:
Gilbert Parker, the Canadian-born novelist of the North and of Egypt, is gathered here in short passages and pictures from his works. His novels move between frontier settlements and drawing rooms, and the passages sample both worlds. Characters recur in brief, vivid turns of speech. Each passage can be traced to its full scene, so a line never has to carry the whole story alone.

Read together, the passages sketch Parker's range: hard country, social codes, and people tested by both. Loyalty, pride, forgiveness, and the weight of a past act recur across them. The volume suits a reader who wants Parker's voice in small doses before choosing a novel. It is a compact way to meet a once-popular storyteller on his own terms.
7557-quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of:
Charles Dudley Warner, the Hartford essayist and novelist, wrote about gardens, travel, and American life for a generation, and this volume gathers quotations from his writings. The contents list his range: Summer in a Garden, Backlog Studies, Baddeck, In the Wilderness, and Spring in New England stand beside Captain John Smith, Pocahontas, and Saunterings.

Being a Boy and On Horseback follow, with For Whom Shakespeare Wrote, Novel and School, and Their Pilgrimage. Later entries cover modern fiction, culture, equality, literature and life, literary copyright, and the education of the Negro. Nine short essays close the list, on truthfulness and the pursuit of happiness among them. The volume is Warner the companionable American, in his own best sentences.
761-a-v-laider:
Max Beerbohm wrote this short tale about A. V. Laider, a man who claims a strange power: he can see, in a flash, the future of those he meets. The narrator hears Laider's account with doubt, then with unease, as the tale turns on fate, chance, and the burden of knowing what is to come. Beerbohm tells it with dry wit.

The story is brief, but it lingers. Its charm lies in the talk between two men, one credulous and one sceptical, and in a twist that leaves the reader unsure what to believe. It shows Beerbohm's gift for the polished, uncanny tale, where a drawing-room chat opens onto mystery.
7841-a-primary-reader:
E Louise Smythe's A Primary Reader offers old-time stories, fairy tales, and myths retold by children. It served first-grade readers in Santa Rosa schools. Its aim is threefold: give small readers sight-word texts, meet heroes of song and story early, and plant a desire for literature.

Following G Stanley Hall's call for true child editions, Smythe tested tales piece by piece. She cut and shaped them to children's minds, and let pupils retell them aloud before they appeared on blackboard or mimeograph. The result is a gentle first reader built from children's own words.
7842-the-rise-of-iskander:
Benjamin Disraeli's The Rise of Iskander opens at sunset behind Athenian mountains, where the plain glows violet and olive groves stir. Turkish pennons twinkle over Piraeus harbor, women process to a fountain, horsemen throw javelins, and nightingales, grasshoppers, and violets fill purple air with music and scent.

On the Acropolis crag, amid Minerva's temple ruins, a lone figure gazes on columns and Caryatides that baffle modern proportion. That figure is Iskander, the Albanian hero also known as Skanderbeg, whose rise against Ottoman power the romance will trace through war, pride, and fate, in Disraeli's early ornate style.
7870-tales-of-daring-and-danger:
G. A. Henty's Tales of Daring and Danger, published in 1890 by Blackie, opens with a merry party on a Poona bungalow verandah, where Colonel Hastings commands a brigade. Tiffin is served as officers and ladies lounge in cane chairs, before tales carry readers far from that calm.

Contents promise bears and dacoits in the Ghauts, the Paternosters, a pipe of mystery, white-faced Dick, and a brush with the Chinese. An illustration sights the wreck of a steamer. Through India, sea, and frontier, Henty gives boys brisk adventures of pluck, loyalty, and quick action.
7964-the-mystery-of-cloomber:
Arthur Conan Doyle set this early mystery in Scotland, where the West family, newly arrived from Edinburgh, finds a strange tenant at Cloomber Hall: Major-General J. B.
