Heatherstone, a retired Indian officer who lives like a man under siege. Chapters follow the family's growing acquaintance with him, a young man with a grey head, a corporal named Rufus Smith. The wreck of the barque Belinda, and three foreign men seen on the coast. The tale is told through journals and statements.

The mystery deepens as Heatherstone's Indian past closes in on him, and the explanation, when it comes, blends the supernatural with revenge. Written before Sherlock Holmes made Doyle famous, the novel already shows his skill at suspense. It is an eerie, fast-moving story for readers who enjoy Victorian tales of hidden guilt.
7970-life-of-luther:
Julius Köstlin wrote this life of Martin Luther in German, and it appears here in English translation with illustrations drawn from authentic sources, including Cranach's portrait in the Weimar town church. Köstlin opens by arguing that no German shaped his people's religious life, and through it their whole history, as powerfully as Luther did. The biography follows the monk, preacher, and reformer through the break with Rome.

The book stresses Luther's personal character as the key to his influence: plain, forceful, and popular in a way that let his teaching take hold. Readers find a scholarly but readable life, attentive to both the man and the movement he started. It remains a solid introduction to the Reformation told through its central figure.
8017-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
Esther is set at the Persian court of King Ahasuerus, who reigns from India to Ethiopia over a hundred and twenty-seven provinces. The Jewish orphan Esther becomes queen, while her cousin Mordecai uncovers a plot and then faces the minister Haman, who schemes to destroy all the Jews in the empire. Through banquets, reversals, and a royal decree, Esther risks her life to expose Haman and save her people.

The book never names God, yet its coincidences and reversals have long been read as providence at work. It explains the Jewish feast of Purim, celebrating deliverance. In the King James Version, Esther reads like a court thriller, and its heroine's courage, for such a time as this, has made her a lasting model of bravery.
8060-the-bible-king-james-version-book-6:
Peter wrote to strangers scattered through Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, Christians living as outsiders in a hostile world. His letter encourages them to endure suffering without retaliation, to live honourably before neighbours, and to hope in an inheritance that does not fade. It gives counsel to wives and husbands, elders and the young, and calls the whole community a royal priesthood and a holy nation.

First Peter is short, warm, and practical, written for people under pressure rather than for theologians. Its image of believers as living stones and its teaching on suffering have comforted persecuted Christians ever since. In the King James Version, its steady, pastoral voice makes it a good first letter for readers facing hardship.
8134-together:
Robert Herrick's novel Together opens in a little chapel on a warm June morning, where a tall. Straight young woman stands before the minister who is to marry her, looking at him rather than at the man beside her. Her father gives her arm a last gentle pressure and steps behind her, while a spray of woodbine sways through the open window behind the altar. The hush of the congregation waits for the ancient words that will unite the couple.

Herrick's novel follows a marriage through American life, asking what togetherness costs and what it means when ideals meet reality. Written in the progressive era, it examines divorce, ambition, and the changing roles of men and women. For readers of American social fiction, it is a serious, thoughtful study of marriage as an institution.
8180-a-phantom-lover:
Vernon Lee published A Phantom Lover in 1890, dedicating it to Count Peter Boutourline at Tagantcha in Russia. Her dedication recalls telling him, one afternoon on a hearthstool at Florence, the story of Mrs Oke of Okehurst, and his urging her to write it out at once. Though she protested that to write is to exorcise, and that printers' ink chases away ghosts as surely as holy water. The tale that follows is that story, of a woman haunted by a lover from the past.

Lee's ghost story works through atmosphere and suggestion rather than shock, with Okehurst house and its portraits carrying the haunting. It is a classic of the Victorian supernatural tale, admired for its psychological subtlety. For readers of ghost fiction, it remains one of Lee's finest, and a model of the quiet, uncanny story.
8244-the-world-english-bible-web-esther:
Esther, in the World English Bible, is set in the days of Ahasuerus, who reigned from India to Ethiopia over one hundred twenty-seven provinces. In the third year of his reign, the king feasts his princes and servants for one hundred eighty days. Displaying the riches of his glorious kingdom, and then feasts all the people of Shushan for seven days. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book follows Esther's rise, Haman's plot, and the Jews' deliverance.

The modern version keeps the court story's suspense and reversals, as banquet follows banquet toward rescue. Esther never names God, yet its deliverance has long been read as providence. For new readers, this rendering makes a thrilling court tale easy to follow, and explains the feast of Purim it celebrates.
8287-the-world-english-bible-web-1-peter:
Peter's first letter speaks to Christians scattered across Asia Minor who faced insults and suspicion from their neighbors. Written in Peter's name, it urges them to live so well that critics have nothing true to charge, to honor rulers, and to bear suffering without returning evil. The letter calls them a chosen people and a royal priesthood, strangers who belong elsewhere.

Household advice, warnings to elders, and a closing note of hope fill the later chapters. Its most quoted image, the devil prowling like a lion, warns readers to stay alert. For believers under pressure, 1 Peter has long offered dignity: suffering is not proof of failure, but part of the road.
8313-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-13-1-pa:
Long lists of names open this book, and patient readers are rewarded with a retelling of Israel's history from Adam to David. Called 1 Paralipomenon in the Douay-Rheims Bible, it is the book modern readers know as 1 Chronicles. Genealogies give way to David's reign: the ark brought to Jerusalem, plans for the temple, and the organization of priests, singers, and gatekeepers.

Where the books of Samuel stress David's sins and wars, Chronicles stresses worship and the temple he planned but did not build. Bishop Challoner's revision from the Latin Vulgate keeps the Greek-derived title, meaning things left out of the earlier histories. It is a book for readers who want the story told through liturgy and lineage.
8314-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-14-2-pa:
Solomon builds the temple, and Judah's kings succeed or fail by how they treat it: that is the spine of 2 Paralipomenon, the Douay-Rheims name for 2 Chronicles. The book opens with Solomon's wisdom and the temple's dedication, then marches through the kings of Judah, praising reformers like Ezechias and Josias, and condemning idolaters, until Babylon destroys the sanctuary.

Like its companion volume, this retelling favors priests, singers, and temple order over battlefield detail. It ends, surprisingly, with Cyrus of Persia sending the exiles home to rebuild. Challoner's text from the Latin Vulgate keeps the Greek title, meaning things omitted from the books of Kings. It is history written as liturgy.
8326-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-26-eccl:
Ecclesiasticus, also called Sirach, is a wisdom book of the Catholic canon, written by Jesus son of Sirach in Jerusalem about two centuries before Christ. It gathers practical advice on friendship, speech, money, table manners, and the fear of God, then closes with a long hymn praising Israel's great ancestors, from Enoch to Simon the high priest.

The book reads like Proverbs expanded into a teacher's manual, with a grandson's preface explaining how he translated it from Hebrew into Greek. Challoner's Douay-Rheims text gives it in Vulgate-based English. Readers meet a Judaism confident in law and wisdom, speaking to young men bound for public life in a Greek-ruled world.
8409-love-letters-between-a-nobleman-and:
Aphra Behn, the first Englishwoman to earn her living by writing, tells this story in letters between a nobleman and his sister. The argument sets it in the time of the Huguenot rebellion in Paris under the Prince of Condé, called Cesario here. Illustrious persons were drawn into conspiracy then, among them a young man of quality, fortune, youth, and beauty.

Behn's epistolary romance mixes politics, passion, and intrigue, in the Restoration manner, with lovers writing across danger. Readers meet Behn at her most daring, in a tale of forbidden love and civil war. The book remains a landmark: a woman writer shaping the novel's early form, in letters that still read with heat.
8450-the-elements-of-character:
Mary G. Chandler wrote The Elements of Character as a study of education and morals, opening with a warning against one-sided training. An exclusively intellectual education leads to hard-heartedness, she argues, an exclusively moral one to fatuity, and an exclusively religious one to worse, unless the influences balance. Character, for Chandler, needs all three.

The book belongs to Victorian moral philosophy for general readers, earnest and plainspoken. Chandler's aim is practical: how to form young people into steady, kind, and sensible adults. Readers interested in nineteenth-century ideas of education will find a clear, period example, with warnings that still sound familiar.
8677-behind-a-mask-or-a-woman-s-power:
A. M. Barnard, Louisa May Alcott's sensational pen name, opens Behind a Mask with a household awaiting its new governess, Miss Jean Muir. Poor, peevish Mrs Coventry sinks into an easy chair, sighing like a martyr, while her pretty daughter Bella hovers about her. A languid young man on a couch asks who they are talking of. His cousin Lucia, bent over tapestry with a happy smile on her usually haughty face, offers to tell him about the governess.

Jean Muir proves far more than the meek governess she seems, and the novella turns on a woman's power to outwit a family that underestimates her. Alcott wrote such thrillers for money and for fun, apart from her domestic fame. The story's pleasure lies in watching Muir play her part, and in Alcott's sharp portrait of a household that mistakes performance for innocence.
8710-the-dore-bible-gallery-complete-con:
Gustave Dore's complete Bible gallery gathers one hundred engravings into a single volume. From the creation of Eve and the expulsion from the garden to the murder of Abel, the Deluge, and the Tower of Babel. The preface explains that the original grand work was too costly for most admirers. That this collection was made to meet a felt and often expressed want among a wider circle. Abraham entertaining strangers, the destruction of Sodom, and Hagar in the wilderness follow in order.

Later scenes run through Joseph, Moses, the judges, and beyond, in the same pairing of Bible text and picture title that made Dore's name. For readers without the pictures, the list itself reads as a tour of the Bible's most pictured moments. The complete gallery stands as a monument of Victorian religious art, and a practical way to survey Scripture's great stories in one sitting.
8802-elizabeth-the-disinherited-daughter:
E. Ben Ez-er tells the story of Elizabeth, a daughter disinherited for leaving her ancestral faith, in a novel shaped as religious testimony. Part one opens with a strange letter, follows Elizabeth's alienation from the faith of her fathers, an alarming message, an order obeyed, a fiery furnace, and great victories. The chapter titles promise a conversion narrative told in the language of trial and deliverance.

Part two, called the great work of life, shows Elizabeth as mistress of the cottage chapel, enjoying religious privileges, labouring as an evangelist. Removing to a wilderness country, with chapters set in Volney, Oswego County, New York, and the hardships of a new colony. The book belongs to nineteenth-century evangelical fiction, written to encourage believers facing family opposition. Readers interested in that tradition will find its patterns, plainly and earnestly told.
8805-from-one-generation-to-another:
Henry Seton Merriman traces a family story across generations in From One Generation to Another, opening with the seed, suburban life, Mercury. A freighted venture, before nineteen years pass and a son takes up his father's cause. Chapters promise the roof of the world, relief, recasting, a last throw, a carpet knight, bad news, thin ice, and the curse of a good intention. The touch of nature, the spider and the fly, two motives, and ships upon the sea follow.

At Hurlingham, in a side path, alone, across the years. Somehow time passes, the novel moves toward a stab in the dark, from the jaws of death, balancing accounts, and at bay. Merriman, a popular novelist of adventure and empire, builds his plot on inheritance, duty, and the debts fathers leave sons.
8848-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Peter, apostle of Jesus Christ, writes in Weymouth's version to God's own people scattered over the earth, living as foreigners in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Roman Asia, and Bithynia. Chosen by the Father's foreknowledge, through the Spirit's sanctifying work, for obedience and sprinkling with Christ's blood, they receive his wish for more and more grace and peace. Blessed be God, he continues, who in great mercy has begotten believers anew to a living hope through Christ's resurrection.

That inheritance, imperishable and kept in Heaven, sustains a letter urging holy living under suffering, respect for authorities, and steadfast faith when tested by fire. Weymouth's modern speech keeps Peter's pastoral encouragement direct. Readers facing hardship, or studying the early Church's diaspora, will find a short, bracing letter that treats suffering as refining rather than as defeat.
8849-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Simon Peter, bondservant and apostle of Jesus Christ, writes in Weymouth's version to those allotted the same precious faith through the righteousness of God and Saviour Jesus Christ. Grace and peace, he wishes, in fuller knowledge of God and Jesus, whose divine power has given all things needful for life and godliness. Through God's precious and wondrous promises, readers may share in the divine nature and escape the world's corruption.

The letter then warns against false teachers, scoffers who doubt the Lord's coming, and those who twist Scripture, while urging diligence, growth in virtue, and remembrance of prophecy. Weymouth's modern speech keeps the letter's urgent, second-generation tone: an old apostle's testament to a church after his death. It is a short, stern book, valuable for its picture of early Christian worries about truth, delay, and deceit.
8878-the-mischief-maker:
E. Phillips Oppenheim, author of The Lighted Way and Havoc, writes The Mischief-Maker, a 1913 novel of diplomacy and intrigue, illustrated by Hanson Booth. Book one moves through sympathy and selfishness, an indiscreet letter, a ruined career, a bunch of violets. A sentimental episode, before reaching the Cafe de l'Athenee, coffee for three, Paris, Madame Christophor, and better acquaintance. A toymaker from Leipzig, the Rat Mort, politics and patriotism, and a meeting of socialists follow.

Behind closed doors, love, offers, and Falkenberg's actions drive book two, as a mischief-maker stirs nations and hearts alike. Oppenheim, the prince of Edwardian thriller writers, blends romance with pre-war espionage. Readers who enjoy suave spies, Paris cafes, and diplomatic danger will find a fast, polished entertainment. A snapshot of Europe on the edge of war, seen through a popular novelist's eyes.
8900-the-london-and-country-brewer:
An anonymous brewer published The London and Country Brewer in 1736, a practical manual running from barley-corn to finished beer. Contents cover the nature of barley and proper soils and manures for improving it, making good malts, telling good malts from bad. The uses of pale, amber, and brown malts. Waters and their use in brewing, grinding malts, and brewing in general follow. The London method for stout, but-beer, and pale and brown ales set beside the country or private way.

Hops, boiling malt liquors, brewing a quantity of drink in a little room with few tubs. Foxing or tainting of liquors, with prevention and cure, complete the advice. The book preserves Georgian brewing before industrial scale and science transformed it. Modern home brewers and food historians will enjoy its concrete, frugal wisdom.
898-the-lesson-of-the-master:
Henry James wrote this novella about Paul Overt, a young writer who seeks the counsel of Henry St. George, a master of fiction grown worldly with success. St. George warns Overt that marriage and comfort will kill his art, and urges him to guard his gift alone. Overt must choose between love and work.

James tells the tale with irony and restraint, leaving the reader to judge whether the master's lesson is wisdom or self-deception. The novella, first printed in book form in 1915, is a classic James study of the artist's life. It rewards readers who like fiction about fiction, where every choice costs.
8997-ritchie-s-fabulae-faciles-a-first-l:
Edited by John Copeland Kirtland Jr., a Latin teacher at Phillips Exeter Academy, this is a first reader for students of Latin. It retells four great Greek myths in easy Latin: Perseus, Hercules, the Argonauts, and Ulysses. Notes and a full word list sit beside the tales, so a beginner can work through them with care.

Short notes first link each myth to English books and art, from Hawthorne to old vase paintings. Then the Latin text itself leads the reader through monsters, quests, and sea voyages. It remains a friendly door into Latin, joining language drill to stories that have shaped the West.
904-her-father-s-daughter:
Gene Stratton-Porter wrote this novel about Linda, a young woman whose chapters carry titles such as What Kind of Shoes Are the Shoes You Wear and Cotyledon of Multiflores Canyon. The House of Dreams follows, and Linda starts a revolution. She faces the smoke of battle, and meets Jane Meredith, Katy, and a bear-cat along the way.

Stratton-Porter sets Linda's growth amid California canyons, flowers, and home life, with her usual love of nature and plucky heroines. The tale turns on a girl finding her own course, with help and hindrance from those around her. The book offers a warm, old-fashioned story of youth, nature, and self-reliance.
905-within-the-law-from-the-play-of-baya:
Marvin Dana novelized Bayard Veiller's play Within the Law into this tale of Mary Turner, a shopgirl wrongly sent to prison for theft. She serves three years, then sets out to live within the law while taking revenge on those who wronged her, using the law's own loopholes against them.

Dana follows Mary through the underworld and the courtroom, with marked money, legal traps, and a love that complicates her plan. The novel keeps the play's pace and its moral bite: a woman punished by law learns to use law as a weapon. It remains a gripping melodrama of justice and revenge.
914-the-uncommercial-traveller:
Charles Dickens wrote these sketches as an uncommercial traveller, a man who travels not for trade but for curiosity. His general line of business is to look, listen, and note, and his chapters take in a shipwreck, Wapping Workhouse, and the byways of London and beyond, with illustrations by Harry Furniss.

Dickens's traveller meets sailors, paupers, and eccentrics, and he tells their tales with warmth and wit. The sketches show the novelist as a reporter, finding stories in docks, inns, and night streets. The volume is a rich, rambling companion for readers who love Dickens's eye for the everyday and the odd.
9248-other-tales-and-sketches-from-the-d:
Hawthorne's other tales and sketches open with My Visit to Niagara, approached with deeper enthusiasm than any pilgrim's. He lingered from the falls, treasuring hope over memory, till the stagecoach from Lewiston brought him near. A Frenchman rode beside him as he listened for the cataract's roar, trembling with a sensation like dread.

The Antique Ring and Graves and Goblins follow in the set. Hawthorne's Niagara passage is among his finest nature writing, awed and personal. The collection remains a good sampler of his sketches, from wonder to gloom, in his early manner.
927-the-lamplighter:
Charles Dickens wrote this short piece about a lamplighter who talks of Murphy and Francis Moore, the almanac makers, gentlemen whose forecasts folk trusted. The lamplighter, a man of the streets, holds forth on weather, fate, and the lights he tends, in Dickens's early comic voice.

The piece is brief and theatrical, a sketch rather than a novel, with the lamplighter as a small philosopher of the night. It shows Dickens finding his voice in London types and talk. The Lamplighter delights readers who enjoy a short, funny Dickens, lit by gaslight and good humour.
932-the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher:
Edgar Allan Poe wrote this tale of a narrator who rides alone, on a dull, dark, and soundless autumn day, to the dreary house of Usher. Roderick Usher, a friend grown strange and nervous, has called him, and his sister Madeline lies ill in the house. The building itself seems alive with decay.

Poe builds dread from setting, sound, and the slow unravelling of minds, until the house and its line fall together. His prose is musical and gothic, full of mirrors, vaults, and storm. The tale is a masterpiece of horror, and the most famous of Poe's stories of a house that shares its owner's fate.
9324-roden-s-corner:
Henry Seton Merriman wrote this novel in 1913, opening with a verse on destiny playing men like chess pieces. Roden's corner lies in St. Jacob Straat, where work and play, a new disciple, and a shadow from the past tangle. Chapters move from the dunes to the Oude Weg, from danger to a combined force, and from gratitude to an ultimatum.

Commerce, plain speaking, and a bright and shining light mark the road to the corner itself. Merriman keeps intrigue and romance in balance. The novel is a solid late work by a master of the adventure tale, brisk and worldly-wise.
936-the-village-watch-tower:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote these stories of village life, headed by the village watch-tower of the title. The introduction notes that Wiggin's name is now little known, yet Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm still brings instant recognition in America. These tales show the same warm, humane art in shorter form.

Wiggin writes of neighbours, children, and small-town ways with humour and tenderness, never with condescension. Her village folk are vivid, and her morals are gentle. The collection suits readers who love Rebecca, and who want more of Wiggin's New England world, in tales that can be read one at a time.
9377-london-pride-or-when-the-world-was-:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon wrote this Restoration romance in 1896, called London Pride, or When the World Was Younger. Chapters move from a harbour from the storm and convent walls, through letters from home and the valley of the shadow, to London at the top of fashion. A Puritan house, a priest's hole, and a Millbank ghost follow.

Falcon and dove, murder as motive, and revelations drive the plot to good-bye, London, and a manor moat. Braddon recreates Charles the Second's age with color and pace. The novel remains a lavish historical romance, full of intrigue and high feeling.
9402-be-courteous-or-religion-the-true-r:
Mrs. M. H. Maxwell wrote Be Courteous, or Religion the True Refiner, a tale of plain folk on a rural plain. The story follows a family at Appledale and their kin, through calls, church days, sickbeds, and small trials. Its thread is simple: true faith shows itself in kind manners, not in fine words. The book first spoke to readers who prized home piety and good conduct.

Scenes move from berry parties and log-house calls to a poor woman's need and a sick child's bedside. Each test asks the same thing: will faith make a person gentler to those near at hand? Maxwell writes in a mild, earnest voice, rich in home detail. A reader gets a quiet lesson in courtesy as a Christian duty, told through daily life.
9403-the-life-and-works-of-friedrich-sch:
Calvin Thomas, a professor at Columbia, wrote this life and works of Friedrich Schiller, the German poet and dramatist. The book opens with parentage and schooling: Captain Schiller and his wife, a sojourn at Lorch, and removal to Ludwigsburg. Duke Karl Eugen's academy at Solitude shapes the boy, from law to medicine, with early poems and plays.

Schiller's dissertation fails, yet The Robbers takes shape, born of morbid melancholy and ardent friendship. Thomas follows the poet's growth with scholarly care. The volume remains a standard English life of Schiller, thorough, sympathetic, and readable.
9404-the-story-of-the-malakand-field-for:
Winston Churchill, then a young cavalry officer, wrote this book in 1898 about war on India's north-west frontier. He served under Major-General Sir Bindon Blood in the Malakand campaign of 1897, when tribal fighters rose against British rule. Churchill frames these frontier wars as the hard edge where a growing empire met fierce, free peoples. The book is both a soldier's report and a young writer's bid for fame.

Chapters map the hills and passes, name the tribes, and follow raids, marches, and sharp fights. Churchill praises his chief, notes the cost in lives, and defends the campaign with verve. A reader gets a first-hand view of late empire war, told with speed and color, and a glimpse of a future prime minister learning his craft.
9456-opera-stories-from-wagner:
Florence Akin wrote Opera Stories from Wagner in 1915, retelling Wagner's great operas as plain tales for young readers. The book covers The Rhine-Gold, The Valkyrie, Siegfried, and The Twilight of the Gods, with verses drawn from Oliver Huckel's translations. Akin breaks each opera into short scenes, so a child can follow gods, heroes, and cursed gold. Plates add pictures of the chief scenes.

Readers meet the Rhine daughters, Alberich's theft, Wotan and Brunhilde, and Siegfried's sword and fire. Greed, love, and doom drive each tale, in prose far simpler than Wagner's verse. A reader gets a clear first path into the Ring cycle, and a story book that makes vast operas feel close and human.
9471-the-vicar-s-daughter:
George MacDonald, a Scots novelist of the Victorian age, first put out The Vicar's Daughter in 1872. A vicar's daughter tells her own tale, from her girlhood home through her wedding and her first years as a wife. London firms and church folk fill the early scenes. The book reads as a home tale, warm and plain, with a keen eye for manners and faith.

Chapters follow her wedding, calls on good society, a foundling child, and the trials of a young wife. A found baby, a friend named Connie, and a run of dinner parties shape the plot. Through it all, the voice stays kind and wry. Readers who like slow, humane Victorian fiction will find a gentle portrait of family duty and love.
9618-the-field-of-ice-part-ii-of-the-adv:
Part two of Jules Verne's Adventures of Captain Hatteras, The Field of Ice, follows the polar party's frozen ordeal. The 1875 Routledge translation, with 126 pictures by Riou, carries the tale from the doctor's inventory to first words with Altamont. Chapters promise winter pleasures, bear tracks, an Arctic spring, and the North-West Passage. Arctic Arcadia and Altamont's revenge add wonder and strife.

The party, trapped in ice, builds shelter, hunts, and plans final marches, as cold and hunger test them. Verne blends science with adventure in brisk, clear prose. A reader gets a classic polar tale's second half, rich in ice, courage, and the lure of the North.
9665-delia-blanchflower:
Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote Delia Blanchflower, a novel that opens in a crowded Tyrolean hotel salon. An Englishman, finding scarcely a Britisher in sight, trades weather talk with a German who lends him matches. Thunder showers splash outside as the dining hall empties. Delia herself soon enters this cosmopolitan scene, where English manners meet foreign ways.

Ward follows Delia through hotels, society, and moral choices, with her usual care for motive and class. The Tyrol setting lends color to a tale of character. A reader gets a late Ward novel of travel, manners, and a young woman's growth, told with grave, polished art.
9747-the-fortune-hunter:
Louis Joseph Vance wrote The Fortune Hunter in 1910, a novel of a young man chasing wealth in a small town. Roland Barnette, aided by Homer Little John and Blinky Lockwood, climbs from small beginnings to business triumph. Chapters promise a window in Radville, a grubstake, and manoeuvres by Josie, toward the rainbow's end. Margaret's daughter and Betty cross Roland's path.

Vance follows Roland's bargains, troubles, and triumphs with brisk, comic energy. The tale asks what fortune costs and what it buys. A reader gets a lively Edwardian success story, full of small-town schemes and a hero's rise.
9785-woodstock-or-the-cavalier:
Sir Walter Scott wrote Woodstock, or The Cavalier, a tale of the year 1651, in the Civil War's shadow. Scott's 1832 introduction recalls how the war displayed each party's genius in striking incidents, fit for fiction. Adventures at Woodstock in 1649, long read and half forgotten, gave him his harvest. The book adds a scuffle and a just devil of Woodstock as appendices.

The Cavalier follows royalists and Roundheads around Woodstock's loyal house, with Scott's rich humor and history. His preface sets the tale's frame. A reader gets a classic Scott romance of king, commons, and loyalty, from the master of historical fiction.
9837-albert-du-rer:
T. Sturge Moore's study of Albrecht Dürer treats the German artist as both craftsman and thinker. It opens with general ideas, including proportion and the pull of religion on art, before placing Dürer in the world he lived in.

Later sections follow his youth and schooling, his time in Venice, his patrons and friends, his links with Luther and the humanists, and his journey to the Netherlands. Moore reads Dürer's prints and paintings as the work of a mind joining faith, science, and skill. Art lovers get a compact, thoughtful life of a master.
9839-the-cavalier:
George W. Cable's 1901 novel is set in Louisiana during the American Civil War. Its opening chapters introduce a young woman who wanted to laugh, a Lieutenant Ferry, and a household living under the strain of war, with rations short and strangers arriving.

Cable, best known for his Louisiana stories, mixes romance with the confusion of occupied country: names mistaken, loyalties tested, and danger close at hand. The novel gives readers a southern, civilian view of the war, told with local color, humor, and a light, ironic touch throughout every chapter.
9871-the-avenger:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's 1908 thriller opens with a mysterious visitor and a horror in a hansom cab, setting a London mystery in motion. Oppenheim, a popular writer of crime and spy tales, builds his novels from secrets, pursuit, and revenge.

The chapters that follow deepen the puzzle as the avenger's purpose comes into view and the net tightens around his quarry. Oppenheim keeps the pace quick and the scenes theatrical, in the style of Edwardian popular fiction. Readers looking for a fast, old-fashioned thriller will find this one easy to finish.
9978-the-happy-foreigner:
Enid Bagnold's 1920 novel follows a traveller journeying through France after the Great War, happy to be a foreigner among new scenes. It opens with a prologue on the eve of departure, then moves to a black hut at Bar and on into Lorraine.

Later parts visit Metz, Verdun, and the forests of Chantilly, ending with spring in Charleville, where Philippe and his mother appear. Bagnold writes with a sharp eye for inns, rivers, and small comedy. Readers get a fresh, observant portrait of a woman travelling light through a Europe remaking itself.
a-biography-of-edmund-spenser:
John W. Hales admits at the start that Spenser's life is wrapped in a similar obscurity to Chaucer's and Shakespeare's: a few meagre entries in official documents are the principal external authorities. His biography, revised in 1896 and taken from the Macmillan Globe edition of Spenser's works, builds what can honestly be built from those records and from the poems themselves.

Four long chapters trace the London schoolboy, the Cambridge scholar, the secretary in Ireland, the planter at Kilcolman, and the poet of The Faerie Queene at Elizabeth's court. Hales weighs dedications, allegories, and state papers for facts with a scholar's caution. The result is a sober Victorian life of a poet whose inner story must be read out of his verse.
a-brief-memoir-with-portions-of-the-diar: Eliza Allen Southall is remembered in this memoir drawn from her diary and letters. Born at Liskeard in Cornwall, she married William Southall of Birmingham and lived a short life among scenes she loved. The selections show her attachment to childhood places and to the people around her. The memoir preserves her voice for American readers as a record of faith and feeling.
a-cathedral-singer: James Lane Allen sets this novel at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine on Morningside Heights. The great church rises on a high rock above the city, and its music draws the story forward. A cathedral singer stands at the center of a tale of pity, faith, and youthful aspiration. Allen writes with warmth about art, worship, and the inner life of his singers.
a-daughter-of-the-sioux-a-tale-of-the-in: Charles King tells a tale of the Indian frontier through a daughter of the Sioux. Its chapters open with foreshadowed events, absence from duty, and a night encounter. The sign of the bar shoe and a grave discovery deepen the mystery. King, a soldier author, writes of army life and frontier conflict with firsthand color.
a-dutch-boy-fifty-years-after: Edward William Bok tells his story as a Dutch boy fifty years after. Adapted from his Americanization, the book follows his first days in America and a first job at fifty cents a week. Chapters treat his hunger for self education, a presidential friend, and going to the theatre with Longfellow. Bok offers schoolboys and schoolgirls a tale of obstacles overcome.
a-first-spanish-reader: Erwin William Roessler gives a first Spanish reader for the very beginning of the Spanish course. Early selections use only the present tense and treat school, family, lessons, and coins of the United States and Spain. Roessler and Alfred Remy designed the book to join simplicity with variety. The reader serves high school pupils starting Spanish.
a-girl-s-student-days-and-after: Jeannette Augustus Marks writes of a girl's student days and after. With an introduction by Mary Emma Woolley, president of Mount Holyoke, the book follows school life into later years. Marks, a Wellesley graduate, writes for girls facing college and its choices. The volume offers counsel drawn from student experience.
a-library-primer: John Cotton Dana gives a library primer for founders of public libraries. Chapters treat library law, preliminary work, trustees, the librarian, and rooms and equipment. Dana draws on Poole, Fletcher, and Plummer for the organization of small libraries. The primer served a generation building public libraries in America. New librarians will find the steps laid out in clear order.
a-lost-leader:
A Lost Leader is a 1907 political novel by E Phillips Oppenheim. Its hero, Mannering, is content with a quiet country life of leisure and study in England. His teenage niece Clara lives with him, and a beautiful widow, Berenice, is staying nearby, so nothing seems likely to disturb him.

Politics disturbs him anyway. Borrowdean believes Mannering's gift for speech and public life is needed in London to save the faltering Liberal party, and he means to fetch him back whatever it takes. The novel follows the pull between private peace and public duty, as the lost leader is drawn toward the career he had left behind.
a-melody-in-silver: Keene Abbott writes a melody in silver in linked stories. Its chapters include the lost cause, rue and rosemary, the world's end, and dead sea fruit. The mug of woe, a fountain in the desert, and the gone away lady follow. Abbott's stories move from guilt and crime toward light and apotheosis.
a-phantom-lover: Vernon Lee frames this ghost story as a tale told at Florence to Count Peter Boutourline, the story of Mrs Oke of Okehurst. The narrator protests that writing such matters exorcises them, since printers' ink chases away ghosts as surely as holy water. Yet the telling survives in print, carrying a haunting worked up by firelight into a little book meant to recall, in a Russian summer, that stranger seasons exist.
a-plea-for-old-cap-collier:
Irvin S. Cobb explains how his essay jelled at last in a small seacoast hotel, where, laid up sick over a Sunday, he ran out of newspapers and magazines. In despair he took an old Fifth Reader to bed and read it through. The night's reading stirred his defense of the cheap story papers of his boyhood.

His plea speaks for Old Cap Collier, hero of the dime novels that boys once hid and devoured. Cobb argues that those crude tales of detectives and Indians fed real hunger for story and did less harm than their critics claimed. The essay is funny, fond, and shrewd about how reading tastes form.
a-practical-illustration-of-woman-s-righ: Marie Elizabeth Zakrzewska, a physician late of Berlin, offers her career as a practical illustration of a woman's right to labour, in a letter edited by Caroline Dall. Dedicated to Samuel Sewall, supporter of a New England college for women in medicine, the volume argues: a woman who does the work claims her licence in the work itself. Its epigraphs from Aurora Leigh frame healing as proof against those who doubt.
a-primary-reader: Emma Louise Smythe retells old-time stories, fairy tales, and myths for beginning readers in this primary reader, grown from lessons for first grade pupils in Santa Rosa. Each story was told, discussed, and then produced orally by the children, whose own expressions shaped the final text. Following the teaching of G. Stanley Hall, the book fits its tales to the minds and hearts of little ones with only a small vocabulary of sight words.
a-roman-singer: Francis Marion Crawford tells this Roman story through Cornelio Grandi, once owner of a castello in the Sabines with corn land, vineyards, and olives, now a poor professor of philosophy. Driven to sell his patrimony, he raised Nino from childhood and schooled him in Latin, hoping for a philosopher, but the boy's voice proved too great for philosophy. As Nino grows famous, Grandi sets down the whole truth about the singer.
a-selection-of-books-published-by-methue: Methuen and Company issue their October 1910 selection from Essex Street, London, with contents pages running from general literature through ancient cities and antiquary's books to the Arden Shakespeare. Fiction occupies page 23, with books for boys and girls, sixpenny books, and novels of Alexandre Dumas following. An asterisk marks books in the press, and colonial editions are published of all the firm's novels.
a-sixth-century-fragment-of-the-letters-: Elias Avery Lowe studies six leaves of a sixth-century uncial manuscript of Pliny the Younger's letters, preserved in the Pierpont Morgan Library in New York. Published by the Carnegie Institution of Washington in 1922, the volume divides into palaeography by Lowe and text by E. K. Rand, professor of Latin at Harvard. The fragment's lettering, layout, and readings are examined leaf by leaf, giving scholars a firm account of a very early witness.
a-texas-matchmaker: Andy Adams tells a Texas matchmaker's story in this 1904 ranch novel, illustrated by E. Boyd Smith and dedicated to Frank Earnest, mounted inspector of customs at Laredo. The chapters run from Lance Lovelace and Shepherd's Ferry through Las Palomas, Christmas, a pigeon hunt, the spring of 1876, and San Jacinto Day. A cat hunt on the Frio, a turkey bake, hide hunting, a two years' drought, and matchmaking itself carry the ranch year toward sunset.
a-texas-ranger:
William MacLeod Raine's A Texas Ranger, dated 1910, begins with a foreword to ye gentle reader. The frontier, Raine writes, has passed from rollicking boyhood to responsible majority within living memory. The ranger who patrolled for bad men has yielded to the forest ranger. Tucson, where he writes, is now more civilized than New York.

Part one, The Man from the Panhandle, opens on a desert meeting. A girl crouched in the bear-grass covers a passing driver with her revolver. Steve, the ranger hero, plays second fiddle, by the part's own subtitle, to the lady's distress. Raine builds a border melodrama of rustlers, disguises, and a ranger's divided duty. His West is already nostalgic in 1910. The saga of the strong, as his quoted poem calls it, sings over country the plough has taken.
a-v-laider:
Max Beerbohm tells a quiet, teasing short story about a narrator resting at a small seaside hotel after illness. Rain falls, time hangs heavy, and the narrator falls into talk with A. V. Laider, a fellow guest who writes books nobody seems to know. Laider shares a strange tale about a palm reading and a fate he believes was foretold for him.

Beerbohm lets the talk unfold slowly, with dry humor and polite doubt on both sides. The joke turns on vanity, fate, and how gladly a man believes a story that makes him seem marked by destiny. Readers prize the story for its gentle wit and its neat, ironic close.
a-woman-hater:
Charles Reade opens at the Golden Star hotel in Homburg, a humble house used by modest travelers, not gay gamblers. At two o'clock on a June day, two strangers sit far apart in the dining room. One is a lady of twenty-four with a high white forehead and gray eyes, looking comely and sedate — and not, the narrator warns, the remarkable person she really is.

The other stranger is a sworn woman-hater, and Reade sets these two against each other for thirty-two chapters of argument, adventure, and reluctant feeling. The heroine argues women's cause with her life as much as her tongue. Reade writes with his usual research, energy, and courtroom love of a good cross-examination.
a-yankee-girl-at-fort-sumter:
A Yankee Girl at Fort Sumter, by Alice Turner Curtis, tells a Civil War story for young readers through a Boston child in Charleston. Curtis sets Sylvia Fulton in the South Carolina city with her parents just before the war opens. The introduction promises her perilous adventure in Charleston Harbor and her warm welcome from new southern friends, whose kindness to a northern girl carries much of the book's point.

Philadelphia printed the volume in 1920, with illustrations by Isabel W Caley, as part of Curtis's historical writing for girls. Early chapters bring a new friend, trouble, and an unexpected journey. Later ones take Sylvia to a plantation with Estralla and Elinor, where ways of life she has never seen raise questions the story treats gently. Loyalty to home and fairness to strangers are held up together as the guns approach.
adventures-of-a-despatch-rider: William Henry Lowe Watson, a captain in the British Expeditionary Force, recounts his service as a despatch rider in the First World War. He describes carrying orders under fire, moving between units, and the confusion and strain of the early campaigns. Maps and a plain soldier's voice ground the book in the daily work of the front, rather than in grand strategy.
albert-du-rer: Thomas Sturge Moore studies the life and art of Albert Dürer, opening with general ideas on proportion and the influence of religion on the creative impulse. The book traces how the German master joined exact craft with deep feeling, in engraving, painting, and theory. Moore writes for readers who want to understand Dürer not only as a maker of images but as a thinker about art.
allan-and-the-holy-flower:
H. Rider Haggard's Allan and the Holy Flower, first published in 1915, begins with Allan Quatermain disclaiming any link to orchids. Yet an orchid hunt of remarkable character, he writes, should not be lost. His companion beyond the Limpopo is Charles Scroope, an English sportsman. Scroope fled to Africa after quarrelling with his fiancée over four dances at a hunt ball.

Brother John, a white-bearded missionary figure of the wilds, leads the party inland. Their goal is a gigantic orchid, the holy flower worshipped by the Ponda people. A slave-raiding stronghold, a great ape, and a tribal war guard the treasure. Haggard mixes botany with his usual African adventure. Quatermain narrates in dry hindsight, older and sadder than in King Solomon's Mines. The flower itself, when found, justifies the madness of the quest.
alphabetical-catalogue-of-books-in-ficti: Chatto and Windus, the London publishing firm, lists its books in fiction and general literature alphabetically in this catalogue of September 1905. Issued from St. Martin's Lane, Charing Cross, the catalogue served booksellers and readers seeking the firm's titles. As a trade list, it now records what a major house offered at the height of the Edwardian book trade.
amy-foster:
Joseph Conrad's story Amy Foster is told by Kennedy, a country doctor in the village of Colebrook on the Kent coast. Kennedy's practice runs from the sea-wall towns inland to Darnford, and his cases bring him the parish's secrets. Among them is the history of Amy Foster, a dull, kind servant girl, and of the stranger the sea delivered to her world.

That stranger is Yanko Goorall, a peasant from Eastern Europe and the sole survivor of a wrecked emigrant ship. He learns no English that the village trusts, marries Amy, and has a child with her. When fever takes him, the gap of language and fear between husband and wife turns fatal. Conrad turns a coast village's suspicion of one foreign man into a study of loneliness.
an-adventure-with-a-genius-recollections:
An Adventure with a Genius records Alleyne Ireland and his recollections of Joseph Pulitzer, the great newspaper publisher. Ireland frames the book in a preface about a life spent meeting remarkable men in a score of countries, from kings and viceroys to judges and ward politicians. His first outstanding adventure, he says, was with a stern and formidable man, and the dedication honors Mrs Joseph Pulitzer.

Inside, the chapters follow Ireland's work beside Pulitzer at close range. The publisher appears through daily demands, sharp judgments, and the running of a newspaper empire built on crusades and circulation wars. Ireland writes as a witness rather than a critic, setting down habits, sayings, and scenes from inside the office and the household. Readers curious about how a press lord actually worked, hour by hour, get a portrait drawn by a man who stood in the room.
an-american-idyll-the-life-of-carleton-h: Cornelia Stratton Parker writes an American idyll on the life of Carleton H. Parker, her husband, published by the Atlantic Monthly Press in Boston. The memoir recalls a scholar and reformer whose work touched labour and social life in California. Tender and clear-eyed, it paints a portrait of a life cut short but widely felt.
an-apache-princess-a-tale-of-the-indian-: Charles King tells a tale of the Indian frontier in An Apache Princess, by the author of A Daughter of the Sioux and Fort Frayne. The story follows army life, Native peoples, and a heroine caught between two worlds on the western border. King's soldier's eye gives the romance its detail and its period colour.
an-arkansas-planter: Opie Percival Read writes An Arkansas Planter, a novel of Southern life centred on a planter and the world around him. Published in Chicago and New York, the story follows character, land, and local custom in the post-war South. Read's warm, anecdotal style gives the book its easy, storytelling charm.
animal-ghosts-or-animal-hauntings-and-th: Elliott O'Donnell writes on animal ghosts, or animal hauntings and the hereafter, by the author of The Sorcery Club and books on haunted houses. The volume collects cases of phantom beasts and asks whether animals survive death. O'Donnell's credulous, story-driven manner made the book popular with ghost-lore readers.
armageddon-and-after: W. L. Courtney reflects on war and peace just after the First World War, asking what the future should learn from the past. He opens with problems of the future, turns to lessons of history, and closes with suggested reforms. Biblical images of a last battle frame his warning against old rivalries and worn ideas. The tone is earnest and civic, urging readers to shape a peace that does not repeat the errors that led to war.
arthur-a-short-sketch-of-his-life-and-hi: Frederick James Furnivall edits a fifteenth century English verse sketch of King Arthur from the Marquis of Bath manuscript. The poem tells how Arthur was begotten by Uther Pendragon on Ygerne, and it follows his labors in short, plain lines. Furnivall keeps the old spelling and adds notes on the manuscript for students of early English. The result is a brief, rare window on Arthur in verse before print.
be-courteous-or-religion-the-true-refine:
Mrs. M. H. Maxwell wrote this religious tale around the apostle's command to be courteous. Her preface calls the story a disconnected diary of one early refined from earthly dross, whose short life proved the divine authority behind the text. Scenes and characters, she says, were once familiar to her. An engraving shows Mary and the sick child at page fifty-six.

Chapter heads map a rural Christian world: a blueberry party on the plain, the family at Appledale, calls at the log-house, and original poetry on the ride home. Trouble enters through Dora, whose religious fits of being disobliging make a sick girl unhappy until her mother forbids Dora the room. Maxwell measures refinement not by manners learned but by faith practised, in the Sunday-school manner of her century.
behind-a-mask-or-a-woman-s-power:
Louisa May Alcott published this sensation tale under her pen name A. M. Barnard, as Behind a Mask, or A Woman's Power. The Coventry family waits on a governess: Mrs. Coventry frets on her cushion, Bella hovers, and the languid Gerald declares his inveterate aversion to the whole tribe of governesses. Jean Muir arrives, small, plain, and thirty years of practiced humility in her manner.

Jean is not what she seems. Her confession, sampled midway, tells of a wild act that convinced a stormy lover of her indomitable dislike. He found her out anyway and wrote; her reply goes by another's hand to Lady Sydney. Alcott, writing thrillers for money while the March girls waited, lets the governess scheme, act, and conquer the house from below stairs. It is her darkest, cleverest fiction.
big-brother:
Annie Fellows Johnston published this children's story in the Cosy Corner Series with Joseph Knight of Boston, copyrighted in 1893. Robin, the big brother of the frontispiece, is followed everywhere by little Steven. The pictures promise the scale of their world. A barefoot girl wears a sunbonnet; a little white cottage stands in New Jersey. A black dancing bear must always be put to bed, and a snow man is in the building.

One scene brings an eccentric old banker, Mr. Dearborn, face to face with the boy who shares his name. He presses a shining half-dollar into the small mittened hand: that's for good luck, for he was a boy himself once. Sometimes, he sighs, he wishes he could have stayed one. Johnston, later famous for The Little Colonel, writes brotherly devotion in the Sunday-school manner, all small change and large sentiment.
black-beetles-in-amber:
Ambrose Bierce published this book of satirical verse in 1892, arranging his Californian enemies like insects in amber. The contents are a rogues' gallery: An Obituarian, A Commuted Sentence, Two Statesmen, Three Kinds of a Rogue, Dennis Kearney, and To My Liars. Each beetle is a public man of the Pacific coast, pinned in couplets meant to outlast him.

Nemesis gets the sampled poem's full music. When devils dance madly in the midmost Hell, beware: she is everywhere. You shall hear her at your back and fancy her eyes burning like a tiger's on your track. She whispers in the breeze to summer trees and calls through the storm while giant billows fall. Bierce's wit here is rarely gentle; the amber is acid, and the preservation eternal, exactly as the victims would not have wished.
bohemians-of-the-latin-quarter:
Henry Murger published Bohemians of the Latin Quarter in French in 1851, and the English text here is the Vizetelly issue of 1888. Murger drew his scenes from poor artists' life in Paris, and the book later fed two operas named La Bohème. Schaunard, Rodolphe, Marcel, and Colline form the club.

Chapters follow the four friends through cold rooms, pawned goods, and sudden small windfalls. Musette, Mimi, and other grisettes move through the tale of love and hunger. Work sells late or not at all, yet the friends keep their jokes. Youth fleets, as the last chapter warns, and success parts the group. Murger writes with warmth for a life he knew. The scenes set the lasting image of the starving artist.
book-of-mormon-1852-front-matter:
Front matter from the 1852 Liverpool edition of the Book of Mormon fills this entry. Publishers Jas. O. Wright and Co. framed Joseph Smith's scripture for British readers. Only the introduction and synopsis appear here, not the full text.

The publisher explains the book's origin and story in brief. A synopsis walks through its peoples, prophets, and wars. Such framing shows how a new faith packaged its core text for converts abroad. The piece is a small historical artifact. It suits students of Mormon history who study how the movement spread in its first decades.
both-sides-the-border-a-tale-of-hotspur-:
G A Henty wrote Both Sides the Border, a tale of Hotspur and Glendower set in the first years of the fourteen hundreds. Henty states the stakes in his preface: Glendower's Welsh rising, Douglas's raid, and the Percy revolt. Young Oswald, of a border hold, carries the plot.

Oswald rides to Alnwick, jousts, and runs missions for Hotspur to Dunbar and Ludlow. He meets Glendower, fights at Homildon Hill, and wins his spurs. The Percy discontent builds to Shrewsbury, where Hotspur falls. Henty threads real battles through a squire's rise, with wrestling and races at a border feast for relief. Boys got hard history here: marches law, clan pride, and a king held by one day's march.
boulogne-sur-mer:
William Fleming, rector of St Mary's, Moorfields, published Boulogne-sur-Mer with Washbourne of London in 1907. Fleming argues a bold claim in his subtitle: this French port was St Patrick's native town. The archbishop of Westminster's imprimatur heads the Catholic case.

Celtic, Roman, and Frankish traces around Boulogne build the ground first. Fleming then reads Patrick's own Confession, where the saint names his father's home, Bonaven Taberniae. Scholiasts and place names are weighed to fix that town on the Armorican coast near Boulogne. Dumbarton's rival claim gets a full hearing and a firm no. Pilgrims get town history along the way. The case shows how saints' lives were fought over with maps and charters.
bound-to-rise-or-up-the-ladder:
Bound to Rise, or Up the Ladder, by Horatio Alger Jr, opens with a life of its author. Alger was a minister turned writer. He settled in New York to work among street boys. The sketch counts more than seventy Alger stories. It also counts over a million copies sold in his lifetime. That frame tells readers what kind of book they hold.

Harry Walton, a poor country boy, carries the story. His family needs his wages. His motto comes from Hiram, the hired man of Chapter III. A calamity opens the tale. An arithmetic sum matters more than sums usually do. The ladder of the subtitle then rises rung by rung. Employers, temptations, and small sums saved mark the climb. Alger's promise sits in the title. Rise is possible, and boys earn it in public, one honest decision at a time.
britannica-1911-abbot-george-writer:
George Abbot the writer, called the Puritan, receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abbot, born at Easington in Yorkshire in 1603, has been long confused with kin of the archbishop. He was no clergyman, but a layman of rare learning, the entry stresses.

Caldecote manor house was his stage in the civil war, held bravely against Princes Rupert and Maurice. His Whole Booke of Job Paraphrased won praise for terse clarity amid prolix Puritan comment. Vindiciae Sabbathi shaped the long Sabbath debate. Notes on the Psalms came out after his death in 1648. A lay theologian of that force, the entry holds, stands near alone in the period's literature. Dugdale and Wood supply the record.
britannica-1911-abd-el-kader:
Abd-el-Kader receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abd-el-Kader, amir of Mascara, was born near Mascara about 1807, of a sherif family famed for piety. Pilgrimage to Mecca and Bagdad, and a sight of Mehemet Ali's Egypt, formed his youth.

France took Algiers in 1830, and Mascara proclaimed him amir in 1832. Fifteen years of war followed, in his favor till Bugeaud took the field. Surrender in 1847 led, against promise, to prison at Amboise till Napoleon the Third freed him in 1852. Damascus gained a sage: in 1860 he saved thousands of Christians from massacre there. France gave him a pension and its grand cross. He died at Damascus in 1883, a writer on faith and the Arab horse.
britannica-1911-abelard-peter:
Peter Abelard receives a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abelard, a Breton noble's son born in 1079, chose learning over knighthood and mastered dialectic young. Paris drew him to William of Champeaux at Notre-Dame, whom he bested in open dispute.

Schools at Melun, Corbeil, and St Geneviève made him Europe's famed teacher by 1115, with crowds in thousands, as the tale runs. Anselm of Laon fell to the same lance in theology. Heloise, canon Fulbert's niece, then entered his house as pupil, and love, a child, and ruin followed the fame. The entry traces the love story at full length, with her learning in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew praised. Pride at its height meets a fall prepared in his own house.
britannica-1911-abner:
Abner receives a Bible entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. Abner, Saul's first cousin and army chief, set Saul's son Ishbaal on Israel's throne at Mahanaim after Gilboa. David, king in Judah at Hebron, warred with that house for years.

A set fight of twelve against twelve at Gibeon, all slain, opens the one full battle told. Abner killed pursuing Asahel in self-defence and earned Joab's blood feud. Ishbaal's rebuke over Rizpah drove Abner to David, who feasted the bargain and took Michal back. Joab then slew Abner at Hebron's gate. David's grief cleared him of the plot, though punishment stayed beyond his power, the entry judges.
britannica-1911-aceto-acetic-ester:
Aceto-acetic ester is a chemical substance whose discovery in 1863 opened a famous quarrel. Geuther found that sodium acting on ethyl acetate gave a sodium compound that yielded a colourless, oily liquid with acids. Frankland and Duppa argued in 1865 that it was a derivative of a keto acid's ethyl ester, while Geuther held his product was itself an acid. Wislicenus investigated thoroughly and sided with Frankland and Duppa.

Preparation and behaviour occupy most of the entry. Dried ethyl acetate is treated with sodium wire, then acidified and fractionated, giving a liquid that boils at a high temperature and reacts as a keto compound should. Its replaceable hydrogen atoms let chemists build many other substances from it, making it a prized synthetic reagent for rings, acids, and ketones.
britannica-1911-actinometer:
Actinometer is an instrument for measuring light's effects. The word joins Greek terms for ray and measure. Sir John Herschel first gave the name to his apparatus. His device measured the heating effect of solar rays. Scientists have since discarded Herschel's instrument. The pyrheliometer replaced it for heat measurement. Usage of the old name shifted accordingly.

Modern actinometers measure chemical effect instead. Actinic rays are the rays that drive chemical change. Such instruments generally depend on photochemical changes. Photography uses practical forms of them daily. Photographers must judge light's strength before exposure. The entry points readers onward for the details. Radiation theory and photochemistry hold the fuller accounts. One name thus covers two generations of instruments.
britannica-1911-adam-alexander:
Alexander Adam (1741-1809) was a Scottish writer on Roman antiquities. He was born near Forres in Morayshire. Poverty and difficulty marked his classical studies. Diligence carried him to Edinburgh University in 1757. His scholarship won him school posts quickly. In 1768 he became rector of Edinburgh's High School. He held that post for life. Pupil numbers grew greatly under him. Sir Walter Scott sat among his pupils. Lord Brougham and Jeffrey did as well.

Reform and writing fill his record. Adam introduced Greek into the school curriculum. Edinburgh University opposed the change, but he prevailed. His grammar of 1772 was written in English. That choice brought a storm of abuse. His Roman Antiquities proved his best work. Many editions and a German translation followed.
britannica-1911-adams-henry-carter:
Henry Carter Adams (born 1852) is an American economist. He was born at Davenport, Iowa, in December 1852. Iowa College gave him his first education. Johns Hopkins University gave him a fellowship. He lectured there from 1880 to 1882. Cornell University employed him as lecturer next. In 1887 Michigan made him professor. His chair covered political economy and finance. Government work claimed him alongside teaching.

Statistics and transport were his public fields. He became statistician to the Interstate Commerce Committee. The 1900 census put him over its transportation department. His books treat the state and industrial action. Taxation history and public debts both feature. The Science of Finance appeared in 1888. Economics and Jurisprudence closed the list in 1897.
britannica-1911-adams-herbert-baxter:
Herbert Baxter Adams (1850-1901) was an American historian and educationalist. He was born at Shutesbury, Massachusetts, in April 1850. Amherst graduated him at his class's head in 1872. German universities then trained him for four years. Gottingen, Berlin, and Heidelberg all hosted his studies. Heidelberg gave him a doctorate with highest honours. Johns Hopkins University claimed him from 1876. He rose there from fellow to full professor. His chair covered American and institutional history.

Building institutions marks his career. Adams founded the Johns Hopkins Studies series in 1882. Forty volumes appeared under his editorship. He co-founded the American Historical Association in 1884. He served as its secretary until 1900. Bureau of Education monographs bore his editing too. Students owed him their training and enthusiasm most.
britannica-1911-agrippina-elder:
Agrippina the Elder, a leading figure of the early Roman empire, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa and Julia, granddaughter of Augustus, and wife of Germanicus. She went with her husband to Germany and stood by him when the Rhine legions revolted after Augustus died in A.D. 14.

Germanicus died at Antioch in A.D. 19, said to be poisoned on the orders of Piso, governor of Syria. Agrippina returned to Rome and boldly accused Piso, who killed himself rather than face public shame. Tiberius and his favourite Sejanus feared her ambition for her children. She was banished to the island of Pandataria, where she died in A.D. 33, starved by her own act or by Tiberius's order. Among her children were Caligula and Agrippina the Younger.
britannica-1911-agrippina-younger:
Agrippina the Younger (A.D. 16–59) clawed her way to power in Rome and died by her own son's order. She was Germanicus's daughter by Agrippina the Elder, Caligula's sister, and Nero's mother. Her birthplace, Oppidum Ubiorum on the Rhine, took a new name in her honour, Colonia Agrippinae, today's Cologne. A life of plots and betrayal is the plain verdict on her.

Nero came from her first match, with Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus. Men charged her with poisoning her second husband, Passienus Crispus. Aided by the freedman Pallas, she got her uncle Claudius to wed her and to adopt Nero as heir in place of Britannicus. She poisoned Claudius next and set her son on the throne. When she threatened to back Britannicus, Nero had the prince murdered. Then he had his mother slain at Baiae, after a boat built to sink failed to drown her.
britannica-1911-ahrweiler:
Wine is close to the whole of trade at Ahrweiler, a German town that keeps a medieval face. The town stands on the river Ahr in the Prussian Rhine province, along the rail line from Remagen to Adenau. Some 5,000 people lived there when the notice was made. Making the district's wines and shipping them out is the work that fills its days.

Old walls gird the town, topped with battlements and pierced by four gates, all in sound repair. A Gothic church in the pointed-arch manner of the middle ages dates from 1245. South of town, on a hill that draws the eye, sits a school run by Ursuline nuns in a convent. For a visitor, the walls and the old look come first; for the town itself, the vineyards rule.
britannica-1911-albert-grand-master:
Albert (1490–1568) began as grand master of a knightly order and ended as the first duke of Prussia. Born at Ansbach in May 1490, he was Frederick of Hohenzollern's third son; his father ruled Ansbach and Bayreuth. His mother Sophia was King Casimir IV of Poland's daughter. A church career was planned for him, and he held a canon's post at Cologne.

Soldiering suited him better. He fought in Italy and Hungary, then joined the Teutonic Order and was picked as grand master early in 1511. Men hoped his kinship with Sigismund I of Poland would calm the quarrels over east Prussia. Albert would not make peace, though, and spent years hunting allies for the war that seemed bound to come. Later he joined the Protestant league of Torgau in 1526 and stood with princes banded against Charles V after the Interim of 1548.
britannica-1911-alcester:
Alcester, pronounced Auster, a market-town in Warwickshire, England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the Stratford-on-Avon division, sixteen miles west-south-west of Warwick, among low wooded hills. The small stream Alne joins the Arrow there, and two railways serve the town's 2,303 people. Its name means the camp on the Alne.

St Nicholas church is mostly a rebuilding of 1734, though its Decorated tower survives, and a fine Chantrey monument honours the second marquess of Hertford. A picturesque town hall of 1641 stands raised on stone columns, and a free grammar school serves the town. Needle-making, once the chief trade, had faded as Redditch absorbed the industry. Implement works, cycle works, and brewing remained. A small Romano-British town once stood on the Roman road through the site, and Alcester appears as a royal borough under Henry I.
britannica-1911-alcinous-philosopher:
Alcinous, a Platonic philosopher, is distinguished in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica from the legendary king of the same name. He probably lived in the time of the Caesars. His work, the Epitome of Plato's doctrines, analyses Plato's philosophy as later writers understood it. It proceeds rather in Aristotle's manner, the entry says.

The Epitome freely credits Plato with ideas from other philosophers that seemed to complete his system. What results is a blend of Plato and Aristotle, mixed with Pythagorean and Eastern thought, close to the Alexandrian school. Alcinous taught a god who cannot be known, with lesser beings, daimones, standing between god and men. He also recognised Ideas and Matter, borrowing largely from Aristotle and the Stoics. The entry closes by listing the book's many translations and editions.
britannica-1911-alder:
Alder names a clan of trees and shrubs, Alnus in Latin, set in the birch order, Betulaceae. The common alder is its best-known member. The clan counts few members, spread through northern lands of mild climate and down the Andes as far as Chile. The British kind stays in the Old World.

Moist ground suits the common alder best, and in good spots it climbs to fifty feet. Its leaves, round and short-stalked, feel a bit sticky when young, which gives the kind its Latin name glutinosa, and hold their green late into the fall. Male catkins, long hanging spikes of bloom, run two to four inches long and glow red. The smaller female catkins harden into woody black cones that cling on through winter once the winged seeds have flown. The tree seeds itself with ease and throws shoots from its roots as well.
britannica-1911-ale-conner:
Ale-conner, an old English officer, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. An ale-conner was appointed yearly at the court-leet of ancient manors to handle the assize of ale and ale-measures, the checking of drink and its vessels. Such officers were sworn men, known in different places as ale-tasters, ale-founders, and ale-conners.

Their duty was to examine beer and ale, making sure the drink was good and wholesome and sold at proper prices. London kept the custom longest. Four ale-conners were still chosen every year by the liverymen in common hall on Midsummer Day. By then their work was checking the measures of beer and liquor sellers against fraud. Elsewhere the office fell out of use once ale and beer became excisable goods, taxed by the state. The entry sends readers to the article on Adulteration for the wider story.
britannica-1911-alger-russell-alexander:
Russell Alexander Alger (1836–1907) lost his parents young and paid for his own schooling by farm work at Richfield Academy in Ohio. He was born in Medina county, in his birth state, in February 1836. He taught for two winters, read law, and joined the bar in 1859.

Law practice at Cleveland soon gave way, in 1860, to the Michigan lumber trade, where pine lands later made him a rich man. He signed up with a Michigan horse regiment in 1861 and climbed from captain to colonel. He fought in the Gettysburg campaign and rode with Sheridan in the Shenandoah Valley, which won him brevet rank as brigadier and then major-general. Michigan made him its governor from 1885 to 1887, and he led the Grand Army of the Republic. As McKinley's war secretary from 1897, he drew harsh blame for how the Spanish-American War contracts were run.
britannica-1911-almoner:
Almoner names an officer charged with managing and distributing alms. Alms are the charitable gifts of a household or religious house. The word descends from the Latin eleemosynarius, through medieval Latin and French forms. In the early sense, the almoner served in religious houses. Ancient canons required monasteries to spend at least a tenth of their income on the poor. Bishops, too, had to keep almoners.

At the French court, the grand almoner became an important official. He superintended the Chapel Royal and court religious ceremonies. He directed a great hospital for the blind. He also nominated professors at the Collège de France. In England, the royal almonry survives within the sovereign's household. Its officers include a hereditary grand almoner, now a merely titular post. The lord high almoner, usually a bishop, distributes royal charity.
britannica-1911-angler:
Angler, also called fishing-frog, frog-fish, or sea-devil, is a fish well known off the coasts of Britain and Europe generally. Its grotesque body and singular habits have drawn naturalists' attention in every age. The head is enormous, broad, flat, and depressed, so that the rest of the body looks like a mere appendage to it. North Sea fishermen know the fish as the monk.

A wide mouth runs around the front of the head, armed with bands of long pointed teeth that incline inward and fold down, letting prey glide toward the stomach while blocking escape. The pectoral and ventral fins work like feet, letting the fish walk along the sea bottom, where it hides in sand or seaweed. Fringed skin appendages resembling seaweed fronds complete its camouflage. The entry maps its range across northern Europe and western North America and names Mediterranean and East Asian relatives.
britannica-1911-ankober: Ankober is a town in Abyssinia. It once served as capital of the kingdom of Shoa. The town stands ninety miles north-east of Adis Ababa. A mountain site holds it 8,500 feet above the sea. Its population is about 2,000. Around 1890 Menelek II changed its role. He made Ankober a detention place for political prisoners. The entry gives coordinates and little more. That brevity reflects a small, remote highland town.
britannica-1911-araroba-powder:
Araroba powder is a drug in powdered form. Its colour is yellowish-brown, varying in tint. Goa powder is its alternative name. The Portuguese colony of Goa introduced it. That introduction came about 1852. The source is the tree Andira Araroba. That tree belongs to the legume family. Bahia's forests hold it in abundance. It prefers low, humid spots there.

The tree grows eighty to 100 feet high. Its leaves are large and pinnate. Purple flowers arrange themselves in panicles. The powder fills crevices in the heartwood. It is a morbid product of the tree. Hot chloroform extracts half its weight as chrysarobin. That substance holds official therapeutic value. Pharmacopoeias include it widely today. Skin diseases are its main application. Psoriasis and eczema receive it locally. It stains skin and linen deep yellow.
britannica-1911-arbuthnot-alexander:
Alexander Arbuthnot (1538–1583) was a Scottish ecclesiastic and poet. St Andrews and Bourges educated him. In 1569 he became principal of King's College, Aberdeen. He held that office until death. Church politics of the period absorbed him. He was twice moderator of the kirk. He served on the St Andrews university inquiry in 1583. Catholic writers commended his correctness of attitude.

James VI disliked his policy and influence. The Assembly elected him to St Andrews church. The king ordered him back to King's College. He had ministered at Arbuthnott in Kincardineshire earlier. Three poems survive from his pen. The Praises of Wemen runs 224 lines. The Miseries of a Pure Scholar runs 189. A Latin family history remains in manuscript. Calderwood and Spottiswood record his life. Pinkerton printed his poems in 1786.
britannica-1911-austria-lower:
Lower Austria is an archduchy and crownland of Austria. Its German name is Niederösterreich. It is also called Austria below the Enns. Hungary bounds it on the east. Bohemia and Moravia bound the north. Upper Austria and Bohemia bound the west. Styria bounds it on the south. Its area is 7,654 square miles. The Danube divides it into two parts.

North of the Danube lies the Waldviertel. That low hilly country continues the Bohemian plateau. The Weinsberger Wald is its high western part. The Peilstein reaches 3,478 feet there. South of the river, mountains dominate. The Lower Austrian Alps occupy that division. Schneeberg is the highest summit at 6,806 feet. Raxalpe and Ötscher follow in height. Vienna sits within this crownland. Illustrated monographs anchor the closing references.
britannica-1911-austria-upper:
Upper Austria is an archduchy and crown-land of Austria. Its German name is Oberösterreich. It means Austria above the river Enns. Bohemia bounds it on the north. Bavaria bounds the west. Salzburg and Styria bound the south. Lower Austria bounds the east. Its area is 4,631 square miles. The Danube divides it into unequal parts.

The smaller northern part prolongs the Bohemian forest. Plöcklstein is its culminating point at 4,510 feet. The southern part belongs to the Eastern Alps. The Salzkammergut district lies there famously. Alpine foothills stretch toward the Danube northward. The Hausruckwald is a wooded chain there. Brown coal enriches that chain. The Danube flows west to east through it. Inn, Traun, and Enns join it there. Salt, stone, and timber lead its exports.
britannica-1911-auxanometer: Auxanometer is an apparatus for measuring growth in plants. It records increase, or the rate of growth, in a plant under observation. The name joins two Greek elements: auxanein, meaning to increase, and metron, meaning measure. The entry is a single-sentence definition only, giving the instrument's purpose and the Greek construction of its name, with no description of its mechanism.
britannica-1911-axminster:
Axminster is a market town in Devonshire, England, on the river Axe east of Exeter, with 2,906 people in 1901. Its minster of St Mary shows every style from Norman to Perpendicular, with old effigies, sedilia, and a piscina in the chancel.

The town was long famed for hand-woven carpets, made like tapestry after the craft began there in 1755; the carpets kept the Axminster name after the work moved to Wilton. Brush factories, corn mills, and an iron foundry took its place. Axminster stands where two great ancient roads cross, held a Cistercian abbey from 1246 until 1539, and still holds the midsummer fair granted then.
britannica-1911-back-s-river:
Back's River, in its native name Thlewechodyeth or Great Fish, is a river of the Mackenzie and Keewatin districts in Canada. It rises in small Sussex Lake and winds north-east through a chain of large lake-expansions, Pelly, Carry, MacDougall, and Franklin among them, to an inlet of the Arctic Ocean.

Rapids and rocks in succession make it unnavigable, like the Coppermine, the only other great river of that region. Sir George Back discovered and explored it in 1834, and his name stayed on the map. The whole course runs 560 miles. A tortuous Arctic river, known through one explorer's journey, is the entry's subject from source to sea.
britannica-1911-backscratcher:
Backscratcher names a long, thin rod of wood, whalebone, tortoiseshell, horn, or cane, tipped with a small carved human hand, usually of ivory. Its name gives its first use, but it also served as a rake for the huge powdered hairstyles women wore through much of the 1700s and early 1800s.

Examples run twelve to twenty inches long; the finer ones, sometimes hung from the waist, are silver-mounted, and the ivory fingers may wear carved rings. Hands appear open or bent, right or left, though the Chinese kind usually bears a right hand; a rake or bird's claw sometimes replaces the hand. Once common, the scratch-back has grown scarce and now draws collectors.
britannica-1911-bacon-roger:
Bacon, Roger (about 1214 to about 1294), was an English philosopher and man of science. He was born near Ilchester in Somerset. Oxford trained him, and Grosseteste and Adam de Marisco befriended him there. Paris, the centre of learning in Europe, drew him next. Family losses under Henry III shadowed his start.
