At Paris, Bacon judged the reigning scholarship rotten. Aristotle was known only in vile translations. Scripture was deserted for Peter Lombard's Sentences. Natural knowledge was argued from authority instead of tested by experiment. He withdrew from the schools' routine for languages and experimental research, respecting only one teacher, a Picard mathematician likely the author of a treatise on the magnet. The long entry follows this critic of his age through his writings and his troubles with his Franciscan order.
britannica-1911-baily-william-hellier:
Baily, William Hellier (1819-1888), was an English fossil scholar. He was a nephew of the sculptor E. H. Baily. Born at Bristol, he worked at the Bristol Museum from 1837 to 1844. He then joined the Geological Survey in London.

In 1854 Baily became assistant naturalist. He served under Edward Forbes and later under Huxley. In 1857 he moved to the Irish branch of the Survey. He stayed there as acting fossil expert for life. His papers covered many fossil subjects. He also wrote notes for Irish Survey memoirs. His book Figures of Characteristic British Fossils ran from 1867 to 1875. Only its first volume appeared. It dealt with the oldest fossil species. Baily drew every figure on stone himself.
britannica-1911-bain-alexander:
Bain, Alexander (1818-1903), was a Scottish philosopher and teacher of teachers. He was born in Aberdeen and schooled there. In early life he worked as a weaver. A punning tag called him the weaver king of philosophers. He entered Marischal College in 1836.

Bain soon won notice in mental philosophy, mathematics, and physics. He wrote for the Westminster Review from 1840. That work began his lifelong friendship with John Stuart Mill. He helped Mill revise the System of Logic. In 1845 he took a Glasgow chair in mathematics and natural philosophy. Later he joined the board of health in London. His two big books followed. The Senses and the Intellect came in 1855. The Emotions and the Will came in 1859.
britannica-1911-balder:
Balder was a god of the Norse peoples, a son of Odin. The 1911 Britannica entry is brief and points to the tale of his death. That tale comes down in two quite different forms, one told by Saxo in his Gesta Danorum and one in the Prose Edda.

Readers who want the full story are sent on to those sources, and to F. Kauffmann's book Balder: Mythus und Sage, printed at Strassburg in 1902. The entry acts as a signpost: it names the god, gives his parentage, and shows where the death story can be read in full, rather than retelling it here.
britannica-1911-bales-peter:
Peter Bales (1547–1610?) was an English calligrapher and one of the inventors of shorthand. Born in London, he spent some years among the scholars of Oxford. Anthony Wood called him most dexterous in his profession, to the wonder of scholars and others, and Holinshed's Chronicle praised his tiny writing.

One feat made him famous. In 1575 Bales wrote the Lord's Prayer, the Creed, the Ten Commandments, two short Latin prayers, his name, and the date, all inside the circle of a single penny. Set in gold and crystal, the work was shown to Queen Elizabeth at Hampton Court. The 1911 Britannica entry also notes his skill at copying handwriting, used by Secretary Walsingham.
britannica-1911-balquhidder:
Balquhidder is a village and parish in Perthshire, Scotland, whose Gaelic name means the farm in the back-lying country. The parish held 605 people in 1901. The village sits at the east end of Loch Voil, below the Braes of Balquhidder, about two miles from its rail station on the Callander to Oban line.

The Maclaurins held the district from as early as the 9th century until the Macgregors drove them out, killing their chief in 1558. Rob Roy carried out some of his exploits here and died at Balquhidder in 1734. The 1911 Britannica entry points to his grave in the old kirkyard, and to a stone said to cover Angus, the Columban missionary.
britannica-1911-baluster:
Baluster is the name for a small moulded shaft, square or round, in stone, wood, or sometimes metal. The word came through French from an Italian term drawn from the flower of the wild pomegranate, and in English it has been corrupted into banister. A row of balusters holding up a rail forms a balustrade.

Earliest examples show in Assyrian palace carvings, where they served as window rails and seem to wear Ionic capitals. Greeks and Romans, the 1911 Britannica entry says, did not use them. They appear in the balconies of Venice and Verona, and under Italian revival builders they grew into major features of windows and roof parapets. A last note covers the baluster shafts splitting Saxon windows.
britannica-1911-bandolier:
Bandolier, or bandoleer, comes from French and Italian words for a little band. It is a belt worn over the shoulder, used above all by soldiers to carry cartridges. The word and the gear both had a long life by 1911.

In the 17th century, wooden cases hung from the belt, each holding a charge of powder. The modern form named in the 1911 Britannica entry carries its cartridges in loops sewn to the belt, or in small pouches holding strips of several rounds. The British army had taken it up widely, the entry notes, most of all for mounted troops who needed their rounds close at hand while on horseback.
britannica-1911-barlow-peter:
Peter Barlow (1776–1862) was an English writer on pure and applied mathematics, born at Norwich in 1776. In 1806 he became mathematical master at the Woolwich Academy, the army's school for engineers and gunners, and he held that post for forty-one years. The Royal Society made him a fellow in 1823 and gave him its Copley medal two years later.

Railways drew much of his attention, and he sat on the railway commissions of 1836, 1839, 1842, and 1845. The 1911 Britannica entry lists his chief books, on number theory, magnetism, and a mathematical dictionary. His work on magnetism led to a means of correcting compass errors in ships, a discovery of direct worth at sea. He also compiled useful tables and wrote for the Encyclopaedia Metropolitana.
britannica-1911-barnard-frederick-august:
Frederick Augustus Porter Barnard (1809–1889) was an American scientist and educationalist, born at Sheffield, Massachusetts, on 5 May 1809. He graduated at Yale in 1828, second on the honour list. He then taught at Yale and at schools for deaf pupils in Hartford and New York, work that opened his career in education.

From 1838 Barnard held chairs at the University of Alabama in mathematics, chemistry, and natural history, and even English literature for two years. Ordained deacon in 1854, he became chancellor of the University of Mississippi until the Civil War, when his Northern sympathies took him to Washington and the Coast Survey. In 1864 he became the tenth president of Columbia College in New York. The 1911 Britannica entry follows that long presidency.
britannica-1911-barometer:
Barometer, from Greek words for pressure and measure, is the instrument that measures the weight or pressure of the atmosphere. The ordinary mercurial barometer uses a tube about 36 inches long, sealed at the top and filled with mercury. In the cistern form the tube's open end stands in a basin of mercury, and pressure is read from the difference of the two levels.

The siphon form bends the tube back on itself and reads the gap between its two limbs. The aneroid uses no liquid at all, relying on a sealed metal chamber that changes volume with pressure. Baroscopes only show that pressure changes; barographs record the changes on their own. The 1911 Britannica entry, a very long one, then traces the instrument's history from Galileo's day and the old puzzle of the suction pump.
britannica-1911-barrow-river:
Barrow is a river of south-eastern Ireland described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It rises in the Slieve Bloom mountains, flows east at first and then almost due south, and joins the Suir to form Waterford Harbour on the south coast. Counting the estuary, its valley runs for rather more than a hundred miles, and the harbour drains about 3500 square miles of country.

Counties and towns give the entry its map. The drainage covers all of County Kilkenny and parts of Waterford, Cork, Limerick, Tipperary, Carlow, and King's and Queen's counties. Chief towns on the banks are Athy, where the river becomes navigable and meets the Grand Canal, Carlow, Bagenalstown, and New Ross. Its main tributary is the Nore, joining from the north-west above New Ross. The entry also notes fine scenery along parts of the banks.
britannica-1911-barry-spranger:
Spranger Barry (1719–1777), a British actor born in Dublin, the son of a silversmith, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Trained for his father's trade, he first acted at Dublin's Smock Alley theatre in 1744 and at once lifted its fortunes. In London from 1746 he played Othello at Drury Lane, then alternated with Garrick in Hamlet and Macbeth, and beat him, in the critics' view, as Romeo.

Rivalry and management fill the middle years. Barry left for Covent Garden in 1750, built Dublin's Crow Street theatre in 1758, and added a theatre in Cork, without success as a manager. Handsome and tall, an advantage Garrick lacked, he returned to London stages and died in January 1777. The entry also traces his second wife, Ann Street Barry, a leading tragic actress as Mrs Dancer and later Mrs Crawford.
britannica-1911-barter:
Barter, from a French word meaning to truck or exchange, is defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as swapping goods for goods, in contrast to swapping goods for money. Among early communities it was the simplest form of trade. Its drawbacks, though, pushed people at a fairly early stage of civilization toward using metals as a medium of exchange, something both sides could accept and carry into later deals.

Old practice had not vanished when the entry was written. Barter stayed very common, the entry says, in dealings with peoples it calls uncivilized. Traders in many countries still stocked goods such as weapons, tools, and ornaments, because those were taken more readily than money. Readers who want the longer story are sent to the article on money, and to books by Jevons, Marshall, and Ridgeway on currency and how exchange developed.
britannica-1911-barton-upon-humber:
Barton-upon-Humber, a market town in Lincolnshire, England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as standing on flat ground by the Humber, with its centre a mile from the river. It ended a Great Central railway branch, forty-four miles north by east of Lincoln. The urban district's population in 1901 was 5671. Barton appears in Domesday Book, when a ferry across the Humber already existed, and it later grew into a port of some weight.

Churches dominate the rest of the entry. St Peter's has a west tower of pre-Conquest work, with round arches below and triangular ones above, apart from its later Norman top. St Mary's is fine Early English work with a later clerestory, the upper window row. Local industries were brick-making, malting, and rope-making. Barton once supplied eight ships and crews for Edward III's expedition to Brittany.
britannica-1911-basselin-olivier:
Olivier Basselin (about 1400–about 1450), a French poet from the Val-de-Vire in Normandy, is the subject of a doubtful 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. By occupation he was a fuller, who cleans and thickens cloth, and tradition still pointed out his mill. His drinking songs became famous under the name Vaux-de-Vire, a title later corrupted into the familiar word vaudeville. Tradition held that the English wars killed him around the middle of the century, possibly at Formigny in 1450.

Authorship is the entry's real problem. Early in the seventeenth century a Norman lawyer, Jean Le Houx, published a collection of songs as Basselin's work. Very little doubt remains that Le Houx wrote those songs himself, along with the ones he admitted were his. Some songs kept in Paris have been suggested as genuinely his, and the question had scholarly literature by 1897.
britannica-1911-bates-henry-walter:
Henry Walter Bates (1825–1892), an English naturalist and explorer born at Leicester, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father, a hosier, meant him for trade, but the boy slipped away to the fields for plants and insects. In 1844 he met Alfred Russel Wallace, and the two planned a trip to a little-known land. They sailed for Pará, at the mouth of the Amazon, in April 1848, planning to pay their way by selling spare specimens.

Eleven years in the Amazon made Bates's name. He went 1400 miles up the great river and brought back some 8000 insect species new to science. Ill health followed him home. From 1864 he served as assistant secretary of the Royal Geographical Society until his death. Darwin urged him to write The Naturalist on the Amazons, and his 1861 paper set out and solved the puzzle of mimicry, how one species copies another to stay safe.
britannica-1911-batter:
Batter is a building term of unknown origin, explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the slight slope of the face of a wall away from the upright. The batter is most often used in retaining walls, which hold back earth. Their lower courses are laid at right angles to the slope, to resist the thrust of the earth inside. For looks alone it is also used in the lowest parts of great buildings.

Great age is the batter's chief claim. The entry calls it the most ancient system of building known. In Egypt and Chaldaea, temples of unburnt brick had to be thicker at the bottom. That need gave the raking, sloping side, which Egypt later copied in stone. Fortress walls also used a batter, as in the tower of David and Herod's walls at Jerusalem. Crusaders took up the plan across Europe.
britannica-1911-baynes-thomas-spencer:
Thomas Spencer Baynes (1823–1887) was an English editor and man of letters, born at Wellington in Somerset. At Edinburgh he studied under Sir William Hamilton and became the chief voice for Hamilton’s views on logic. His Essay on the New Analytic of Logical Forms came out in 1850.

Baynes edited the Edinburgh Guardian, worked on the Daily News, and from 1864 held a chair at St Andrews in logic, metaphysics and English literature. In 1873 the ninth edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica was placed in his hands. He ran it alone until 1881, then with W. Robertson Smith, and stayed at work until his death in May 1887.
britannica-1911-bell-john-political-lead:
John Bell (1797–1869) was an American political leader born near Nashville, Tennessee. He graduated at Nashville in 1814, served one term in the state senate, then spent ten years at the law. From 1827 to 1841 he sat in the national House of Representatives and was its speaker for nine months.

Bell began as a Democrat, broke with President Jackson, and led the Southern Whigs after 1835. He was Harrison’s secretary of war in 1841 and a senator from 1847 to 1859, voting against the Kansas-Nebraska Bill. A firm Union man, he tried in vain to hold Tennessee back from secession in 1861, then took no part in the war.
britannica-1911-bell-john-traveller:
John Bell (1691–1780) was a Scottish traveller born at Antermony and trained as a doctor. In 1714 he went to St Petersburg and joined the Persian embassy as its medical attendant, travelling from 1715 to 1718. The next four years took him on an embassy to China, across Siberia and the Tatar deserts.

Bell then attended Peter the Great on the hard Derbend expedition to the Caspian Gates, writing closely of that ruler’s life. A winter mission to Constantinople followed in 1738, and he later traded there before retiring home in 1747. His travels, printed at Glasgow in 1763, were soon turned into French and read across Europe.
britannica-1911-belle-ile-en-mer:
Belle-Île-en-Mer is an island off the west coast of France, eight miles south of the Quiberon peninsula. It forms a canton of Morbihan, covers thirty-three square miles, and held 9,703 people in 1906. Four communes share it: Le Palais, Bangor, Sauzon and Locmaria.

The island is a treeless plateau about 130 feet high, edged by a rugged, broken coast, with moors inland. Mild air lets fig and myrtle grow in sheltered spots, and the soil repays farming where it is worked. Fishing and the packing of sardines and anchovies employ many hands, the draught horses are prized, and Le Palais keeps an old citadel above its small port.
britannica-1911-belper:
Belper is a market town of Derbyshire, England, on the river Derwent, seven miles north of Derby. Its urban district held 10,934 people in 1901. The chapel of St John is said to go back to Edmund Crouchback, son of Henry III, in the mid-1200s.

Cotton made Belper. The Strutt family set up works there in 1776, and the town flourished as one of the county’s busiest; the Strutts later took their baron’s title from it. Linen, hosiery, silk and earthenware are also made, and the Derwent drives the mills. Nail-making faded, but engineering shops and iron foundries took its place, while collieries and lead mines work the hills near by.
britannica-1911-bemis-edward-webster:
Edward Webster Bemis (born 1860) was an American economist born at Springfield, Massachusetts. Amherst and Johns Hopkins University educated him. He taught history and political economy at Vanderbilt University from 1887 to 1892, then held a post in political economy at Chicago until 1895.

Bemis worked for the Illinois bureau of labour statistics and in 1901 became superintendent of the Cleveland water works. His writing centred on how cities should run their services. Books named include Municipal Ownership of Gas in the United States of 1891 and Municipal Monopolies of 1899, plus chapters in a history of co-operation in America. The entry is a plain career summary.
britannica-1911-bender:
Bender, more correctly Bendery, is a town of Russia in the government of Bessarabia, on the right bank of the Dniester. It lies thirty-seven miles by rail south-east of Kishinev. A tobacco factory, candle-works and brick-kilns stand in the town, and its people grew from 24,443 in 1867 to 33,741 by 1900, most of them Jews.

Bender works as a river port: corn, wine, wool, cattle, flour and tallow are landed there for the road to Odessa and to Yassy in Rumania, and timber floats down the Dniester. Genoese traders settled the site as early as the 1100s. Charles XII of Sweden camped here after Poltava from 1709 to 1713, and Russia took the town three times before holding it for good in 1812.
britannica-1911-beni-amer:
Beni-Amer, or Amir, are a tribe of African “Arabs” of Hamitic stock, standing between Abyssinians and Nubians in descent. They belong to the Beja family. Their ground is the Red Sea coast south of Suakin and parts of the Eritrean shore country north of Abyssinia.

Their blood mixes Beja and Abyssinian strains, and their speech, called Hassa, is half Beja and half Tigré. They take wives from the Bogos and other mountain tribes. Pride runs the other way, though: they will not let their own daughters marry Abyssinians. The entry is a short placing of the tribe, its stock, its tongue and its marriage custom, with books named for more.
britannica-1911-beni-river:
Bení is a river of Bolivia and a tributary of the Madeira. It rises in the high Cordilleras near La Paz, where it is first called the Rio de La Paz. From there it flows east and north-east until it joins the Mamoré and the two together form the Madeira.

Half its course runs through mountain country, fed by streams from snow-clad peaks, a raging torrent in that stretch. Below Reyes it crosses forested hills and open plains where old Indian missions stood, and boats can travel 217 miles of it before the Esperanza rapids bar the way. Its great affluent, the Madre de Dios, is in size the larger river of the two.
britannica-1911-bentley-richard-publishe:
Richard Bentley (1794–1871) was a British publisher born in London, son of a part-owner of the General Evening Post. St Paul’s school was followed by an apprenticeship in printing under John Nichols. With his brother Samuel he set up as printers, then in 1829 began publishing with Henry Colburn in New Burlington Street.

Colburn retired in 1832, leaving Bentley alone. In 1837 he started Bentley’s Miscellany, edited for three years by Charles Dickens, whose Oliver Twist ran in its pages with Cruikshank’s pictures. The firm, later Richard Bentley & Son, issued the Library of Standard Novels and Mrs Henry Wood’s East Lynne. Macmillan absorbed the business in 1898, after Bentley’s son and grandson had carried it on.
britannica-1911-beresford-lord-charles-w:
Lord Charles William de la Poer Beresford (born 1846) was a British admiral, second son of the fourth marquess of Waterford. Born in Ireland, he entered the training ship Britannia as a cadet in 1859. He was lieutenant by 1868 and commander by 1875, and sat in parliament for Waterford as a Conservative from 1874 to 1880.

Beresford won popular fame at the bombardment of Alexandria in 1882, taking his gunboat Condor close under the forts until the admiral signalled “Well done, Condor!” He then commanded the naval brigade in the Sudan expedition of 1884–1885 and rescued Sir Charles Wilson’s wrecked party from the Nile. Later years brought a loud public campaign on naval policy and a return to parliament for Portsmouth in 1910.
britannica-1911-berners-john-bourchier:
John Bourchier, 2nd Baron Berners (1469–1533), was an English courtier and translator. He inherited his title in 1474 from his grandfather, a descendant of Edward III. He fled to Brittany in 1484 after a plot to crown Henry of Richmond. Back in favour, he served Henry VIII in France and at court. In 1516 he became chancellor of the exchequer. In 1518 he went to Madrid to treat with Charles of Spain.

The 1911 Britannica entry stresses his writing as much as his career. He translated Froissart's chronicle into English. He also rendered Huon of Bordeaux and other French works. His letters from Spain describe bull-fights and court life for Henry and Wolsey. A lost comedy and a book on Calais duties are also credited to him.
britannica-1911-berserker:
Berserker, in Scandinavian mythology, names the twelve sons of the hero Berserk. The word comes from the sark, or shirt, of bear skin or other animal skins worn by them. Berserk was grandson of the eight-handed Starkadder and Alfhilde. He was famed for reckless fury in battle. He always fought without armour. His twelve sons matched him in bravery.

This short 1911 Britannica entry explains how the word widened in meaning. In Old Norse, berserker came to mean reckless courage itself. Later the term was applied to the bodyguards of several Scandinavian heroes. The entry gives no named sagas or kings. It stays with the mythic family and the word's later use.
britannica-1911-bessemer:
Bessemer is a town in Jefferson County, Alabama, about 12 miles south-west of Birmingham. It lies near the centre of the state, in Jones's Valley. The 1911 Britannica entry tracks fast growth: 4,544 people in 1890, 6,538 in 1900, and 10,864 in 1910. Five railway lines serve the town. Red ore mountains rise to the east, and the Warrior coalfields lie north-west.

Mining, iron smelting, and iron and coke making are its chief trades. Truck farming also counts as an important industry. Limestone quarries stand close by the town. In 1900 Bessemer ranked eighth in Alabama for population but second for capital in manufacturing. The town was laid out in 1887 and incorporated in 1889. Its name matches the famous steel process of the same era.
britannica-1911-bicester:
Bicester is a market town in Oxfordshire, England, 12 miles north-north-east of Oxford. A branch of the London and North-Western railway serves it. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 3,023 people in the urban district in 1901. The town sits by the flat plain of Ot Moor, in pastoral country. Its church of St Eadburg is cruciform, with a western tower. Norman work and every later style appear in its fabric.

The town holds a large farm and market trade, plus a brewing industry. It is also a favoured hunting centre, the entry notes. An Augustinian priory was founded here in 1182 by Gilbert Basset. Scant remains of it survive inside a farmhouse. The ending cester does not prove Roman origin here, the article warns. Nearby Alchester holds the true small Roman site.
britannica-1911-bichat-marie-francois-xa:
Marie François Xavier Bichat (1771–1802) was a French anatomist and physiologist, born at Thoirette in the Jura. His father, a physician, was his first teacher. He studied at Nantua and then at Lyons under the surgeon Petit. Revolutionary troubles drove him to Paris in 1793. There he became the pupil of Desault at the Hôtel Dieu. Desault treated him almost as an adopted son.

When Desault died suddenly in 1795, Bichat repaid the debt at once. He supported the widow and finished Desault's surgical journal. The 1911 Britannica entry then follows his own research on tissues and remedies. He ran direct experiments on the effects of drugs. A fall at the Hôtel Dieu brought a fever, and overwork did the rest. He died in July 1802, aged only thirty.
britannica-1911-bicker: Bicker is an Old English word, traced from the 13th century, that implies conflict or disputation, a verbal fight or quarrel. The 1911 Britannica note links it, on Skeat's authority, with the word bike, meaning to thrust or to strike. That link fits the word's sense of sharp, repeated blows exchanged between opponents. A poetical use drawn from noise is also recorded: Tennyson, in his poem The Brook, uses the phrase to bicker down the valley, for the sound of the stream on its course.
britannica-1911-bidder-george-parker:
George Parker Bidder (1806–1878) was an English engineer, born at Moreton Hampstead in Devon. His father was a stone-mason. From a very early age the boy showed an extraordinary gift for mental calculation. His father exhibited him as a calculating boy for profit. Schooling at Camberwell and classes at Edinburgh University rescued his education. Sir John Herschel and Sir Henry Jardine both took interest in him.

He joined the ordnance survey in 1824, then drifted into engineering. Robert Stephenson gave him a post on the London and Birmingham railway in 1834. The 1911 Britannica entry names the Victoria Docks in London as his design. Critics had mocked his plan to use the Essex marshes for docks. Governments often sought his advice on naval and military engineering. He died at Dartmouth in September 1878.
britannica-1911-bidding-prayer:
Bidding-prayer is the formula of prayer, or call to prayer, said before the sermon on special occasions. It was used in English cathedrals, at university sermons, and in the Inns of Court. The word bid here comes from the Old English biddan, to pray. Ancient Greek and Gallican liturgies held like forms. Pre-Reformation English liturgies held them too. In each case the minister tells the people what to pray for.

Over time the old sense of bid faded from speech. Hearers confused it with bid meaning to command, from beodan, to offer or announce. So the bidding-prayer came to mean the exhortation itself, the 1911 Britannica entry explains. The 55th canon of the Church of England, from 1603, prints a set form for it. Preachers were told to move the people to join in that prayer.
britannica-1911-bio-bio-river:
Bio-Bio is a river of southern Chile, named for its flow across the country's south. It rises in the Pino Hachado pass across the Andes, at 38 degrees 45 minutes south latitude. From there it runs in a general north-westerly direction. It reaches the Pacific Ocean at Concepción. At that mouth it is two miles wide and forms an excellent harbour. The river's total length is about 225 miles in all.

Nearly half of that length is navigable, the 1911 Britannica entry states. The entry runs to two short sentences and a heading line in total. It gives the source pass, the course, the mouth, and the width and length figures. No tributaries, towns, or bridges are named in the text. The harbour at Concepción and the navigable share of the course are its practical points. The river shares its name with the Chilean province treated nearby.
britannica-1911-bion-philosopher:
Bion of Borysthenes was a Greek moralist and philosopher of the early 3rd century BC. He came from Olbia in Sarmatia, and his birth was low. His mother was a courtesan, and his father dealt in salt fish and smuggling. Sold young as a slave to a rhetorician, Bion won freedom and the man's inheritance. He then went to Athens to study philosophy. He attached himself in turn to the Academy, the Cynics, the Cyrenaics, and the Peripatetics.

Like the sophists he travelled Greece and Macedonia as a speaker. Antigonus Gonatas admitted him to his court's literary circle. He later taught at Rhodes and died at Chalcis in Euboea. The 1911 Britannica entry calls him essentially a popular writer. His Diatribae mocked the follies of mankind for a low-class audience. Traces of his wit survive in Teles, Stobaeus, and Seneca. Horace nods to his caustic salt in the Epistles.
britannica-1911-birger:
Birger (died 1266) was a Swedish statesman of the great Folkunge family. He was nephew of Birger Brosa and became its most famous member. King Erik Eriksson made him jarl of Bjälbo in 1248. He married the king's sister that era. When Erik died in 1250, Birger's son Valdemar was elected king. Birger ruled as regent for the boy. Sweden advanced greatly in fame and wealth across his sixteen years of sway.

In 1249 he led an expedition into Finland and built the fortress of Tavastehus. That work laid the base of Sweden's oversea empire, the 1911 Britannica entry says. He also built Stockholm and made it the chief mart for Lübeck trade. A commercial treaty with Lübeck sealed that gain. As a lawgiver he laboured hard in the cause of civilization. A statue of him stands in Stockholm's Riddarholm church, raised in 1884.
britannica-1911-bischweiler: Bischweiler is a German town in the imperial territory of Alsace-Lorraine, in the district of Lower Alsace, 23 miles north by east of Strassburg by rail. The 1911 Britannica entry is two sentences long. It gives the town a population of 7,897 in the 1900 census and names its industries in one short list: manufactures of jute and machinery, together with brewing and iron-founding. No history, buildings, or events are recorded; the entry itself supplies only the place, the people, and the trades.
britannica-1911-blackwater:
Blackwater is the name of several rivers in England, Scotland, and Ireland, and the entry deals with the two best known. The Essex Blackwater rises near Saffron Walden and runs about 40 miles to the North Sea. The larger river of the name flows through the south of Ireland.

The Irish river rises on the Cork and Kerry border, runs east to Cappoquin, then turns sharply south to Youghal Bay. Its valley is about 90 miles long and drains some 1300 square miles. Only a few miles near the mouth can be sailed, but its salmon fisheries draw sportsmen and bring in real trade. Fine scenery along its banks is also noted.
britannica-1911-blackwater-fever:
Blackwater fever is a dangerous fever found in hot countries and often grouped with malaria. Attacks come as sharp chills, bilious vomiting, and yellow skin, and the urine turns dark with blood pigment, which gives the disease its name. It occurs across tropical Africa, parts of Asia, the West Indies, and the southern United States, and in Greece, Sicily, and Sardinia in Europe.

What causes it was still disputed when the entry was written. Some blamed heavy quinine use against malaria, a view Koch backed, but cases did not match quinine use closely. A newer school blamed a tiny parasite in the blood, akin to the one behind redwater fever in cattle. Confusion with yellow fever is also discussed.
britannica-1911-bladder: Bladder, in this very short 1911 Britannica entry, names the urine sac found in animals. It gives the word's Old English root, linked to a verb meaning to blow, with the German blase beside it. It calls the bladder a thin-walled sac that takes in urine sent down from the kidneys. The term is then widened to like-shaped sacs. The gall-bladder is one, and the swim-bladder in fishes is another. Small bladders in some seaweeds also take the name.
britannica-1911-bolsover:
Bolsover is a small town in north-east Derbyshire, England, 5½ miles east of Chesterfield, with 6844 people in 1901. It stands high on a sharp slope above a stream that runs to the river Rother. Branch lines of two railway companies served it.

The town grew around its castle. William Peveril founded a stronghold there soon after the Conquest, and the fine castellated house on the site was built in 1613. The Cavendish family, who gained the castle in the 1500s, have monuments in St Mary's church, a Norman and later building with early stone carving. Traces of the town's old defences remain, the entry notes, and coal mining and quarrying were worked nearby.
britannica-1911-bondager: Bondager is a word for a servant, used in a special sense in the south of Scotland and in Northumberland. There it names a woman field worker whom a married farm labourer, living in a farm cottage, must supply as a term of his tenancy. Sometimes he must also feed and house her. The entry is short and gives the reason the custom arose. Farms could not get enough hands for field work, so the duty to bring a bondager was written into the labourer's bargain for his cottage.
britannica-1911-boulanger:
Boulanger is the shared name of several French artists. The entry sorts them in a few lines. Two Jeans open the list. One (1606–1660) was a pupil of Guido Reni at Bologna. He kept an academy at Modena. His cousin Jean (1607–1680) was a famed line engraver. That Jean's son Matthieu also engraved.

Louis Boulanger (1806–1867) was a subject painter. He was a friend of Victor Hugo. He directed the imperial art school at Dijon. The best known of the name is Gustave Rodolphe Clarence Boulanger (1824–1888). He was a pupil of Delaroche. He painted Oriental and classical subjects, and joined the Institute in 1882. Clément Boulanger (1805–1842), a pupil of Ingres, closes the roll.
britannica-1911-boulder: Boulder, short for boulder-stone, is a word of uncertain birth, set out in a very short entry. A Swedish kin word names a great stone that sets stream water rippling. In plain use a boulder is a large stone, smoothed by weather or worn by water. In geology it is a mass of rock carried far from its home bed. Miners use it for a lump of ore found far from its vein.
britannica-1911-breughel-pieter:
Pieter Breughel was a Flemish painter, son of a peasant in the village of Breughel near Breda, from which the family name is drawn. He learned painting from Koek, whose daughter he married, spent time in France and Italy, then joined the Antwerp academy in 1551 before settling at Brussels, where he died.

His pictures lean to comic peasant scenes, full of spirit and humour, though lacking the fine touch and silvery clearness of Teniers. Dates for his death differ, some giving about 1570 at age sixty, others 1590. Two sons carry the name on: Pieter the younger (1564–1637), dubbed Hell Breughel. Jan (about 1569–1642), Velvet Breughel, famed for flowers, fruit and landscapes so fine that Rubens used his hand for landscape parts in small works.
britannica-1911-brickfielder:
Brickfielder is the Australian name for a hot, scorching wind that blows out of the dry interior. Bare sandy wastes, stripped of plants in summer, bake under the sun and heat the air that sweeps outward. The wind can blow hard for days at a stretch, parching plants and beating every effort to keep dust down.

One gain is claimed for it: being very dry and hot, it kills many harmful germs of disease. A northern brickfielder is almost always followed by a strong southerly buster, cool and cloudy off the ocean. Both winds spring from one cause, a storm system over the Australian Bight with a narrow V-shaped dip inland. As it passes east the wind can swing from north to south so fast that the thermometer has dropped fifteen degrees in twenty minutes.
britannica-1911-bridgwater:
Bridgwater is a market town, port and borough in Somerset, England, on the river Parret 10 miles from its mouth and about 152 miles west by south of London. It held 15,209 people in 1901. Level, well-wooded country surrounds it, with the Mendip range east and the Quantock hills west, and an iron bridge joins the two banks in town.

Sea trade keeps the port busy, bringing in grain, coal, wine, hemp, tallow and timber, and sending out Bath brick, farm goods, pottery, cement and plaster of Paris. Ships of 700 tons can reach it, though spring tides send a bore up the river that can rise 9 feet in rough weather. St Mary Magdalene's church, a house in Blake Street where Admiral Blake was born in 1598. The Sedgemoor battlefield 3 miles off, where the Monmouth rising was crushed in 1685, close the account.
britannica-1911-brodie-peter-bellinger:
Peter Bellinger Brodie (1815–1897) was an English geologist and clergyman born in London in 1815, son of a barrister and nephew of Sir Benjamin Collins Brodie. Living at Lincoln's Inn Fields, he picked up natural history and a love of fossils at the museum of the Royal College of Surgeons under curator W. Clift, whose influence got him elected fellow of the Geological Society early in 1834.

At Emmanuel College, Cambridge, Sedgwick's spell settled his course, and all his leisure went to geology thereafter. Ordained in 1838, he served curacies at Wylye and Steeple Claydon, then became rector of Down Hatherley and in 1855 vicar of Rowington, publishing geological records from every district. At Cambridge he found fossil shells in Pleistocene beds at Barnwell, in the Vale of Wardour he discovered the isopod named Archaeoniscus Brodiei in Purbeck beds. In Buckinghamshire and the Vale of Gloucester he described Purbeck, Portland, Lias and Oolite outcrops.
britannica-1911-brogger-waldemar-christo:
Waldemar Christofer Brogger (born 1851) was a Norwegian geologist born in Christiania on 10 November 1851 and educated in that city. In 1876 he became curator of the geological museum there and assistant on the Geological Survey. He held the chair of mineralogy and geology at Stockholm from 1881 to 1890, then at Christiania from 1890, rising to rector of its royal university.

His studies of the igneous rocks of south Tirol set against those of Christiania shed much light on how granitic and basic rocks relate. He gave close attention to how rock types split apart as one magma hardens into plutonic or volcanic rock. Also worked on Norway's Palaeozoic rocks and on late glacial and post-glacial shifts of level around Christiania. Honours named include doctorates from Heidelberg and Glasgow and the Murchison medal of the Geological Society of London in 1891.
britannica-1911-broker:
Broker, in its first sense, names a trade agent. His office is to bring intending buyers and sellers together and make a contract between them. He is paid by a fee called brokerage or commission. Cotton, wool and produce brokers fit that first sense exactly. Word roots are traced to Latin brocca, a spit or spike, and broccare, to broach, with a French phrase for selling wine from the tap behind the dealing sense.

Use has widened far beyond goods: stockbrokers, insurance brokers, ship brokers and bill brokers all now fall under the word. Pawnbrokers do not, since they deal as principals rather than as agents. The long entry then takes up the legal questions of modern interest, dealing first with brokers as agents for buying and selling goods before turning to the newer classes.
britannica-1911-brome-alexander:
Alexander Brome (1620–1666) was an English poet who worked by profession as an attorney. Verse, not law, made his name: he wrote many drinking songs and satirical verses backing the Royalists and mocking the Rump. His wit and gaiety won him the title of the English Anacreon in Edward Phillips's Theatrum Poetarum.

In 1661 he published Songs and other Poems, holding songs on many subjects, political songs, ballads, epistles, elegies, epitaphs, epigrams and translations, with an introductory eclogue in his praise by Izaak Walton. In 1666 came a translation of Horace by himself and others. He also wrote a comedy, The Cunning Lovers, in 1654, and edited two volumes of the plays of Richard Brome, the dramatist who shares his surname.
britannica-1911-browne-peter:
Peter Browne (about 1665–1735) was an Irish divine and bishop of Cork and Ross, born in County Dublin not long after the Restoration. He entered Trinity College, Dublin, in 1682 and after ten years took a fellowship. In 1699 he became provost of the college, and that same year printed his Letter answering Toland's book Christianity not Mysterious.

That reply was recognised as the ablest yet written to Toland, and it held in germ his whole later theory of analogy. Made bishop in 1710, a post he held until his death in 1733 by the entry's dating, he won notoriety in 1713 for pamphlets attacking the fashion of drinking healths. His two great works are the Procedure, Extent, and Limits of the Human Understanding of 1728, a critique of Locke. The Divine Analogy of 1733, holding that God's attributes can be known only by analogy with things natural and human, an answer to deist use of Locke.
britannica-1911-buchan-peter:
Peter Buchan (1790–1854) was a Scottish printer and editor. He is known for collecting old Scottish ballads. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his short career. He was born at Peterhead, in Aberdeenshire. In 1816 he set up as a printer there. His business did well enough to let him retire. He then gave his time to ballads.

His Ancient Ballads and Songs of the North of Scotland appeared in 1828. It held many ballads never printed before. It also held new versions of known ballads. The Percy Society issued a second collection in 1845. Its title was Scottish Traditional Versions of Ancient Ballads. Two more volumes of his collecting stay unpublished. They rest in the British Museum. Buchan died on 19 September 1854. The entry is brief, and it rests his name on this rescue work.
britannica-1911-calder:
Calder is an ancient district of Midlothian, in Scotland. This 1911 Britannica entry describes its parishes and industries. The district splits into Mid-Calder and West-Calder. East-Calder belongs to the parish of Kirknewton. Mid-Calder held 3132 people in 1901. West-Calder held 8092, and Kirknewton 3221. The district owes its prosperity to one great industry. That is the mineral oil trade, hugely developed there.

Coal-mining is also carried on widely in Calder. Sandstone and limestone are quarried as well. Paper-mills flourish in the district too. Mid-Calder town stands on the river Almond. It has an ancient church and a notable minister. John Spottiswood, the Scottish reformer, served there for years. His sons John and James were both born in the town. West-Calder is the district's chief centre. It stands on Breich Water, south-west of Edinburgh. At Addiewell, works make ammonia, naphtha and paraffin oil.
britannica-1911-calender:
Calender is a word with two quite separate meanings. This 1911 Britannica entry sets out both senses. The first is a machine used in cloth and paper making. It consists of two or more rollers in close contact. The rollers are often heated in use. Cloth passes between them under pressure. The process flattens the fibres of the fabric. It removes unevenness and gives a smooth finish. It can also leave a glaze on the surface.

Paper manufacture uses the same machine in its finishing. The second sense is a religious one. A calender was a member of an order of dervishes. The order split from the Baktashite order in the 14th century. Its members were vowed to perpetual travelling. The name appears in several other forms as well. Kalenderis and Qalandarites are among them. The entry points readers to the article on dervishes for more.
britannica-1911-california-lower:
Lower California is a long, narrow peninsula of Mexico. It is also called Baja California. It lies between the Gulf of California and the Pacific Ocean. This 1911 Britannica article surveys the territory. Its population was 42,245 in 1895. By 1900 it had risen to 47,624. The peninsula runs about 760 miles long. It is only 30 to 150 miles wide. Its area is 58,328 square miles.

A range of barren mountains runs the peninsula's full length. It slopes gently toward the Pacific side. Toward the Gulf it breaks down in steep faces. The land looks arid and desolate in general. Rain is too scant for most plants to grow. Volcanic remains add to the barren look. The north is hot and dry, like southern California. The south gets more rain and has fertile tracts. Orchil is the chief natural product named. With irrigation, farmers grow sugar cane, cotton and grapes.
britannica-1911-caponier:
A caponier is a work built in the ditch of a fort. This short 1911 Britannica entry defines the term. The word comes from the French caponnière. That word properly means a capon-cote, or house. The work's fire sweeps the bottom of the ditch. Muskets, machine-guns and case shot can all fire from it. Its guns stop an enemy from settling in the ditch.

The term appears in military use by the late 17th century. In some bastioned systems the caponier had a second role. It served as a covered way to the outworks. The main parapet then defended the ditch by its own fire. The bastion trace made that plan possible. The whole notice is a short paragraph in the original. It gives the word's origin, the work's purpose, and its variant use. Readers get a plain definition of a fortification detail.
britannica-1911-carlyle-alexander:
Alexander Carlyle (1722–1805) was a Scottish divine. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born in Dumfriesshire on 26 January 1722. He passed his youth at Prestonpans, in the east. There he witnessed the battle of 1745 as a young man. He was educated at Edinburgh, Glasgow and Leiden. From 1748 until his death he was minister at Inveresk.

Carlyle rose to high eminence in the Scottish church. He led the moderate, or “broad,” party within it. He was moderator of the General Assembly in 1770. In 1789 he became dean of the Chapel Royal. His striking looks earned him the name “Jupiter Carlyle.” His autobiography appeared in 1860, long after his death. It stops at the year 1770 in its narrative. Still, it pictures 18th-century Scottish life in rich detail. He remembered the Porteous Riots of 1736 in it. Adam Smith, David Hume and John Home were his friends.
britannica-1911-carrier:
Carrier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the law that governs people who carry the goods of others for hire. In common speech the word covered the wagoners who hauled goods by road, a trade the railways had largely replaced. In law it covers all conveyers of property, by land or by water. The growth of world transit made the subject more important, not less.

The entry grounds the carrier's duty in Roman law. A praetorian edict, preserved in the Pandects, promised judgment against shipmasters, innkeepers, and stable-keepers who failed to return what they had received safely. From that short rule grew the principle that a carrier's promise to the public is a contract of indemnity. He must deliver what he took in, or pay its value. The entry traces how that simple Roman rule shaped commercial law across the civilised world.
britannica-1911-carrying-over:
Carrying over is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry defining a stock exchange term, also called continuation. It names the operation by which settlement of a bargain made for money, or for a given account, is put off from one settling day to the next. The delay is not free: the party who carries over pays a consideration for it. That charge is called a contango or a backwardation.

The entry explains the mechanics in terms of sale and repurchase. A continuation equals a sale for the day joined to a repurchase for the succeeding account, or a purchase for the day joined to a resale. The price used to adjust such deals is the “making-up” price of the day. The entry is brief and points readers onward to the articles on Account and Stock Exchange for the fuller treatment of how accounts and settlements worked.
britannica-1911-cartwright-peter:
Peter Cartwright (1785–1872) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an American Methodist Episcopal preacher born in Amherst county, Virginia. His father, a veteran of the War of Independence, moved the family to Kentucky in 1790. Peter had little schooling and gambled at cards and horse racing until 1801, when a sermon by John Page brought him into the church.

He was licensed as an exhorter in May 1802 and soon known as the “Kentucky Boy.” Ordained deacon in 1806 and presiding elder in 1808, he served districts in Kentucky and, from 1823, in Illinois, where he stayed until 1869. By 1856 he had preached some 14,600 times, received about 10,000 people into the church, and baptized about 12,000. The entry calls him a typical backwoods preacher, able and strong, and gives his death near Pleasant Plains, Illinois, in September 1872.
britannica-1911-cavalier:
Cavalier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a word for a horseman. It meant in particular a horse soldier, or a man of gentle birth trained in knightly exercises. The word comes from French forms that go back to the late Latin caballarius, a horseman. That in turn comes from caballus, a pack horse. The same root gave French the word chevalier, the regular term for a knight.

In English the word took on a sharp political sense. It was first used with contempt for a swaggering gallant. Then it fastened to the Royalists, the supporters of Charles I against Parliament. Their opponents coined it as a reproach. The king's party soon adopted it as a title of honour. They answered with the name Roundhead for their foes. The court party kept the name at the Restoration, until the term Tory rose.
britannica-1911-chateau-gontier:
Château-Gontier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of western France, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Mayenne. It stands on the Mayenne river, 18 miles south by east of Laval. Its population in 1906 was 6871. Of its churches, St Jean dates from the eleventh century and is a relic of the castle. The town has a tribunal, a communal college for boys, and a small museum.

Local work includes spinning wool and cotton. Serge, flannel, and oil are made there. The town is also an agricultural market, and chalybeate springs lie close by. Its name and origin come from a castle built in the first half of the eleventh century by Gunther, steward of Fulk Nerra of Anjou. The site had been a farm of the monks of St Aubin. Louis XI later gave the lordship to Philippe de Comines. The Vendeans occupied the town in 1793.
britannica-1911-cheffonier:
Cheffonier is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a piece of furniture, a sideboard like cabinet with doors closing its whole front. The hosted text begins in mid description, so the entry's opening lines are not present here. Its name comes from the French for a rag gatherer. That hints at its first purpose: a place for odds and ends. It now usually serves as a sideboard.

The entry judges it a remote and illegitimate descendant of the cabinet. It has rarely been elegant and never beautiful. The earliest cheffoniers date from the Empire period in England. They are usually of rosewood, with brass knobs and handles. A raised shelf with a pierced brass gallery often stands at the back. The doors are well panelled. The feet are pads, claws, or gilded bronze sphinxes. Cheap forms are still made in England in great number.
britannica-1911-cher:
Cher is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a department of central France. It takes in the eastern part of the old province of Berry. Loiret bounds it in the north, Allier and Creuse in the south, and Nièvre in the east. Its population in 1906 was 343,484. Its area is 2819 square miles. The south and east are elevated, one point reaching 1654 feet. A wide limestone table land fills the centre.

The Cher river becomes navigable where the Arnon and Yèvre join it. The Canal du Berry crosses the department from east to west. The climate is temperate and the rainfall moderate. Apart from the Sologne plain in the north, the soil is generally fertile. Wheat and oats are the main crops, with hemp, vegetables, and fruit. Vines flourish in the east, near Sancerre. Wide pastures support a strong trade in horses, cattle, and sheep.
britannica-1911-chichester:
Chichester is a city and municipal borough in Sussex, England, 69 miles south-south-west of London, lying in a plain at the foot of the South Downs. Its people numbered 12,224 in 1901, and it stands a mile from the head of Chichester Harbour. The cathedral church of the Holy Trinity was founded late in the 11th century, after the see moved here from Selsey in 1075. Fires in 1114 and 1187 kept building going for two centuries.

Norman work fills the nave and choir, while fine Early English work crowns the eastern parts, and the nave has rare double aisles. A detached campanile, unique among English cathedrals, stands beside the church, and the spire rises 277 feet. The market cross, town walls, St Mary's hospital and a grammar school founded in 1497 fill the town account. Cattle trade, farming trade, breweries and tanneries support the city.
britannica-1911-clever:
Clever is an adjective implying dexterous activity of mind or body, and ability to meet emergencies with readiness and adroitness. Its etymology and early history are obscure, and the earliest instance quoted comes from a Bestiary of about 1200. There the adder is called cof and the devil cliver on sins, quick to seize hold. That use would connect the word with cliver or clivre, a talon or claw, and the root seen in claw and cling.

Earlier uses seem confined to bodily dexterity, nimble and skilful use of the hands, as when a horse is called clever at his fences. Sir Thomas Browne listed the word among terms of common use in Norfolk but no general reception in English. A link with Old English gleaw, wise, has also been suggested through Scots gleg. The earliest dictionary use for mental quickness comes from Addison in 1716.
britannica-1911-cloister:
Cloister, from the Latin claustrum, now names the four-sided enclosure with covered ambulatories usually attached to conventual and cathedral churches, and sometimes to colleges. Originally the word signified the entire monastery, a sense frequent in earlier English literature and still used in poetry. The Latin word first denoted only the enclosing wall of a religious house. It then came to cover the whole building enclosed within that wall, as German Kloster still does.

In the common modern sense the cloister is the quadrilateral area round which the principal buildings are ranged. A covered way runs all round it, giving communication between the centres of ecclesiastical life without exposure to weather. Under the Benedictine arrangement, generally adopted in the West, the church forms one side. The refectory occupies the side opposite the church, so that worshippers suffer least annoyance from noise or smells at meals.
britannica-1911-clothier:
Clothier is a manufacturer of cloth, or a dealer who sells either the cloth itself or made-up clothing, the entry states. Those two trades, making and selling, share the one occupational name here. A dealer may sell the raw fabric to buyers, or sell garments already made up from it. No place, date or person is attached to the term in this notice, which is a trade definition only.

American use has shifted with time, and the entry records that shift as its second fact. In the United States the word formerly applied only to those who dressed or fulled cloth during manufacture. Fulling, the cleansing and thickening of woven cloth, was thus the clothier's work there. Now the word is used in the general sense given above, for makers and sellers alike, and the older narrow American sense has faded.
britannica-1911-clover:
Clover, in botany, is the English name for plants of the genus Trifolium, from Latin words for three and a leaf, after its three leaflets. Trefoil is its popular name, and it belongs to the family Leguminosae, with about three hundred species. Most species live in north temperate regions, though some grow on mountains in the tropics. The plants are small herbs with heads or dense spikes of small red, purple, white or rarely yellow flowers.

Eighteen species are native in Britain, and several are extensively cultivated as fodder plants, with red or purple clover the most widely grown. Sown alone or mixed with rye grass, it long formed the staple crop for soiling cattle. Its power to shoot again after repeated mowings and its bulk entitled it to that preference. Except on certain rich calcareous clay soils it has now become an exceedingly precarious crop.
britannica-1911-coffer:
Coffer, in building terms, is a sunk panel in a ceiling or vault. The word comes through French from a Latin term for a basket. It also names a casket or chest for jewels and rich goods. Large coffers held clothes instead. Form and use thus split in two.

One thread of the entry treats carved work. Marriage coffers in Italy stood out for rich carving and gilding. Great artists at times painted them. That fact lifts a storage chest into the rank of art. The entry stays short, with no list of makers or dates. A reader gains the two senses of the word and one note on Italian craft. The panel sense belongs to building, the chest sense to the home.
britannica-1911-colchester:
Colchester is a market town and river port in Essex, England, 52 miles north-east of London by rail. Its people numbered 38,373 in 1901. It stands on the river Colne, twelve miles from the open sea. Old buildings fill the town with points of note. First among them is the ruined keep of the castle.

That keep is the largest of its kind in England. It covers near twice the ground of the White Tower in London. Kings William I or William II raised it. Roman stone from the old town went into its walls. The Essex Archaeological Society keeps its museum there, rich in Roman finds. Ruins of Saint Botolph's priory add a second Norman sight. The entry also traces the borough's early growth. Domesday Book names 276 burgesses there. Roman walls and finds mark the site throughout.
britannica-1911-collins-william-painter:
William Collins (1787–1847) was an English painter born in London, son of an Irish picture dealer and man of letters. He studied under Etty in 1807. In 1809 he showed his first works of note, Boys at Breakfast and Boys with a Bird's Nest. He became an associate of the Royal Academy in 1815 and a full member in 1820.

For sixteen years he showed work without pause. His fishermen, shrimp-catchers, boats and nets won wide love. His rustic children pleased most of all. On Wilkie's advice he went abroad and spent two years in Italy. In 1840 he became librarian to the Academy and first tried history painting. In 1842 he went back to his early themes. His last years brought his greatest fame. The entry calls him a good colourist and a fine draughtsman.
britannica-1911-cooper-alexander:
Alexander Cooper (died 1660) was an English miniature painter whose works are of great rarity. His chief works form a series of the king and queen of Bohemia and their children. Those pieces belong to the German emperor. Other fine portraits belong to the queen of Holland and to the king of Sweden. He was brother to Samuel Cooper, the famed miniaturist.

Which brother was the elder is not known for sure. Swedish sources put his birth in 1605, four years before Samuel, on slight proof. He lived in Holland before he came to Sweden in 1646. There he entered Queen Christina's service as her miniature painter. He held that post until she gave up the crown in 1654. Two years later he worked in Denmark for Christian IV. In 1657 he was back in Stockholm, where he died early in the next decade.
britannica-1911-cooper-peter:
Peter Cooper (1791–1883) was an American manufacturer, inventor and philanthropist born in New York city on 12 February 1791. His grandfathers and his father all served in the War of Independence. He had next to no schooling. He worked with his father at hat-making, brewing and brick-making in turn. At seventeen he was set to a coach-builder in New York.

On coming of age he made machines for shearing cloth at Hempstead. Three years later he set up in that trade for himself. He held the sole right to make such gear in New York state. The War of 1812 fattened the business, and peace thinned it. He turned to furniture, then to groceries for a short spell. Next came a glue and isinglass factory that ran for twenty-one years in Manhattan. His name clings most to the school he founded.
britannica-1911-cooper-thomas-writer:
Thomas Cooper (1805–1892) was an English Chartist and writer, son of a working dyer, born at Leicester on 20 March 1805. His mother ran a dyeing and box-making trade at Gainsborough after his father's death. The boy was set to a shoemaker. A hunger for knowledge drove him to Greek, Latin and Hebrew in his spare time. In 1827 he left cobbling to teach school.

Preaching and newspaper work followed, at Lincoln and then in London. In 1840 he joined the Leicestershire Mercury staff. His backing of the Chartists cost him that post. In 1841 he edited a Chartist journal instead. He rose to lead the extreme wing of the movement. For urging on the strike of 1842 he spent two years in Stafford gaol. There he wrote The Purgatory of Suicides, an epic in ten books. Later years turned to teaching and a sharp change of belief.
britannica-1911-cope-edward-drinker:
Edward Drinker Cope (1840–1897) was an American palaeontologist born in Philadelphia on 28 July 1840. His family came from Wiltshire and crossed the Atlantic about 1687. Natural history drew him at an early age. In 1859 he sent a paper on the Salamandridae to the Academy of Natural Sciences at Philadelphia. He studied in part at the University of Pennsylvania.

After more study and travel in Europe he became curator of that academy in 1865. He held the post until 1873. He taught natural science at Haverford College from 1864 to 1867. In 1889 he took the chair of geology and palaeontology at Pennsylvania. Fossil vertebrates of America held his chief zeal. He dug in Kansas, Wyoming and Colorado from 1871 to 1877. In time he made known at least 600 species new to science. He died in Philadelphia on 12 April 1897.
britannica-1911-copper:
Copper, symbol Cu, is a metal known and used by mankind from the most remote ages. Its alloy with tin, bronze, was the first metal compound in common use. That vast use gave a whole age its name, the Bronze Age. Greeks and Romans used one word for the metal and its alloys alike. Rome drew its chief supply from Cyprus, and the name cuprum grew from that source.

The metal shows a brilliant red colour of its own. A fresh fracture of the pure metal takes a pink or yellow tinge. With cuprous oxide in it the hue turns purple. Weight for its bulk runs near 8.9 times that of water. Ore dressing, smelting and refining fill great parts of it. One method wets broken ore in heaps with a mix of salts. The sheer scale marks it as a full trade treatise.
britannica-1911-cover:
Cover, from a French word for covering, names that which hides, shuts in or hides from view. A lid to a box or vessel bears the name. So does the binding of a book or the wrapper of a parcel. As a hunting term it names the wood or brush that shelters game. Trade gives the word a sharper and more set sense.

It is a deposit lodged with a broker to keep him from loss if stocks fall against his client. The client must pay the difference if he can, and the deposit guards that gap. A court case of 1898 gives that sense in set words. Men who wish to cap their risk at a small sum use the mode most. Outside brokers, not members of the Exchange, run most of that trade in England.
britannica-1911-cracker:
Cracker is a word built on crack, a term for a sharp break or snap. It names, first, a firework made to pop with report after report. The piece jumps at each bang as it lies on the ground. It names, second, a roll of coloured paper with a snap strip inside. Sweets, cheap trinkets and paper caps fill that roll for party use.

Third, it names a thin, crisp biscuit. In America the word serves as the general name for a biscuit of any kind. A fourth sense carries a sting in the southern states of America. There cracker is a term of scorn for the poor or mean whites, most of all in Georgia and Florida. That use is old and runs back to the Revolution. Men trace it to the cracked corn that formed the staple food of that class.
britannica-1911-cratippus-philosopher:
Cratippus of Mitylene, a Peripatetic philosopher of the first century before Christ, was a contemporary of Cicero. He taught Cicero's son at Athens in his school. Cicero praises him in the De officiis as the greatest man of his school. Pompey counted him as a friend as well. After the battle of Pharsalia he shared Pompey's flight from the field.

Men said his aim in that flight was to sway Pompey to trust in providence. Brutus heard his lectures at Athens after the killing of Caesar. One work is laid to his name, a treatise on divination. In 44 before Christ the Areopagus asked him to head the school in place of Andronicus of Rhodes. Motion, sense and appetite, he held, cannot live apart from the body. Thought gains its peak when most free of the body's curb.
britannica-1911-credit-foncier:
The Crédit Foncier was a French body that lent money on mortgage of real property. It was created by a government decree of 28 February 1852. Its loans carried low interest, ran for long terms, and were repaid by yearly payments that included capital. It began in Paris as the Banque Foncière de Paris with a capital of 25,000,000 francs. Sister bodies at Nevers and Marseilles soon merged into it.

Under the name Crédit Foncier de France its capital rose, and the state named its governor and two deputies. It could issue bonds repayable in fifty or sixty years, some carrying prizes. Loans could not pass half the worth of the mortgaged property. It also lent to local bodies, and its charter was renewed in 1881 for ninety-nine years. A linked Crédit Agricole failed after heavy loans to Egypt, and the bank suffered with it.
britannica-1911-crofter:
A crofter is a tenant who rents and works a small holding of land, a use strongest in the Highlands and islands of Scotland. The word croft first meant an enclosed field. The Crofters' Holdings Act of 1886 fixes the legal sense. A crofter there is a tenant who lives on his holding, in a crofting parish, at a rent of not more than thirty pounds a year. Clearances in the 1800s stripped many tenants of such holdings.

Those clearances, made against what tenants claimed was an implied security of tenure, stirred long agitation. Royal commissions studied the grievances, and laws followed in some number. The entry judges that the Act of 1886, with its later amending acts, markedly improved the crofters' condition. Much of the agitation had died out by the time of writing. For the history of the crofter laws the entry sends readers to the article on Scotland.
britannica-1911-cromer:
Cromer is a watering-place in the northern division of Norfolk, England, 139 miles north-east of London by rail. Its urban district held 3,781 people in 1901. The town stands on high cliffs and has often suffered from the ravages of the sea. A wall and esplanade run along the cliff foot, with a fine stretch of sandy beach and a short pier. The church of St Peter and St Paul is Perpendicular, with a lofty tower.

On a three-acre site stands the convalescent home of the Norfolk and Norwich hospital, and the town has an excellent golf course. Herring, cod, lobster, and crab fisheries are prosecuted from the town. The village of Sheringham, lying to the west, also draws visitors. A so-called Roman camp on a height above the sea is, the entry notes, actually a modern beacon.
britannica-1911-cromwell-oliver:
Oliver Cromwell (1599–1658), lord protector of England, was the fifth and only surviving son of Robert Cromwell of Huntingdon. His grandfather was Sir Henry Cromwell of Hinchinbrook, and his line ran back to a nephew of Thomas Cromwell, Henry VIII's minister. Born on 25 April 1599, he was schooled under the puritan Dr Thomas Beard at Huntingdon. In 1616 he entered Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge. He married Elizabeth Bourchier in 1620 and settled at Huntingdon.

In 1628 Cromwell entered parliament for Huntingdon and spoke at once for puritan doctrine. The entry, a full-scale biography, follows him from those beginnings through the wars and governments of the next thirty years. It ends with his rule as lord protector. A detailed bibliography, arranged by period and topic, closes the long text. Works listed cover the legal side of his rule, the navy, the church, foreign relations, and the mission of Menasseh Ben Israel.
britannica-1911-cross-river:
Cross River is a river of West Africa, more than 500 miles long. It rises in the mountains of Cameroon and flows first north-west. A series of rapids marks its course, and below them the river is navigable for shallow-draught boats. At its most northern point it turns south-west and then south. It enters the Gulf of Guinea through the Calabar estuary.

The Calabar river runs parallel to the Cross, ten to twenty miles east of it, and the town of Calabar stands near its mouth. Cross, Calabar, Kwa, and other streams from the Cameroon Mountains form a large delta together. The Calabar and Kwa lie wholly within the British protectorate of Southern Nigeria. So does the Cross from its mouth up to the rapids. The upper course of the river lay in German territory.
britannica-1911-cross-springer: Cross springer is a term in architecture for the block from which the diagonal ribs of a vault spring or start. The top of that block carries its own name, the skewback. The hosted entry is a single sentence and gives no more than that definition and cross-reference. For the wider subject it sends the reader to the article on the arch. Nothing else, no history, use, or example, is stated in the entry as hosted.
britannica-1911-csoma-de-koros-alexander:
Alexander Csoma de Körös (about 1790–1842) was a Hungarian traveller and philologist born at Körös in Transylvania, of a noble family sunk in poverty. Educated at Nagy-Enyed and Göttingen, he split his study between medicine and Oriental languages. His youthful dream was to find the origin of his countrymen. In 1820, backed by a friend's promise of 100 florins a year, he set out for the East. He passed through Egypt and reached Tibet.

In Tibet Csoma spent four years in a Buddhist monastery, studying the language and its sacred books. The search for Hungarian origins gained nothing there, to his disappointment. In Bengal the Asiatic Society employed him for its Tibetan library of over 1,000 volumes. His Tibetan dictionary and grammar appeared at Calcutta in 1834, with an analysis of the Kah-Gyur. Early in 1842 he set out again on the quest. He died at Darjiling on 11 April 1842.
britannica-1911-cucumber:
The cucumber, Cucumis sativus, is a creeping plant of the order Cucurbitaceae, grown across the world. It likely began in northern India, where it may have been grown for three thousand years. It spread west to Europe and was known to the ancient Greeks. China received it two hundred years before the Christian era. The plant is an annual with a rough trailing stem, hairy lobed leaves, and branched tendrils for climbing.

Male and female flowers grow on the same plant, the female known by the swollen ovary below the bloom. That ovary becomes the fruit without fertilization. The entry sorts the many garden kinds into forcing and field varieties. Long pages give the hot-bed craft in full detail. A closing note describes a way of turning the pulp to a drink inside the fruit, and names the squirting cucumber as the source of the drug elaterium.
britannica-1911-demeter:
Demeter, in Greek mythology, was a daughter of Cronus and Rhea and a sister of Zeus, goddess of agriculture and civilized life. Her name is read as grain-mother or as earth-mother. She is rare in Homer and not counted among the Olympian gods. The central fact of her cult is the story of her daughter Persephone, carried off by Hades from the Nysian plain with Zeus's connivance.

Demeter wandered the earth seeking her daughter, learned the truth from Helios, and came in an old woman's shape to Celeus at Eleusis. In her wrath she laid a great dearth on the earth until Zeus let Persephone spend two-thirds of the year above ground. Before leaving, she taught the rulers of Eleusis agriculture and her rites, the mysteries that promised a future life.
brother-and-sister:
Josephine Lawrence's Brother and Sister opens the Morrison family at breakfast on a rainy morning. Brother will not drink his milk because rain stops outdoor growing. His brother Ralph promises a birthday present next week, if Brother is tall enough by Wednesday. Louise, the older sister, calls him silly.

Twenty-two short chapters follow Brother and Sister through party preparations and presents. Dick's buttons, a haunted house, and a very sick doll supply the adventures. Mickey Gaffney, a poorer neighbour boy, needs plans and finally owns up. Lawrence wrote the first of her Brother and Sister series for young children. The episodes are gentle, funny, and exact about family life: spilled treats, small jealousies, and making up. Grandma Hastings and Miss Putnam keep the grown-up world kindly in view.
bucky-o-connor-a-tale-of-the-unfenced-bo:
William MacLeod Raine dedicates Bucky O'Connor to his brother Edgar. The Denver letter is dated March 1910. It offers the tale of the unfenced border as a companion for a long northern winter. Sheriff Bucky O'Connor of Arizona enters with Bear-Trap Collins in chapter one. Taxation without representation and a called bluff follow in the contents.

Bucky crosses into revolutionary Mexico and survives the hold-up of the M C P flyer. He pursues a kidnapped girl and stolen money, through stone walls that do not a prison make. He climbs stairs three at a time to meet brown eyes after the night's hazards. Raine, a Colorado schoolteacher turned Westerner, writes clean action with a romantic shine.
business-correspondence-vol-1-how-to-wri:
An anonymous manual, Business Correspondence, Volume One: How to Write the Business Letter, teaches the art of selling and persuading by post. Its twenty-four chapters draw proved principles and practical schemes from extracts of 217 actual letters.

Early chapters prepare the writer: what a postage stamp can do, the advantages of doing business by letter, and gathering talking points. Later parts show how to open a letter, present a proposition convincingly, close effectively, and acquire a forceful, original style. The volume adapts selling appeal to different prospects and aims at orders by letter. Modern readers will find it a vivid record of early twentieth-century salesmanship.
cabin-fever:
B M Bower named Cabin Fever for the malady her first chapter diagnoses: the restlessness that snow, isolation, and a failing marriage breed in a northern cabin. Bud, a young rancher, quarrels with his wife Marie and heads south with ten dollars and a job. The contents promise deserts, barren months, and cabin fever in its worst form.

Bud partners with the older Cash, whose sourdough loaves and silence steady the partnership through mining disappointments. A child, Lovin Child, enters the tangle, and Marie takes a desperate chance of her own. Bower resolves the fever with facts faced and a cure complete. Her Westerns ground romance in work, weather, and money, and this one adds a rare honest look at marriage.
cap-n-dan-s-daughter:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Cap'n Dan's Daughter is a Cape Cod story set in the village of Trumet Centre, where the Metropolitan Dry Goods and Variety Store opens for business with no customers at all. August should bring city visitors hunting white duck hats, oilskin coats, post cards and chocolates, but the shop stands quiet.

Lincoln peoples his village with shopkeepers, sailors and summer folk, telling their doings in the dry, affectionate dialect humour that made his Cape Cod books famous. The daughter of the title, Cap'n Dan's own girl, stands at the centre of the village's hopes and gossip. Readers who enjoy gentle American local-colour fiction, with salt air and small-town comedy, will feel at home in Trumet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-deer:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Deer describes a once-famous Scottish monastery on the Ugie in Buchan. Celtic legend tells how St. Columcille, with his disciple Drostan, founded a missionary centre there on lands given by the local chief, whose son Columcille's prayers had healed.

Columcille soon moved on, leaving Drostan as abbot until his death about 606, and Aberdour's veneration of Drostan supports the legend. In 1219 the Earl of Buchan founded the Cistercian abbey of New Deer two miles west, granting it part of Old Deer's lands. Later a titular abbot held the lands in commendam, and the flourishing monastery fell prey to the troubles of the age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-dorc:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Dorchester describes an abbey founded in 1140 by Alexander of Lincoln for Augustinian canons, or Black Canons. Dorchester, a Roman city of Mercia nine miles from Oxford, had held a bishopric from 634, when St. Birinus arrived, until the see moved to Lincoln in 1085.

The abbey, dedicated to Peter, Paul and Birinus, drew rich gifts from the old bishopric's lands and tithes, with twelve parishes subject to it. Its first abbot appears to have been Alured, and its last, John Mershe, elected in 1533, subscribed to the king's supremacy and took a pension of twenty-two pounds a year. Henry the Eighth kept much of the property for a college of his own founding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abner:
Abner, son of Ner and cousin of Saul, served as commander-in-chief of Saul's army. After Saul and three of his sons fell at Mount Gelboe, Abner made Isboseth, Saul's fourth son, king over all Israel except Judea, which held to David. For seven and a half years he fought for Isboseth's throne, and near Gabaon he reluctantly slew Asael, brother of Joab, who pursued him hotly.

That killing embittered Joab, who counted himself his brother's avenger. When Isboseth rebuked Abner for marrying Respha, a concubine of Saul, Abner angrily opened talks with David, restored Saul's daughter Michol to him as demanded, and reached a full understanding. Joab then called him back and killed him at the city gate, and David mourned him and charged Solomon to avenge the murder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adalbert-stif:
Adalbert Stifter was a poet and pedagogue born at Oberplan in Bohemia on 23 October 1805. He died at Linz on 28 October 1868; his father had been a linen weaver and flax dealer. The boy's first stimulus came from his mother and grandmother, tellers of fairy tales, stories, and legends. School proved him apt, with talent for music and drawing. After his father's sudden death in 1817, his grandfather placed him at the Benedictine school at Kremsmunster.
