He stands as the model Canadian landed proprietor, pious, upright, and honourable. He died in 1717.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-joseph:
Pierre-Joseph Pelletier was a Paris pharmacist and chemist whose work on plant medicines gave the world quinine in usable form. He was born in Paris in 1788 to a pharmacist father. He turned to materia medica, the study of healing substances, and to the alkaloids, the active chemicals found in plants.

With Joseph Caventou he isolated quinine, the fever drug from cinchona bark. He published the result openly instead of keeping it secret for profit. He won the Montyon prize in 1827 for the discovery. He also helped identify strychnine, taught at the Paris school of pharmacy, and joined the Academy of Sciences in 1840.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-vernie:
Pierre Vernier was the French mathematician and official who invented the fine scale that still bears his name. He was born at Ornans about 1580 and taught science by his father. He became captain and castellan of Ornans castle for the king of Spain. He also served as director of coinage in the County of Burgundy.

His 1631 treatise described a movable scale that lets a reader measure fractions of a degree. The reader sees which of its lines lines up with a line on the main scale. The device is now fitted to sextants, barometers, and other graduated instruments. It owes its name to Lalande, who showed that the older term nonius belonged to a different contrivance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pirkheimer:
Charitas Pirkheimer was the abbess of Saint Clara's convent at Nuremberg and sister of the humanist Willibald Pirkheimer. She was born at Nuremberg in 1466 and formed in the cloister from the age of twelve. She was chosen abbess in December 1503 after serving as teacher and perhaps mistress of novices.

For twenty years she lived in contemplative peace, reading Latin authors and the church fathers, above all Jerome, with her brother as guide. Her later years were stormed when Lutheran doctrines reached Nuremberg and the peace of the convent ceased. She defended her house with learning and firmness, and the entry draws on her letters and friendships with humanists such as Celtes, Scheurl, and Dürer until her death in 1532.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-placidus-fixl:
Placidus Fixlmillner was an Austrian Benedictine astronomer who directed the observatory at Kremsmünster Abbey. He was born near Kremsmünster in 1721 and joined the Benedictines at sixteen. He showed early talent for mathematics and, after publishing a theological treatise in 1756, returned to mathematics when the transit of Venus in 1761 rekindled his interest.

As observatory director he rebuilt its instruments and fixed the latitude and longitude of the site. He amassed observations of great variety until his death in 1791. He was among the first to compute the orbit of Uranus after Herschel's discovery, and his many observations of Mercury helped Lalande build tables of that planet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-christop:
Pope Christopher reigned in 903 and 904, a figure some call antipope and others accept as true pope. Once Cardinal-Priest of Saint Damasus, a Roman and son of Leo, he took the papacy by forcibly dethroning Leo V and imprisoning him, seemingly about October 903. As Leo soon died in prison, Christopher may count as pope from his death.

His name stands in contemporary catalogues of popes. His portrait hangs among the popes at Saint Paul Outside the Walls. Leo IX, confirming Corbie Abbey's privileges, cited grants of Benedict and Christopher. That Corbie privilege is the only act of his that survives. A Greek document claims he first stated in his profession of faith to Constantinople that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son. No Patriarch Sergius then existed, however.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-porter-doorke:
Porter, also called doorkeeper, comes from the Latin ostiarius, a door-keeper. Among Romans the porter was the slave guarding a house entrance. Better houses all had one, though the duties ranked very low. From the late second century, as Christian communities owned houses for worship and business, church ostiaries appear, at least in larger cities.

Cornelius's letter to Fabius of Antioch in 251 counts Rome's clergy: forty-six priests, seven deacons, seven subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists, lectors, and ostiaries. The Liber Pontificalis says an ostiary named Romanus was martyred in 258 with St Lawrence. In Western Europe the ostiary was the lowest minor order. A 377 law of the Theodosian Code gives ostiaries personal immunity among Italian clergy. Gelasius wrote in 494 that clergy candidates must be able to read; a man without that could at most become an ostiary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prayer:
Prayer, from Greek euchesthai, Latin precari, and French prier, means to plead, to beg, to ask with earnestness. It is an act of the virtue of religion, asking fit gifts and graces from God. In a wider sense it is the mind's turn to Divine things, as a road to union with God. The Fathers call it the mind's lift to God, converse with God, and plain talk with God.

It voices our wants to God, not to school or steer Him, but to plead His goodness. Church use opens and closes the day with prayer. Morn and eve prayer bind no strict duty, yet long neglect counts more or less as sin, by its cause, most oft sloth. Prayer divides as vocal or mental, private or public. Vocal prayer joins an outward act, most oft words, to the inward act found in all prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prosper-louis:
Dom Prosper Guéranger, Benedictine monk and prolific writer, was born at Sablé-sur-Sarthe on 4 April 1805 and died at Solesmes on 30 January 1875. Ordained priest in 1827, he left parish work in Paris, returned to the Mans region, and in December 1832 bought the priory of Solesmes, then up for sale. There he set out to plant Benedictine monastic life again in France after the Revolution had wiped it out.

Guéranger's long campaign pushed the Roman liturgy in place of the many local French uses, and he lived to see that effort win across the country. He also battled Gallican and Jansenist leanings, arguing that error must be replaced rather than merely attacked. His books ranged from early political pamphlets to liturgical studies, a life of Saint Cecilia, and rules for Benedictine novices, closing a career that reshaped French Catholic worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quimper:
The Diocese of Quimper covers the Department of Finistère. This encyclopedia entry explains that the Concordat of 1802 rebuilt it from a large part of Quimper, also called Cornouailles. It added the whole Diocese of Saint Pol de Léon, and small parts of Tréguier and Vannes. From 1802 to 1859 it answered to Tours, and since 1859 it has answered to Rennes. Two bishop lists survive, from Quimperlé in the twelfth century and Quimper in the fifteenth.

Both name Saint Corentinus as first bishop, though his biography is very late. Some suppose Martin ordained him in the fourth century, others place him in the sixth. Later pages praise Albert Le Grand, whose Lives of the Saints of Brittany of 1636 fed a revival, and Maunoir, founder of Breton philology with his Breton dictionary. Quimper Cathedral's cornerstone was laid in 1424, and Alexander the Sixth's grant of Jubilee indulgences at last funded its completion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rafael-ferrer:
Rafael Ferrer, Spanish missionary and explorer, was born at Valencia in 1570 and died at San José, Peru, in 1611. This encyclopedia entry tells that his father meant him for a soldier's career, but he entered the Society of Jesus and was sent to Quito, Ecuador, in 1593. In 1601 he entered the land of the Cofanis, a hostile tribe. Within three years religion had so civilized several villages that the surrounding country lay open to colonists.

In 1605, at the viceroy of Quito's command, Ferrer travelled among the uncivilized tribes of the River Napo. He journeyed two and a half years and 3,600 miles into the interior. He returned with a chart of the Napo basin, a map of the explored country, and a herbarium. His grammar of the Cofani tongue survives, with his translations of the catechism and Sunday Gospel readings, though his longer manuscript was lost and never fully published.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raoul-glaber:
Raoul Glaber, Benedictine chronicler, was born in Burgundy before 1000 and died at Cluny about 1050. This encyclopedia entry paints a wayward boy, so mischievous that his uncle, a monk, forced him into Saint-Léger de Champeaux at twenty to keep him safe. Glaber took only the monastic habit. Pride made him resist and disobey his superiors and quarrel with his brethren, until he was expelled.

He then entered Notre-Dame du Moutier and Saint-Benignus at Dijon. Abbot William of Dijon, valuing his literary gifts, befriended him and took him to Susa in Italy in 1028. Yielding again to a roving temper, Glaber slipped away to Saint-Germain d'Auxerre, sure his learning would win him refuge anywhere. His chronology and geography fall short, yet his work stays interesting and useful, opening a window on the customs and morals of an age when continental Christianity had sunk low.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reform-of-a-r:
Reform of a religious order means restoring an order from mitigated, relaxed observance to its primitive rule's rigour. This encyclopedia entry first allows that mitigations may be lawful. They may come by the Holy See's authority, or by decree of the order's superiors within their power. Established prescription or custom may also allow them, so long as relaxations do not touch the vows. Obligations springing directly from vows cannot be changed by custom or prescription.

Abolishing abuses in vow matters is therefore not reform in the proper sense of the word. Where a rule's mitigation came about through authority, reform may be set on foot by the Holy See or by the order's superiors, the entry notes. They work through the channels the order's constitutions allow. Pellizzario, Schmalzgrüber, Bouix, Bachofen and Aichner supply the canon-law sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-dow:
Religious dower, the Latin dos religiosa, takes its name by analogy from the dower a bride brings her husband. It is the money or property a nun brings into her convent for her own maintenance, set apart for her support after profession. It is neither a gift to the convent nor the payments for a postulant or novice before profession. The custom was unknown in the ancient Church and came in only gradually for nuns under solemn vows.

The convent gained no possession of the dower until profession itself, and a novice who left beforehand recovered it, as the Council of Trent laid down. Dispensation from solemn vows was almost unheard of, so no rule covered restitution when a professed religious left; equity, not law, supplied the answer. The decree Perpensis of 3 May 1902 changed this, requiring three years under simple vows before solemn profession.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-remi-ceillier:
Remi Ceillier, patrologist, was born at Bar-le-Duc on 14 May 1688 and died at Flavigny on 26 May 1763. Schooled at the Jesuit College of Bar-le-Duc, he entered the monastery of Moyen-Moutier in the Vosges in 1705, a house of the Benedictine congregation of Saint-Vannes and Saint-Hydulphe. He taught there as professor for six years, became dean of Moyen-Moutier in 1716, and prior of Saint Jacques de Neufchâteau in 1718.

In 1724 he became assistant to Dom Charles de Vassimont at the priory of Flavigny-sur-Moselle, succeeding him as prior on his death in 1733. Under his wise rule the monastery flourished materially, spiritually, and intellectually. His first great work, begun while professor at Moyen-Moutier, defended the morals of the Fathers. Charges of Jansenism against him find no support in his writings, as Benedict the Fourteenth's treatment of him shows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-francois:
René-François Rohrbacher, ecclesiastical historian, was born at Langatte in the present Diocese of Metz on 27 September 1789 and died in Paris on 17 January 1856. After a few months' study at Sarrebourg and Phalsebourg, he had finished his classical studies by seventeen. He taught three years at the college of Phalsebourg, entered the seminary at Nancy in 1810, and was ordained priest in 1812.

He served briefly as assistant priest at Insming, then moved to Lunéville after six months. A mission he preached at Flavigny in 1821 led to a diocesan mission band, and he later joined the Congregation of Saint Peter founded by Félicité and Jean de La Mennais. From 1827 to 1835 he directed the philosophical and theological studies of young churchmen preparing to assist the two brothers. His great history of the Church crowns a life of teaching and preaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-chall:
Richard Challoner, Bishop of Debra and Vicar Apostolic of the London District, was born on 29 September 1691 and died on 12 January 1781. The leading figure of English Catholicism through most of the eighteenth century, he was no cradle Catholic: his father was a Presbyterian wine cooper of Lewes. After his father's death his mother kept house for the Catholic Gages at Firle. The boy entered the Church at about thirteen, at Warkworth, seat of the Catholic Holman family.

Challoner's Bible became the groundwork of nearly all English versions. Its Old Testament appeared in 1750, a third edition in 1752 carried over two thousand text and note changes, and an American edition followed at Philadelphia in 1805. In 1753 he published his Meditations for Every Day of the Year, many times reprinted and translated into French and Italian. His spiritual and controversial works carried that leadership into print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-franc:
A wandering Franciscan preacher known only as Richard appears in the record for a few crowded years, 1428 to 1431. His birthplace and nationality are unknown. He is linked by guesswork to the followers of Bernardine of Siena and Vincent Ferrer. Like them, he promoted devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus and warned that the end of the world was near. From the Holy Land he reached France and preached at Troyes and Paris.

Crowds flocked to his long morning sermons. Listeners burned dice and finery after hearing him. Threatened by the Paris theology faculty, he left the city. He met Joan of Arc at Troyes, helped bring that town over to Charles VII, and served as Joan's confessor and chaplain. Differences over a visionary woman cooled the friendship. After preaching Lent at Orleans in 1431, he was barred from preaching. No trace of him survives after that year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-of-ci:
Richard of Cirencester was a Westminster monk whose chronicle covered English kings from 447 to 1066. Almost nothing is known of his life beyond a pilgrimage to Jerusalem in 1391, his presence at Westminster in 1397, and a spell of sickness in the infirmary around 1400. His four-book Speculum Historiale de Gestis Regum Angliae is judged of little historical value, though it preserves several charters granted to Westminster Abbey.

His name gained a stranger fame centuries later. In the eighteenth century, Charles Bertram forged a work on Roman Britain and passed it off under Richard's name. The forgery fooled leading antiquaries, including Stukeley and Lingard, and was only exposed in 1866-67. The entry also lists two further works ascribed to Richard, neither of which survives today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-riemenschneid:
Tilman Riemenschneider was one of the most important sculptors of Franconia, working in Wurzburg from 1483 until his death in 1531. Born at Osterode am Harz in or after 1460, he joined the Guild of St Luke at Wurzburg and never left the city. His early tomb work still followed the Gothic manner. His carvings for the Marienkapelle moved toward the Renaissance style, keeping traces of older art.

He excelled at character and at female saints. The Marienkapelle holds his famed Adam and Eve and his larger-than-life Christ, Baptist, and apostles. Graceful figures of Dorothea and Margaret stand there too. His masterpiece is the tomb of Emperor Henry II at Bamberg Cathedral, with ideal recumbent figures and lively scenes from the couple's lives on its sides. Other works, including Lamentations over Christ and a suspended rosary Madonna at Volkach, survive across Germany. Faults in some pieces are blamed on apprentices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-joseph:
Robert Joseph Pothier was a French lawyer whose treatises shaped the Code Napoleon. Born at Orleans in 1699, son of a petty-court judge, he later held his father's judgeship and a professorship of French law at Orleans, both from 1750. His quiet life of teaching and judging was marked by austerity, modesty, and deep religion.

His chief early work rearranged the texts of Roman law in the Pandectae Justinianeae of 1748-52, under Chancellor d'Aguesseau's patronage. He then wrote on the customs of Orleans and a long series of treatises, collected in 1781. They covered duties, sales, rents, exchange, hiring, leases, contracts, marriage, community, dowry, possession, and title. Jurists drafting the new French Civil Code kept his clear, well-planned works in hand and owed them much, especially on duties and contracts. From a religious angle, his treatise on the marriage contract sets out Gallican doctrines in full. He died at Orleans in 1772.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-stephe:
Robert Stephen Hawker was a Cornish poet and antiquary who spent forty years as vicar of the wreck-strewn parish of Morwenstow. Born at Plymouth in 1803, son of a doctor turned vicar of Stratton, he was schooled at Liskeard and placed with a Plymouth solicitor. The law disgusted him, so an aunt paid for Cheltenham Grammar School, where he published Tendrils in 1821.

At Pembroke College, Oxford, from 1823, he married Charlotte I'ans, a Cornishwoman twenty years older. He won the Newdigate Prize for a poem on Pompeii in 1827 and took orders in 1831. As vicar of Morwenstow from 1834, he restored church and parsonage, founded a school, held synods as rural dean, succoured shipwrecked sailors, and buried drowned bodies. His poems and essays drew on Cornish history and legend. Finest among them is the Quest of the San Graal; most famous, the Ballad of Trelawney. Tractarian in views, he died at Plymouth in 1875.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rochester:
Rochester is the oldest and smallest of the suffragan sees of Canterbury, founded by St Augustine in 604. Augustine consecrated St Justus as its first bishop. The diocese covered roughly western Kent, divided from the rest of the county by the Medway, though its bounds did not follow the river closely. Its cathedral, founded by King Ethelbert and dedicated to St Andrew, was served by secular priests and endowed with land called Priestfield.

After the Conquest, Bishop Gundulf began a new cathedral. He replaced secular chaplains with Benedictine monks, and enshrined St Paulinus in a silver shrine that drew pilgrims. His nave is the oldest in England, and the cathedral has a Norman crypt. Consecrated in 1130 amid a great fire, it gained a rebuilt choir and central tower from offerings at St William of Perth's tomb by 1343. The right to nominate bishops passed from Canterbury archbishops to the cathedral monks in 1148.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roger-bishop-:
Roger, Bishop of Worcester, was a loyal friend of St Thomas of Canterbury. Younger son of Robert, Earl of Gloucester, he was schooled with the future Henry II, ordained priest, and consecrated Bishop of Worcester by Thomas on 23 August 1163. Though sent to the pope with the king's appeal against Thomas, he took no active part in the embassy. He refused to join the bishops' appeal of 1166, earning the king's enmity.

When Thomas asked him to share his exile, Roger went without leave in 1167 after Henry refused permission. He boldly rebuked the king at Falaise in 1170, and a reconciliation followed. After Thomas's martyrdom, when England faced an interdict, Roger pleaded with the pope and won high esteem in England and at Rome. Alexander III called him and Bartholomew of Exeter the two great lights of the English Church. He died at Tours in 1179.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roger-of-wend:
Roger of Wendover was a Benedictine monk and the first of the great chroniclers of St Albans Abbey. His birth date is unknown, and he died in 1236. Probably a native of Wendover in Buckinghamshire, he was made prior of the Belvoir cell. Deposed from that office, he retired to St Albans, where he likely wrote his chronicle, the Flores Historiarum, running from Creation to 1235.

From 1202 the chronicle stands as an original and valuable authority, though Matthew Paris later reworked the whole in his Chronica Majora. Wendover shows less prejudice than Paris but also less colour. Where Paris generalizes about causes and anticipates the modern historian, Wendover simply discharges a chronicler's task. The Flores was edited for the English Historical Society in 1841 by Coxe in five volumes, starting at 447 for British history. Its most valuable part, 1154 to 1235, was re-edited by Hewlett for the Rolls Series in 1886-89.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roman-hindere:
Roman Hinderer, known in Chinese as Te, was a German Jesuit missionary and mapmaker in China. Born at Reiningen near Mulhausen in Alsace in 1668, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1688 in the German province and reached China in 1707. Emperor K'ang-hi personally asked him to join the great mapping work the Jesuits were carrying out under imperial orders. With de Mailla and Regis he mapped the provinces of Ho-nan, Kiang-nan, Che-kiang, and Fu-kien.

Hinderer was more than a man of science. For forty years he laboured as an apostle, winning substantial results by zeal and efficiency, and twice headed the mission as visitor. He earns special recognition for introducing and fostering among converts the devotion to the Sacred Heart. He died at Shang-ho in Kiang-nan in 1744.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-herbert:
Herbert of Derwentwater, whose birth date is unknown, died on 20 March 687. He was a seventh-century hermit living on the small island in Derwentwater that still bears his name. For years he was the friend and disciple of Cuthbert of Lindisfarne, and each year he visited him to seek guidance in the spiritual life. In 686, hearing Cuthbert was at Carlisle to give the veil to Queen Eormenburg, Herbert went to meet him there instead of at Lindisfarne.

After they had talked, Cuthbert told him they would never meet again in this world, for his own death was near. Weeping, Herbert begged that both might be admitted to heaven at the same time, and Cuthbert prayed and assured him the wish was granted. Herbert fell ill on returning to his hermitage and died on the very day Cuthbert died on Holy Island.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-ludger:
Ludger, missionary to the Frisians and Saxons and first bishop of Münster in Westphalia, was born at Zuilen near Utrecht about 744. He died on 26 March 809. His parents Thiadgrim and Liafburg were wealthy Frisians of noble line.

In 753 he saw Boniface, apostle of Germany, and the saint's later martyrdom left a deep mark on the boy. Sent to Gregory of Utrecht's school, he made good progress, and in 767 he went with Alubert to York, where he received the diaconate and studied under Alcuin. Ordained at Cologne in 777, he took charge of the missions of Ostergau in East Friesland, with Dokkum as his centre, and taught each autumn at Utrecht's cathedral school. After Widukind drove out the missionaries, Ludger escaped with his disciples and later visited Rome in 785.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santander:
Santander, a Spanish diocese suffragan of Burgos, takes its name not from Andrew, as the sound suggests, but from Hemeterius, one of the city's patron martyrs with Celedonius. Bounded by the Bay of Biscay, Vizcaya, Burgos, Palencia, León, and Oviedo, it covers most of Santander province with parts of Álava and Burgos. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia corrects a common error at the start.

In Roman times the town was Portus Victoriae, named for Agrippa's conquest from the Cantabrians, and in the reconquest it counted among the Asturias between the Saja and Miesa rivers. Alfonso I repeopled the land, Alfonso II founded the abbey of Hemeterius and Celedonius where the martyrs' heads were kept, and Alfonso VII made it collegiate. The entry follows the abbey's rise to a diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sarah-peter:
Sarah Peter, philanthropist, was born at Chillicothe, Ohio, on 10 May 1800 and died at Cincinnati on 6 February 1877. Her father Thomas Worthington governed Ohio from 1814 to 1818 and served in the United States Senate. She married Edward King, son of Rufus King, in 1816, and after his death married William Peter, British consul at Philadelphia, in 1844. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows wealth spent well.

At Philadelphia she founded the School of Design for Women on 2 December 1850. Back in Cincinnati she patronised art and charity and converted at Rome in March 1855 under Mgr Mermillod. She gave generously to the Good Shepherd Sisters, the Sisters of Mercy, and the Little Sisters of the Poor. In 1862 she nursed with sisters following Grant's army after Pittsburg Landing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schottenklost:
Schottenkloster, Scotch Monasteries, is the name for houses founded by Irish and Scottish missionaries on the continent. Above all it means the Scottish Benedictine monasteries of Germany, joined in the early thirteenth century into one congregation under the abbot of St James at Ratisbon. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows wandering monks from Ireland to the continent.

The earliest known Schottenkloster was Säckingen in Baden, founded by the Irishman Fridolin late in the fifth century, who is also said to have founded one at Constance. A century later Columbanus arrived with twelve companions and founded Annegray, Luxeuil, and Fontaines in France and Bobbio in Italy. His disciples and other Irish and Scottish missionaries then planted a long list of houses across France, Germany, Belgium, and Switzerland, St Gall chief among them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastian-bru:
Sebastian Brunner, a versatile and voluminous writer, was born in Vienna on 10 December 1814 and died there on 27 November 1893. Schooled by the city's Benedictines and trained in philosophy and theology at Vienna university, he was ordained priest in 1838 and taught for years in the university's philosophy faculty. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a fearless Catholic journalist.

Freiburg university honoured him with a doctorate in theology. In the revolutionary year 1848 he founded the Wiener Kirchenzeitung, editing it until 1865 and scourging with sharp satire the Josephinist bondage of the Church. Largely through his fearless championship, which more than once clashed with the authorities, Austria's Church breathes more freely today. He also wrote ascetical books, many sermon volumes, a life of Clemens Hofbauer, and keen travel books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shrine-of-oos:
Oostacker, a hamlet two miles from Ghent in East Flanders, gives its name to a shrine of the Virgin and a place of pilgrimage for Belgium, Holland, and northern France. Its pilgrimage origin is recent, dating from 1873. In 1871 the Marquise de Calonne de Courtebourne had built an aquarium shaped as an artificial grotto in her park. On a visit, the parish priest suggested setting a statue of Our Lady of Lourdes among the rocks.

For two years the grotto stayed a mere aquarium, but the family fell into the habit of pausing there for a Hail Mary. A public blessing of the statue on 23 June 1873 drew nearly the whole village. Flemish peasants asked leave to come often, and Sunday afternoons soon failed to hold the throngs. The park was thrown open, a large Gothic church rose with its cornerstone laid in 1875, and the shrine came to count about 450 organized pilgrimages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-george-bo:
George Bowyer, baronet, writer on jurisprudence and defender of the Holy See, was born at Radley House, Berkshire, on 8 October 1811 and died in London on 7 June 1883. His family had settled at Denham Court early in the 1600s, and his grandfather fought in Howe's victory off Ushant in 1794. Meant for the army, Bowyer left Woolwich for law, entering the Middle Temple in 1836 and reaching the Bar in 1839. Oxford made him an honorary master of arts five days later.

He practiced as an equity draftsman while writing steadily. The English Constitution of 1841 and Commentaries on the Civil Law of 1844 won him Oxford's highest honor, and his Commentaries on Universal Public Law of 1854 stands as his greatest book. Converted about 1850, he sat for Dundalk from 1852 to 1868. In Parliament he denounced the spoliation of the pope's temporal lands and the Italian revolutionaries' deeds. He then sat for Wexford from 1874 to 1880 as a Home Ruler.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-slander:
Slander means attributing to another a fault of which the speaker knows him innocent. It carries a double malice: damage unjustly done to a neighbour's good name, and lying as well. Theologians note the offence against truth alone may not be grave, yet it will often be wise to mention it in confession, so the extent and method of reparation can be settled.

Slander wounds a neighbour's right to his reputation, and moralists hold it is not specifically distinct from detraction. The difference is that real misdeeds may sometimes lawfully be exposed, while no one may ever be charged with what he has not done. A lie is evil by nature, and no cause can ever justify it. Slander breaks commutative justice, so the slanderer must retract his false statement and compensate his victim for losses the false charge foreseeably caused.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-speyer:
Speyer was a Bavarian diocese whose city grew from the Roman stronghold of Noviomagus on the left bank of the Rhine, in the land of the Nemetes tribe. This entry follows the place from a Roman municipality, wiped out by Attila in 451, to the new city of Spira that rose from its ashes, with Christianity arriving in Roman times.

Its first bishop, Jesse, appears in the synod acts of Sardica in 343 and Cologne in 346. Though his historicity is uncertain. Bishop Hilderich at Paris in 614 begins an unbroken succession. Made suffragan to Mainz in 748, Speyer laid the first stone of its Romanesque cathedral of Our Lady in 1030, planned as the mausoleum of the Salian emperors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anselm-of-:
St. Anselm of Lucca the Younger was born at Mantua about 1036. He died in the same city on 18 March 1086. This entry follows the nephew of Anselm of Lucca the Elder, who became Pope Alexander II in 1061. In 1071 Alexander named the younger Anselm bishop of Lucca. He sent him to Germany for investiture from Henry IV.

Anselm travelled there, but he shrank from receiving the signs of spiritual power from a temporal ruler. He returned without investiture. Gregory VII, Alexander's successor, also named him bishop in 1073. He advised Anselm not to take ring and crosier from Henry. Anselm took investiture anyway, then felt such remorse that he resigned and entered the Benedictine monastery of Padilirone near Mantua. Gregory ordered him back to Lucca, and he returned reluctantly, still living as a monk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-christophe:
St. Christopher, from Greek christos, Christ, and pherein, to bear, in Latin Christophorus, Christbearer, was a third-century martyr. This entry follows one of the most popular saints in East and West, about whose life and death little is certain. The legend says a heathen king in Canaan or Arabia, through his wife's prayers to the Blessed Virgin, had a son. He called him Offerus, or Offro, Adokimus, or Reprebus, and dedicated him to Machmet and Apollo.

In time, Offerus grew to extraordinary size and strength, and resolved to serve only the strongest and bravest. He served in turn a mighty king and Satan. Both lacked courage: the former dreaded even the devil's name, the latter a roadside cross. For a time his search for a new master was in vain. At last a hermit, perhaps Babylas, told him to offer his almighty service to Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-francis-xa:
Francis Xavier, co-founder of the Jesuits, carried the Gospel from Paris classrooms to the coasts of Asia in a decade of travel. Born at Xavier castle in Navarre on 7 April 1506, he studied at Sainte-Barbe in Paris, where he befriended Pierre Favre and fell under Ignatius Loyola's influence. With five others they made the Montmartre vow of 15 August 1534. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death near China to 2 December 1552.

After Venice hospital work and ordination, he sailed east, preaching nearly three years in western India and Ceylon despite persecuting petty kings and scandalous Portuguese soldiers. Malacca and the Moluccas followed, then Japan, learned from a Japanese named Anger at Malacca in 1547. Whether he ever landed in the Philippines remains unproved, the entry warns, despite his canonization bull's claim.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-isidore-th:
Isidore the Labourer, Spanish farmhand of Madrid, prayed before work and, legend says, had angels plough beside him. Born near Madrid about 1070, he served Juan de Vargas on a farm outside the city. Each morning before labour he heard Mass at a Madrid church. Fellow workers complained he was always late, but his master found him at prayer while an angel ploughed. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Madrid to 15 May 1130.

On another day his master saw an angel ploughing on either side of him, so his work equalled three men's. He is also said to have raised his master's dead daughter and to have struck fresh water from dry earth for his master's thirst. His wife Maria Torribia, honoured as Maria della Cabeza, is carried in procession in drought, head and all. The entry joins field labour to wonder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-james-the-:
James the Greater, son of Zebedee and Salome, brother of John, stands among the apostles as fisherman turned martyr. His name, Hebrew Yakob, was a favourite among later Jews. Called Greater to set him apart from James the Less, probably the shorter man, he came of means: Zebedee fished Galilee with hired men, and Salome ministered to Christ from her substance. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 traces him from Bethsaida's boats to Jerusalem's sword.

With his mother he once sought thrones at Christ's right and left, still ignorant of a spiritual kingdom. Tradition, given serious weight in the entry, says he preached in Spain, returned to Judea, and died by Herod Agrippa I's order at Passover in 44. His body was miraculously carried to Iria Flavia, then to Compostela, which became a famous pilgrimage town through the Middle Ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-fishe:
John Fisher, cardinal bishop of Rochester, died for denying Henry VIII's supremacy over the Church. Born at Beverley in Yorkshire in 1459, or 1469, eldest son of merchant Robert Fisher and Agnes, he studied at his town's collegiate school, then at Michaelhouse, Cambridge, from 1484. He took his B.A. in 1487, M.A. in 1491, fellowship, and the vicarage of Northallerton. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 22 June 1535.

In 1494 he resigned his benefice to serve as university proctor, became Master of Michaelhouse three years later, and chaplain and confessor to Lady Margaret Beaufort, Henry VII's mother. As vice-chancellor in 1501 he guided her foundations of St. John's and Christ's Colleges and two Lady Margaret divinity chairs. Refusing the supremacy oath, he was sent to the Tower on 26 April 1534, attainted, and stripped of goods and see. Made cardinal in prison, he was tried at Westminster on 17 June for treason and beheaded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-the-a:
John the Almsgiver, patriarch of Alexandria from 606 to 616, called the poor his lords and masters. Born at Amathus in Cyprus about 550, he was son of Epiphanius, the island's governor, of noble descent. He married young and had children, but wife and children soon died, and he entered religious life. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death in Cyprus to 616.

When Patriarch Theodorus died, Alexandrians begged Emperor Phocas to appoint John, and Phocas did. In youth John had dreamed of a beautiful maiden with an olive garland, calling herself Compassion, eldest daughter of the Great King. That vision marked him deeply. Given scope for benevolence, he listed several thousand needy persons under his special care and became famous across the East for munificent liberality. The poor, he said, held mighty influence at God's court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-macrina-th:
Macrina the Elder, grandmother of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, fled Diocletian's persecution and schooled a family of fathers. Her life is known mainly through her grandchildren: Basil's letters, Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Macrina the Younger, and Gregory of Nazianzus's panegyric on Basil. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 places her home at Neocaesarea in Pontus.

Mother of the elder Basil, father of Basil, Gregory, and other known children including Macrina the Younger, she knew in childhood Gregory Thaumaturgus, first bishop of her native town. That venerable doctor, who won Neocaesarea almost wholly for Christianity, died between 270 and 275, so Macrina must have been born before 270. Under Diocletian she fled her town with her husband, whose name is unknown, enduring many privations as a confessor of the faith.

Macrina the Younger, eldest child of Basil and Emmelia, shaped her brothers' minds, including Gregory of Nyssa's. Born about 330, granddaughter of Macrina the Elder and sister of Cappadocian Fathers Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, she received excellent training, based more on Bible study than profane literature. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death to 379.

At twelve her father arranged her marriage to a young advocate of excellent family, but her betrothed died suddenly soon after, and Macrina resolved on perpetual virginity and Christian perfection. She greatly influenced her younger brothers' religious training, especially Peter, later bishop of Sebaste, and through her Gregory received his greatest intellectual stimulation. On their father's death, Basil took her and their mother to the family's Pontus estate on the Iris River, where her community life unfolded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-melania-th:
Melania the Younger, a Roman heiress of the great Valerii family, gave away a vast fortune to live as a nun. Born at Rome about 383 and married at thirteen to her kinsman Pinianus, she lost two children young and then won her husband's consent to a celibate life. Step by step the couple shed their wealth and turned to prayer and charity.

Fleeing the Visigothic invasions, they spent two years near Messina, seven years in Africa beside Augustine and Alypius, and then sailed for Palestine in 417. There she founded a nunnery, which she ruled, while Pinianus led a monks' house nearby. She died at Jerusalem on 31 December 439. The entry follows a fortune transformed into monasteries, pilgrimage, and care for the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-omer:
Omer, bishop of Thérouanne in seventh-century Gaul, restored Christianity among the Morini, where almost every trace of faith had vanished. Born near the close of the sixth century at Guldendal in Switzerland, he entered Luxeuil with his father about 615 and studied Scripture under Eustachius. King Dagobert sought a bishop for Thérouanne, and Omer was consecrated in 637.

Monks from Luxeuil, including Bertin, Mommolin, and Ebertran, joined his mission, and the true religion soon stood firm again. About 654 he founded the abbey of St Peter at Sithiu, now St Bertin's, and later raised the church of Our Lady there. He died about 670. The entry follows a missionary bishop rebuilding a diocese from near ruin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-peter-clav:
Peter Claver, a Catalan Jesuit, spent forty-four years as apostle to enslaved Africans landed at Cartagena. Born at Verdú in 1581 to a farmer, he studied at Barcelona and entered the Jesuit novitiate at Tarragona at twenty. At Majorca in 1605 the porter Alphonsus Rodriguez urged him toward the Spanish American missions, and in 1610 he landed at Cartagena.

Cartagena was the chief slave market of the New World, receiving a thousand captives at a time from Guinea, Congo, and Angola. Claver met each ship, carried food and medicine to the holds, baptised, catechised, and defended the newcomers against brutal masters. He died on 8 September 1654, after a lifetime spent among the slave ships and hospitals of Cartagena. The entry honours a ministry of mercy inside a cruel trade.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-peter-four:
Peter Fourier, the good father of Mattaincourt, rebuilt a corrupt Lorraine parish and founded free schools for poor girls. Born at Mirecourt on 30 November 1565, he studied at Pont-à-Mousson, became a Canon Regular at Chaumousey, and was ordained in 1589. He knew the Summa of Thomas by heart and mastered patristic theology.

Made parish priest of Mattaincourt in 1597, he restored religion by prayer, teaching, and example. He set up a mutual help bank for the fallen poor. He formed sodalities for men, women, and girls. To make his work last, he founded in 1598 the Congregation of Notre-Dame, whose sisters teach poor girls without charge. He died at Gray on 9 December 1640, beloved as a pastor and educator.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-robert-of-:
Robert of Newminster, a Cistercian abbot, planted the order in the north of England. Born in Craven, Yorkshire, probably at Gargrave, he studied at Paris, where he is said to have written a commentary on the Psalms. He served as parish priest at Gargrave, became a Benedictine at Whitby, and joined the founders of Fountains with his abbot's leave.

About 1138 he led the first colony from Fountains and founded Newminster near Ralph de Merlay's castle at Morpeth. Under his abbacy three daughter houses rose: Pipewell in 1143, Roche in 1147, and Sawley in 1148. Capgrave's tale of a misconduct charge answered before Bernard is doubted by the entry. His tomb at Newminster drew pilgrims, and his feast falls on 7 June. He died on 7 June 1159.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-simeon-sty:
Simeon Stylites the Elder, the first and most famous pillar hermit, spent decades atop a column near Antioch. Born about 388 at Sisan near Syria's northern border, he began as a shepherd boy and entered a monastery before sixteen. His austerity seemed so extreme that his brethren judged him unsuited to community life.

Forced to leave, he shut himself in a hut at Tell-Neschin for three years, passing whole Lents without food or drink. That became his regular practice, joined to other mortifications. At last he took up life atop a pillar, the strange asceticism that gave the stylites their name. The entry rests on very reliable first-hand evidence, which modern critics no longer dispute.

Simeon Stylites the Younger, a pillar hermit of Antioch, lived atop columns for sixty-eight years. Born at Antioch in 521 to an Edessan father and Martha, later revered as a saint, he was drawn very young to austerity. He joined ascetics within the enclosure of another pillar hermit, John, who directed them spiritually.

Still a boy, he had a pillar raised for himself close to John's, and he wrote that he already lived on a pillar when he lost his first teeth. He moved pillars several times, and on one descent the patriarch of Antioch and the bishop of Seleucia ordained him deacon. For eight years until John's death he stayed near his master's column, close enough to converse. He died at Antioch on 24 May 597.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vincent-fe:
Vincent Ferrer, a Dominican missionary, preached repentance across Europe during the Western Schism. Born at Valencia on 23 January 1350, fourth child of William Ferrer and Constantia Miguel, he completed philosophy at fourteen. In 1367 he entered the Dominicans, studied at Barcelona, and taught philosophy at Lérida in 1370.

Returning to Barcelona's school of Arabic and Hebrew studies in 1373, he foretold during famine that wheat ships were near, and they came. He preached through Spain, France, Italy, and Brittany, drawing vast crowds and many conversions, and worked to end the Schism, first backing Benedict XIII, then urging his resignation. He died at Vannes in Brittany on 5 April 1419, famed as the Angel of the Apocalypse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-wendelin-o:
Wendelin of Trier, a herdsman saint of the Saarland, is known only through biographies written after 1417. Their narrative calls him son of a Scottish king who secretly left home on pilgrimage to Rome. Returning, he settled as a hermit in Westrich in the diocese of Trier. When a great landowner blamed his idle life, he served as herdsman.

A miracle then obliged the lord to let him return to solitude, and he gathered a company of hermits from which the Benedictine abbey of Tholey sprang. Later legends call him abbot about 597, though Tholey seems founded as a collegiate body about 630. Buried in his cell, with a chapel over his grave, he drew the town of St Wendel around him. His intercession was sought in pestilence and cattle disease. He died probably in 617.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stabat-mater:
The Stabat Mater, opening words of two companion hymns, mourns Mary at the Cross and rejoices with her at the Manger. The Dolorosa, in liturgical use, and the Speciosa, not in use, celebrate her emotions at Calvary and Bethlehem respectively, differentiated by their third words. The Speciosa holds thirteen double stanzas of six lines, the Dolorosa ten.

Otherwise the hymns run in quite perfect parallelism of phrase, as their first stanzas show: dolorosa beside the weeping cross, speciosa beside the joyful hay. The Dolorosa was known to all classes by the late fourteenth century, sung by Flagellants in 1388 and by the Albati of Provence about 1399. The entry weighs which hymn came first, surveys authorship claims from Jacopone da Todi onward, and traces liturgical use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-steinamanger:
Steinamanger, in Hungarian Szombathely, is a diocese in Hungary, suffragan of Gran, founded in 1777 under Maria Theresa. Originally Colonia Claudia Sabaria, capital of Pannonia in Roman times, it was laid waste by Huns in 445. In the ninth century, already an episcopal see before the Hun invasion, it fell under Salzburg's archbishop, and King Stephen is said to have given it to Veszprém's bishop.

The see was reconstituted in 1777 at the expense of Agram and Veszprém. It covers Vas and Zala counties and land along the Mura. Its first bishop, John Szily, from 1777 to 1799, built the episcopal residence and cathedral. His successor, Cardinal Franz Herzen, served as Joseph II's envoy to the Holy See. The abbey of Jaák, a chief Romanesque edifice of Hungary, lies in the diocese, whose chapter sprang from Vasvár's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephan-jakob:
Stephan Jakob Neher, a church historian of Württemberg, pioneered ecclesiastical geography and statistics. Born at Ebnat on 24 July 1829 to country people of that village in the Neresheim district, he studied theology at Tübingen after the gymnasium. Ordained, he served as pastor of Dorfmerkingen, then Zübingen, and finally Nordhausen in the Ellwangen district.

Through life he pursued intellectual work, chiefly canon law and church history, above all ecclesiastical geography and statistics, where he achieved great results. His first considerable work, of 1861, treated the privileged altar. The first volume of his great planned work, Kirchliche Geographie und Statistik, appeared in 1864, the three volumes running to 1868, for its day indispensable to historians. He died at Nordhausen on 7 October 1902.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephan-ladis:
Stephan Ladislaus Endlicher, an Austrian botanist, linguist, and historian, ordered plant knowledge and Chinese grammar alike. Born at Pressburg on 24 June 1804 to a physician, he studied philosophy at Pest and Vienna and theology at Vienna from 1823 to 1826, without entering the priesthood. From 1826 at Pressburg he turned to languages, above all Chinese, shown in his Anfangsgründe der chinesischen Grammatik of 1844 and his Atlas of China of 1843.

Urged by his father, he took up botany in 1826, giving all spare time to it during 1828 to 1836, when he kept the Imperial Library's manuscripts at Vienna. As librarian he issued works on classical, German, and Hungarian letters and the manuscript catalogue's first volume in 1836. In 1836 he became curator of the botanical department, and in 1840 professor of botany at Vienna and director of its botanical garden. He died at Vienna on 28 March 1849.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-lochn:
Stephen Lochner, a Cologne painter of the fifteenth century, is famed for the Adoration of the Magi triptych. Born at Meersburg on Lake Constance, date unknown, he died at Cologne in 1452. He reached Cologne about 1430 from Meersburg. His style recalls Master Wilhelm of the fourteenth century more than his Cologne successors, who show Dutch influence, and he brought from Upper Germany the vivid realism of Moser and Witz.

His chief work, meant for the town hall altar, moved in 1810 to the cathedral's choir chapel. Its brilliant triptych shows in the centre, almost life size, the Magi worshipping, with Ursula and her companions on one side panel and Gereon with his warriors on the other. In the middle sits the Madonna with the Child, humble yet majestic, in traditional ideal garments, a miraculous star above and angels overhead. Kings pray and offer beside the throne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-suger:
Suger, abbot of St-Denis, statesman, and historian, was born near St-Denis about 1081 and died there on 13 January 1151. Offered to the monastery about 1091, he studied beside the future Louis VI, and served as secretary to Abbot Adam from 1106. He held provostships at Berneval and Toury before missions took him to the courts of Gelasius II and Callistus II.

Elected abbot during his Roman stay of 1121 to 1122, he attended the First Lateran Council in 1123 and reformed his monastery from 1127, while advising Louis VI and Louis VII. As regent during Louis VII's crusade absence from 1147 to 1149, he ruled so well that the king named him Father of the Country. His lives of Louis VI and Louis VII remain key sources for the period.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-suitbert-baeu:
Suitbert Baeumer, born at Leuchtenberg near Kaiserswerth on 28 March 1845, was a historian of the Breviary and a leading patrologist of the nineteenth century. He studied at Bonn and Tübingen, entered the new Benedictine abbey of Beuron in 1865, and was ordained priest in 1869.

Years at Maredsous in Belgium and Erdington in England followed, before his return to Beuron in 1890. As critical adviser to the Tournai printers Desclée, he shaped editions of the Missal, Breviary, Ritual, and Pontifical. His essays covered the Stowe Missal, the Micrologus, and the Gelasian Sacramentary, while his classic History of the Breviary appeared at Freiburg in 1895. He died there in 1894.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-supernatural-:
The supernatural order is the whole of effects that exceed created powers, freely produced by God to lift rational creatures toward a God-like life and destiny. This entry shows how the phrase shifts with its opposite, the natural order. Readers who count nature as matter alone, or as mere mechanism, will call spiritual facts and free acts supernatural, and the entry allows that usage with a warning.

It must not be used to hide a denial of the supernatural in the strict sense. Theologians also speak of accidentally supernatural ways of producing natural effects, and of relatively supernatural endowments like freedom from death and suffering. The strict sense starts from nature in its widest reach, including man's highest gifts, and sets the supernatural beyond it all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sylvester-jos:
Sylvester Joseph Hunter, born at Bath on 13 September 1829, was an English Jesuit priest and educator. His father, a Protestant minister, won wider fame as an antiquarian and Shakespeare critic. The family moved to London in 1833, when the elder Hunter became Keeper of the Public Records, and the boy entered St Paul's School in 1840.

A Cambridge scholarship followed in 1848, where he shone in mathematics and took eighth place as wrangler in 1852. Law studies at Lincoln's Inn and two praised legal textbooks came next, before his reception into the Church in 1857. He joined the Jesuits in 1861, was ordained in 1870, and is best known for his three-volume Outlines of Dogmatic Theology of 1894.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teutonic-orde:
The Teutonic Order was a medieval military order modelled on the Hospitallers of St John. It changed residence as often as they did. Acre in Palestine was its cradle from 1190 to 1309. Marienburg in Prussia centred its military principality from 1309 to 1525. Mergentheim in Franconia held its diminished lands from 1524 to 1805. Finally Vienna holds it as a purely hospital order. A Protestant branch also subsists in Holland.

A Teutonic hospital for German pilgrims stood in the Latin Kingdom, with a church to the Blessed Virgin, still the order's patroness, giving members the name Mariani. Saladin's conquest of Jerusalem in 1187 broke it up. In 1190, under Acre's besieged walls, pilgrims from Bremen and Lübeck, with the Duke of Holstein, raised a tent hospital from ships' sails. After Acre's capture the hospital stood permanently, with knights for pilgrims' defence, and the Order took its place beside Hospitallers and Templars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-apostlesh:
A league of prayer joined to the Heart of Jesus is described here, founded at Vals in France in 1844 by Francis Gautrelet. Its spread owed much to Henry Ramière, a Jesuit. In 1861 he reshaped it for parishes and Catholic institutions and made it widely known through his book on the subject, translated into many languages.

Statutes approved by Pius IX in 1879 and revised under Leo XIII in 1896 set out its nature and order. Members offered each day's prayers, works, and sufferings, said a decade of beads for the pope's monthly intentions, and joined a monthly hour of prayer. Three grades of membership, local centres, and a worldwide network made it one of the most popular devotions of its age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-benedicti:
Monks living under the Rule of Saint Benedict, commonly called black monks, fill this vast survey, the longest in this stretch of the encyclopedia. Unlike other orders, the Benedictines form no single body under one general; each monastery keeps its own abbot, linked in congregations rather than ruled from a centre. That loose structure shapes everything that follows.

Six sections carry the story: history from Benedict's Monte Cassino to medieval expansion, lay brothers, oblates, confraters, and nuns, then the order's influence on learning, farming, art, and missions. Present condition, monks of special distinction, and daughter foundations close the account. It is less a sketch than a library in miniature on Western monastic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-carmelite:
Mendicant friars of Our Lady of Mount Carmel trace their story here, from disputed origins to worldwide spread. The order claims Elias and Eliseus as founders, while modern historians, starting with Baronius, deny its existence before the second half of the twelfth century. Sons of the Prophets under Samuel offer a distant parallel, living in community under superiors such as Elias on Carmel.

Later hermits on the holy mountain took a rule, migrated westward, and won papal approval. Reforms, the Teresian branch, missions, and the order's Marian devotion follow in turn. Present houses, saints, and scholars close an entry that balances legend against documents with unusual fairness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-carthusia:
Silence, solitude, and the charterhouse give this entry its character, tracing an order named from the French chartreuse, through Latin cartusia. Saint Bruno's foundation stands behind it, and eight heads organise the survey: rule, daily life, organisation, development, present state, distinguished members, the English province, and Carthusian nuns.

Guibert of Nogent and Peter the Venerable supply the earliest pictures. Thirteen monks lived on a ridge, each in his own cell to work, sleep, and eat, meeting for Sunday bread and vegetables cooked alone. Later centuries added provinces, printed books, and martyrs. For readers drawn to contemplative life, few entries capture its rigour so concretely.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-hon-georg:
Youngest son of the second Earl Spencer, George Spencer turned from Anglican rector to Passionist missionary, and this entry follows his striking path. Born at the Admiralty, London, in 1799, he went from Eton to Trinity College, Cambridge, took Anglican orders in 1824, served as chaplain to Bishop Blomfield, and became rector of Brington.

Conversion came in 1830. Rome ordained him priest in 1832, and he returned burning to win England back, begging prayers across the Continent for that cause. West Bromwich, where he built a church at his own cost, Oscott, and finally the Passionist novitiate in 1846 fill his later years. He died at Carstairs in 1864, an apostle of England's conversion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-last-supp:
Christ's final meal with his disciples, on the eve of his Passion, when he instituted the Holy Eucharist, is examined here. Evangelists and critics agree on the week: supper on Thursday, death on Friday, rising on Sunday. The month's day divides opinion, since synoptic Gospels and John seem to differ on whether the meal fell on the 14th of Nisan.

Matthew, Mark, and Luke place it on the first day of unleavened bread, when the pasch was killed. Critics who reject one account or both face Christians who hold Scripture free of contradiction, and the entry weighs harmonies that reconcile the texts. Place, guests, and institution words round out a careful Gospel study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-old-chapt:
English Catholics without bishops found a governing body in the Old Chapter, whose origin this entry dates to 1623. After more than half a century without episcopal government, William Bishop became vicar apostolic, surviving under a year yet organising archdeacons and rural deans across the country. His scheme lasted with little change until the hierarchy returned in 1850.

A chapter of twenty-four canons, with John Colleton as dean, formed its core. Canon law knows no chapter without a diocese, and Rome never formally recognised it, yet never censured it either, despite its wide claims. Existing with the Apostolic See knowing and silent, it steered English Catholic life through penal times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-primer:
Laity's prayer book from the thirteenth to the sixteenth century is the subject here, under the common English name primer. Contents varied greatly from book to book, yet certain elements almost never failed to appear. Chief among them stood the Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary, lavishly adorned with miniatures and ornament. 

Liturgical centres shaped the Office differently. Rome, Salisbury, York, and Paris each left its mark, so title pages often named the use followed, such as Romanum or Sarum. Psalms at Prime differed by use, and the entry traces editions, illustrations, and the Primer's slow eclipse by later prayer books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-rambler:
English Catholic thought in the nineteenth century found a sharp voice in the Rambler, a periodical not to be confused with Johnson's journal of a century earlier. Launched on 1 January 1848 as a weekly review covering home and foreign letters, politics, science, and art, it aimed to join hearty acceptance of Catholic dogma with free enquiry and discussion.

Lord Acton, Richard Simpson, and briefly Newman himself steered a convert phase opposed to the extreme ultramontanism of Ward and Manning. Friction with the new English hierarchy grew as the journal pressed its line. Its final number under the old name, May 1862, announced enlargement, closing a stormy chapter in Victorian Catholic journalism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-besc:
Jesuit Theodore Beschefer spent his best years in Canada's early missions. Born at Châlons-sur-Marne on 25 May 1630, he died at Reims on 4 February 1711. He joined the Society at Nancy in 1647 and learned philosophy and theology at Pont-à-Mousson. He taught letters and rhetoric for seven years in France, then sailed to Canada in 1665 after a third year of trial.

Quebec kept him for three years. A mission to the Mohawks and the Dutch at Albany turned back when Indian war broke out. He worked among the Iroquois in 1670 and 1671, came back to Quebec in 1672, and led the Canadian missions from 1680 to 1687. Quebec College then made him prefect of classes, and the Ursulines praised his wise counsel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-andrew:
Thomas Andrew Becker, sixth Bishop of Savannah, was born at Pittsburgh in 1832 to German Protestant parents and became a Catholic in early manhood. He trained for the priesthood at the College of Propaganda in Rome and was ordained in 1859. After parish work in West Virginia and teaching at Mount St. Mary's College, he served as secretary to Archbishop Spalding.

In 1868 he became the first Bishop of Wilmington, Delaware, and in 1886 he moved to Savannah, where he served until his death in 1899. Known as a skilled linguist, he acted as a secretary of the Fourth Plenary Council of Baltimore and wrote often for Catholic reviews. His will left funds to educate deserving young men, on condition they abstain from drink.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-bourch:
Thomas Bourchier, cardinal and Archbishop of Canterbury, was born in 1406, third son of the Earl of Eu and a Plantagenet mother. Oxford-educated, he rose fast through church preferment, becoming Bishop of Worcester in 1434, then Archbishop of Canterbury in 1454 after a contested move from Ely. His high birth opened doors, though no record shows him as a notable scholar.

As archbishop he crowned Edward IV in 1461 and his queen Elizabeth Woodville in 1465, and received the cardinal's hat in 1473. In 1483 he coaxed the widowed queen from sanctuary to hand over her younger son, pledging his honour for the boy's safety, yet within weeks he crowned Richard III. He crowned Henry VII in 1485 and died the next year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-dempst:
Thomas Dempster, a Scottish scholar born at Cliftbog in 1579, lived a restless life across the universities of Europe before dying at Bologna in 1625. The son of the Baron of Muresk, he studied at Turriff and Aberdeen, then moved through Cambridge, Paris, Louvain, Rome, Tournai and Douai, helped at points by papal and royal funds. At seventeen he held a professorial chair at the College de Navarre in Paris.

Later posts took him to Toulouse, Nimes and other schools, often cut short by quarrels and lawsuits. His learning was wide, his temper quarrelsome, and his books on antiquity and law kept his name in circulation. The entry follows his wanderings in detail, showing a brilliant scholar who could never settle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-ebendo:
Thomas Ebendorfer, a German chronicler and statesman born at Haselbach in 1385, spent his life at the University of Vienna, where he died in 1464. He took his arts degree in 1412, taught Aristotle and Latin grammar, and became master of theology in 1428 and dean of the theological faculty. Three times he served as rector of the university.

Ebendorfer defended Vienna's rights with zeal, represented the university at the Council of Basle, and met the Hussites at Prague as a council delegate. From 1440 to 1444 he acted as ambassador for Emperor Frederick III, but his defence of the university cost him the emperor's favour. His chronicles remain a key source for fifteenth-century Austria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-falkne:
Thomas Falkner, a Jesuit missionary born in 1707, spent more than thirty years among the peoples of Patagonia. The son of a Manchester apothecary, he trained in medicine under Richard Mead and sailed as a ship's surgeon about 1731 on a vessel trading slaves to Buenos Aires. Left ill there, he recovered in the care of the Jesuit superior and entered the Society in 1732.

After study at Cordoba he worked among the Puelches and, from about 1740, helped Father Strobel's mission to the Patagonian Indians at Cape San Antonio. His medical and mechanical skill won him influence with the Indians. Expelled with the Jesuits in 1768, he returned to England, joined the English province, and served as chaplain at Spetchley until his death in 1784.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-franci:
Thomas Francis Meagher, soldier and politician, was born at Waterford in 1823 and drowned in the Missouri River in 1867. Educated at Clongowes and Stonyhurst, he threw his oratory behind O'Connell's Repeal cause, then broke with constitutional agitation for the Young Irelanders. Tried for treason after the abortive rising of 1848, he was sentenced to hang, saw the sentence commuted to transportation, and reached Tasmania in 1849.

Escaping in 1852, he landed in New York, studied law, was admitted to the bar in 1855, and founded the Irish News. During the Civil War he raised and led the Irish Brigade for the Union, and after the war he became Territorial Secretary of Montana in July 1865. While travelling on that office's business, he went overboard from a steamer into the Missouri at night and drowned; his body was never found.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-ignati:
Thomas Ignatius Maria Forster, astronomer and naturalist, was born in London in 1789 and died at Brussels in 1860. His father, a noted botanist and follower of Rousseau, left his literary schooling thin, but Forster taught himself many modern languages. He compiled a Journal of the Weather in 1805 and took up phrenology after reading Gall, then turned to astronomy when the comet of 1811 caught his eye.

On 3 July 1819 he found a new comet of his own. He studied law at Cambridge, switched to medicine, and took a medical degree the same year. Travel on the Continent led to his Perennial Calendar in 1824 and to his conversion to Catholicism. Back in England he joined the Royal Astronomical Society and helped found a short-lived meteorological society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-morton:
Thomas Morton Harper, priest, philosopher and preacher, was born in London in 1821 to Anglican parents and died in 1893. Educated at St. Paul's School and Queen's College, Oxford, he served five years as an Anglican curate, first at Barnstaple and then at a proprietary chapel in Pimlico. Clashes with his bishops over ritual pushed him steadily toward Rome.

The spur came oddly from reading an attack on the Jesuits, whose weak argument convinced him instead of the order's case. Received into the Catholic Church in 1852, he entered the Society of Jesus that October, studied in Belgium, Wales, Rome and Louvain, and was ordained priest. His Metaphysics of the School, in three volumes from 1879 to 1884, is his chief philosophical work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-murner:
Thomas Murner, the greatest German satirist of the sixteenth century, was born at Oberehnheim, Alsace, in 1475 and died there in 1537. His parents settled at Strasburg in 1481, and at sixteen he joined the Franciscans. He studied theology at Paris, philosophy and mathematics at Cracow, and law at Freiburg, taking a doctorate in theology in 1506 and in laws at Basle in 1518.

From 1519 he fought Luther in print, translating Henry VIII's book on the sacraments into German and visiting England in 1523. His satires, above all Von dem grossen Lutherischen Narren, turned the whole reform movement into a single Great Fool, with the new church as Luther's daughter Adelheid. Driven from Strasburg by rebels, he kept writing until his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-netter:
Thomas Netter, theologian and controversialist, was born at Saffron Walden about 1375 and died at Rouen in 1430. Called Waldensis from his birthplace, he joined the Carmelites in London, studied at Oxford, and taught across philosophy, Scripture, canon law and theology. His public career began in 1409, when he was sent to the Council of Pisa.

Back in England he took a leading part against Wycliffites and Lollards. He helped at the trials of William Taylor in 1410, Sir John Oldcastle in 1413 and William White in 1428, and preached at St. Paul's Cross. As confessor to Henry V he rose to provincial of his order. His Doctrinale, printed in 1523, defends Catholic doctrine and ritual against the Lollards at length.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-of-dov:
Thomas of Dover, martyr, died on 2 or 5 August 1295, when French raiders sacked Dover and attacked the Benedictine priory of St. Martin. All the monks fled except one old and infirm brother, Thomas Hales, whom sailors found in the dormitory. He refused to reveal where the church treasures were hidden, and they killed him for it.

Miracles were soon reported at his relics, and pilgrims honoured him as a martyr at the black monks' house under Dover Castle. Richard II, at his mother's urging, asked the pope to canonize Thomas, and an inquiry opened in 1382, though nothing more followed. Locally he was long treated as a saint, with an altar at Dover Priory endowed in 1500.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-vincen:
Thomas Vincent Faustus Sadler, a Benedictine born in 1604, spent his life editing and translating books of devotion, dying at Dieulward, Flanders, in January 1681. Received into the Church at seventeen by his uncle Dom Walter Sadler, he joined the Benedictines at Dieulward and was professed in 1622. Little is known of his missionary work, though he probably served the Sheldons of Weston and the Tichbornes in Hampshire as chaplain before working for years in London.

He edited spiritual books, often with Dom Anselm Crowther, signing himself T.V. His chief works include The Christian Pilgrim of 1652 and Jesus, Maria, Joseph of 1657. His Daily Exercise of the Devout Rosarists later grew into the well-known Daily Exercise of the Devout Christian. He also translated Bona's Guide to Heaven and Lallemant's Holy Desires of Death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tobias-lohner:
Tobias Lohner, a Jesuit born at Neuotting in 1619, became a noted preacher and a prolific writer on practical theology. He entered the Society at Landsberg in August 1637 and taught classics in his early years. At Dillingen he held chairs in philosophy for seven years, speculative theology for four, and moral theology thereafter. He also served as rector at Lucerne and Dillingen and as master of novices.

His sermons won him a name as a great preacher, but his books secured his lasting fame. They cover asceticism and moral theology in Latin and German. Chief among them is his four-volume Instructissima Bibliotheca Manualis Concionatoria from 1681, with practical instructions on the Mass, the divine office, apostolic life and the duties of pastors. He died in May 1697.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tomb-of-st-pe:
The Tomb of St. Peter treats a puzzle at the heart of early Christian Rome: where the bodies of Peter and Paul first lay, and how they reached their present tombs. No one doubts that they now rest in the Vatican and on the Ostian Way, but a third tomb at the catacombs of St. Sebastian also claims to have held them once. The question is when that stay occurred, and whether the relics moved once or twice.

The simplest theory fitting the evidence is a single translation at a known date, for reasons history can grasp, with all early allusions referred to that one move. Both apostles, it argues, were first buried near the scenes of their deaths. They lay on ground owned by Christians beside roads out of Rome, Peter on the Via Cornelia and Paul on the Via Ostiana.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trier:
A diocese, suffragan of Cologne, covering the governmental departments of Trier and Coblenz in the Prussian Rhine province, with the principality of Birkenfeld. In 1912 it counted 711 parish priests, 28 parish vicars and 1,249,700 Catholics against 450,000 people of other faiths, spread across 46 deaneries.

Trier was capital of Belgica Prima and often an imperial residence, with Christians present from the second century. It claims the oldest episcopal see in Germany, its first clearly authenticated bishop being Agricius, at Arles in 314, and its churches include St. Matthias, holding the only grave of an Apostle in Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-unions-of-pra:
Unions of prayer are associations of the faithful banded together for shared prayer and penance, a tendency the entry notes as recently spreading. First comes the Association of Prayer and Penitence in honour of the Heart of Jesus. Founded at Dijon in 1879, it moved to Montmartre and became an archconfraternity under Leo XIII in 1894. Its aims were reparation for sin and for outrages against church and pope, plus the church's welfare, the pope's freedom, and the world's salvation.

Next stands the Archconfraternity of Our Lady of Compassion for the return of England to the Catholic faith, founded at Saint-Sulpice in Paris by a brief of Leo XIII in 1897. It carried on the zeal of Jean-Jacques Olier for England's conversion. The entry lists further unions of the same kind, their founders, and their stated ends, giving a snapshot of organized lay prayer at the turn of the century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Münster in Westphalia gained its university in 1771 through the prince-bishop's vicar general, Freiherr von Fürstenberg. Its foundation was the cathedral school, dating from the Middle Ages, which flourished late in the fifteenth century under the humanist Rudolph von Langen. The Anabaptist disturbances of 1533 to 1535 depressed it, but Dean Gottfried von Raesfeld restored it by handing its supervision to the Jesuits in 1588.

The school, now called Gymnasium Paulinum, grew by adding philosophy and theology courses for the scientific training of priests. Pope Urban VIII raised it to university rank, and the entry follows its faculties, its professors, and its later growth under Prussian rule. It closes with the modern university's place in Westphalian Catholic life, a school that rose from a medieval cathedral classroom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-urbain-jean-j:
Urbain Jean Joseph Le Verrier was an astronomer and director of the Paris observatory, born at Saint-Lô in northwestern France on 11 May 1811, who died at Paris on 25 September 1877. From 1831 he studied at the École Polytechnique with such success that he was kept on as an instructor. He favoured mathematical studies above all, especially the problems Laplace had treated in his celestial mechanics.

Le Verrier later served in the government tobacco administration, taught at the Collège Stanislas in Paris, and became professor of celestial mechanics at the University of Paris. As early as 1839 he published calculations on the planets, and his later work on Uranus's irregular motion led to the discovery of Neptune. The entry follows his career, his disputes, and his direction of the observatory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valentin-thal:
Valentin Thalhofer was a German theologian born at Unterroth near Ulm on 21 January 1825, who died in the same place on 17 September 1891. He studied at the gymnasium and in philosophy at Dillingen, then from 1845 studied theology at Munich. In 1848 he earned his doctorate in theology and was ordained priest. He then served as prefect at Dillingen's seminary for priests from 1850 to 1863.

From 1863 to 1876 he taught exegesis at Dillingen's lyceum, then directed the Georgianum seminary at Munich and taught liturgy at Eichstätt. He ranked as an able, respected teacher of noble character, zealous in the confessional, in the pulpit, and in catechizing, and he wrote fruitfully, thoroughly, and with intellect. The entry lists his works on liturgy and pastoral care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valliscaulian:
The Valliscaulian Order takes its name from Vallis Caulium, or Val-des-Choux, its first monastery in Burgundy. Viard, a lay brother of the Carthusian priory of Loubigny in the Langres diocese, founded it near the twelfth century's end. His superior let him live as a hermit in a woodland cave, where prayer and austerity won him a saint's repute.

The Duke of Burgundy, fulfilling a vow, built a church and monastery on the hermitage site. Viard became prior in 1193 and framed rules drawn partly from Carthusian and partly from Cistercian observance. Innocent III later gave formal confirmation to the Brethren of the Cabbage Valley. The entry follows its houses, chiefly in Scotland and France, and its later decline.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vallumbrosan-:
The Vallumbrosan Order takes its name from Vallombrosa, Latin for shady valley, its motherhouse twenty miles from Florence on Monte Secchieta's northwest slope, 3,140 feet above the sea. Its founder St John Gualbert was the son of the noble Florentine Gualbert Visdomini. He was born in 985 or 995 and died at Passignano on 12 July 1073, his feast day, having been canonized in 1193.

When a kinsman was murdered, duty bound John to avenge him. He met the murderer in a narrow lane, sword in hand, but when the man threw himself down with arms spread like a cross, John pardoned him for Christ's love. On his way home he prayed at San Miniato, where the crucifix bowed its head to him. The entry follows his founding of Vallombrosa and the order's growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vancouver:
Vancouver's archdiocese covers the mainland of British Columbia south of 54 degrees north and west of the Strait of Georgia, together with the Queen Charlotte Islands, about 150,000 square miles in all. The first resident of what is now British Columbia was a Catholic, as were the great explorers Simon Fraser and his lieutenant Quesnel. Catholics in Hudson Bay Company service gave natives their first notion of Christianity.

Later Father De Smet visited the Kootenays, and in 1843 Father Demers travelled widely among the Okanagans, Shuswaps, and Carriers. In 1843 the district joined the Vicariate Apostolic of Columbia under Bishop Blanchet, and three years later a Jesuit, Father Nobili, arrived. The entry follows the archdiocese's growth, its bishops, parishes, and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-charles-b:
Charles Baker, rightly David Henry Lewis by his own entry at the English College, was an English Jesuit martyr born in Monmouthshire in 1616, who died at Usk on 27 August 1679. His father Morgan Lewis was a lax Catholic later converted, and his mother Margaret Pritchard was devout. David grew up Protestant and attended the Royal Grammar School at Abergavenny, where his father was headmaster.

At sixteen he spent three months in Paris with the son of Earl Rivers and was received into the church there by Father Talbot. After his parents' deaths he sought the priesthood, entered the English College at Rome on 3 November 1638, and was ordained in 1642.
